lessons.title: Charge and Its Properties
lessons.notes_html:
Electric charge is the fundamental property of matter by virtue of which a body experiences a force in an electric field. There are two kinds: positive charge, as on a glass rod rubbed with silk, and negative charge, as on an ebonite rod rubbed with fur.

Properties of Charge

  • Like charges repel and unlike charges attract each other.
  • Charge is quantized - it occurs only in whole multiples of the elementary charge.
  • Charge is conserved - it can neither be created nor destroyed, only transferred.
  • Charge is additive - the total charge is the algebraic sum of all charges.

Q = n e

  • Q - total charge, unit C; n - whole number of electrons or protons; e = 1.6 x 10-19 C, the elementary charge

A point charge is a charged body whose size is negligible compared with the distances involved. A test charge is a very small positive charge used to explore a field without disturbing it.

Worked Example: Electrons in One Coulomb

How many electrons are contained in 1 C and 3 C of charge?

Step 1: Use Q = n e, so n = Q / e, with e = 1.6 x 10-19 C.

Step 2: For 1 C: n = 1 / (1.6 x 10-19) = 6.25 x 1018.

Step 3: For 3 C: n = 3 / (1.6 x 10-19) = 1.875 x 1019, about 1.9 x 1019.

Answer: 1 C contains 6.25 x 1018 electrons and 3 C contains about 1.9 x 1019 electrons.

mcqs.q: What is electric charge?
options: The fundamental property of matter by virtue of which a body experiences a force in an electric field
The property of matter by virtue of which a body experiences a force only in a magnetic field
A form of energy stored inside every neutral body
The mass carried by an electron or a proton
mcqs.why: The notes define electric charge as the fundamental property of matter by virtue of which a body experiences a force in an electric field.

mcqs.q: A glass rod rubbed with silk acquires which kind of charge?
options: Negative charge
Positive charge
No charge at all
Both positive and negative charge in equal amounts
mcqs.why: The notes give the glass rod rubbed with silk as the standard example of a body carrying positive charge.

mcqs.q: An ebonite rod rubbed with fur acquires which kind of charge?
options: Positive charge
No charge at all
Negative charge
A charge that keeps changing sign
mcqs.why: The notes give the ebonite rod rubbed with fur as the standard example of a body carrying negative charge.

mcqs.q: How do like charges and unlike charges behave towards each other?
options: Like charges attract and unlike charges repel each other
Both like and unlike charges attract each other
Both like and unlike charges repel each other
Like charges repel and unlike charges attract each other
mcqs.why: One of the stated properties of charge is that like charges repel each other while unlike charges attract each other.

mcqs.q: Charge is quantized. What does this mean?
options: Charge occurs only in whole multiples of the elementary charge
Charge can have any value, including fractions of the elementary charge
Charge always occurs in whole multiples of one coulomb
Charge is divided equally between any two bodies that touch
mcqs.why: Quantization means charge is never found in fractions of the elementary charge e; the total charge is always Q = n e with n a whole number.

mcqs.q: Charge is conserved. What does this mean?
options: Charge can be created but never destroyed
Charge can neither be created nor destroyed, only transferred
Charge can be destroyed but never created
The charge of a body can never be transferred to another body
mcqs.why: The law of conservation of charge in the notes states that charge can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be transferred from one body to another.

mcqs.q: Charge is additive. What does this mean?
options: The total charge is the product of all the charges
The total charge is always equal to the largest single charge
The total charge is the algebraic sum of all the charges
Positive and negative charges are counted separately and never combined
mcqs.why: Additivity means the charges are added with their signs, so the total charge of a system is the algebraic sum of all the individual charges.

mcqs.q: What is a point charge?
options: A charge placed exactly at the centre of a sphere
A very small positive charge used to explore a field
A charge that has no electric field around it
A charged body whose size is negligible compared with the distances involved
mcqs.why: The notes define a point charge as a charged body whose size is negligible compared with the distances involved; the small exploring charge in the distractors is the test charge.

mcqs.q: How many electrons are contained in 1 C of charge? (e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C)
mcqs.why: Using Q = n e, n = Q / e = 1 / (1.6 x 10^-19) = 6.25 x 10^18 electrons, as worked out in the notes example.

mcqs.q: How many electrons are contained in 3 C of charge? (e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C)
mcqs.why: Using Q = n e, n = Q / e = 3 / (1.6 x 10^-19) = 1.875 x 10^19, about 1.9 x 10^19 electrons, as in the notes example.

lessons.title: Coulomb's Law
lessons.notes_html:
Coulomb's law states that the electrostatic force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. It acts along the line joining the charges.

F = k q1 q2 / r2

  • F - force, unit N; q1, q2 - charges, unit C; r - separation, unit m; k = 9 x 109 N m2 C-2

Effect of the Medium

In a medium the force is reduced. The relative permittivity or dielectric constant is the ratio of the permittivity of the medium to that of free space. For free space it is 1 and for material media it is greater than 1.

F = k q1 q2 / (εr r2)

  • εr - relative permittivity, a pure number with no unit; the force in the medium is 1 / εr times the free-space force

The electrostatic force is independent of the temperature of the charges. It depends only on the charges, their separation and the medium between them.

Worked Example: Force Between Two Electrons

Determine the force of repulsion between two free electrons spaced 0.5 angstrom apart. 1 angstrom = 10-10 m.

Step 1: Each electron has charge e = 1.6 x 10-19 C and r = 0.5 x 10-10 m = 5 x 10-11 m.

Step 2: Use F = k e2 / r2 = (9 x 109) x (1.6 x 10-19)2 / (5 x 10-11)2.

Step 3: Numerator is 9 x 109 x 2.56 x 10-38 = 2.304 x 10-28. Denominator is 2.5 x 10-21.

Step 4: Divide: 2.304 x 10-28 / 2.5 x 10-21 = 9.216 x 10-8 N, about 92 nN.

Answer: The force of repulsion is about 92 nN.

mcqs.q: According to Coulomb's law, the electrostatic force between two point charges is:
options: Directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the distance between them
Directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them
Directly proportional to the sum of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them
Inversely proportional to the product of the charges and directly proportional to the square of the distance between them
mcqs.why: Coulomb's law states the force is proportional to q1 q2 and inversely proportional to r^2, which is why the formula is F = k q1 q2 / r^2.

mcqs.q: What is the value of the constant k in Coulomb's law, F = k q1 q2 / r^2?
mcqs.why: The notes list k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2 in the Coulomb's law formula; 1.6 x 10^-19 C is the elementary charge, a different constant.

mcqs.q: Along which line does the electrostatic force between two point charges act?
options: Along a line perpendicular to the line joining the charges
Along the direction of the electric field of a third charge
In a circle around the midpoint of the two charges
Along the line joining the two charges
mcqs.why: Coulomb's law as stated in the notes says the force acts along the line joining the charges, attractive for unlike charges and repulsive for like charges.

mcqs.q: Two point charges of 1 microC each are separated by 0.1 m in free space. What is the force between them? (k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2)
options: 9 N

mcqs.q: What is the force of repulsion between two free electrons spaced 0.5 angstrom apart? (1 angstrom = 10^-10 m, e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C)
options: 9.216 x 10^-8 N, about 92 nN

mcqs.q: When the space between two charges is filled with a medium of relative permittivity epsilon_r, the force becomes:
options: F = epsilon_r k q1 q2 / r^2, which is epsilon_r times the free-space force
F = k q1 q2 / r^2, exactly the same as in free space
F = k q1 q2 / (epsilon_r r^2), which is 1 / epsilon_r times the free-space force
F = k q1 q2 / (epsilon_r r), falling only as 1 / r
mcqs.why: The notes state that in a medium the force is reduced, becoming 1 / epsilon_r times the free-space force, so epsilon_r divides the free-space expression.

mcqs.q: The relative permittivity (dielectric constant) of free space is:
mcqs.why: Relative permittivity is the ratio of the permittivity of the medium to that of free space, so for free space itself the ratio is 1; for material media it is greater than 1.

mcqs.q: The force between two charges in free space is 80 N. What is the force if the same charges at the same separation are placed in a medium of relative permittivity 2?
mcqs.why: In a medium the force is 1 / epsilon_r times the free-space force, so F = 80 / 2 = 40 N.

mcqs.q: If the distance between two point charges is doubled, the force between them becomes:
options: One half of its original value
One quarter of its original value
Twice its original value
Four times its original value
mcqs.why: F is proportional to 1 / r^2, so doubling r multiplies the force by (1 / 2)^2 = 1 / 4 of its original value.

mcqs.q: The electrostatic force between two charges depends on:
options: The charges, their separation, the medium and the temperature of the charges
Only the charges, and not on their separation or the medium
The charges, their separation and the medium between them, but not on the temperature of the charges
Only the separation and the temperature of the charges
mcqs.why: The notes state clearly that the electrostatic force is independent of the temperature of the charges; it depends only on the charges, their separation and the medium between them.

lessons.title: Electric Field and Electric Field Intensity
lessons.notes_html:
The concept of the electric field was introduced by Faraday. An electric field is the region around a charge in which another charge experiences a force. A charge sets up a field, and a second charge placed in it experiences a force.

Electric field intensity at a point is the force per unit positive test charge placed at that point. Its direction is the direction of the force on a small positive test charge.

E = F / q

  • E - field intensity, unit N C-1; F - force on the test charge; q - test charge

Field Due to a Point Charge

E = k Q / r2

  • Q - source charge; r - distance from the charge; the field points away from a positive charge and towards a negative charge

Inside a charged metallic sphere placed in a field, and inside a hollow charged shell, the field is zero, because all the charge resides on the outer surface.

Worked Example: Electron in an Electric Field

Find the force that an electron experiences in an electric field of 1000 N C-1. If the electron is free to move, find the distance covered by it in 10 ns. Mass of electron is 9.11 x 10-31 kg.

Step 1: Force F = e E = (1.6 x 10-19) x 1000 = 1.6 x 10-16 N.

Step 2: Acceleration a = F / m = (1.6 x 10-16) / (9.11 x 10-31) = 1.756 x 1014 m s-2.

Step 3: Time t = 10 ns = 1 x 10-8 s. Starting from rest, s = (1 / 2) a t2.

Step 4: s = 0.5 x (1.756 x 1014) x (1 x 10-8)2 = 8.78 x 10-3 m = 8.78 mm.

Answer: The force is 1.6 x 10-16 N and the distance covered is 8.78 mm. (The book's printed answer of 0.88 mm is wrong; the correct value is 8.78 mm.)

mcqs.q: Who introduced the concept of the electric field?
options: Coulomb
Gauss
Faraday
Ampere
mcqs.why: The notes state that the concept of the electric field was introduced by Faraday: a charge sets up a field, and a second charge placed in it experiences a force.

mcqs.q: Electric field intensity at a point is defined as:
options: The work per unit positive test charge placed at that point
The force multiplied by the test charge placed at that point
The total force exerted by all the charges in the field
The force per unit positive test charge placed at that point
mcqs.why: The notes define field intensity as the force per unit positive test charge, E = F / q; work per unit charge is the electric potential, not the field.

mcqs.q: What is the unit of electric field intensity E?
options: N C^-1
J C^-1
C m^-2
mcqs.why: Since E = F / q, its unit is newtons per coulomb, N C^-1; J C^-1 is the volt, the unit of potential.

mcqs.q: The direction of the electric field intensity at a point is:
options: The direction of the force on a small negative test charge at that point
The direction of the force on a small positive test charge at that point
Always directed towards the nearest charge, whatever its sign
Always directed away from the nearest charge, whatever its sign
mcqs.why: By the notes, the direction of E is the direction of the force on a small positive test charge, so it points away from a positive charge and towards a negative charge.

mcqs.q: The electric field due to a point charge Q at distance r is E = k Q / r^2. Its direction is:
options: Always away from the charge, whatever the sign of Q
Always towards the charge, whatever the sign of Q
Away from the charge if Q is positive and towards the charge if Q is negative
Perpendicular to the line joining the charge to the point
mcqs.why: The notes state that the field points away from a positive charge and towards a negative charge, following the force on a positive test charge.

mcqs.q: Find the force that an electron experiences in an electric field of 1000 N C^-1. (e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C)
mcqs.why: F = e E = (1.6 x 10^-19) x 1000 = 1.6 x 10^-16 N, exactly as calculated in the notes worked example.

mcqs.q: The electron in the previous field has mass 9.11 x 10^-31 kg and experiences a force of 1.6 x 10^-16 N. What is its acceleration?
mcqs.why: a = F / m = (1.6 x 10^-16) / (9.11 x 10^-31) = 1.756 x 10^14 m s^-2, as worked out step by step in the notes.

mcqs.q: Starting from rest, what distance does that electron cover in 10 ns in the same field? (a = 1.756 x 10^14 m s^-2)
mcqs.why: t = 1 x 10^-8 s and s = (1 / 2) a t^2 = 0.5 x (1.756 x 10^14) x (1 x 10^-8)^2 = 8.78 x 10^-3 m = 8.78 mm; the notes note the printed 0.88 mm answer is wrong.

mcqs.q: Inside a charged metallic sphere placed in a field, and inside a hollow charged shell, the electric field is:
options: Maximum, because all the charge collects at the centre
The same as the field just outside the surface
Zero, because all the charge resides on the outer surface
Zero only at the exact centre and large everywhere else inside
mcqs.why: The notes state the field inside is zero because all the charge resides on the outer surface, leaving no field-producing charge inside.

mcqs.q: What is the electric field intensity at a distance of 3 m from a point charge of 2 x 10^-9 C? (k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2)

lessons.title: Electric Field Lines
lessons.notes_html:
Electric field lines, also called lines of force, are imaginary lines drawn so that the tangent at any point gives the direction of the electric field at that point. Their closeness shows the strength of the field.

Characteristics of Field Lines

  • They start from a positive charge and end on a negative charge, or go to infinity.
  • They never cross each other, because the field at a point has only one direction.
  • They are closer together where the field is stronger and farther apart where it is weaker.
  • They leave or enter a charged surface normally.
  • They do not pass through a conductor.

Common Patterns

For a single positive charge the lines radiate straight outwards in all directions. For a single negative charge they converge straight inwards. For two identical positive charges the lines curve away from each other and there is a neutral point midway between them where the field is zero. For two identical negative charges the pattern is the same but the arrows point inwards.

The direction of intensity at a point can also be found from the force on a positive test charge: away from a positive charge and towards a negative charge.

mcqs.q: Electric field lines are drawn so that:
options: The tangent at any point gives the magnitude of the electric field at that point
Each line shows the path that a free electron must follow
The length of each line shows the strength of the field
The tangent at any point gives the direction of the electric field at that point
mcqs.why: Field lines, also called lines of force, are imaginary lines whose tangent at any point gives the field direction there; their closeness, not their length, shows strength.

mcqs.q: What does the closeness of electric field lines show?
options: The strength of the field: lines are closer where the field is stronger
The sign of the charge: lines are closer near negative charges only
The potential of the field: lines are closer where the potential is lower
Nothing; the spacing of the lines is purely decorative
mcqs.why: The notes state that field lines are closer together where the field is stronger and farther apart where the field is weaker.

mcqs.q: Electric field lines start and end as follows:
options: They start from a negative charge and end on a positive charge
They start from a positive charge and end on a negative charge, or go to infinity
They form closed loops around every charge
They start and end on the same charge
mcqs.why: One of the listed characteristics is that field lines start from a positive charge and end on a negative charge, or go to infinity if there is no negative charge.

mcqs.q: Electric field lines never cross each other because:
options: The lines repel each other like charges
Crossing would make the field zero at that point
The field at a point has only one direction
The lines are made of a material that cannot bend
mcqs.why: If two lines crossed, the field at the crossing point would have two directions at once, which is impossible because the field at a point has only one direction.

mcqs.q: How do field lines leave or enter a charged surface?
options: Tangentially, running along the surface
At 45 degrees to the surface
In random directions depending on the material
Normally, that is, perpendicular to the surface
mcqs.why: The notes list as a characteristic that field lines leave or enter a charged surface normally, meaning at right angles to the surface.

mcqs.q: Do electric field lines pass through a conductor?
options: No, they do not pass through a conductor
Yes, they pass straight through any conductor
Yes, but only through a conductor carrying a current
Only the lines from positive charges pass through
mcqs.why: The notes state as a characteristic of field lines that they do not pass through a conductor, which matches the zero field inside a conductor.

mcqs.q: For a single positive charge, the field line pattern is:
options: Straight lines converging inwards from all directions
Straight lines radiating outwards in all directions
Concentric circles around the charge
Parallel straight lines on one side of the charge
mcqs.why: The notes describe the pattern for a single positive charge as lines radiating straight outwards in all directions, away from the charge.

mcqs.q: For a single negative charge, the field line pattern is:
options: Straight lines radiating outwards in all directions
Concentric circles around the charge
Straight lines converging inwards towards the charge
Lines that curve away from each other
mcqs.why: For a single negative charge the notes say the lines converge straight inwards, because the field points towards a negative charge.

mcqs.q: For two identical positive charges, what is found midway between them?
options: A point where the electric field is maximum
A point where the field lines cross each other
A point where all the field lines end
A neutral point where the electric field is zero
mcqs.why: The notes state that for two identical positive charges the lines curve away from each other and there is a neutral point midway between them where the field is zero.

mcqs.q: For two identical negative charges, the field pattern compared with two identical positive charges is:
options: The same pattern, but the arrows on the lines point inwards
Completely different, with no neutral point between them
The same pattern with the arrows also pointing outwards
A pattern of parallel lines between the charges
mcqs.why: The notes state that for two identical negative charges the pattern is the same as for two positive charges, but the arrows point inwards towards the charges.

lessons.title: Electric Dipole
lessons.notes_html:
An electric dipole is a pair of equal and opposite charges +q and -q separated by a small distance d. The dipole axis is the line passing through both charges, directed from the negative charge towards the positive charge.

p = q d

  • p - dipole moment, a vector along the dipole axis; q - magnitude of each charge; d - separation of the charges; unit of p is C m, also measured in debye

Field Due to a Dipole

Far from the dipole, on the axial line the field is along the dipole moment, and on the equatorial line (the perpendicular bisector) it is opposite to the dipole moment. In both cases the field falls as 1 / r3.

E = k x 2p / r3

  • E - axial field at distance r from the midpoint, for r much greater than d; the equatorial field is half of this, k p / r3

In a uniform field a dipole experiences a torque that tends to align its moment along the field.

Worked Example: Field on the Axial Line

An electric dipole consists of charges +10 microC and -10 microC separated by 0.5 cm. Calculate the field intensity on the axial line at 5 cm from the midpoint.

Step 1: Dipole moment p = q d = (10 x 10-6) x (0.5 x 10-2) = 5 x 10-8 C m.

Step 2: Distance r = 5 cm = 0.05 m. Use E = k x 2p / r3.

Step 3: E = (9 x 109) x (2 x 5 x 10-8) / (0.05)3 = 900 / (1.25 x 10-4).

Step 4: E = 7.2 x 106 N C-1.

Answer: The field intensity on the axial line is 7.2 x 106 N C-1.

mcqs.q: What is an electric dipole?
options: A pair of equal and opposite charges +q and -q separated by a small distance d
A pair of equal positive charges separated by a small distance d
A single point charge placed near a neutral body
A pair of unequal charges separated by a large distance
mcqs.why: The notes define an electric dipole as a pair of equal and opposite charges +q and -q separated by a small distance d.

mcqs.q: The dipole axis is directed:
options: From the positive charge towards the negative charge
From the negative charge towards the positive charge
Perpendicular to the line joining the two charges
In whichever direction the dipole is moving
mcqs.why: The notes state that the dipole axis is the line through both charges, directed from the negative charge towards the positive charge, and the dipole moment is a vector along this axis.

mcqs.q: What is the unit of dipole moment p?
options: C m^-1
N C^-1
C m, also measured in debye
J C^-1
mcqs.why: Since p = q d, its unit is coulomb times metre, C m; the notes add that dipole moment is also measured in debye.

mcqs.q: In a uniform electric field, a dipole experiences a torque that tends to:
options: Align its dipole moment opposite to the field
Rotate its dipole moment perpendicular to the field
Move the dipole without rotating it at all
Align its dipole moment along the field
mcqs.why: The notes state that in a uniform field a dipole experiences a torque that tends to align its moment along the field direction.

mcqs.q: Far from a dipole, the field on the axial line is directed:
options: Along the dipole moment
Opposite to the dipole moment
Perpendicular to the dipole moment
In a circle around the dipole moment
mcqs.why: The notes state that on the axial line the field is along the dipole moment, while on the equatorial line it is opposite to the dipole moment.

mcqs.q: Far from a dipole, the field on the equatorial line (the perpendicular bisector) is directed:
options: Along the dipole moment
Opposite to the dipole moment
Towards the positive charge of the dipole
Away from both charges equally in all directions
mcqs.why: The notes state that on the equatorial line the field is opposite to the dipole moment, whereas on the axial line it is along the moment.

mcqs.q: How does the field of a dipole fall off with distance r far from the dipole?
options: As 1 / r^2, like the field of a point charge
As 1 / r, like the potential of a point charge
As 1 / r^3, on both the axial and the equatorial lines
It stays constant, independent of r
mcqs.why: The notes state that in both the axial and equatorial cases the dipole field falls as 1 / r^3, faster than the 1 / r^2 fall of a point-charge field.

mcqs.q: A dipole consists of charges +10 microC and -10 microC separated by 0.5 cm. What is its dipole moment?
mcqs.why: p = q d = (10 x 10^-6) x (0.5 x 10^-2) = 5 x 10^-8 C m, converting 0.5 cm to 0.005 m before multiplying, as in the notes example.

mcqs.q: For that dipole (p = 5 x 10^-8 C m), what is the field intensity on the axial line at 5 cm from the midpoint?
At the same distance of 5 cm, what is the field intensity on the equatorial line of that dipole?
mcqs.why: The notes state the equatorial field is half the axial field, k p / r^3, so E = (7.2 x 10^6) / 2 = 3.6 x 10^6 N C^-1.

lessons.title: Electric Flux
lessons.notes_html:
Electric flux through a surface is a measure of the number of electric field lines passing through it. It depends on the field, the area and their relative direction, but not on the shape of the surface.

Φ = E A cos θ

  • Φ - electric flux, unit N m2 C-1; E - field strength; A - area; θ - angle between the field and the area vector (the normal to the surface)

Maximum and Minimum Flux

  • Flux is maximum when θ = 0 degrees: the field is parallel to the area vector and perpendicular to the surface, so Φ = E A.
  • Flux is minimum, zero, when θ = 90 degrees: the field is parallel to the surface, so no lines cross it.

Flux Through a Surface Enclosing a Charge

For a closed surface, the total flux depends only on the charge enclosed inside it. Charges outside the surface contribute no net flux, because every line from them that enters also leaves. This idea leads directly to Gauss's law in the next lesson. The surface charge density is the charge per unit area.

σ = Q / A

  • σ - surface charge density, unit C m-2; Q - charge on the surface; A - area of the surface

mcqs.q: Electric flux through a surface is:
options: A measure of the charge stored on the surface
A measure of the number of electric field lines passing through the surface
The total force exerted on the surface by the field
The work done in moving a charge across the surface
mcqs.why: The notes define electric flux as a measure of the number of electric field lines passing through a surface, given by Phi = E A cos theta.

mcqs.q: In the flux formula Phi = E A cos theta, the angle theta is:
options: The angle between the field and the surface itself
The angle between the field and the nearest charge
The angle between the field and the area vector, the normal to the surface
Always 45 degrees for any tilted surface
mcqs.why: The notes specify that theta is the angle between the field and the area vector, which is the normal to the surface, not the angle with the surface itself.

mcqs.q: What is the unit of electric flux?
options: N C^-1
C m^-2
J C^-1
mcqs.why: Flux is E times A, so its unit is (N C^-1) x (m^2) = N m^2 C^-1, as listed in the notes for Phi = E A cos theta.

mcqs.q: Electric flux through a surface is maximum when:
options: Theta = 0 degrees, the field is parallel to the area vector and perpendicular to the surface, so Phi = E A
Theta = 90 degrees, the field is parallel to the surface
Theta = 45 degrees, the field crosses the surface diagonally
Theta = 180 degrees, the field is opposite to the area vector
mcqs.why: Cos 0 degrees = 1, so Phi = E A is the largest possible value; the notes describe this as the field being parallel to the area vector and perpendicular to the surface.

mcqs.q: Electric flux through a surface is zero when:
options: Theta = 0 degrees, the field is perpendicular to the surface
Theta = 90 degrees, the field is parallel to the surface so no lines cross it
The area of the surface is very large
The field is very strong
mcqs.why: Cos 90 degrees = 0, so Phi = 0; the notes explain that the field is then parallel to the surface and no field lines cross it.

mcqs.q: A field of 200 N C^-1 passes perpendicularly through an area of 0.5 m^2 (theta = 0 degrees). What is the flux?
mcqs.why: Phi = E A cos theta = 200 x 0.5 x cos 0 degrees = 200 x 0.5 x 1 = 100 N m^2 C^-1, the maximum flux for this field and area.

mcqs.q: A field of 100 N C^-1 crosses an area of 1 m^2 with theta = 60 degrees. What is the flux?
mcqs.why: Phi = E A cos theta = 100 x 1 x cos 60 degrees = 100 x 0.5 = 50 N m^2 C^-1; 86.6 would come from using sin 60 degrees by mistake.

mcqs.q: Electric flux through a surface depends on:
options: The field, the area and their relative direction, but not on the shape of the surface
The field, the area and the shape of the surface only
The shape of the surface and the charge on it
Only the field strength, whatever the area or direction
mcqs.why: The notes state that flux depends on the field, the area and their relative direction, but not on the shape of the surface.

mcqs.q: For a closed surface, charges outside the surface contribute no net flux because:
options: Their field cannot reach the surface at all
Every field line from them that enters the surface also leaves it
Their flux is exactly cancelled by the charges inside
Gauss's law forbids outside charges from producing any field
mcqs.why: The notes explain that the total flux through a closed surface depends only on the enclosed charge, since every line from an outside charge that enters also leaves, giving zero net contribution.

mcqs.q: A surface carries a charge of 10 C spread over an area of 2 m^2. What is the surface charge density?
mcqs.why: Surface charge density sigma = Q / A = 10 / 2 = 5 C m^-2, the charge per unit area as defined in the notes.

lessons.title: Gauss's Law
lessons.notes_html:
Gauss's law states that the total electric flux through any closed surface is equal to 1 / εo times the total charge enclosed by the surface. It follows from Coulomb's law and is most useful when the charge distribution has symmetry.

Φ = Q / εo

  • Φ - total flux through the closed surface; Q - total charge enclosed; εo - permittivity of free space, 8.85 x 10-12 C2 N-1 m-2

The Gaussian Surface

A Gaussian surface is an imaginary closed surface chosen to apply Gauss's law. It is selected so that the field is either constant and parallel to the area vector, or perpendicular to it, which makes the flux easy to calculate.

  • For a point charge or spherical distribution, choose a sphere.
  • For a line charge, choose a cylinder.
  • For a sheet of charge, choose a pill-box (flat cylinder).

For example, for a point charge on a spherical Gaussian surface, Φ = E x 4 π r2 = Q / εo, which gives the familiar point-charge field E = k Q / r2.

mcqs.q: Gauss's law states that:
options: The total electric flux through any closed surface is equal to epsilon_o times the total charge enclosed
The total electric flux through any surface equals the total charge enclosed, with no constant
The total electric flux through any closed surface is equal to 1 / epsilon_o times the total charge enclosed by the surface
The electric field inside any closed surface is always zero
mcqs.why: The notes state Gauss's law as Phi = Q / epsilon_o: the flux through a closed surface is 1 / epsilon_o times the charge enclosed by the surface.

mcqs.q: What is the value of epsilon_o, the permittivity of free space?
options: 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1
mcqs.why: The notes list epsilon_o = 8.85 x 10^-12 C^2 N^-1 m^-2 in Gauss's law; 9 x 10^9 is the Coulomb constant k, a different quantity.

mcqs.q: Gauss's law is most useful when:
options: The charge distribution has symmetry
The charges are all moving rapidly
The charge distribution has no symmetry at all
Only one charge is present and it is at rest
mcqs.why: The notes state that Gauss's law follows from Coulomb's law and is most useful when the charge distribution has symmetry, so a suitable Gaussian surface can be chosen.

mcqs.q: A Gaussian surface is:
options: A real metal surface placed around a charge
An imaginary closed surface chosen to apply Gauss's law
The outer surface of any charged conductor
A surface that must always be a sphere
mcqs.why: The notes define the Gaussian surface as an imaginary closed surface chosen to apply Gauss's law; its shape depends on the symmetry of the charge distribution.

mcqs.q: A Gaussian surface is selected so that:
options: The field is zero everywhere on the surface
The surface passes through all the charges present
The field is either constant and parallel to the area vector, or perpendicular to it, making the flux easy to calculate
The field changes direction many times along the surface
mcqs.why: The notes explain the surface is chosen so the field is constant and parallel to the area vector, or perpendicular to it, which makes the flux calculation simple.

mcqs.q: For a point charge or a spherical charge distribution, the Gaussian surface chosen is:
options: A cylinder
A pill-box (flat cylinder)
A cube
A sphere
mcqs.why: The notes list the choices matched to symmetry: a sphere for a point charge or spherical distribution, a cylinder for a line charge and a pill-box for a sheet of charge.

mcqs.q: For a line charge, the Gaussian surface chosen is:
options: A cylinder
A sphere
A pill-box (flat cylinder)
A cone
mcqs.why: The notes state that for a line charge a cylindrical Gaussian surface is chosen, matching the cylindrical symmetry of the charge distribution.

mcqs.q: For a sheet of charge, the Gaussian surface chosen is:
options: A sphere
A pill-box (flat cylinder)
A long cylinder
A hollow shell
mcqs.why: The notes state that for a sheet of charge the Gaussian surface is a pill-box, a flat cylinder straddling the sheet, matching its symmetry.

mcqs.q: A closed surface encloses a total charge of 8.85 x 10^-12 C. What is the total flux through the surface? (epsilon_o = 8.85 x 10^-12 C^2 N^-1 m^-2)
mcqs.why: By Gauss's law, Phi = Q / epsilon_o = (8.85 x 10^-12) / (8.85 x 10^-12) = 1 N m^2 C^-1.

mcqs.q: Applying Gauss's law to a point charge on a spherical Gaussian surface, Phi = E x 4 pi r^2 = Q / epsilon_o, gives:
options: The potential formula V = k q / r
The dipole field E = k x 2p / r^3
The result that the field inside the sphere is zero
The familiar point-charge field E = k Q / r^2
mcqs.why: The notes show this example: equating E x 4 pi r^2 with Q / epsilon_o leads directly to the familiar point-charge field E = k Q / r^2.

lessons.title: Applications of Gauss's Law
lessons.notes_html:
Point Charge and Charged Sphere

Outside a charged spherical shell or solid sphere the field is the same as that of a point charge at the centre. Inside a hollow charged shell the field is zero at every point, because a Gaussian sphere drawn inside encloses no charge.

E = k Q / r2

  • E - field outside the sphere at distance r from the centre; Q - total charge on the sphere; inside a hollow shell E = 0

Infinite Line of Charge

E = λ / (2 π εo r)

  • λ - charge per unit length, unit C m-1; r - perpendicular distance from the line

Infinite Sheet and Parallel Plates

E = σ / (2 εo)

  • E - field of one infinite sheet, independent of distance; σ - surface charge density

Between two oppositely charged parallel plates the fields of the two sheets add up, giving E = σ / εo between the plates and zero outside them. This result is used for the parallel plate capacitor.

mcqs.q: Outside a charged spherical shell or solid sphere, the field is:
options: Zero at every point outside the sphere
Constant, with the same value at all distances
The same as the field of an infinite sheet of charge
The same as that of a point charge at the centre, E = k Q / r^2
mcqs.why: The notes state that outside a charged spherical shell or solid sphere the field is the same as that of a point charge Q at the centre.

mcqs.q: Inside a hollow charged shell, the field is zero at every point because:
options: A Gaussian sphere drawn inside encloses no charge
The charge on the shell cancels its own field by heating up
The field lines are absorbed by the material of the shell
The charges inside the shell neutralise the field
mcqs.why: By Gauss's law the flux, and so the field, depends on enclosed charge; a Gaussian sphere inside the hollow shell encloses no charge, so E = 0 there.

mcqs.q: What is the field at a distance of 2 m from the centre of a charged sphere carrying 4 x 10^-9 C, measured outside the sphere? (k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2)
For an infinite line of charge, the field is E = lambda / (2 pi epsilon_o r). The quantity lambda is:
options: The charge per unit area, with unit C m^-2
The total charge on the whole line, with unit C
The charge per unit length, with unit C m^-1
The dipole moment per unit length, with unit C m
mcqs.why: The notes define lambda as the charge per unit length of the line, with unit C m^-1; charge per unit area is the surface charge density sigma.

mcqs.q: For an infinite line of charge, if the perpendicular distance r from the line is doubled, the field:
options: Becomes one quarter of its original value
Becomes twice its original value
Stays exactly the same
Becomes half of its original value
mcqs.why: E = lambda / (2 pi epsilon_o r) is proportional to 1 / r, so doubling r multiplies the field by 1 / 2, halving it.

mcqs.q: The field of one infinite sheet of charge, E = sigma / (2 epsilon_o), has the special feature that it is:
options: Independent of the distance from the sheet
Proportional to the distance from the sheet
Inversely proportional to the square of the distance
Zero everywhere except very close to the sheet
mcqs.why: The notes emphasise that the field of one infinite sheet, sigma / (2 epsilon_o), does not contain r at all, so it is independent of distance.

mcqs.q: What is the field due to an infinite sheet with surface charge density 17.7 x 10^-12 C m^-2? (epsilon_o = 8.85 x 10^-12 C^2 N^-1 m^-2)
Between two oppositely charged parallel plates, the field is:
options: E = sigma / (2 epsilon_o), the same as for one sheet alone
Zero, because the fields of the two sheets cancel there
E = sigma / epsilon_o, because the fields of the two sheets add up
Twice the field outside the plates
mcqs.why: The notes state that between the plates the fields of the two sheets add up, giving E = sigma / epsilon_o, and this result is used for the parallel plate capacitor.

mcqs.q: What is the field between two oppositely charged parallel plates with surface charge density 17.7 x 10^-12 C m^-2? (epsilon_o = 8.85 x 10^-12 C^2 N^-1 m^-2)
mcqs.why: Between the plates, E = sigma / epsilon_o = (17.7 x 10^-12) / (8.85 x 10^-12) = 2 N C^-1; 1 N C^-1 would be the field of one such sheet alone.

mcqs.q: Outside two oppositely charged parallel plates, the total field is:
options: Zero
Sigma / epsilon_o, the same as between the plates
Sigma / (2 epsilon_o), the same as for one sheet
Twice the field between the plates
mcqs.why: The notes state that the fields of the two sheets add between the plates to give sigma / epsilon_o and cancel outside them, giving zero field outside.

lessons.title: Electric Potential
lessons.notes_html:
Electric potential at a point is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a small test charge from infinity to that point. It is a scalar quantity. The absolute potential uses infinity, where the potential is taken as zero, as the reference point.

V = W / q

  • V - electric potential, unit volt (V), which is J C-1; W - work done; q - charge moved; the dimension of potential is work per unit charge

Work and Potential Energy

The work done by an external agent in moving a charge through a potential difference is stored as a change in the electrical potential energy of the charge.

W = q V

  • W - work done, equal to the potential energy gained; q - charge; V - potential difference crossed

The potential due to several charges is the algebraic sum of the individual potentials, because potential is a scalar, unlike the field, which is added as a vector.

mcqs.q: Electric potential at a point is defined as:
options: The work done per unit positive charge in bringing a small test charge from infinity to that point
The force per unit positive charge at that point
The total work done in bringing a test charge from infinity to that point
The work done per unit distance in moving a charge at that point
mcqs.why: The notes define potential as work done per unit charge, V = W / q, measured from infinity; force per unit charge is the field intensity, not the potential.

mcqs.q: Electric potential is what kind of quantity?
options: A vector quantity
A scalar quantity
A tensor quantity
A quantity with direction but no magnitude
mcqs.why: The notes state that electric potential is a scalar quantity, which is why potentials from several charges simply add algebraically.

mcqs.q: For absolute potential, the reference point is:
options: The surface of the earth, where the potential is taken as zero
The centre of the charge distribution
Infinity, where the potential is taken as zero
Any point where the electric field is maximum
mcqs.why: The notes state that the absolute potential uses infinity as the reference point, where the potential is taken as zero.

mcqs.q: The unit of electric potential, the volt, is equal to:
options: N C^-1, one newton per coulomb
J m^-1, one joule per metre
C s^-1, one coulomb per second
J C^-1, one joule per coulomb
mcqs.why: Since V = W / q, the volt is work per unit charge, J C^-1; the notes add that the dimension of potential is work per unit charge. N C^-1 is the unit of field.

mcqs.q: 20 J of work is done in bringing a charge of 4 C from infinity to a point. What is the potential at that point?
options: 5 V
mcqs.why: V = W / q = 20 / 4 = 5 V, using the defining relation for electric potential from the notes.

mcqs.q: The work done by an external agent in moving a charge through a potential difference is:
options: Always lost completely as heat in the surroundings
Stored as a change in the electrical potential energy of the charge
Converted into the mass of the charge
Stored as kinetic energy of the charge in every case
mcqs.why: The notes state that this work is stored as a change in the electrical potential energy of the charge, with W = q V.

mcqs.q: How much work is done in moving a charge of 3 C through a potential difference of 5 V?
options: 8 J
2 J
mcqs.why: W = q V = 3 x 5 = 15 J; the work equals the potential energy gained by the charge, as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: The potential at a point due to several charges is found by:
options: Adding the individual potentials as vectors
Multiplying all the individual potentials together
Taking only the largest individual potential
Taking the algebraic sum of the individual potentials
mcqs.why: The notes state that because potential is a scalar, the total potential is the algebraic sum of the individual potentials, unlike the field, which is added as a vector.

mcqs.q: Two charges produce potentials of 5 V and 3 V at a point. What is the total potential at that point?
options: 8 V
2 V
mcqs.why: Potential is a scalar, so the potentials add algebraically: V = 5 + 3 = 8 V, with no direction to consider.

mcqs.q: How do electric field and electric potential differ in the way they combine from several charges?
options: Both the field and the potential are added as vectors
The field is added as a vector, while the potential is added as a scalar (algebraically)
Both the field and the potential are added as scalars
The field is added as a scalar, while the potential is added as a vector
mcqs.why: The notes contrast the two directly: potential is a scalar added algebraically, unlike the field, which is added as a vector.

lessons.title: Electric Field as Potential Gradient and Potential Due to a Point Charge
lessons.notes_html:
The potential gradient is the rate of change of potential with distance. The electric field at a point is equal to the negative of the potential gradient at that point.

E = - dV / dr

  • E - electric field; dV / dr - potential gradient; the negative sign shows that the field points in the direction in which the potential decreases most rapidly

For a uniform field, such as between parallel plates, this becomes a simple ratio of potential difference to separation.

E = V / d

  • V - potential difference between the plates; d - plate separation; unit of E here is V m-1, the same as N C-1

Potential Due to a Point Charge

The work done against the field in bringing a unit charge from infinity to a distance r from a charge gives the potential at that point. It is positive for a positive charge and negative for a negative charge.

V = k q / r

  • V - potential at distance r from point charge q; note that V falls as 1 / r, while the field falls as 1 / r2

mcqs.q: The potential gradient at a point is:
options: The rate of change of the field with distance
The rate of change of potential with distance
The total change of potential between two plates
The potential divided by the charge at that point
mcqs.why: The notes define the potential gradient as the rate of change of potential with distance, written dV / dr, and the field equals its negative.

mcqs.q: The relation between the electric field and the potential gradient is E = -dV / dr. The negative sign shows that:
options: The field is always negative in value
The potential always increases along the field
The field points in the direction in which the potential decreases most rapidly
The field and the potential have opposite units
mcqs.why: The notes explain that the negative sign shows the field points in the direction in which the potential decreases most rapidly.

mcqs.q: For a uniform field, such as between parallel plates, the field is given by:
options: E = V d, the potential difference multiplied by the separation
E = d / V, the separation divided by the potential difference
E = V / q, the potential difference divided by the charge
E = V / d, the potential difference divided by the separation
mcqs.why: The notes state that for a uniform field the gradient relation becomes the simple ratio E = V / d, potential difference over plate separation.

mcqs.q: Using E = V / d, the unit of the field can also be written as:
options: V m^-1, the same as N C^-1
V C^-1, the same as N C^-1
J m^-1, the same as N C^-1
C m^-1, the same as N C^-1
mcqs.why: The notes point out that with E = V / d the unit of E is V m^-1, which is the same unit as N C^-1 obtained from E = F / q.

mcqs.q: The potential at a distance r from a point charge q is:
options: V = k q / r^2
V = k q / r
V = k q r
V = q / (k r)
mcqs.why: The notes give the point-charge potential as V = k q / r, found from the work done bringing a unit charge from infinity to distance r; k q / r^2 is the field.

mcqs.q: The potential due to a point charge is:
options: Positive for both positive and negative charges
Negative for a positive charge and positive for a negative charge
Positive for a positive charge and negative for a negative charge
Always zero, because the signs cancel
mcqs.why: The notes state the potential V = k q / r carries the sign of the charge: positive for a positive charge and negative for a negative charge.

mcqs.q: How do the potential and the field of a point charge fall off with distance r?
options: Both V and the field fall as 1 / r^2
Both V and the field fall as 1 / r
V falls as 1 / r^2, while the field falls as 1 / r
V falls as 1 / r, while the field falls as 1 / r^2
mcqs.why: The notes highlight this contrast: V = k q / r falls as 1 / r, while E = k Q / r^2 falls as 1 / r^2, so the potential decreases more slowly.

mcqs.q: The potential difference between two parallel plates is 200 V and their separation is 0.04 m. What is the uniform field between them?
mcqs.why: E = V / d = 200 / 0.04 = 5000 V m^-1, using the uniform-field form of the potential gradient relation.

mcqs.q: What is the potential at a distance of 3 m from a point charge of 2 x 10^-9 C? (k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2)
options: 6 V
2 V
mcqs.why: V = k q / r = (9 x 10^9) x (2 x 10^-9) / 3 = 18 / 3 = 6 V; note the potential falls as 1 / r, not 1 / r^2.

mcqs.q: A uniform field of 2000 V m^-1 exists between two points 0.03 m apart along the field. What is the potential difference between the points?
options: 6 V
mcqs.why: From E = V / d, V = E d = 2000 x 0.03 = 60 V, rearranging the uniform-field relation given in the notes.

lessons.title: Electron Volt
lessons.notes_html:
An electron volt is a small unit of energy used for atomic and nuclear physics. One electron volt is the energy gained or lost by an electron when it is moved across a potential difference of one volt. It is a unit of energy, not of charge, current or potential.

W = q V

  • For an electron, q = e = 1.6 x 10-19 C and V = 1 V, so the energy is found from this relation

1 eV = 1.6 x 10-19 J

  • Because (1.6 x 10-19 C) x (1 V) = 1.6 x 10-19 J

Using the Electron Volt

An electron accelerated through 1000 V gains 1000 eV of energy. In joules this is 1000 x 1.6 x 10-19 J = 1.6 x 10-16 J. Larger multiples are also used: 1 keV = 103 eV, 1 MeV = 106 eV and 1 GeV = 109 eV, each converted to joules by multiplying by 1.6 x 10-19.

The electron volt keeps atomic energies in convenient numbers, instead of very small values in joules.

mcqs.q: One electron volt is defined as:
options: The charge carried by one electron
The potential difference produced by one electron
The energy gained or lost by an electron when it is moved across a potential difference of one volt
The energy gained by a proton moved across one volt
mcqs.why: The notes define the electron volt through an electron crossing a potential difference of one volt, with the energy found from W = q V.

mcqs.q: The electron volt is a unit of:
options: Charge
Current
Potential
Energy
mcqs.why: The notes state explicitly that the electron volt is a unit of energy, not of charge, current or potential, and is used in atomic and nuclear physics.

mcqs.q: One electron volt is equal to how many joules?
options: 1 J
mcqs.why: 1 eV = e x 1 V = (1.6 x 10^-19 C) x (1 V) = 1.6 x 10^-19 J, using W = q V as shown in the notes.

mcqs.q: The value 1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 J comes from the relation:
options: W = q / V, with q = 1.6 x 10^-19 C and V = 1 V
W = q V, with q = 1.6 x 10^-19 C and V = 1 V
W = V / q, with q = 1.6 x 10^-19 C and V = 1 V
W = q V^2, with q = 1.6 x 10^-19 C and V = 1 V
mcqs.why: The notes derive it directly: (1.6 x 10^-19 C) x (1 V) = 1.6 x 10^-19 J, because the work done is charge times potential difference.

mcqs.q: An electron accelerated through a potential difference of 1000 V gains an energy of:
options: 1 eV
mcqs.why: By the definition, an electron crossing 1 V gains 1 eV, so crossing 1000 V it gains 1000 eV, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: How many joules is 1000 eV?
mcqs.why: 1000 eV = 1000 x (1.6 x 10^-19 J) = 1.6 x 10^-16 J, exactly the conversion worked out in the notes.

mcqs.q: One kilo-electron volt (1 keV) is equal to how many joules?
mcqs.why: 1 keV = 10^3 eV, so in joules it is 10^3 x (1.6 x 10^-19) = 1.6 x 10^-16 J, using the conversion given in the notes.

mcqs.q: One mega-electron volt (1 MeV) is equal to how many joules?
mcqs.why: 1 MeV = 10^6 eV, so in joules it is 10^6 x (1.6 x 10^-19) = 1.6 x 10^-13 J; 1.6 x 10^-10 J is the value for 1 GeV.

mcqs.q: One giga-electron volt (1 GeV) is equal to how many joules?
mcqs.why: 1 GeV = 10^9 eV, so in joules it is 10^9 x (1.6 x 10^-19) = 1.6 x 10^-10 J, following the multiples listed in the notes.

mcqs.q: Why is the electron volt used for atomic and nuclear physics?
options: It is a larger unit than the joule, so energies look bigger
Joules cannot be used for charged particles
It removes the need to know the charge of the electron
It keeps atomic energies in convenient numbers instead of very small values in joules
mcqs.why: The notes state that the electron volt keeps atomic energies in convenient numbers, instead of the very small values they would have in joules.

lessons.title: Capacitor and Its Capacitance
lessons.notes_html:
A capacitor is a device that stores electric charge, and hence energy in its electric field. It usually consists of two conductors separated by an insulator called a dielectric.

Capacitance is the ratio of the charge stored on either plate to the potential difference between the plates. It measures the ability to store charge per unit potential difference.

C = Q / V

  • C - capacitance, unit farad (F); Q - charge on either plate; V - potential difference between the plates; one farad stores one coulomb at one volt

Capacitance depends on the area of the plates, the separation between them and the medium between them. It does not depend on the material of the plates themselves.

Combinations of Capacitors

In series, the same charge flows onto each capacitor and the total voltage is the sum of the individual voltages. The equivalent capacitance is smaller than the smallest one.

1 / C = 1 / C1 + 1 / C2

  • Series rule - reciprocals add

In parallel, all capacitors have the same voltage and the total charge is the sum of the individual charges, so the equivalent capacitance is the sum and is larger than any one of them.

C = C1 + C2

  • Parallel rule - capacitances add directly

mcqs.q: A capacitor is a device that:
options: Produces electric charge from mechanical energy
Stores electric current in a coil of wire
Converts electric charge into heat energy
Stores electric charge, and hence energy in its electric field
mcqs.why: The notes define a capacitor as a device that stores electric charge, and hence energy in its electric field, usually two conductors separated by a dielectric.

mcqs.q: The insulator placed between the conductors of a capacitor is called:
options: A dielectric
An electrolyte
A semiconductor
A dielectric constant
mcqs.why: The notes state that a capacitor usually consists of two conductors separated by an insulator called a dielectric.

mcqs.q: Capacitance is defined as:
options: The ratio of the potential difference between the plates to the charge on either plate
The ratio of the charge stored on either plate to the potential difference between the plates
The total charge stored on both plates added together
The energy stored divided by the charge on either plate
mcqs.why: The notes define capacitance by C = Q / V: it measures the ability to store charge per unit potential difference between the plates.

mcqs.q: One farad is the capacitance of a capacitor that:
options: Stores one coulomb of charge at any potential difference
Stores one joule of energy at one volt
Stores one coulomb of charge at a potential difference of one volt
Allows one ampere to flow for one second
mcqs.why: From C = Q / V, one farad means Q = 1 C when V = 1 V, as stated in the notes for the unit of capacitance.

mcqs.q: Capacitance depends on:
options: The material of the plates, the charge stored and the voltage applied
Only the charge stored on the plates
Only the material from which the plates are made
The area of the plates, the separation between them and the medium between them, but not on the material of the plates themselves
mcqs.why: The notes state that capacitance depends on the plate area, the separation and the medium between the plates, and does not depend on the material of the plates themselves.

mcqs.q: A capacitor stores a charge of 20 microC when the potential difference between its plates is 4 V. What is its capacitance?
options: 5 microF
80 microF
0.2 microF
24 microF
mcqs.why: C = Q / V = 20 / 4 = 5 microF, using charge in microC and voltage in volts so the answer comes out in microF.

mcqs.q: When capacitors are connected in series:
options: All the capacitors have the same voltage and the total charge is the sum of the charges
The same charge flows onto each capacitor and the total voltage is the sum of the individual voltages
The equivalent capacitance is larger than any one of them
The charge on each capacitor is different and the voltages are equal
mcqs.why: The notes describe series connection this way, and add that the equivalent capacitance in series is smaller than the smallest one.

mcqs.q: For two capacitors in series, the equivalent capacitance is found from:
options: C = C1 + C2, the capacitances add directly
C = C1 x C2, the capacitances multiply
1 / C = 1 / C1 + 1 / C2, the reciprocals add
1 / C = 1 / C1 - 1 / C2, the reciprocals subtract
mcqs.why: The notes give the series rule as reciprocals adding: 1 / C = 1 / C1 + 1 / C2; direct addition is the parallel rule.

mcqs.q: Two capacitors of 6 microF and 3 microF are connected in series. What is the equivalent capacitance?
options: 9 microF
4.5 microF
18 microF
2 microF
mcqs.why: 1 / C = 1 / 6 + 1 / 3 = 1 / 6 + 2 / 6 = 3 / 6 = 1 / 2, so C = 2 microF, smaller than the smallest capacitor as the notes require.

mcqs.q: Two capacitors of 6 microF and 3 microF are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent capacitance?
options: 9 microF
2 microF
4.5 microF
18 microF
mcqs.why: In parallel all capacitors have the same voltage and the charges add, so C = C1 + C2 = 6 + 3 = 9 microF, larger than any one of them; 2 microF is the series value.

lessons.title: Capacitance of a Parallel Plate Capacitor
lessons.notes_html:
A parallel plate capacitor has two parallel metal plates of area A separated by a small distance d. Between the plates the field is uniform, and the potential difference is the field times the separation.

E = σ / εo

  • E - field between the plates; σ = Q / A, the surface charge density

V = E d

  • V - potential difference between the plates; d - separation

Combining C = Q / V with these results gives the capacitance. It increases with plate area and decreases with separation.

C = εo A / d

  • C - capacitance in free space or air; A - area of each plate; d - separation; εo = 8.85 x 10-12 C2 N-1 m-2

With a dielectric filling the space between the plates, the capacitance is multiplied by the dielectric constant.

C = εo εr A / d

  • εr - relative permittivity of the dielectric

mcqs.q: A parallel plate capacitor consists of:
options: Two parallel metal plates of area A separated by a small distance d
Two concentric metal spheres separated by a dielectric
A single metal plate rolled into a cylinder
Two perpendicular metal plates of area A
mcqs.why: The notes describe the parallel plate capacitor as two parallel metal plates of area A separated by a small distance d, with a uniform field between them.

mcqs.q: Between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor, the field is E = sigma / epsilon_o, where sigma is:
options: The total charge on both plates, sigma = 2 Q
The surface charge density, sigma = Q / A
The charge per unit length of the plate edge
The capacitance per unit area, sigma = C / A
mcqs.why: The notes define sigma = Q / A for the plates, and this field between the plates leads, through V = E d, to the capacitance formula.

mcqs.q: The potential difference between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor is related to the field by:
options: V = E / d, the field divided by the separation
V = E A, the field times the plate area
V = E d, the field times the separation
V = d / E, the separation divided by the field
mcqs.why: The notes state that between the plates the field is uniform and the potential difference is the field times the separation, V = E d.

mcqs.q: The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor in free space or air is:
options: C = epsilon_o d / A
C = A / (epsilon_o d)
C = epsilon_o A d
C = epsilon_o A / d
mcqs.why: Combining C = Q / V with E = sigma / epsilon_o and V = E d gives C = epsilon_o A / d, as derived step by step in the notes.

mcqs.q: The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor increases when:
options: The plate area increases or the separation decreases
The plate area decreases or the separation increases
The plate area and the separation both increase together
The voltage applied to the plates increases
mcqs.why: From C = epsilon_o A / d, capacitance is proportional to A and inversely proportional to d, so it increases with area and decreases with separation.

mcqs.q: In the formula C = epsilon_o A / d, epsilon_o has the value:
mcqs.why: The notes list epsilon_o = 8.85 x 10^-12 C^2 N^-1 m^-2, the permittivity of free space; 9 x 10^9 is the Coulomb constant k.

mcqs.q: A parallel plate capacitor has plate area 0.1 m^2 and separation 0.001 m. What is its capacitance in air? (epsilon_o = 8.85 x 10^-12 C^2 N^-1 m^-2)
When a dielectric fills the space between the plates, the capacitance becomes:
options: C = epsilon_o A / (epsilon_r d), divided by the dielectric constant
C = epsilon_o A / d, completely unchanged
C = epsilon_r A / d, with epsilon_o removed
C = epsilon_o epsilon_r A / d, multiplied by the dielectric constant epsilon_r
mcqs.why: The notes state that with a dielectric filling the space, the capacitance is multiplied by the dielectric constant, giving C = epsilon_o epsilon_r A / d.

mcqs.q: The capacitor of plate area 0.1 m^2 and separation 0.001 m has capacitance 8.85 x 10^-10 F in air. What is its capacitance when filled with a dielectric of epsilon_r = 3?
mcqs.why: The dielectric multiplies the capacitance by epsilon_r, so C = 3 x (8.85 x 10^-10) = 2.655 x 10^-9 F.

mcqs.q: If the separation between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor is halved, its capacitance:
options: Halves
Doubles
Becomes four times as large
Stays exactly the same
mcqs.why: C = epsilon_o A / d is inversely proportional to d, so halving d multiplies C by 1 / (1 / 2) = 2, doubling the capacitance.

lessons.title: Electric Polarization of a Dielectric
lessons.notes_html:
Electric polarization is the process in which the molecules of a dielectric placed in an electric field develop dipole moments. In a polar dielectric the permanent dipoles align with the field. In a non-polar dielectric the positive and negative charge centres of each molecule are displaced, creating induced dipoles.

How the Field is Reduced

Polarization charges appear on the dielectric surfaces: negative charge near the positive plate and positive charge near the negative plate. These charges set up an internal field opposite to the applied field, so the net field between the plates is reduced.

E = Eo / εr

  • E - net field with the dielectric; Eo - field without the dielectric; εr - dielectric constant

Effect on Capacitance

For the same stored charge, the reduced field means the potential difference also falls by the factor εr. Since C = Q / V, the capacitance therefore increases by the same factor.

C = εr Co

  • C - capacitance with dielectric; Co - capacitance without dielectric

A dielectric also allows the capacitor to store more energy and to withstand a higher voltage without breakdown.

mcqs.q: Electric polarization is the process in which:
options: The molecules of a conductor placed in a field lose their electrons
The molecules of a dielectric placed in an electric field develop dipole moments
A dielectric is charged by rubbing it with another material
The plates of a capacitor develop equal charges of the same sign
mcqs.why: The notes define electric polarization as the process in which the molecules of a dielectric placed in an electric field develop dipole moments.

mcqs.q: In a polar dielectric placed in an electric field:
options: The charge centres of each molecule are displaced to create dipoles
The molecules break down into free ions
The permanent dipoles align with the field
The dipoles align opposite to the field
mcqs.why: The notes state that in a polar dielectric the permanent dipoles align with the field; displaced charge centres creating induced dipoles describe a non-polar dielectric.

mcqs.q: In a non-polar dielectric placed in an electric field:
options: The permanent dipoles align with the field
Free electrons flow from one face to the other
The molecules gain a permanent charge
The positive and negative charge centres of each molecule are displaced, creating induced dipoles
mcqs.why: The notes state that in a non-polar dielectric the positive and negative charge centres of each molecule are displaced, creating induced dipoles.

mcqs.q: Polarization charges appear on the dielectric surfaces and set up an internal field that:
options: Is opposite to the applied field, so the net field between the plates is reduced; negative charge appears near the positive plate and positive charge near the negative plate
Is in the same direction as the applied field, so the net field increases
Is opposite to the applied field, with positive charge near the positive plate
Cancels the charge stored on the plates completely
mcqs.why: The notes explain that negative charge appears near the positive plate and positive charge near the negative plate, and these charges set up an internal field opposite to the applied field, reducing the net field.

mcqs.q: With a dielectric between the plates, the net field is given by:
options: E = epsilon_r E_o, increased by the factor epsilon_r
E = E_o / epsilon_r, reduced by the factor epsilon_r
E = E_o, unchanged by the dielectric
E = E_o / epsilon_r^2, reduced by the square of epsilon_r
mcqs.why: The notes give the net field with the dielectric as E = E_o / epsilon_r, where E_o is the field without the dielectric.

mcqs.q: The field between the plates of a capacitor without a dielectric is 90 N C^-1. What is the net field when a dielectric of epsilon_r = 3 is inserted?
mcqs.why: E = E_o / epsilon_r = 90 / 3 = 30 N C^-1, because polarization sets up an internal field opposing the applied field.

mcqs.q: For the same stored charge, inserting a dielectric makes the potential difference between the plates:
options: Rise by the factor epsilon_r, because the field is reduced
Stay the same, because the charge is unchanged
Fall to zero, because the field is cancelled completely
Fall by the factor epsilon_r, because the field is reduced by that factor
mcqs.why: The notes state that for the same stored charge the reduced field means the potential difference also falls by the factor epsilon_r, which is why the capacitance rises.

mcqs.q: The capacitance with a dielectric is related to the capacitance without it by:
options: C = epsilon_r C_o
C = C_o / epsilon_r
C = C_o + epsilon_r
C = epsilon_r / C_o
mcqs.why: Since C = Q / V and V falls by the factor epsilon_r for the same charge, the notes give the capacitance with dielectric as C = epsilon_r C_o.

mcqs.q: A capacitor has capacitance 5 microF without a dielectric. What is its capacitance with a dielectric of epsilon_r = 4?
options: 1.25 microF
20 microF
5 microF
9 microF
mcqs.why: C = epsilon_r C_o = 4 x 5 = 20 microF, because the dielectric multiplies the capacitance by its dielectric constant.

mcqs.q: Besides increasing the capacitance, a dielectric also allows the capacitor to:
options: Store less energy and break down at a lower voltage
Work without any charge on its plates
Store more energy and withstand a higher voltage without breakdown
Pass a steady direct current between its plates
mcqs.why: The notes state that a dielectric also allows the capacitor to store more energy and to withstand a higher voltage without breakdown.

lessons.title: Charging and Discharging of a Capacitor
lessons.notes_html:
An RC circuit contains a resistor R and a capacitor C in series with a source. The resistor limits the current, so the capacitor charges and discharges gradually, following an exponential curve. RC circuits are used in timing circuits, filters and camera flashes.

Charging

When the capacitor is connected through the resistor to a battery, charge accumulates on the plates, rising quickly at first and then more slowly. It reaches about 63 percent of its maximum in one time constant and is approximately fully charged after about five time constants, when its voltage equals the battery e.m.f. and the current stops.

q = Qo (1 - e-t / RC)

  • q - charge at time t; Qo - final maximum charge

Discharging

When the charged capacitor is connected across a resistor, the stored charge flows back and falls exponentially, dropping to about 37 percent of its initial value in one time constant and to practically zero after about five time constants.

q = Qo e-t / RC

  • q - charge remaining at time t

Time Constant

τ = R C

  • τ - time constant, unit second (s); the product R C has the unit of time, since ohm x farad = second

mcqs.q: An RC circuit contains:
options: A resistor R and an inductor L in series with a source
Two capacitors in parallel with a source and no resistor
A resistor R and a capacitor C in series with a source; the resistor limits the current so the capacitor charges and discharges gradually
A resistor that lets the capacitor charge instantly
mcqs.why: The notes define the RC circuit this way and add that RC circuits are used in timing circuits, filters and camera flashes because the charging is gradual and exponential.

mcqs.q: During charging, the charge on a capacitor in an RC circuit:
options: Rises at a steady constant rate until it is full
Rises slowly at first and then suddenly jumps to full
Stays at zero and then jumps instantly to its maximum
Rises quickly at first and then more slowly, following an exponential curve
mcqs.why: The notes describe charge accumulating quickly at first and then more slowly as charging proceeds, following the exponential charging curve.

mcqs.q: The charge on a charging capacitor at time t is given by:
options: q = Q_o e^(-t / RC)
q = Q_o t / RC
mcqs.why: The notes give the charging equation as q = Q_o (1 - e^(-t / RC)), where Q_o is the final maximum charge; Q_o e^(-t / RC) is the discharging equation.

mcqs.q: In one time constant, a charging capacitor reaches about:
options: 37 percent of its maximum charge
63 percent of its maximum charge
50 percent of its maximum charge
100 percent of its maximum charge
mcqs.why: The notes state that the charge reaches about 63 percent of its maximum in one time constant during charging; 37 percent is the discharging figure.

mcqs.q: A capacitor with maximum charge Q_o = 100 microC is charging. What charge does it hold after one time constant?
options: 37 microC
100 microC
63 microC
50 microC
mcqs.why: After one time constant the charge is about 63 percent of the maximum, so q = 0.63 x 100 = 63 microC.

mcqs.q: A capacitor in an RC circuit is approximately fully charged after:
options: Exactly one time constant, when the current stops
About two time constants, when its voltage is half the e.m.f.
About ten time constants, when its voltage exceeds the e.m.f.
About five time constants, when its voltage equals the battery e.m.f. and the current stops
mcqs.why: The notes state full charging takes about five time constants; for example with tau = 2 s this is 5 x 2 = 10 s, at which point the voltage equals the e.m.f. and the current stops.

mcqs.q: The charge remaining on a discharging capacitor at time t is given by:
options: q = Q_o e^(-t / RC)
q = Q_o - t / RC
mcqs.why: The notes give the discharging equation as q = Q_o e^(-t / RC): the stored charge flows back through the resistor and falls exponentially.

mcqs.q: A charged capacitor with initial charge Q_o = 100 microC discharges through a resistor. What charge remains after one time constant?
options: 63 microC
37 microC
0 microC
50 microC
mcqs.why: During discharging the charge drops to about 37 percent of its initial value in one time constant, so q = 0.37 x 100 = 37 microC.

mcqs.q: The time constant of an RC circuit is:
options: Tau = R / C, with unit second
Tau = C / R, with unit ohm
Tau = R C, with unit second, since ohm x farad = second
Tau = R C^2, with unit farad
mcqs.why: The notes give the time constant as tau = R C and state that the product R C has the unit of time, the second, since ohm x farad = second.

mcqs.q: What is the time constant of an RC circuit with R = 2000 ohm and C = 500 microF?
options: 4 s
1 s
mcqs.why: Tau = R C = 2000 x (500 x 10^-6) = 2000 x 0.0005 = 1 s, using the time constant relation from the notes.

lessons.title: Energy Stored in a Capacitor
lessons.notes_html:
Work must be done to charge a capacitor, against the repulsion of the charge already on the plates. This work is stored as potential energy in the field between the plates, and is released as heat when the capacitor discharges.

U = 1 / 2 C V2

  • U - energy stored, unit J; C - capacitance; V - potential difference between the plates

Using Q = C V, the same energy can also be written in two other useful forms.

U = Q2 / (2 C)

  • Useful form when the charge Q is kept constant

U = 1 / 2 Q V

  • Useful form when both Q and V are known

Worked Example: Charge and Energy Stored

A capacitor of 5 microF is charged by a 12 V battery. Find the charge and energy stored on it.

Step 1: Charge Q = C V = (5 x 10-6) x 12 = 60 x 10-6 C = 60 microC.

Step 2: Energy U = (1 / 2) C V2 = 0.5 x (5 x 10-6) x (12)2.

Step 3: (12)2 = 144, so U = 0.5 x (5 x 10-6) x 144 = 360 x 10-6 J.

Answer: The charge stored is 60 microC and the energy stored is 3.6 x 10-4 J.

Key Points

  • Charge is quantized, Q = n e, conserved and additive; like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
  • Coulomb's law: F = k q1 q2 / r2; a dielectric reduces the force by the factor εr.
  • Field intensity E = F / q and E = k Q / r2 for a point charge; field lines never cross.
  • A dipole has moment p = q d; its far field falls as 1 / r3.
  • Electric flux Φ = E A cos θ is maximum at θ = 0 degrees and zero at 90 degrees.
  • Gauss's law: Φ = Q / εo; the field inside a hollow charged shell is zero.
  • Potential V = W / q, V = k q / r for a point charge, and E = - dV / dr.
  • 1 eV = 1.6 x 10-19 J.
  • Capacitance C = Q / V and C = εo A / d for parallel plates; a dielectric multiplies C by εr.
  • Energy stored U = (1 / 2) C V2; the RC time constant is τ = R C and full charging takes about five time constants.

mcqs.q: The work done in charging a capacitor is stored as:
options: Kinetic energy of the charges on the plates
Chemical energy in the dielectric
Magnetic energy in the connecting wires
Potential energy in the field between the plates, released as heat when the capacitor discharges
mcqs.why: The notes state that work done against the repulsion of charge already on the plates is stored as potential energy in the field between the plates and released as heat on discharging.

mcqs.q: The energy stored in a capacitor is given by:
options: U = C V^2
U = 1 / 2 C V
U = C / V^2
mcqs.why: The notes give the stored energy as U = 1 / 2 C V^2, where C is the capacitance and V is the potential difference between the plates.

mcqs.q: The form U = Q^2 / (2 C) is most useful when:
options: The potential difference V is kept constant
The charge Q is kept constant
Both Q and V are unknown
The capacitance is changing rapidly
mcqs.why: Using Q = C V the energy can be rewritten in three forms; the notes state that U = Q^2 / (2 C) is the useful form when the charge Q is kept constant.

mcqs.q: The form U = 1 / 2 Q V is most useful when:
options: Only the capacitance C is known
The charge Q is kept constant and V is unknown
Both Q and V are known
Neither Q nor V is known
mcqs.why: The notes state that U = 1 / 2 Q V is the useful form when both the charge and the potential difference are known.

mcqs.q: A capacitor of 5 microF is charged by a 12 V battery. What charge is stored on it?
options: 17 microC
2.4 microC
600 microC
60 microC
mcqs.why: Q = C V = (5 x 10^-6) x 12 = 60 x 10^-6 C = 60 microC, exactly as in the notes worked example.

mcqs.q: What is the energy stored in that capacitor of 5 microF charged to 12 V?
Using U = 1 / 2 Q V, what is the energy stored when Q = 60 microC and V = 12 V?
mcqs.why: U = (1 / 2) Q V = 0.5 x (60 x 10^-6) x 12 = 360 x 10^-6 J = 3.6 x 10^-4 J, the same energy as found from (1 / 2) C V^2.

mcqs.q: Using U = Q^2 / (2 C), what is the energy stored when Q = 60 microC and C = 5 microF?
According to the key points of this unit, inserting a dielectric into a capacitor:
options: Divides the capacitance by epsilon_r
Leaves the capacitance unchanged
Multiplies the capacitance by epsilon_o
Multiplies the capacitance by epsilon_r
mcqs.why: The key points in the notes summarise that capacitance is C = epsilon_o A / d for parallel plates and a dielectric multiplies C by epsilon_r.

mcqs.q: According to the key points of this unit, the RC time constant and full charging are:
options: Tau = R C, and full charging takes about five time constants
Tau = R / C, and full charging takes about one time constant
Tau = R C, and full charging takes about one time constant
Tau = C / R, and full charging takes about five time constants
mcqs.why: The key points in the notes state that the RC time constant is tau = R C and full charging takes about five time constants.

lessons.title: Steady Current
lessons.notes_html:
Steady current is a continuous flow of charge whose magnitude remains constant with time, as supplied by a cell or battery. Electric current is the rate of flow of charge.

I = Q / t

  • I - current, unit ampere (A); Q - charge flowing, unit C; t - time, unit s

Conventional and Electronic Current

Conventional current is taken to flow from the positive terminal of a source to the negative terminal through the external circuit. Electronic current is the actual flow of free electrons in a metal, from the negative terminal to the positive terminal. The two are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction. In an electrolyte or plasma, both positive and negative ions carry the current in opposite directions.

Drift of Free Electrons

Without a field, free electrons move randomly and there is no net current. When a potential difference is applied, they gain a slow average motion opposite to the field, called the drift velocity. It is very small, of the order of millimetres per second, yet it constitutes the current. The direction of current is found in practice with a galvanometer or ammeter.

Worked Example: Electrons Through a Bulb

How many electrons flow through a light bulb each second, if the current through the bulb is 0.8 A?

Step 1: Charge per second Q = I x t = 0.8 x 1 = 0.8 C.

Step 2: Number of electrons n = Q / e = 0.8 / (1.6 x 10-19).

Step 3: n = 5 x 1018.

Answer: 5 x 1018 electrons flow through the bulb each second.

mcqs.q: What is steady current?
options: A flow of charge that keeps changing direction every second
A continuous flow of charge whose magnitude remains constant with time
A flow of charge that grows larger with time
A momentary flow of charge that stops after one second
mcqs.why: The notes define steady current as a continuous flow of charge whose magnitude remains constant with time, as supplied by a cell or battery.

mcqs.q: Electric current is defined as which of the following?
options: The total charge stored in a conductor, I = Q x t
The rate of flow of energy, I = W / t
The rate of flow of charge, I = Q / t
The charge per unit area, I = Q / A
mcqs.why: Current is the rate of flow of charge, I = Q / t, with I in ampere, Q in coulomb and t in second, as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: What is the unit of electric current?
options: Coulomb (C)
Volt (V)
Ohm
Ampere (A)
mcqs.why: In I = Q / t the current I is measured in ampere (A), while charge Q is in coulomb and time t is in second.
