mcqs.q: In the external circuit, conventional current is taken to flow in which direction?
options: From the positive terminal of the source to the negative terminal
From the negative terminal of the source to the positive terminal
From the negative terminal back to the negative terminal
In a circle inside the source only
mcqs.why: Conventional current flows from the positive terminal to the negative terminal through the external circuit, opposite to the actual electron flow.

mcqs.q: What is electronic current in a metal?
options: The flow of positive ions from positive to negative terminal
The actual flow of free electrons from the negative terminal to the positive terminal
The flow of protons through the external circuit
The flow of charge assumed from positive to negative terminal
mcqs.why: Electronic current is the actual flow of free electrons in a metal, from negative to positive terminal, equal in magnitude but opposite in direction to conventional current.

mcqs.q: In an electrolyte or plasma, what carries the current?
options: Only free electrons moving in one direction
Only positive ions moving in one direction
Both positive and negative ions moving in opposite directions
Only neutral atoms moving randomly
mcqs.why: The notes state that in an electrolyte or plasma both positive and negative ions carry the current in opposite directions, unlike a metal where electrons carry it.

mcqs.q: What is drift velocity?
options: The fast random motion of electrons when no field is applied
The motion of electrons along the direction of the field
The speed of the current signal around the whole circuit
The slow average motion gained by free electrons opposite to the field when a potential difference is applied
mcqs.why: Without a field electrons move randomly with no net current; with a potential difference they gain a slow average motion opposite to the field, called drift velocity.

mcqs.q: How many electrons flow through a bulb each second if the current is 0.8 A? Use e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C.
mcqs.why: Charge per second Q = I x t = 0.8 x 1 = 0.8 C. Number n = Q / e = 0.8 / (1.6 x 10^-19) = 5 x 10^18 electrons, as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: A steady current of 0.8 A flows for 5 s. How much charge flows?
mcqs.why: Using I = Q / t, Q = I x t = 0.8 x 5 = 4.0 C. The charge is the current multiplied by the time for which it flows.

mcqs.q: A charge of 1.6 C flows through a wire in 2 s. What is the current?
mcqs.why: Current I = Q / t = 1.6 / 2 = 0.8 A. Current is charge divided by time, so 1.6 coulomb in 2 seconds gives 0.8 ampere.

lessons.title: Sources of Steady Current
lessons.notes_html:
A source of steady current maintains a potential difference by converting some other form of energy into electrical energy, so that charge keeps flowing in one direction.

SourceEnergy Converted
Cell and batteryChemical energy
Dynamo and generatorMechanical energy
PhotocellLight energy
ThermocoupleHeat energy

The Simple Voltaic Cell

The first source of e.m.f. was discovered by Volta. In a simple voltaic cell the zinc plate is the negative electrode: zinc atoms give up electrons and enter the electrolyte as positive ions. The copper plate is the positive electrode: it accepts electrons from the external circuit, where positive ions gain electrons and are deposited or liberated. The chemical reactions at the plates maintain the potential difference.

Cells differ in type: a Leclanche cell is not rechargeable, while nickel-cadmium and lead-acid cells are rechargeable. A photocell converts light energy into electrical energy.

mcqs.q: What does a source of steady current do?
options: It stores charge without converting any energy
It converts electrical energy only into heat energy
It maintains a potential difference by converting another form of energy into electrical energy
It removes the potential difference so charge stops flowing
mcqs.why: A source of steady current maintains a potential difference by converting some other form of energy into electrical energy, so charge keeps flowing in one direction.

mcqs.q: What energy conversion takes place in a cell and battery?
options: Mechanical energy into electrical energy
Light energy into electrical energy
Heat energy into electrical energy
Chemical energy into electrical energy
mcqs.why: The table in the notes shows that a cell and battery convert chemical energy into electrical energy to maintain the potential difference.

mcqs.q: What energy conversion takes place in a dynamo and generator?
options: Mechanical energy into electrical energy
Chemical energy into electrical energy
Light energy into electrical energy
Heat energy into electrical energy
mcqs.why: The notes table shows that a dynamo and generator convert mechanical energy into electrical energy, unlike a cell which uses chemical energy.

mcqs.q: What energy conversion takes place in a photocell?
options: Heat energy into electrical energy
Light energy into electrical energy
Chemical energy into electrical energy
Mechanical energy into electrical energy
mcqs.why: A photocell converts light energy into electrical energy, as listed in the sources table and repeated at the end of the lesson notes.

mcqs.q: What energy conversion takes place in a thermocouple as a source?
options: Light energy into electrical energy
Chemical energy into electrical energy
Heat energy into electrical energy
Mechanical energy into electrical energy
mcqs.why: The sources table in the notes lists the thermocouple as converting heat energy into electrical energy to act as a source of steady current.

mcqs.q: Who discovered the first source of e.m.f.?
options: Ohm
Faraday
Wheatstone
Volta
mcqs.why: The notes state that the first source of e.m.f. was discovered by Volta, and the simple voltaic cell is named after this work.

mcqs.q: In a simple voltaic cell, which plate is the negative electrode?
options: The zinc plate
The copper plate
Both plates equally
Neither plate is an electrode
mcqs.why: In the simple voltaic cell the zinc plate is the negative electrode: zinc atoms give up electrons and enter the electrolyte as positive ions.

mcqs.q: In a simple voltaic cell, what happens at the copper plate?
options: It is the negative electrode and gives up electrons to the electrolyte
It is the positive electrode and accepts electrons from the external circuit
It dissolves into the electrolyte as positive ions
It blocks all electrons from the external circuit
mcqs.why: The copper plate is the positive electrode: it accepts electrons from the external circuit, where positive ions gain electrons and are deposited or liberated.

mcqs.q: Which cell is NOT rechargeable according to the notes?
options: Nickel-cadmium cell
Lead-acid cell
Leclanche cell
Both nickel-cadmium and lead-acid cells
mcqs.why: The notes state that a Leclanche cell is not rechargeable, while nickel-cadmium and lead-acid cells are rechargeable types of cell.

mcqs.q: What maintains the potential difference in a voltaic cell?
options: The heating of the electrolyte by the current
The magnetic field around the cell
The light falling on the plates
The chemical reactions at the plates
mcqs.why: The notes explain that the chemical reactions at the plates maintain the potential difference in the simple voltaic cell.

lessons.title: Ohm's Law
lessons.notes_html:
Ohm's law states that, at constant temperature, the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends.

V = I R

  • V - potential difference, unit V; I - current, unit A; R - resistance, unit ohm (Ω)

Ohmic Devices

An ohmic device obeys Ohm's law: its V-I graph is a straight line through the origin and its resistance stays constant. Metals such as copper, silver and gold at constant temperature are ohmic. If the length of a wire is doubled, its resistance also doubles.

Non-Ohmic Devices

A non-ohmic device does not obey Ohm's law: its V-I graph is a curve, because its resistance changes with voltage, current or temperature. Examples are the filament of an electric bulb, a semiconductor diode, germanium and a thermistor. For such devices R = V / I gives only the resistance at that particular point.

mcqs.q: What does Ohm's law state?
options: At constant temperature, the current is inversely proportional to the potential difference
At any temperature, the resistance is directly proportional to the current
The current is directly proportional to the resistance at constant voltage
At constant temperature, the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its ends
mcqs.why: Ohm's law states that at constant temperature the current is directly proportional to the potential difference across the ends, giving V = I R.

mcqs.q: Which relation expresses Ohm's law?
options: V = I R
V = I / R
V = R / I
I = V x R
mcqs.why: Ohm's law is written V = I R, where V is potential difference in volt, I is current in ampere and R is resistance in ohm.

mcqs.q: What is the unit of resistance?
options: Ampere
Ohm
Volt
Siemen
mcqs.why: In V = I R the resistance R is measured in ohm, while V is in volt and I is in ampere, as listed in the notes.

mcqs.q: What does the V-I graph of an ohmic device look like?
options: A curve bending away from the origin
A horizontal line at constant voltage
A straight line through the origin
A vertical line at constant current
mcqs.why: An ohmic device obeys Ohm's law: its V-I graph is a straight line through the origin and its resistance stays constant.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an ohmic device at constant temperature?
options: Semiconductor diode
Filament of an electric bulb
Thermistor
Copper
mcqs.why: Metals such as copper, silver and gold at constant temperature are ohmic, while a diode, bulb filament and thermistor are listed as non-ohmic.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a non-ohmic device?
options: Germanium
Silver at constant temperature
Gold at constant temperature
Copper at constant temperature
mcqs.why: Germanium is listed among non-ohmic devices with the bulb filament, diode and thermistor, because its resistance changes and its V-I graph is a curve.

mcqs.q: If the length of a wire is doubled, what happens to its resistance?
options: Its resistance becomes half
Its resistance also doubles
Its resistance becomes four times
Its resistance stays exactly the same
mcqs.why: The notes state directly that if the length of a wire is doubled, its resistance also doubles, showing resistance grows in proportion to length.

mcqs.q: A wire of resistance 6 ohm has its length doubled. What is its new resistance?
options: 3 ohm
6 ohm
12 ohm
36 ohm
mcqs.why: Resistance is proportional to length, so doubling the length doubles the resistance: R = 6 x 2 = 12 ohm, following the rule given in the notes.

mcqs.q: A current of 2 A flows through a 5 ohm resistor. What is the potential difference across it?
options: 7 V
mcqs.why: Using Ohm's law V = I R = 2 x 5 = 10 V. Potential difference equals current multiplied by resistance for an ohmic conductor.

mcqs.q: A potential difference of 12 V is applied across a 4 ohm resistor. What current flows?
options: 3 A
8 A
mcqs.why: From V = I R, I = V / R = 12 / 4 = 3 A. The current is the potential difference divided by the resistance.

lessons.title: Resistivity and Conductivity
lessons.notes_html:
Resistivity is a property of the material of a conductor, not of its size. It is the resistance of a unit cube of the material.

R = ρ L / A

  • R - resistance; ρ - resistivity, unit ohm m; L - length; A - area of cross-section

Conductivity is the reciprocal of resistivity. Its unit is ohm-1 m-1, and the unit of conductance is the siemen, which is equal to the mho.

σ = 1 / ρ

  • σ - conductivity; ρ - resistivity

Effect of Temperature

For metals, resistivity increases with temperature, because vibrating lattice ions obstruct the electrons more. For semiconductors and insulators it decreases, because heating frees more charge carriers. For alloys such as constantan and manganin it stays almost constant. A positive coefficient means resistance rises with temperature, as in metals; a negative coefficient means it falls, as in semiconductors. Its unit is per degree C.

Rt = Ro (1 + α t)

  • Rt - resistance at temperature t; Ro - resistance at 0 degrees C; α - temperature coefficient of resistivity

Worked Example: Resistance of a Metal Rod

A metal rod is 4 m long and 6 mm in diameter. Compute its resistance if the resistivity of the metal is 1.76 x 10-8 ohm m.

Step 1: Radius r = 6 mm / 2 = 3 mm = 3 x 10-3 m.

Step 2: Area A = π r2 = 3.14 x (3 x 10-3)2 = 2.83 x 10-5 m2.

Step 3: R = ρ L / A = (1.76 x 10-8 x 4) / (2.83 x 10-5) = 7.04 x 10-8 / 2.83 x 10-5.

Step 4: R = 2.49 x 10-3 ohm, about 2.5 x 10-3 ohm.

Answer: The resistance of the rod is about 2.5 x 10-3 ohm.

Worked Example: Resistance at a Higher Temperature

A copper wire has a resistance of 3 ohm at 0 degrees C. What is its resistance at 60 degrees C? The temperature coefficient of copper is 0.0039 per degree C.

Step 1: Use Rt = Ro (1 + α t) with Ro = 3 ohm, α = 0.0039 and t = 60.

Step 2: α t = 0.0039 x 60 = 0.234, so 1 + α t = 1.234.

Step 3: R = 3 x 1.234 = 3.702 ohm, about 3.70 ohm.

Answer: The resistance at 60 degrees C is about 3.70 ohm. (The book's printed answer of 3.77 ohm is wrong; the correct value is 3.70 ohm.)

mcqs.q: What is resistivity?
options: A property of the material, the resistance of a unit cube of the material
A property that depends only on the length of the wire
The total resistance of any wire of the material
The reciprocal of the resistance of a wire
mcqs.why: Resistivity is a property of the material, not of its size: it is the resistance of a unit cube of the material, as defined in the notes.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the resistance of a conductor?
options: R = rho A / L
R = rho L / A
R = L / (rho A)
R = rho / (L A)
mcqs.why: Resistance is R = rho L / A, where rho is resistivity in ohm m, L is length and A is area of cross-section.

mcqs.q: What is the unit of resistivity?
options: Ohm per m
Ohm m^-1
Ohm m
Siemen
mcqs.why: In R = rho L / A, resistivity rho has unit ohm m, as stated in the notes alongside the resistance formula.

mcqs.q: Conductivity is defined as which of the following?
options: The product of resistivity and length, sigma = rho L
The reciprocal of resistance, sigma = 1 / R
The ratio of length to resistivity, sigma = L / rho
The reciprocal of resistivity, sigma = 1 / rho
mcqs.why: Conductivity sigma is the reciprocal of resistivity, sigma = 1 / rho, with unit ohm^-1 m^-1 as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: How does the resistivity of a metal change with temperature?
options: It increases, because vibrating lattice ions obstruct the electrons more
It decreases, because heating frees more charge carriers
It stays exactly constant at all temperatures
It first decreases and then becomes zero
mcqs.why: For metals resistivity increases with temperature because vibrating lattice ions obstruct the electrons more, giving a positive temperature coefficient.

mcqs.q: For which materials does resistivity stay almost constant with temperature?
options: Pure metals such as copper
Alloys such as constantan and manganin
Semiconductors such as germanium
Insulators
mcqs.why: The notes state that for alloys such as constantan and manganin resistivity stays almost constant with temperature, unlike metals and semiconductors.

mcqs.q: A metal rod is 4 m long and 6 mm in diameter. What is its area of cross-section? Use pi = 3.14.
mcqs.why: Radius r = 3 mm = 3 x 10^-3 m. Area A = pi r^2 = 3.14 x (3 x 10^-3)^2 = 3.14 x 9 x 10^-6 = 2.83 x 10^-5 m^2, as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: For the rod in the worked example, resistivity 1.76 x 10^-8 ohm m, length 4 m and area 2.83 x 10^-5 m^2, what is the resistance?
options: About 2.5 x 10^-2 ohm
About 2.5 ohm
About 1.24 x 10^-3 ohm
About 2.5 x 10^-3 ohm

mcqs.q: A copper wire has resistance 3 ohm at 0 degrees C, with alpha = 0.0039 per degree C. What is its resistance at 60 degrees C?
options: About 3.70 ohm
About 3.77 ohm
About 2.30 ohm
About 3.23 ohm
mcqs.why: Rt = Ro (1 + alpha t) = 3 x (1 + 0.0039 x 60) = 3 x (1 + 0.234) = 3 x 1.234 = 3.702 ohm, about 3.70 ohm. The book value 3.77 ohm is wrong.

mcqs.q: What is the conductivity of a metal with resistivity 1.76 x 10^-8 ohm m?
options: About 1.76 x 10^8 ohm^-1 m^-1
About 5.68 x 10^7 ohm^-1 m^-1
About 5.68 x 10^6 ohm^-1 m^-1
About 0.57 ohm^-1 m^-1
mcqs.why: Conductivity sigma = 1 / rho = 1 / (1.76 x 10^-8) = 5.68 x 10^7 ohm^-1 m^-1. Conductivity is the reciprocal of the given resistivity.

lessons.title: Thermistor
lessons.notes_html:
A thermistor is a temperature-dependent resistor made of a semiconductor material, usually a metal oxide. Its resistance varies markedly even with a small change of temperature.

Behaviour

Most thermistors have a negative temperature coefficient: their resistance falls as the temperature rises, because heating frees more charge carriers in the semiconductor. This is the opposite behaviour to a metal, whose resistance rises with temperature. A thermistor is therefore a non-ohmic, heat-sensitive device.

Applications in Daily Life

  • Temperature sensors and controllers in thermostats
  • Fire alarms and digital thermometers
  • Automatic temperature control of refrigerators and air conditioners
  • Temperature compensation and surge protection in electronic circuits

Because a small temperature change produces a large resistance change, a thermistor can detect and control temperature accurately with a simple circuit.

mcqs.q: What is a thermistor?
options: A temperature-dependent resistor made of pure copper wire
A temperature-dependent resistor made of a semiconductor material, usually a metal oxide
A device made of two dissimilar metal wires joined at two junctions
A long uniform wire used to compare e.m.f.s
mcqs.why: A thermistor is a temperature-dependent resistor made of semiconductor material, usually a metal oxide, whose resistance varies markedly with small temperature changes.

mcqs.q: Most thermistors have which temperature coefficient?
options: Positive: resistance rises as temperature rises
Zero: resistance never changes with temperature
Negative: resistance falls as temperature rises
Positive at first and then exactly zero
mcqs.why: Most thermistors have a negative temperature coefficient: resistance falls as temperature rises because heating frees more charge carriers in the semiconductor.

mcqs.q: Why does the resistance of a thermistor fall when it is heated?
options: Heating makes the lattice ions vibrate less
Heating removes charge carriers from the material
Heating changes the thermistor into a metal
Heating frees more charge carriers in the semiconductor
mcqs.why: The notes explain that heating frees more charge carriers in the semiconductor, so the resistance of the thermistor falls as temperature rises.

mcqs.q: How does a thermistor differ from a metal in its temperature behaviour?
options: A thermistor resistance falls with rising temperature, while a metal resistance rises
Both resistances fall with rising temperature
Both resistances rise with rising temperature
A thermistor resistance rises, while a metal resistance falls
mcqs.why: The thermistor behaviour is the opposite of a metal: the thermistor resistance falls with temperature while a metal resistance rises with temperature.

mcqs.q: A thermistor is an example of which kind of device?
options: An ohmic device with constant resistance
A non-ohmic, heat-sensitive device
A source of steady current
A potential divider with a sliding contact
mcqs.why: The notes describe the thermistor as a non-ohmic, heat-sensitive device, and it is also listed as a non-ohmic example in the Ohm's law lesson.

mcqs.q: Which is an application of a thermistor?
options: Measuring high temperatures inside furnaces directly as a junction
Comparing the e.m.f.s of two cells
Temperature sensors and controllers in thermostats
Balancing a Wheatstone bridge to find resistance
mcqs.why: Thermistors are used as temperature sensors and controllers in thermostats, one of the daily-life applications listed in the notes.

mcqs.q: Which pair is a correct thermistor application?
options: Dynamos and generators
Photocells and solar panels
Rheostats and potentiometers
Fire alarms and digital thermometers
mcqs.why: Fire alarms and digital thermometers are both listed in the notes as applications that use the thermistor temperature-sensitive resistance.

mcqs.q: Thermistors are used for automatic temperature control of which appliances?
options: Refrigerators and air conditioners
Electric bulbs and heaters only
Furnaces and engines only
Voltmeters and ammeters
mcqs.why: The applications list includes automatic temperature control of refrigerators and air conditioners using thermistors as the sensing element.

mcqs.q: Why can a thermistor detect temperature accurately with a simple circuit?
options: A large temperature change produces no resistance change
A small temperature change produces a large resistance change
A small temperature change produces an e.m.f. at a junction
Its resistance stays constant so the current is steady
mcqs.why: Because a small temperature change produces a large resistance change, a thermistor can detect and control temperature accurately with a simple circuit.

mcqs.q: In electronic circuits, thermistors are also used for which purpose?
options: Converting light energy into electrical energy
Storing charge between two plates
Temperature compensation and surge protection
Producing a magnetic field around a wire
mcqs.why: The notes list temperature compensation and surge protection in electronic circuits as an application of thermistors in daily life.

lessons.title: Electromotive Force and Potential Difference
lessons.notes_html:
Electromotive force (e.m.f.) is the work done by a source per unit charge in moving charge once around a complete circuit - the energy supplied by the source per coulomb. Its unit is the volt. Potential difference, or terminal voltage, is the work done per unit charge in the external circuit, and equals the energy converted per coulomb outside the source.

Internal Resistance

Every real source has internal resistance r. When current flows, part of the e.m.f. is used up inside the source, so the terminal voltage is less than the e.m.f.

V = E - I r

  • V - terminal potential difference; E - e.m.f. of the source; I - current drawn; r - internal resistance; hence E is greater than V when current flows

The two are equal only when no current is drawn (open circuit, I = 0) or when the internal resistance is zero, as for an ideal source.

Electrical Power and Maximum Power Transfer

P = V I

  • P - electrical power, unit watt (W); also P = I2 R and P = V2 / R for a resistor

A source delivers maximum power to the external circuit when the load resistance R equals the internal resistance r. Then half the total power is delivered to the load and half is wasted as heat inside the source, so the efficiency is only 50 percent.

Pmax = E2 / (4 r)

  • Maximum power delivered, obtained when R = r

mcqs.q: What is electromotive force (e.m.f.)?
options: The work done per unit charge in the external circuit only
The force that pushes electrons through a resistor only
The work done by a source per unit charge in moving charge once around a complete circuit
The potential difference across a resistor in the circuit
mcqs.why: E.m.f. is the work done by a source per unit charge around a complete circuit, the energy supplied per coulomb, with unit volt.

mcqs.q: What is potential difference, or terminal voltage?
options: The work done per unit charge around the complete circuit including the source
The energy wasted as heat inside the source per coulomb
The total energy supplied by the source per coulomb
The work done per unit charge in the external circuit
mcqs.why: Potential difference is the work done per unit charge in the external circuit, the energy converted per coulomb outside the source, unlike e.m.f. which covers the whole circuit.

mcqs.q: Which relation gives the terminal voltage of a real source?
options: V = E - I r
V = E + I r
V = E x I r
V = I r - E
mcqs.why: Terminal voltage V = E - I r, where E is e.m.f., I is current drawn and r is internal resistance, so V is less than E when current flows.

mcqs.q: When are terminal voltage and e.m.f. equal?
options: When the largest possible current is drawn
When no current is drawn, on open circuit with I = 0
When the load resistance equals the internal resistance
When the source is delivering maximum power
mcqs.why: V and E are equal only when no current is drawn (open circuit, I = 0) or when internal resistance is zero, as for an ideal source.

mcqs.q: A source has e.m.f. 12 V and internal resistance 1 ohm, and supplies 2 A. What is its terminal voltage?
options: 6 V
mcqs.why: Terminal voltage V = E - I r = 12 - (2 x 1) = 12 - 2 = 10 V. Part of the e.m.f. is used up inside the source when current flows.

mcqs.q: Which is a correct formula for electrical power in a resistor?
options: P = I / R
P = V / I
P = R / I^2
P = I^2 R
mcqs.why: Electrical power is P = V I, and for a resistor it can also be written P = I^2 R and P = V^2 / R, as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: A current of 2 A flows through a 5 ohm resistor. What power is dissipated?
options: 5 W
mcqs.why: Power P = I^2 R = (2)^2 x 5 = 4 x 5 = 20 W. This uses the resistor form of the power formula given in the notes.

mcqs.q: When does a source deliver maximum power to the external circuit?
options: When the load resistance is zero
When the load resistance R equals the internal resistance r
When the load resistance is much larger than r
When no current is drawn from the source
mcqs.why: Maximum power is delivered when load resistance R equals internal resistance r, with Pmax = E^2 / (4 r), as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: At maximum power transfer, what is the efficiency of the source?
options: 100 percent
75 percent
Only 50 percent
25 percent
mcqs.why: At maximum power transfer half the total power goes to the load and half is wasted as heat inside the source, so the efficiency is only 50 percent.

mcqs.q: A source has e.m.f. 8 V and internal resistance 2 ohm. What is the maximum power it can deliver?
options: 4 W
8 W
mcqs.why: Maximum power Pmax = E^2 / (4 r) = (8)^2 / (4 x 2) = 64 / 8 = 8 W, obtained when the load resistance equals the internal resistance.

lessons.title: Thermocouple
lessons.notes_html:
A thermocouple is a device made of two dissimilar metal wires joined at two junctions. It converts heat energy into electrical energy and is used to measure temperature.

Working Principle - Seebeck Effect

A thermocouple works on the Seebeck effect: when the two junctions are kept at different temperatures, an e.m.f. is produced in the circuit. This thermo-e.m.f. depends on the temperature difference between the hot junction and the cold (reference) junction, and increases as that difference increases.

Function and Uses

The thermo-e.m.f. is measured with a galvanometer or voltmeter calibrated to read temperature directly. Thermocouples are used for measuring high temperatures in furnaces, engines and laboratories, and as temperature sensors in industry, where ordinary thermometers cannot be used.

Note the difference in purpose: a thermocouple produces an e.m.f. from heat, while a thermistor changes its resistance with heat.

mcqs.q: What is a thermocouple?
options: A semiconductor resistor made of a metal oxide
A long uniform wire with a sliding jockey contact
A coil of wire wound on an insulating cylinder
A device made of two dissimilar metal wires joined at two junctions
mcqs.why: A thermocouple is made of two dissimilar metal wires joined at two junctions; it converts heat energy into electrical energy and measures temperature.

mcqs.q: On what effect does a thermocouple work?
options: The Seebeck effect
The heating effect of current
The magnetic effect of current
The photoelectric effect
mcqs.why: A thermocouple works on the Seebeck effect: when the two junctions are at different temperatures, an e.m.f. is produced in the circuit.

mcqs.q: When is an e.m.f. produced in a thermocouple?
options: When both junctions are kept at exactly the same temperature
When the two junctions are kept at different temperatures
When light falls on one of the junctions
When a current is forced through the junctions
mcqs.why: The Seebeck effect produces an e.m.f. only when the two junctions are kept at different temperatures, one hot and one cold reference junction.

mcqs.q: What does the thermo-e.m.f. of a thermocouple depend on?
options: The length of the wires only
The resistance of the wires only
The temperature difference between the hot junction and the cold reference junction
The colour of the two metal wires
mcqs.why: The thermo-e.m.f. depends on the temperature difference between the hot junction and the cold reference junction, and increases as that difference increases.

mcqs.q: How does the thermo-e.m.f. change when the temperature difference increases?
options: It decreases
It stays exactly the same
It becomes zero
It increases
mcqs.why: The notes state that the thermo-e.m.f. increases as the temperature difference between the hot and cold junctions increases.

mcqs.q: How is temperature measured with a thermocouple?
options: The thermo-e.m.f. is measured with a galvanometer or voltmeter calibrated to read temperature directly
The change in resistance is measured on an ohm scale
The balancing length on a uniform wire is measured
The deflection of a bridge galvanometer is brought to zero
mcqs.why: The thermo-e.m.f. is measured with a galvanometer or voltmeter calibrated to read temperature directly, as described in the notes.

mcqs.q: Thermocouples are especially used for measuring which temperatures?
options: Only body temperature in clinics
High temperatures in furnaces, engines and laboratories
Only very low temperatures near zero
Only room temperature in homes
mcqs.why: Thermocouples measure high temperatures in furnaces, engines and laboratories, where ordinary thermometers cannot be used.

mcqs.q: What energy conversion does a thermocouple perform?
options: Light energy into electrical energy
Chemical energy into electrical energy
Heat energy into electrical energy
Electrical energy into heat energy only
mcqs.why: Like the sources table, this lesson states that a thermocouple converts heat energy into electrical energy by producing a thermo-e.m.f.

mcqs.q: How does a thermocouple differ in purpose from a thermistor?
options: A thermocouple changes its resistance, while a thermistor produces an e.m.f.
Both produce an e.m.f. from heat in the same way
Both change resistance and neither produces an e.m.f.
A thermocouple produces an e.m.f. from heat, while a thermistor changes its resistance with heat
mcqs.why: The notes contrast the two directly: a thermocouple produces an e.m.f. from heat, while a thermistor changes its resistance with heat.

mcqs.q: In industry, thermocouples are used as what?
options: Temperature sensors
Charge storage devices
Variable resistors for current control
Instruments for comparing e.m.f.s
mcqs.why: Thermocouples are used as temperature sensors in industry, in places where ordinary thermometers cannot be used, according to the notes.

lessons.title: Kirchhoff's Laws
lessons.notes_html:
Circuit analysis means finding the currents and voltages in every part of a circuit. Ohm's law alone is enough for simple circuits, but complex networks need Kirchhoff's laws. A node is a point where three or more conductors meet; a node at zero potential is the datum node. A loop is any closed conducting path.

First Law - Junction Rule

The algebraic sum of the currents at any junction is zero: the total current entering a junction equals the total current leaving it. It is based on the conservation of charge, because charge cannot accumulate at a junction. By convention, currents towards a node are taken positive and currents away from it negative.

Second Law - Loop Rule

The algebraic sum of the potential changes around any closed loop is zero: the sum of the e.m.f.s equals the sum of the IR drops. It is based on the conservation of energy. Going through a source from negative to positive, the e.m.f. is taken positive; going through a resistor in the direction of the current, the potential falls by I R, and against the current it rises.

Node analysis applies the first law at the junctions, and loop analysis applies the second law around the independent loops. Together they give enough equations to solve the circuit.

Worked Example: Currents in a Two-Loop Circuit

Determine the currents in a circuit where R1 is 10 ohm, R2 is 6 ohm, R3 is 10 ohm, E1 is 6 V and E2 is 3 V. I1 flows through R1, I2 through R2 and I3 downwards through R3.

Step 1: At the middle junction, I1 + I2 = I3 by the first law.

Step 2: Left loop clockwise: 6 - 10 I1 - 10 I3 = 0, so I1 + I3 = 0.6.

Step 3: Right loop clockwise: 6 I2 - 3 + 10 I3 = 0, so 6 I2 + 10 I3 = 3.

Step 4: From Steps 1 and 2, I2 = 2 I3 - 0.6. Substituting gives 22 I3 = 6.6, so I3 = 0.3 A.

Step 5: Then I1 = 0.6 - 0.3 = 0.3 A and I2 = 2(0.3) - 0.6 = 0 A.

Answer: I1 is 0.3 A, I2 is 0 A and I3 is 0.3 A. No current flows through R2 because the two loop voltages balance.

mcqs.q: What is a node in a circuit?
options: A point where three or more conductors meet
Any closed conducting path in the circuit
A point where exactly two conductors meet
The positive terminal of a source
mcqs.why: A node is a point where three or more conductors meet; a node at zero potential is called the datum node, as defined in the notes.

mcqs.q: What is a loop in a circuit?
options: A point where conductors meet
Any closed conducting path
A single resistor in the circuit
An open path from one terminal to the other
mcqs.why: A loop is any closed conducting path, and Kirchhoff's second law is applied around such closed loops to analyse the circuit.

mcqs.q: What does Kirchhoff's first law (junction rule) state?
options: The sum of e.m.f.s equals the sum of IR drops around a loop
The current through every branch is exactly the same
The total current entering a junction equals the total current leaving it
Charge accumulates at a junction until it is full
mcqs.why: The first law says the algebraic sum of currents at a junction is zero: current entering equals current leaving, because charge cannot accumulate at a junction.

mcqs.q: Kirchhoff's first law is based on conservation of what?
options: Energy
Momentum
Mass
Charge
mcqs.why: The junction rule is based on conservation of charge, since charge cannot accumulate at a junction, while the loop rule is based on conservation of energy.

mcqs.q: What does Kirchhoff's second law (loop rule) state?
options: The sum of the e.m.f.s around a closed loop equals the sum of the IR drops
The total current entering a junction equals the current leaving it
The resistance around a loop is always zero
The potential is the same at every point of the loop
mcqs.why: The second law says the algebraic sum of potential changes around any closed loop is zero: the sum of e.m.f.s equals the sum of the IR drops.

mcqs.q: Kirchhoff's second law is based on conservation of what?
options: Charge
Energy
Momentum
Mass
mcqs.why: The loop rule is based on conservation of energy, because the net potential change around a closed loop must be zero, unlike the first law which uses charge.

mcqs.q: In the two-loop worked example with R1 = 10 ohm, R2 = 6 ohm, R3 = 10 ohm, E1 = 6 V and E2 = 3 V, what is the current I3 through R3?
options: 0 A
3 A
mcqs.why: From I1 + I2 = I3, I1 + I3 = 0.6 and 6 I2 + 10 I3 = 3, substitution gives 22 I3 = 6.6, so I3 = 6.6 / 22 = 0.3 A, as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: In the same two-loop worked example, what is the current I1 through R1?
options: 0 A
mcqs.why: The left loop gives I1 + I3 = 0.6. With I3 = 0.3 A from the full solution, I1 = 0.6 - 0.3 = 0.3 A, as worked out in the notes.

mcqs.q: In the same two-loop worked example, what is the current I2 through R2?
options: 0 A
mcqs.why: I2 = 2 I3 - 0.6 = 2(0.3) - 0.6 = 0 A. No current flows through R2 because the two loop voltages balance, as the notes conclude.

mcqs.q: What is node analysis?
options: Applying Kirchhoff's second law around the loops
Applying Kirchhoff's first law at the junctions
Applying Ohm's law to a single resistor only
Balancing a bridge to zero galvanometer current
mcqs.why: Node analysis applies the first law at the junctions, while loop analysis applies the second law around the independent loops, together solving the circuit.

lessons.title: Rheostat
lessons.notes_html:
A rheostat is an electrical device that controls the current in a circuit. It is a long wire of high-resistance material such as constantan wound on an insulating cylinder, with a sliding contact that can move along the wire.

Working Principle

The resistance between one end of the wire and the sliding contact is proportional to the length of wire between them. Moving the contact changes the resistance, and hence changes the current or the voltage taken from the device.

As a Variable Resistance

Connected in series with the circuit, the rheostat varies the total resistance. Sliding the contact to include more wire increases the resistance and decreases the current.

As a Potential Divider

Connected across a source, with the output taken between one end and the sliding contact, the rheostat gives any desired fraction of the source voltage. The output voltage is the fraction of the source voltage corresponding to the fraction of the wire length used.

Vout = (l / L) x V

  • Vout - output voltage; l - length used; L - total length; V - source voltage

mcqs.q: What is a rheostat?
options: A device that compares e.m.f.s using a long uniform wire
A device that controls the current in a circuit, made of high-resistance wire wound on an insulating cylinder with a sliding contact
A bridge of four resistances used to find an unknown resistance
A semiconductor device whose resistance changes with heat
mcqs.why: A rheostat is a long wire of high-resistance material such as constantan wound on an insulating cylinder, with a sliding contact that moves along the wire.

mcqs.q: What material is named in the notes for the rheostat wire?
options: Copper
Silver
Constantan
Germanium
mcqs.why: The rheostat uses a long wire of high-resistance material such as constantan wound on an insulating cylinder, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: On what does the resistance used in a rheostat depend?
options: It is proportional to the area of the cylinder only
It depends only on the voltage of the source
It stays fixed whatever the contact position
It is proportional to the length of wire between one end and the sliding contact
mcqs.why: The resistance between one end of the wire and the sliding contact is proportional to the length of wire between them, so moving the contact changes the resistance.

mcqs.q: How is a rheostat connected when used as a variable resistance?
options: In series with the circuit
Across the source with output from the sliding contact
In parallel with every component
Across a galvanometer as a shunt
mcqs.why: Connected in series with the circuit, the rheostat varies the total resistance; more wire increases resistance and decreases the current.

mcqs.q: What happens to the current when the sliding contact includes more rheostat wire in series?
options: The resistance decreases and the current increases
The resistance increases and the current decreases
The resistance increases and the current increases
The resistance stays the same and the current decreases
mcqs.why: Sliding the contact to include more wire increases the resistance and decreases the current, which is how the rheostat controls current in series use.

mcqs.q: How is a rheostat connected when used as a potential divider?
options: In series with the circuit only
Across a galvanometer to protect it
Across a source, with the output taken between one end and the sliding contact
In place of the source in the circuit
mcqs.why: As a potential divider the rheostat is connected across a source and the output is taken between one end and the sliding contact, giving any fraction of the source voltage.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the output voltage of a rheostat potential divider?
options: Vout = (L / l) x V
Vout = l x L x V
Vout = V / (l x L)
Vout = (l / L) x V
mcqs.why: The output voltage is Vout = (l / L) x V, where l is the length used, L is the total length and V is the source voltage.

mcqs.q: A 12 V source is connected across a rheostat divider and half the wire length is used. What is the output voltage?
options: 6 V
3 V
mcqs.why: Vout = (l / L) x V = (1/2) x 12 = 6 V. The output is the same fraction of the source voltage as the fraction of wire length used.

mcqs.q: A 12 V source is connected across a rheostat divider and one quarter of the wire length is used. What is the output voltage?
options: 6 V
3 V
9 V
mcqs.why: Vout = (l / L) x V = (1/4) x 12 = 3 V. Using one quarter of the length gives one quarter of the source voltage at the output.

mcqs.q: What two uses of a rheostat are described in the notes?
options: As an ammeter and as a voltmeter
As a source and as a thermocouple
As a variable resistance and as a potential divider
As a bridge and as a potentiometer
mcqs.why: The notes describe the rheostat used in series as a variable resistance and connected across a source as a potential divider.

lessons.title: Wheatstone Bridge
lessons.notes_html:
A Wheatstone bridge is a circuit of four resistances P, Q, R and S connected in a diamond. A cell is connected across one diagonal and a galvanometer across the other diagonal.

Working Principle

The bridge works on the null-deflection principle. It is balanced when the galvanometer shows no deflection, which happens when the two junctions joined by the galvanometer are at the same potential.

P / Q = R / S

  • Balance condition of the bridge; if three resistances are known, the fourth unknown resistance is found from this ratio

S = (Q / P) x R

  • S - unknown resistance, found when P, Q and R are known

Because the measurement is made at zero galvanometer current, the bridge measures an unknown resistance accurately.

mcqs.q: What is a Wheatstone bridge?
options: A long uniform wire used with a jockey and driver cell
A single variable resistor with a sliding contact
A circuit of four resistances P, Q, R and S connected in a diamond
Two metal wires joined at two junctions
mcqs.why: A Wheatstone bridge is a circuit of four resistances P, Q, R and S connected in a diamond, with a cell across one diagonal and a galvanometer across the other.

mcqs.q: How are the cell and galvanometer connected in a Wheatstone bridge?
options: Both across the same diagonal
The cell in one arm and the galvanometer in another arm
Both in series with the unknown resistance
The cell across one diagonal and the galvanometer across the other diagonal
mcqs.why: In the bridge a cell is connected across one diagonal and a galvanometer across the other diagonal of the diamond of four resistances.

mcqs.q: On what principle does the Wheatstone bridge work?
options: The null-deflection principle
The Seebeck effect
The maximum power transfer principle
The potential gradient principle
mcqs.why: The bridge works on the null-deflection principle: it is balanced when the galvanometer shows no deflection at all.

mcqs.q: When is a Wheatstone bridge balanced?
options: When the galvanometer shows maximum deflection
When the galvanometer shows no deflection, with its two junctions at the same potential
When the current through every arm is equal
When all four resistances are exactly equal
mcqs.why: The bridge is balanced when the galvanometer shows no deflection, which happens when the two junctions joined by the galvanometer are at the same potential.

mcqs.q: What is the balance condition of the Wheatstone bridge?
options: P x Q = R x S
P / R = S / Q with P + Q = R + S
P / Q = R / S
P + Q = R + S
mcqs.why: The balance condition is P / Q = R / S; if three resistances are known, the fourth unknown resistance is found from this ratio.

mcqs.q: Which formula finds the unknown resistance S in a Wheatstone bridge?
options: S = (P / Q) x R
S = (Q x R) / S
S = P x Q x R
S = (Q / P) x R
mcqs.why: Rearranging P / Q = R / S gives S = (Q / P) x R, where S is the unknown resistance found when P, Q and R are known.

mcqs.q: In a balanced bridge P = 10 ohm, Q = 20 ohm and R = 15 ohm. What is the unknown resistance S?
options: 30 ohm
7.5 ohm
15 ohm
45 ohm
mcqs.why: S = (Q / P) x R = (20 / 10) x 15 = 2 x 15 = 30 ohm. This follows directly from the balance condition P / Q = R / S.

mcqs.q: In a balanced bridge P = 5 ohm, Q = 10 ohm and R = 4 ohm. What is the unknown resistance S?
options: 2 ohm
8 ohm
4 ohm
20 ohm
mcqs.why: S = (Q / P) x R = (10 / 5) x 4 = 2 x 4 = 8 ohm. The unknown is the known resistance R scaled by the ratio Q / P.

mcqs.q: Why does the Wheatstone bridge measure resistance accurately?
options: The measurement is made at maximum galvanometer current
The bridge draws a very large current from the cell
The measurement is made at zero galvanometer current
The four resistances heat up to a steady temperature
mcqs.why: Because the measurement is made at zero galvanometer current (null deflection), the bridge measures an unknown resistance accurately, as the notes state.

mcqs.q: At balance, what is true of the two junctions joined by the galvanometer?
options: They are at opposite potentials of the cell
One is at zero potential and the other at full cell voltage
They carry the largest current in the bridge
They are at the same potential
mcqs.why: Balance occurs when the two junctions joined by the galvanometer are at the same potential, so no current flows through the galvanometer.

lessons.title: Potentiometer
lessons.notes_html:
A potentiometer is a long uniform wire, usually 1 to 10 metres, across which a steady current is maintained by a driver cell, so the potential falls uniformly along the wire. It compares e.m.f.s and measures e.m.f. accurately.

Working Principle

The unknown source is balanced against a length l of the wire at which the galvanometer shows no deflection (the null method). At balance no current is drawn from the source, so the measurement is exact and unaffected by its internal resistance.

E = k l

  • E - unknown e.m.f.; k - potential gradient, the fall of potential per unit length of wire; l - balancing length

E1 / E2 = l1 / l2

  • Comparing two cells - their e.m.f.s are in the ratio of their balancing lengths

Applications

  • Comparing the e.m.f.s of two cells
  • Measuring the internal resistance of a cell
  • Calibrating voltmeters and ammeters
  • Measuring small potential differences accurately

Worked Example: E.M.F. From Balancing Lengths

The e.m.f. of a battery is balanced by a length of 80 cm on a potentiometer wire, while the e.m.f. of 1.03 V of a standard cell is balanced by a length of 55 cm. Determine the e.m.f. of the battery.

Step 1: E.m.f. is proportional to balancing length, so E / Es = l / ls.

Step 2: E = 1.03 x (80 / 55) = 1.03 x 1.4545.

Step 3: E = 1.498 V, about 1.5 V.

Answer: The e.m.f. of the battery is about 1.5 V.

Key Points

  • Steady current I = Q / t; conventional current flows from positive to negative, electrons flow the opposite way with a small drift velocity.
  • Sources convert other energy into electrical energy: cells chemical, generators mechanical, photocells light, thermocouples heat.
  • Ohm's law: V = I R; ohmic devices give a straight V-I line, non-ohmic devices give a curve.
  • Resistivity R = ρ L / A and conductivity σ = 1 / ρ; metal resistivity rises with temperature, semiconductor resistivity falls.
  • A thermistor is a heat-sensitive semiconductor resistor, usually with a negative temperature coefficient.
  • Terminal voltage V = E - I r; V and E are equal only on open circuit or if r = 0.
  • Maximum power is transferred when the load resistance equals the internal resistance, R = r.
  • A thermocouple uses the Seebeck effect to measure temperature, especially high temperatures.
  • Kirchhoff's first law is conservation of charge at a node; the second law is conservation of energy around a loop.
  • Wheatstone bridge balance: P / Q = R / S. Potentiometer: E = k l, measured at null deflection with no current drawn.

mcqs.q: What is a potentiometer?
options: A bridge of four resistances in a diamond shape
A short thick wire with a sliding contact for current control
A pair of dissimilar wires joined at two junctions
A long uniform wire, usually 1 to 10 metres, across which a steady current is maintained by a driver cell
mcqs.why: A potentiometer is a long uniform wire, usually 1 to 10 metres, with a steady current from a driver cell so the potential falls uniformly along the wire.

mcqs.q: Why does the potential fall uniformly along the potentiometer wire?
options: The wire is uniform and a steady current is maintained by the driver cell
The wire resistance changes from point to point
The driver cell e.m.f. keeps increasing along the wire
No current flows in the wire at any time
mcqs.why: Because the wire is uniform and the driver cell maintains a steady current, the potential falls uniformly along the potentiometer wire.

mcqs.q: What happens at the balancing point of a potentiometer?
options: The galvanometer shows maximum deflection and maximum current is drawn
The galvanometer shows no deflection and no current is drawn from the source being measured
The full driver current flows through the source being measured
The wire current stops completely
mcqs.why: At balance (null method) the galvanometer shows no deflection and no current is drawn from the source, so the measurement is exact and unaffected by internal resistance.

mcqs.q: Which relation gives the e.m.f. measured by a potentiometer?
options: E = k / l
E = l / k
E = k l
E = k x l^2
mcqs.why: The unknown e.m.f. is E = k l, where k is the potential gradient (fall of potential per unit length) and l is the balancing length.

mcqs.q: What is the potential gradient k of a potentiometer wire?
options: The total fall of potential along the whole wire
The e.m.f. of the driver cell
The resistance per unit length multiplied by the balancing length
The fall of potential per unit length of wire
mcqs.why: In E = k l, k is the potential gradient, defined in the notes as the fall of potential per unit length of the wire.

mcqs.q: How are the e.m.f.s of two cells compared with a potentiometer?
options: E1 / E2 = l1 / l2, the ratio of their balancing lengths
E1 / E2 = l2 / l1, the inverse ratio of lengths
E1 x E2 = l1 x l2
E1 - E2 = l1 - l2 in volts
mcqs.why: Comparing two cells, their e.m.f.s are in the ratio of their balancing lengths: E1 / E2 = l1 / l2, as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: A battery balances at 80 cm and a 1.03 V standard cell balances at 55 cm. What is the e.m.f. of the battery?
options: About 0.71 V
About 1.5 V
About 1.03 V
About 2.5 V
mcqs.why: E = Es x (l / ls) = 1.03 x (80 / 55) = 1.03 x 1.4545 = 1.498 V, about 1.5 V, exactly as in the worked example in the notes.

mcqs.q: What is the ratio of the balancing lengths 80 cm to 55 cm in the worked example?
options: About 0.69
About 1.25
About 1.45
About 25
mcqs.why: The ratio l / ls = 80 / 55 = 1.4545, about 1.45. The battery e.m.f. is this ratio times the standard cell e.m.f. of 1.03 V.

mcqs.q: Which is an application of the potentiometer listed in the notes?
options: Measuring high temperatures in furnaces
Controlling current as a variable resistance
Detecting temperature with a semiconductor resistor
Measuring the internal resistance of a cell
mcqs.why: Applications listed include comparing e.m.f.s, measuring internal resistance of a cell, calibrating voltmeters and ammeters, and measuring small potential differences accurately.

mcqs.q: Why is the potentiometer measurement unaffected by the internal resistance of the source?
options: At balance no current is drawn from the source
The internal resistance becomes zero during measurement
A very large current cancels the internal resistance drop
The driver cell has no internal resistance
mcqs.why: At balance no current is drawn from the source, so there is no drop across its internal resistance and the measured e.m.f. is exact.

lessons.title: Magnetic Field
lessons.notes_html:
A magnetic field is the region around a magnet or a moving charge where another magnet or moving charge feels a magnetic force. Field lines show its direction and strength.

Field Around a Straight Conductor

A current in a straight wire makes circular field lines around the wire. Use the right-hand grip rule: point the thumb along the conventional current, and the curled fingers show the field direction.

In a diagram, a dot means current coming out of the page and a cross means current going into the page. Out of the page gives an anticlockwise field; into the page gives a clockwise field.

B = μo I / (2 π r)

  • B - magnetic flux density at distance r, unit T
  • I - current in the wire, unit A; r - distance from the wire, unit m
  • μo - permeability of free space, 4 π x 10-7 T m A-1

B grows with current and falls as distance grows. For a coil, curl the fingers along the current; the thumb points to the north pole face of the coil.

mcqs.q: What is a magnetic field?
options: The region inside a wire where current flows
The total number of field lines through a surface
The region around a magnet or a moving charge where another magnet or moving charge feels a magnetic force
The force on a stationary charge near a magnet
mcqs.why: A magnetic field is the region around a magnet or moving charge where another magnet or moving charge feels a force; field lines show its direction and strength.

mcqs.q: What shape are the field lines around a straight current-carrying wire?
options: Straight lines radiating out from the wire
Straight lines parallel to the wire
Spirals running along the wire
Circles around the wire
mcqs.why: A current in a straight wire makes circular field lines around the wire, with direction given by the right-hand grip rule.

mcqs.q: What does the right-hand grip rule state for a straight wire?
options: Point the thumb along the conventional current and the curled fingers show the field direction
Point the thumb along the field and the fingers show the current direction
Hold thumb, forefinger and middle finger at right angles for field, current and force
Curl the fingers along the current and the thumb gives the force direction
mcqs.why: For a straight wire, thumb along conventional current and curled fingers show the field direction; the three-finger rule is Fleming's rule for force, not this one.

mcqs.q: In a field diagram, what does a dot mean?
options: Current going into the page
Current coming out of the page
Field going into the page
A north pole pointing sideways
mcqs.why: A dot means current coming out of the page and a cross means current going into the page; out of the page gives an anticlockwise field.

mcqs.q: Current into the page produces a field in which sense around the wire?
options: Anticlockwise
Straight outwards
Clockwise
Along the wire
mcqs.why: The notes state that current out of the page gives an anticlockwise field, while current into the page gives a clockwise field around the wire.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the flux density at distance r from a straight wire carrying current I?
options: B = mu_o I x 2 pi r
B = mu_o r / (2 pi I)
B = 2 pi mu_o I / r
B = mu_o I / (2 pi r)
mcqs.why: The field of a straight wire is B = mu_o I / (2 pi r), where mu_o is the permeability of free space, 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1.

mcqs.q: What is the value of the permeability of free space mu_o?
options: 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1
mcqs.why: The notes give mu_o = 4 pi x 10^-7 T m A^-1 for the permeability of free space in the straight-wire field formula.

mcqs.q: A straight wire carries 10 A. What is B at a distance of 0.05 m from it?
A straight wire carries 10 A. What is B at a distance of 0.10 m from it?
mcqs.why: B = mu_o I / (2 pi r) = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 10) / (2 pi x 0.10) = (2 x 10^-6) / 0.10 = 2 x 10^-5 T. Doubling the distance halves B.

mcqs.q: For a coil, how is the north pole face found?
options: Point the thumb along the current in one straight wire
Curl the fingers against the current; the thumb gives the south pole
Hold the left hand with fingers for field and current
Curl the fingers along the current; the thumb points to the north pole face
mcqs.why: For a coil the grip rule is applied as: curl the fingers along the current and the thumb points to the north pole face of the coil.

lessons.title: Force on a Current Carrying Conductor in a Magnetic Field
lessons.notes_html:
A conductor carrying current in a field feels a force because the field acts on its moving charges. This is the basis of the electric motor.

The Force Formula

F = B I L sin θ

  • F - force on the conductor, unit N
  • B - magnetic flux density, unit T; I - current, unit A; L - length in the field, unit m
  • θ - angle between the conductor and the field

The force is maximum when θ = 90°, with the conductor across the field, and zero when θ = 0°, with the conductor along the field.

Direction of the Force

Fleming's left-hand rule: hold thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand at right angles. Forefinger = field, middle finger = current, thumb = force. For electrons the force is opposite, because they move against the conventional current.

Worked Example: Force on a Conductor

A conductor of length 20 cm carrying 10 A is placed in a uniform field of 2 T at 60° to the field. Find the force on it.

Step 1: Write the data. B = 2 T, I = 10 A, L = 20 cm = 0.20 m, θ = 60°.

Step 2: Use F = B I L sin θ.

Step 3: F = 2 x 10 x 0.20 x sin 60° = 4 x 0.866.

Answer: F = 3.46 N, about 3.5 N.

mcqs.q: Why does a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field feel a force?
options: The field heats the conductor until it expands
The conductor becomes a permanent magnet
The field acts only on the insulation around the wire
The field acts on the moving charges inside the conductor
mcqs.why: A conductor carrying current feels a force because the field acts on its moving charges; this effect is the basis of the electric motor.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the force on a conductor in a magnetic field?
options: F = B I L sin theta
F = B I L cos theta
F = B / (I L sin theta)
F = q v B sin theta for the whole wire length
mcqs.why: The force on a conductor is F = B I L sin theta, with B in tesla, I in ampere, L the length in the field and theta the angle to the field.

mcqs.q: At what angle is the force on a conductor maximum?
options: Theta = 0 degrees, with the conductor along the field
Theta = 90 degrees, with the conductor across the field
Theta = 45 degrees to the field
Theta = 180 degrees, opposite to the field
mcqs.why: Since F = B I L sin theta and sin theta is largest at 90 degrees, the force is maximum when the conductor lies across the field.

mcqs.q: What is the force when the conductor lies along the field, theta = 0 degrees?
options: Maximum, B I L
Half the maximum value
Zero
B I L sin 90 degrees
mcqs.why: F = B I L sin theta with sin 0 degrees = 0 gives F = 0. A conductor along the field feels no force, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: In Fleming's left-hand rule, what does the forefinger represent?
options: Current
Force (motion)
Velocity of an electron
Field
mcqs.why: In Fleming's left-hand rule the forefinger is the field, the middle finger is the current and the thumb is the force, all held at right angles.

mcqs.q: In Fleming's left-hand rule, what does the thumb represent?
options: Force
Field
Current
Flux density direction into the page
mcqs.why: The thumb in Fleming's left-hand rule gives the force (motion), while forefinger is field and middle finger is current.

mcqs.q: How is the force on electrons different from the force given by Fleming's rule for conventional current?
options: It is in the same direction and twice as large
It is opposite, because electrons move against the conventional current
It is zero because electrons have no charge in a field
It acts along the field instead of across it
mcqs.why: For electrons the force is opposite to the conventional-current direction, because electrons move against the conventional current, as the notes state.

mcqs.q: A conductor of length 20 cm carrying 10 A is in a field of 2 T at 60 degrees to the field. What is the force on it?
options: About 3.46 N
About 1.73 N
mcqs.why: F = B I L sin theta = 2 x 10 x 0.20 x sin 60 degrees = 4 x 0.866 = 3.46 N, about 3.5 N, exactly as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: The same conductor (2 T, 10 A, length 0.20 m) is placed across the field at 90 degrees. What is the force?
options: About 3.46 N
2 N
4 N
mcqs.why: At 90 degrees sin theta = 1, so F = B I L = 2 x 10 x 0.20 = 4 N. This is the maximum force for these values of B, I and L.

mcqs.q: The force on a current-carrying conductor in a field is the basis of which device?
options: The electric motor
The thermocouple
The potentiometer
The Wheatstone bridge
mcqs.why: The notes state that the force on a current-carrying conductor in a field is the basis of the electric motor.

lessons.title: Magnetic Flux and Magnetic Flux Density
lessons.notes_html:
Magnetic flux is the total number of field lines passing through a surface. Magnetic flux density is the flux per unit area and measures how strong the field is at a point.

Flux Through a Surface

Φ = B A cos θ

  • Φ - magnetic flux, unit weber (Wb)
  • B - flux density, unit T; A - area of the surface, unit m2
  • θ - angle between B and the normal to the surface

Flux is maximum, Φ = B A, when θ = 0°, so the field is normal to the surface. Flux is zero when θ = 90°, so the field runs along the surface and no lines pass through it.

Flux Density

B = Φ / A

  • B - flux density, unit T, also written Wb m-2 or N A-1 m-1
  • One tesla is the field in which a 1 m conductor carrying 1 A across the field feels a force of 1 N.

The gauss is the smaller CGS unit: 1 T = 104 G, so 1 G = 10-4 T. Tesla measures field strength; weber measures total flux.

mcqs.q: What is magnetic flux?
options: The total number of field lines passing through a surface
The flux per unit area at a point
The force on a conductor per unit length
The field produced by a solenoid per turn
mcqs.why: Magnetic flux is the total number of field lines passing through a surface, while flux density is the flux per unit area.

mcqs.q: What is magnetic flux density?
options: The total flux through any closed surface
The flux per unit area, measuring how strong the field is at a point
The number of turns per unit length of a coil
The force on a unit charge at rest
mcqs.why: Magnetic flux density B is flux per unit area, B = Phi / A, and measures how strong the field is at a point.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the magnetic flux through a surface?
options: Phi = B A sin theta
Phi = B / (A cos theta)
Phi = B A cos theta
Phi = B A / cos theta
mcqs.why: Flux is Phi = B A cos theta, where theta is the angle between B and the normal to the surface, with Phi in weber.

mcqs.q: When is the magnetic flux through a surface maximum?
options: When theta = 90 degrees, so the field runs along the surface
When theta = 45 degrees to the normal
When the area is reduced to zero
When theta = 0 degrees, so the field is normal to the surface and Phi = B A
mcqs.why: Flux is maximum, Phi = B A, when theta = 0 degrees so the field is normal to the surface; it is zero at 90 degrees.

mcqs.q: What is the flux when theta = 90 degrees, with the field along the surface?
options: Zero, because no lines pass through the surface
Maximum, equal to B A
Half the maximum, B A / 2
Equal to B divided by A
mcqs.why: At theta = 90 degrees cos theta = 0, so Phi = 0: the field runs along the surface and no lines pass through it.

mcqs.q: What is the unit of magnetic flux?
options: Tesla (T)
Weber (Wb)
Gauss (G)
Ampere (A)
mcqs.why: Magnetic flux Phi is measured in weber (Wb), while flux density B is measured in tesla; tesla measures field strength and weber measures total flux.

mcqs.q: One tesla is defined in the notes as the field in which what happens?
options: A 1 C charge at rest feels a force of 1 N
A flux of 1 Wb passes through every surface
A 1 m conductor carrying 1 A across the field feels a force of 1 N
A solenoid of 1 turn produces a flux of 1 Wb
mcqs.why: One tesla is the field in which a 1 m conductor carrying 1 A across the field feels a force of 1 N, from F = B I L with all values one.

mcqs.q: How are tesla and gauss related?
mcqs.why: The gauss is the smaller CGS unit: 1 T = 10^4 G, so 1 G = 10^-4 T, as given in the notes on flux density.

mcqs.q: A field of 0.5 T is normal to a surface of area 0.02 m^2. What is the flux through it?
options: 25 Wb
mcqs.why: With the field normal, theta = 0 degrees and Phi = B A cos theta = 0.5 x 0.02 x 1 = 0.01 Wb. Flux is flux density multiplied by area at maximum orientation.

mcqs.q: A flux of 0.01 Wb passes through an area of 0.02 m^2 with the field normal to it. What is the flux density?
options: 2 T
mcqs.why: Flux density B = Phi / A = 0.01 / 0.02 = 0.5 T. Flux density is the flux divided by the area it passes through.

lessons.title: Ampere's Law
lessons.notes_html:
Ampere's law links the magnetic field around a closed path to the current enclosed by that path. It holds in this simple form only for steady currents.

Using Ampere's Law

Choose an Amperian loop, an imaginary closed path where B is constant along the path or at right angles to it, so B can be taken out of the sum around the loop.

B l = μo n l I

  • For a solenoid loop of length l inside the solenoid, only the inside side adds to the sum.
  • n - turns per unit length; I - current in each turn, so n l I is the enclosed current

Field of a Solenoid

B = μo n I

  • B - field inside a long solenoid, unit T, uniform and along the axis
  • It does not depend on position inside the solenoid. Outside, the field is very weak, almost zero.

Worked Example: Solenoid Flux and Flux Density

An air core solenoid of radius 2 cm has 4000 turns per unit length and carries 5 A. Find B inside it and the flux through its cross-section.

Step 1: B = μo n I = 4 π x 10-7 x 4000 x 5.

Step 2: B = 2.51 x 10-2 T.

Step 3: Area A = π r2 = 3.14 x (0.02)2 = 1.257 x 10-3 m2.

Step 4: Φ = B A = 2.51 x 10-2 x 1.257 x 10-3.

Answer: B = 2.51 x 10-2 T and Φ = 3.15 x 10-5 Wb.

mcqs.q: What does Ampere's law link together?
options: The flux through a surface and the area of the surface
The magnetic field around a closed path and the current enclosed by that path
The force on a conductor and its length in the field
The torque on a coil and its number of turns
mcqs.why: Ampere's law links the magnetic field around a closed path to the current enclosed by that path, in this simple form only for steady currents.

mcqs.q: For what kind of currents does Ampere's law hold in this simple form?
options: Rapidly alternating currents only
Currents in insulators only
Steady currents only
All currents including changing ones in the same simple form
mcqs.why: The notes state that Ampere's law holds in this simple form only for steady currents, so the enclosed current must not be changing.

mcqs.q: What is an Amperian loop?
options: A real coil of wire carrying the enclosed current
The circular path of an electron in a field
A closed path drawn only inside a magnet
An imaginary closed path where B is constant along the path or at right angles to it
mcqs.why: An Amperian loop is an imaginary closed path chosen so B is constant along it or at right angles to it, letting B be taken out of the sum around the loop.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the field inside a long solenoid?
options: B = mu_o n I
B = mu_o I / (2 pi r)
B = mu_o n / I
B = n I / mu_o
mcqs.why: Inside a long solenoid B = mu_o n I, where n is turns per unit length and I is the current in each turn; the field is uniform and along the axis.

mcqs.q: What is n in the solenoid formula B = mu_o n I?
options: Total number of turns in the whole solenoid
Turns per unit length
Number of amperes in each turn
Length of the solenoid in metres
mcqs.why: In B = mu_o n I, n is turns per unit length, so n l I is the enclosed current for a loop of length l inside the solenoid.

mcqs.q: How does the field inside a long solenoid vary with position?
options: It is strongest at the ends and zero at the centre
It falls as 1 / r from the axis
It is uniform and does not depend on position inside the solenoid
It increases steadily from one end to the other
mcqs.why: The solenoid field B = mu_o n I does not depend on position inside the solenoid; it is uniform and along the axis, while outside it is almost zero.

mcqs.q: What is the field outside a long solenoid?
options: Equal to the field inside
Twice the field inside
Uniform outside, with the same value mu_o n I as inside
Very weak, almost zero
mcqs.why: Outside a long solenoid the field is very weak, almost zero, while inside it is uniform with value B = mu_o n I.

mcqs.q: An air core solenoid has 4000 turns per unit length and carries 5 A. What is B inside it?
mcqs.why: B = mu_o n I = 4 pi x 10^-7 x 4000 x 5 = 4 x 3.14 x 10^-7 x 20000 = 2.51 x 10^-2 T, as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: The solenoid in the worked example has radius 2 cm. What is its cross-sectional area?
mcqs.why: Area A = pi r^2 = 3.14 x (0.02)^2 = 3.14 x 4 x 10^-4 = 1.257 x 10^-3 m^2, using radius 2 cm = 0.02 m as in the example.

mcqs.q: For that solenoid, B = 2.51 x 10^-2 T and area = 1.257 x 10^-3 m^2. What is the flux through its cross-section?
mcqs.why: Flux Phi = B A = 2.51 x 10^-2 x 1.257 x 10^-3 = 3.15 x 10^-5 Wb, completing the solenoid worked example in the notes.

lessons.title: Force on a Moving Charged Particle in a Magnetic Field
lessons.notes_html:
A moving charge in a field feels a force at right angles to both its velocity and the field. A charge at rest feels no force at all.

Magnitude and Direction

F = q v B sin θ

  • F - magnetic force, unit N; q - charge, unit C
  • v - speed of the particle, unit m s-1; B - flux density, unit T
  • Direction is given by Fleming's left-hand rule for a positive charge, and reversed for an electron.

The force does no work, so it changes only the direction of motion, never the speed. If the motion is along the field, θ = 0° and F = 0.

Circular Path

Moving across the field, the particle follows a circle, because the force acts as a centripetal force toward the centre.

r = m v / (q B)

  • r - radius of the circular path, unit m; m - mass of the particle, unit kg
  • An electron and a proton with the same speed curve in opposite directions, and the electron's circle is far smaller because its mass is about 1836 times smaller.

Worked Example: Speed of an Electron

An electron moves at right angles to a field of 0.2 T and feels a force of 2 x 10-12 N. Find its speed. (The book's printed answer is wrong; the correct value is found below.)

Step 1: At right angles, F = e v B, so v = F / (e B).

Step 2: v = 2 x 10-12 / (1.6 x 10-19 x 0.2).

Step 3: Denominator = 3.2 x 10-20, so v = 6.25 x 107 m s-1.

Answer: v = 6.25 x 107 m s-1. The book prints 6.25 x 1017 m s-1, which is wrong by a factor of 1010 and faster than light.

mcqs.q: What force does a charge at rest feel in a magnetic field?
options: A force along the field
A force of q v B with v equal to zero giving a small force
No force at all
The maximum force q B
mcqs.why: A charge at rest feels no magnetic force at all; the force F = q v B sin theta acts only on a moving charge in the field.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the magnetic force on a moving charge?
options: F = q v B cos theta
F = B I L sin theta with L as the speed
F = q B / (v sin theta)
F = q v B sin theta
mcqs.why: The force on a moving charge is F = q v B sin theta, at right angles to both its velocity and the field, with direction from Fleming's rule.

mcqs.q: What does the magnetic force on a moving charge do to its motion?
options: It does no work and changes only the direction of motion, never the speed
It increases the speed steadily along the field
It does work and increases the kinetic energy
It stops the particle when the motion is across the field
mcqs.why: The magnetic force acts at right angles to the motion, so it does no work: it changes only the direction of motion, never the speed.

mcqs.q: What is the force when the charge moves along the field, theta = 0 degrees?
options: Maximum, q v B
Zero
Half the maximum value
q v B
mcqs.why: F = q v B sin theta with sin 0 degrees = 0 gives F = 0. Motion along the field feels no magnetic force, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: What path does a charge follow when moving across the field?
options: A straight line, because the force is zero
A spiral that speeds up along the field
A circle, because the force acts as a centripetal force toward the centre
A parabola like a projectile
mcqs.why: Moving across the field, the force is always toward the centre and acts as a centripetal force, so the particle follows a circle of radius r = m v / (q B).

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the radius of the circular path in a magnetic field?
options: r = q B / (m v)
r = m v q B
r = m / (q B v)
r = m v / (q B)
mcqs.why: The radius is r = m v / (q B), where m is the particle mass, v its speed, q its charge and B the flux density, as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: An electron and a proton enter the same field with the same speed. How do their paths compare?
options: They curve in opposite directions and the electron circle is far smaller
They curve in the same direction with equal circles
They both go straight because their charges cancel
The proton circle is far smaller because it is heavier
mcqs.why: Opposite charges curve in opposite directions, and the electron circle is far smaller because its mass is about 1836 times smaller than the proton mass.

mcqs.q: An electron moves at right angles to a field of 0.2 T and feels a force of 2 x 10^-12 N. What is its speed?
mcqs.why: At right angles F = e v B, so v = F / (e B) = 2 x 10^-12 / (1.6 x 10^-19 x 0.2) = 2 x 10^-12 / 3.2 x 10^-20 = 6.25 x 10^7 m s^-1. The book value 10^17 is wrong.

mcqs.q: What force does an electron of charge 1.6 x 10^-19 C moving at 6.25 x 10^7 m s^-1 across a 0.2 T field feel?
mcqs.why: F = q v B sin theta = 1.6 x 10^-19 x 6.25 x 10^7 x 0.2 x 1 = 2 x 10^-12 N, the reverse of the worked example calculation.

mcqs.q: How is the direction of the force on an electron found?
options: Use Fleming's left-hand rule with no change
Use the right-hand grip rule for a straight wire
The force is along the velocity direction
Use Fleming's left-hand rule for a positive charge and then reverse it
mcqs.why: Direction is given by Fleming's left-hand rule for a positive charge and reversed for an electron, because the electron charge is negative.

lessons.title: Determination of e/m of an Electron
lessons.notes_html:
The ratio e/m is the charge of an electron divided by its mass. It is found by selecting electrons of known speed and then bending them in a known field.

Velocity Selector

In a velocity selector, crossed electric and magnetic fields are set so an electron passes straight through. Then the electric force balances the magnetic force.

v = E / B

  • v - selected speed, unit m s-1; E - electric field, unit V m-1; B - magnetic field, unit T
  • Only electrons with this speed pass undeflected; faster or slower ones are pushed aside.

Measuring e/m

The selected electrons then enter a magnetic field alone and move in a circle of radius r. Combining r = m v / (e B) with v = E / B gives:

e / m = E / (B2 r)

  • e/m - charge to mass ratio of the electron, about 1.76 x 1011 C kg-1
  • Measure E, B and r, and e/m follows directly.

mcqs.q: What is the ratio e/m for an electron?
options: Its mass divided by its charge, about 1.76 x 10^11 kg C^-1
Its charge multiplied by its mass
Its speed divided by the field, about 1.76 x 10^11 m s^-1
Its charge divided by its mass, about 1.76 x 10^11 C kg^-1
mcqs.why: The ratio e/m is the electron charge divided by its mass, about 1.76 x 10^11 C kg^-1, found by bending speed-selected electrons in a known field.

mcqs.q: What is a velocity selector?
options: Crossed electric and magnetic fields set so an electron of one speed passes straight through
A magnetic field alone that bends all electrons into a circle
A solenoid that increases the speed of electrons
A galvanometer that measures the speed of electrons
mcqs.why: In a velocity selector crossed electric and magnetic fields balance for one speed only, so only electrons with v = E / B pass undeflected.

mcqs.q: In a velocity selector, when does an electron pass straight through?
options: When both forces are zero because the fields are off
When the electric force balances the magnetic force on it
When the magnetic force is twice the electric force
When the electron moves along both fields
mcqs.why: The selector is set so the electric force balances the magnetic force; then the electron passes straight through with no net deflection.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the selected speed in a velocity selector?
options: v = E x B
v = B / E
v = E / B
v = E / (B r)
mcqs.why: Balancing electric force eE with magnetic force e v B gives v = E / B, where E is in V m^-1 and B is in tesla.

mcqs.q: In a velocity selector E = 2000 V m^-1 and B = 0.5 T. What speed is selected?
mcqs.why: Selected speed v = E / B = 2000 / 0.5 = 4000 m s^-1. Only electrons with this speed pass through the selector undeflected.

mcqs.q: What happens to electrons in a selector whose speed is not E / B?
options: Faster or slower ones are pushed aside and do not pass straight through
They also pass straight through at the same point
They stop completely inside the selector
They reverse direction and leave backwards
mcqs.why: Only electrons with speed v = E / B pass undeflected; faster or slower ones have unbalanced forces and are pushed aside, as the notes state.

mcqs.q: After selection, how is e/m measured?
options: The electrons are stopped and their charge is collected
The electrons enter a magnetic field alone and move in a circle of measured radius r
The electrons pass through a second electric field only
The electrons strike a screen and their colour is noted
mcqs.why: The selected electrons enter a magnetic field alone and move in a circle of radius r; combining r = m v / (e B) with v = E / B gives e/m.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives e/m from the selector and circle measurements?
options: e / m = E x B^2 r
e / m = B^2 r / E
e / m = E / (B^2 r)
e / m = E / (B r^2)
mcqs.why: Combining r = m v / (e B) with v = E / B gives e / m = E / (B^2 r), so measuring E, B and r gives e/m directly.

mcqs.q: Using e/m = E / (B^2 r) with E = 2000, B = 0.1 T and r = 0.2 m, what value is obtained?
options: 4 C kg^-1

mcqs.q: What three quantities must be measured to find e/m by this method?
options: E, B and r
I, L and theta
N, A and I
P, Q and R
mcqs.why: The notes state: measure E, B and r, and e/m follows directly from e/m = E / (B^2 r), after the speed has been selected.

lessons.title: Torque on a Current Carrying Coil in a Magnetic Field
lessons.notes_html:
A coil in a field feels equal and opposite forces on its two sides. The forces act on different lines, so they form a couple that turns the coil. This torque runs motors and galvanometers.

Torque Formula

τ = N I A B sin θ

  • τ - torque on the coil, unit N m
  • N - number of turns; I - current, unit A; A - area of the coil, unit m2; B - field, unit T
  • θ - angle between the field and the normal to the coil
