Torque is maximum when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field, and zero when the plane is across the field. Increase torque by increasing N, I, A or B.

Worked Example: Maximum Torque on a Coil

A rectangular coil of sides 10 cm and 6 cm has 2000 turns and carries 5 A in a field of 0.5 T. Find its maximum torque.

Step 1: Area A = 0.10 x 0.06 = 0.006 m2.

Step 2: Maximum torque has sin θ = 1, so τ = N I A B.

Step 3: τ = 2000 x 5 x 0.006 x 0.5.

Step 4: 2000 x 5 = 10000; 10000 x 0.006 = 60; 60 x 0.5 = 30.

Answer: Maximum torque = 30 N m.

mcqs.q: Why does a current-carrying coil in a field turn?
options: Equal and opposite forces on its two sides form a couple that turns the coil
A single force pushes the whole coil sideways
The field heats one side more than the other
The coil becomes magnetised and is attracted to one pole only
mcqs.why: The two sides feel equal and opposite forces on different lines, forming a couple (torque) that turns the coil; this runs motors and galvanometers.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the torque on a coil in a magnetic field?
options: Tau = N I A B cos theta
Tau = N I A B sin theta
Tau = B I L sin theta
Tau = N B / (I A sin theta)
mcqs.why: Torque is tau = N I A B sin theta, with N turns, I current, A coil area, B field and theta the angle between field and normal to the coil.

mcqs.q: In the torque formula, what is theta?
options: The angle between the field and the plane of the coil used in the conductor force formula
The angle between the current and the coil wire
The angle between the field and the normal to the coil
The deflection angle of a galvanometer pointer
mcqs.why: In tau = N I A B sin theta, theta is the angle between the field and the normal to the coil, as defined in the notes for this lesson.

mcqs.q: When is the torque on a coil maximum?
options: When the plane of the coil is across the field
When the current in the coil is zero
When the normal to the coil is parallel to the field
When the plane of the coil is parallel to the field
mcqs.why: Torque is maximum when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field (normal across the field, sin theta = 1) and zero when the plane is across the field.

mcqs.q: When is the torque on a coil zero?
options: When the plane of the coil is across the field
When the plane of the coil is parallel to the field
When the number of turns is largest
When the current is at its maximum value
mcqs.why: With the plane across the field, the normal to the coil lies along the field so theta = 0 degrees and sin theta = 0, giving zero torque in tau = N I A B sin theta.

mcqs.q: Which change increases the torque on a coil?
options: Decreasing the number of turns N
Increasing N, I, A or B
Decreasing the coil area A
Decreasing the field B
mcqs.why: Since tau = N I A B sin theta, the torque is increased by increasing any of N, I, A or B, as stated directly in the notes.

mcqs.q: A rectangular coil has sides 10 cm and 6 cm. What is its area?
mcqs.why: Area A = 0.10 x 0.06 = 0.006 m^2. The sides 10 cm and 6 cm are 0.10 m and 0.06 m, as in step 1 of the worked example.

mcqs.q: That coil has 2000 turns, carries 5 A in a field of 0.5 T. What is its maximum torque?
options: 3 N m
60 N m
15 N m
30 N m
mcqs.why: Maximum torque tau = N I A B = 2000 x 5 x 0.006 x 0.5. 2000 x 5 = 10000; 10000 x 0.006 = 60; 60 x 0.5 = 30 N m, as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: For the same coil, what is the torque when sin theta = 0.5?
options: 15 N m
30 N m
60 N m
7.5 N m
mcqs.why: Tau = N I A B sin theta = 30 x 0.5 = 15 N m. The maximum torque is 30 N m, so at sin theta = 0.5 the torque is half of maximum.

mcqs.q: The torque on a coil in a field is the working principle of which instruments?
options: Thermocouples and thermistors
Motors and galvanometers
Potentiometers and bridges
Photocells and dynamos only as sources
mcqs.why: The notes state that this torque runs motors and galvanometers, both based on a current-carrying coil turning in a magnetic field.

lessons.title: Galvanometer
lessons.notes_html:
A galvanometer detects small currents and shows their direction. Its working principle is the torque on a coil in a magnetic field.

Construction and Working

A coil of many turns is pivoted between concave pole pieces of a magnet, with a soft iron core inside the coil. The pole shape and core make the field radial, so the field is always in the plane of the coil and the torque does not depend on the deflection angle. A spring gives a restoring torque and a pointer moves over a scale. Deflection is directly proportional to current.

Conversion to an Ammeter

Connect a low resistance, called a shunt, in parallel. Most current passes through the shunt and only a small known part through the coil.

Rs = Ig Rg / (I - Ig)

  • Rs - shunt resistance; Ig - full scale current of the galvanometer; Rg - its resistance; I - new current range

Conversion to a Voltmeter

Connect a high resistance in series, so the coil current stays at full scale value for the chosen voltage range.

R = V / Ig - Rg

  • R - series resistance; V - voltage range of the voltmeter

Worked Example: Making a Voltmeter

A galvanometer of resistance 40 Ω deflects full scale at 4 mA. Find the series resistance to make it a 100 V voltmeter.

Step 1: Ig = 4 mA = 0.004 A, V = 100 V, Rg = 40 Ω.

Step 2: V / Ig = 100 / 0.004 = 25000 Ω.

Step 3: R = 25000 - 40 = 24960 Ω.

Answer: Connect 24960 Ω in series.

mcqs.q: What does a galvanometer do?
options: It measures large currents directly without any shunt
It detects small currents and shows their direction
It measures resistance directly in ohms only
It compares the e.m.f.s of two cells
mcqs.why: A galvanometer detects small currents and shows their direction, working on the principle of torque on a coil in a magnetic field.

mcqs.q: What is the working principle of a galvanometer?
options: The Seebeck effect at two junctions
The balance condition of a four-resistance bridge
The torque on a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field
The potential gradient along a uniform wire
mcqs.why: The galvanometer working principle is the torque on a coil in a magnetic field, tau = N I A B sin theta, as in the previous lesson.

mcqs.q: Why are the pole pieces concave and a soft iron core used in a galvanometer?
options: They make the field stronger at one end only
They remove the need for a restoring spring
They convert the galvanometer into an ohmmeter
They make the field radial, so the field is always in the plane of the coil and torque does not depend on deflection angle
mcqs.why: The pole shape and core make the field radial, so the field is always in the plane of the coil and the torque does not depend on the deflection angle.

mcqs.q: How does galvanometer deflection depend on current?
options: Deflection is directly proportional to current
Deflection is inversely proportional to current
Deflection is proportional to the square of the current
Deflection does not change with current
mcqs.why: A spring gives a restoring torque and the pointer deflection is directly proportional to current, so the scale can be marked in current units.

mcqs.q: How is a galvanometer converted into an ammeter?
options: Connect a high resistance in series with it
Connect a low resistance shunt in parallel with it
Connect a low resistance in series with it
Remove the spring and pointer
mcqs.why: An ammeter uses a low resistance shunt in parallel: most current passes through the shunt and only a small known part through the coil.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the shunt resistance for an ammeter?
options: Rs = V / Ig - Rg
Rs = Ig x I x Rg
Rs = Ig Rg / (I - Ig)
Rs = (I - Ig) / (Ig Rg)
mcqs.why: The shunt is Rs = Ig Rg / (I - Ig), where Ig is the galvanometer full scale current, Rg its resistance and I the new current range.

mcqs.q: A galvanometer has Ig = 0.1 A and Rg = 9 ohm. What shunt converts it to a 1 A ammeter?
options: 9 ohm
0.9 ohm
10 ohm
1 ohm
mcqs.why: Rs = Ig Rg / (I - Ig) = (0.1 x 9) / (1 - 0.1) = 0.9 / 0.9 = 1 ohm. The low shunt in parallel carries most of the 1 A range current.

mcqs.q: How is a galvanometer converted into a voltmeter?
options: Connect a high resistance in series with it
Connect a low resistance shunt in parallel with it
Connect a high resistance in parallel with it
Connect it across a thermocouple junction
mcqs.why: A voltmeter uses a high resistance in series, so the coil current stays at its full scale value for the chosen voltage range.

mcqs.q: A galvanometer of 40 ohm deflects full scale at 4 mA. What series resistance makes it a 100 V voltmeter?
options: 40 ohm
mcqs.why: V / Ig = 100 / 0.004 = 25000 ohm. Series resistance R = V / Ig - Rg = 25000 - 40 = 24960 ohm, exactly as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: In the same voltmeter example, what is V / Ig before subtracting Rg?
options: 400 ohm
25 ohm
mcqs.why: V / Ig = 100 / 0.004 = 25000 ohm. Subtracting the galvanometer resistance Rg = 40 ohm then gives the required series resistance of 24960 ohm.

lessons.title: Avometer (Multimeter)
lessons.notes_html:
An Avometer, or multimeter, is one instrument that measures current, voltage and resistance. Its name comes from Ampere, Volt and Ohm.

Parts and Functions

PartJob
Moving coil meter or displayShows the reading
Selector switchChooses function and range
TerminalsConnect the leads to the circuit
Internal batteryDrives the ohmmeter section

As an ammeter it uses shunts in parallel; as a voltmeter it uses high resistances in series. An Avometer does not measure charge.

Ohmmeter

An ohmmeter is a galvanometer in series with a battery and a known resistance, with the scale marked in ohms. Short the terminals first to set zero, which is at full scale deflection. Then connect the unknown resistance: a larger resistance gives a smaller current and a smaller deflection, so the scale reads resistance directly, with infinity at zero deflection.

Analogue and Digital

AnalogueDigital
Pointer on a printed scaleValue shown as digits
Less precise, parallax error possibleMore accurate, no parallax error
Shows a changing value wellNeeds a battery for its circuits

Key Points

  • A current makes circular field lines around a wire; direction by the right-hand grip rule.
  • Force on a conductor: F = B I L sin θ, maximum across the field.
  • Flux Φ = B A cos θ, unit Wb; flux density B = Φ / A, unit tesla, 1 T = 104 G.
  • Ampere's law gives B = μo n I inside a solenoid, and almost zero outside.
  • Force on a moving charge: F = q v B sin θ; across the field it moves in a circle, r = m v / (q B).
  • A stationary charge feels no magnetic force, and the force does no work.
  • Velocity selector: v = E / B, and e/m = E / (B2 r), about 1.76 x 1011 C kg-1.
  • Torque on a coil: τ = N I A B sin θ, the principle of motors and galvanometers.
  • Shunt in parallel makes an ammeter; high resistance in series makes a voltmeter.
  • An Avometer measures current, voltage and resistance, but not charge.

mcqs.q: What is an Avometer?
options: One instrument that measures current, voltage and charge
An instrument that only measures resistance
One instrument that measures current, voltage and resistance
A galvanometer with a shunt only
mcqs.why: An Avometer, or multimeter, is one instrument that measures current, voltage and resistance; its name comes from Ampere, Volt and Ohm.

mcqs.q: From what does the name Avometer come?
options: Ampere, Volt and Weber
Average, Volt and Ohm
Ampere, Voltage and Output
Ampere, Volt and Ohm
mcqs.why: The name Avometer comes from Ampere (current), Volt (voltage) and Ohm (resistance), the three quantities the instrument measures.

mcqs.q: What does an Avometer NOT measure, according to the notes?
options: Charge
Current
Voltage
Resistance
mcqs.why: An Avometer measures current, voltage and resistance, but it does not measure charge, as stated directly in the notes and key points.

mcqs.q: What is the job of the selector switch on an Avometer?
options: It supplies power to the ohmmeter section
It chooses the function and range
It connects the leads to the circuit
It shows the reading as a pointer deflection
mcqs.why: The parts table states that the selector switch chooses function and range, while the terminals connect the leads and the display shows the reading.

mcqs.q: What drives the ohmmeter section of an Avometer?
options: The circuit being tested in every case
A driver cell and uniform wire
An internal battery
A thermocouple junction
mcqs.why: The parts table lists the internal battery as driving the ohmmeter section, since resistance measurement needs its own current source.

mcqs.q: How does an Avometer work as an ammeter and as a voltmeter?
options: As an ammeter it uses high resistances in series; as a voltmeter shunts in parallel
It uses shunts in parallel for both functions
It uses high resistances in series for both functions
As an ammeter it uses shunts in parallel; as a voltmeter it uses high resistances in series
mcqs.why: Like galvanometer conversions, the Avometer uses shunts in parallel as an ammeter and high resistances in series as a voltmeter.

mcqs.q: What is an ohmmeter?
options: A galvanometer in series with a battery and a known resistance, with the scale marked in ohms
A galvanometer with a shunt in parallel and scale marked in amperes
A long uniform wire with the scale marked in volts
A coil in a radial field with the scale marked in tesla
mcqs.why: An ohmmeter is a galvanometer in series with a battery and a known resistance, with the scale marked in ohms, as described in the notes.

mcqs.q: Before using an ohmmeter, what must be done and where is zero on its scale?
options: Leave the terminals open to set zero at no deflection
Short the terminals to set zero, which is at full scale deflection
Connect a known resistance to set zero at half deflection
Short the terminals to set zero at zero deflection
mcqs.why: Short the terminals first to set zero, which is at full scale deflection; infinity is at zero deflection on the reversed ohmmeter scale.

mcqs.q: On an ohmmeter, what does a larger unknown resistance give?
options: A larger current and a larger deflection
Full scale deflection for every large resistance
A smaller current and a smaller deflection, with infinity at zero deflection
No change in deflection at all
mcqs.why: A larger resistance gives a smaller current and smaller deflection, so the scale reads resistance directly, with infinity at zero deflection.

mcqs.q: How do analogue and digital Avometers differ?
options: Analogue shows digits and digital uses a pointer
Both are equally precise and neither can have parallax error
Digital needs no battery for its circuits while analogue does
Analogue uses a pointer on a printed scale and can have parallax error; digital shows digits and is more accurate with no parallax error
mcqs.why: The comparison table states analogue uses a pointer with possible parallax error, while digital shows digits, is more accurate and has no parallax error but needs a battery.

lessons.title: Induced e.m.f.
lessons.notes_html:
An induced e.m.f. is a voltage set up in a conductor or coil when the magnetic flux linked with it changes. The current it drives is called an induced current. No battery is needed.

When is it Induced?

Move a bar magnet toward a coil joined to a galvanometer and the needle deflects. Move it away and the needle deflects the other way. Hold the magnet still, even very close to the coil, and there is no deflection at all.

So the source is relative motion between magnet and coil, or any change of flux. The flux can change by moving the magnet or coil, changing the field strength, changing the area in the field, turning the coil, or changing the current in a nearby coil.

Key Idea

It is the rate of change of flux, not the flux itself, that sets the size of the induced e.m.f. The e.m.f. lasts only while the flux keeps changing, and its unit is the volt.

mcqs.q: What is an induced e.m.f.?
options: A voltage supplied by a battery connected in the circuit
A voltage that appears only when a conductor carries a steady current
A voltage stored permanently inside a magnet
A voltage set up in a conductor or coil when the magnetic flux linked with it changes
mcqs.why: The notes define induced e.m.f. as a voltage set up when the flux linked with a conductor or coil changes; no battery is needed.

mcqs.q: A bar magnet is held still very close to a coil joined to a galvanometer. What happens?
options: There is no deflection at all
The needle deflects strongly in one direction
The needle deflects and stays deflected
The needle swings back and forth continuously
mcqs.why: With the magnet still, the flux is not changing, so no e.m.f. is induced even though the magnet is very close to the coil.

mcqs.q: Moving a bar magnet away from a coil, compared with moving it toward the coil, makes the galvanometer needle
options: Deflect in the same direction
Deflect in the opposite direction
Stay exactly at zero
Deflect twice as far in the same direction
mcqs.why: Moving the magnet away reverses the direction of flux change, so the induced e.m.f. and current reverse and the needle deflects the other way.

mcqs.q: What actually sets the size of an induced e.m.f.?
options: The value of the magnetic flux itself
The total flux that has ever passed through the coil
The rate of change of magnetic flux
The strength of the magnet alone, even with no change
mcqs.why: The key idea in the notes is that the rate of change of flux, not the flux itself, sets the size of the induced e.m.f.

mcqs.q: For how long does an induced e.m.f. last?
options: For as long as any flux is present in the coil
Permanently, once it has been induced once
Only after the flux has stopped changing
Only while the flux keeps changing
mcqs.why: The e.m.f. lasts only while the flux keeps changing; once the change stops, the induced e.m.f. falls to zero.

mcqs.q: Which of these changes can produce an induced e.m.f.?
options: Turning the coil in a magnetic field
Keeping the coil completely still in a steady field
Holding a magnet fixed near the coil
Leaving the current in a nearby coil perfectly steady
mcqs.why: Turning the coil changes the flux linked with it. The notes list turning the coil, moving magnet or coil, changing field, area or nearby current as ways flux changes.

mcqs.q: What is the current driven by an induced e.m.f. called?
options: A conduction current from a battery
An induced current
A displacement current in empty space
A steady direct current
mcqs.why: The notes state directly that the current driven by an induced e.m.f. is called an induced current.

mcqs.q: What is the unit of induced e.m.f.?
options: The weber
The ampere
The volt
The tesla
mcqs.why: Induced e.m.f. is a voltage, so its unit is the volt; the weber is flux, the ampere is current and the tesla is magnetic field.

mcqs.q: The flux through a coil can be changed by changing the current in a nearby coil because
options: The two coils must be joined by a wire for any effect
A steady current in the nearby coil keeps growing the flux
The nearby coil supplies charge directly to the first coil
The nearby coil's field, and so the flux it sends through the first coil, changes
mcqs.why: Changing the current in a nearby coil changes its magnetic field, which changes the flux linked with the first coil and induces an e.m.f. there.

mcqs.q: A magnet is pushed toward a coil slowly, then pushed again much faster. The second push gives
options: A larger induced e.m.f. because the flux changes faster
A smaller induced e.m.f. because the flux changes faster
Exactly the same e.m.f. because the magnet is the same
No e.m.f. because fast motion stops induction
mcqs.why: Faster motion means a greater rate of change of flux, and the induced e.m.f. is set by that rate, so the second push induces more.

lessons.title: Motional e.m.f.
lessons.notes_html:
A motional e.m.f. is induced in a conductor purely by its motion through a magnetic field. It is the basis of the generator.

Why Charge Separates

As a rod moves across a field, its free electrons feel the force F = e v B, which pushes them to one end of the rod. Charge builds up until the electric force balances the magnetic force, e E = e v B, so E = v B.

ε = v B l

  • ε - motional e.m.f., unit V
  • v - speed of the rod, unit m s-1; B - field, unit T; l - length of the rod, unit m
  • If the motion makes angle θ with the field, use ε = v B l sin θ.

Worked Example: e.m.f. in a Moving Conductor

A 60 m long conductor moves at 7 m s-1 at right angles to a uniform field of 0.9 T. Find the induced e.m.f.

Step 1: At right angles, ε = v B l.

Step 2: ε = 7 x 0.9 x 60.

Step 3: 7 x 0.9 = 6.3; 6.3 x 60 = 378.

Answer: ε = 378 V.

mcqs.q: What is a motional e.m.f.?
options: An e.m.f. induced in a conductor purely by its motion through a magnetic field
An e.m.f. induced by heating a conductor in a field
An e.m.f. produced by a battery moving with the conductor
An e.m.f. that appears in a stationary coil only
mcqs.why: The notes define motional e.m.f. as induced purely by motion through a magnetic field, and it is the basis of the generator.

mcqs.q: As a rod moves across a magnetic field, its free electrons are pushed to one end by the force
options: F = e E / B
F = e v B
F = v B / e
F = e v / B
mcqs.why: The notes give the magnetic force on a moving electron as F = e v B, which pushes electrons to one end of the rod.

mcqs.q: Charge stops building up in a moving rod when
options: All the electrons have left the rod completely
The magnetic field is used up by the moving rod
The electric force balances the magnetic force, e E = e v B, so E = v B
The rod reaches the edge of the magnetic field
mcqs.why: Charge builds up until e E = e v B; cancelling e gives E = v B, the balance condition stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: The motional e.m.f. for a rod moving at right angles to a field is
options: epsilon = v B / l
epsilon = B l / v
epsilon = v l / B
epsilon = v B l
mcqs.why: The notes give epsilon = v B l, with v in m s-1, B in tesla and l, the rod length, in metres, giving epsilon in volts.

mcqs.q: A 60 m long conductor moves at 7 m s-1 at right angles to a uniform field of 0.9 T. The induced e.m.f. is
mcqs.why: At right angles epsilon = v B l. Substituting: epsilon = 7 x 0.9 x 60 = 6.3 x 60 = 378 V, the worked example in the notes.

mcqs.q: If the conductor in the worked example moved at only 3.5 m s-1 instead of 7 m s-1, its e.m.f. would be
mcqs.why: epsilon = v B l = 3.5 x 0.9 x 60 = 3.15 x 60 = 189 V. Halving the speed halves the motional e.m.f., since epsilon is proportional to v.

mcqs.q: A rod moves at an angle theta to the magnetic field. The motional e.m.f. is
options: epsilon = v B l cos theta
epsilon = v B l tan theta
epsilon = v B l sin theta
epsilon = v B l / sin theta
mcqs.why: The notes state that when the motion makes angle theta with the field, only the component across the field counts, giving epsilon = v B l sin theta.

mcqs.q: In epsilon = v B l, the symbol l stands for
options: The inductance of the rod, in henry
The distance the rod has travelled, in metres
The number of turns on the rod
The length of the rod, in metres
mcqs.why: The notes define l as the length of the rod in metres; v is its speed and B is the field strength in tesla.

mcqs.q: Motional e.m.f. is described in the notes as the basis of
options: The generator
The transformer
The choke coil
The capacitor
mcqs.why: A conductor moving through a field is how a generator produces its e.m.f., so the notes call motional e.m.f. the basis of the generator.

mcqs.q: If a rod moves parallel to the magnetic field lines, the motional e.m.f. induced is
options: Maximum, because the rod moves along the field
Zero, because sin theta = 0 when theta = 0
Equal to v B l, the same as at right angles
Equal to half of v B l
mcqs.why: Using epsilon = v B l sin theta with theta = 0 gives sin 0 = 0, so epsilon = 0; no flux is cut by motion parallel to the field.

lessons.title: Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
lessons.notes_html:
Faraday's law, given by Faraday, states that the induced e.m.f. in a circuit is directly proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linked with it.

The Law in Symbols

ε = - N ΔΦ / Δt

  • ε - induced e.m.f., unit V; N - number of turns of the coil
  • ΔΦ / Δt - rate of change of flux, unit Wb s-1
  • The negative sign states Lenz's law: the e.m.f. opposes the change that makes it.

Push a magnet into a coil quickly and the galvanometer deflects more than for a slow push, because the flux changes faster. More turns also give a larger e.m.f. for the same flux change.

Worked Example: Flux Reversed in a Coil

A coil of 200 turns is linked by a flux of 40 mWb. The flux is reversed in 4 ms. Find the average induced e.m.f. (The book's printed answer is wrong; the correct value is found below.)

Step 1: Reversal changes the flux from +40 mWb to -40 mWb, so ΔΦ = 80 mWb = 0.08 Wb.

Step 2: Δt = 4 ms = 0.004 s, and N = 200.

Step 3: ε = N ΔΦ / Δt = 200 x 0.08 / 0.004 = 200 x 20.

Answer: ε = 4000 V. The book prints 2000 V, which uses a change of only 40 mWb, as if the flux fell to zero instead of reversing.

mcqs.q: Faraday's law states that the induced e.m.f. in a circuit is directly proportional to
options: The total magnetic flux linked with it
The rate of change of magnetic flux linked with it
The resistance of the circuit
The time for which the flux has been present
mcqs.why: Faraday's law, as stated in the notes, makes the induced e.m.f. directly proportional to the rate of change of flux linkage.

mcqs.q: Faraday's law in symbols is
options: epsilon = - N delta t / deltaPhi
epsilon = - deltaPhi / (N delta t)
epsilon = - N deltaPhi / delta t
epsilon = N deltaPhi x delta t
mcqs.why: The notes write epsilon = - N deltaPhi / delta t, where N is the number of turns and deltaPhi / delta t is the rate of change of flux in Wb s-1.

mcqs.q: The negative sign in Faraday's law represents
options: That the e.m.f. is always negative in value
That flux must always decrease in a coil
That the current flows only in one chosen direction
Lenz's law: the e.m.f. opposes the change that makes it
mcqs.why: The notes explain the minus sign states Lenz's law: the induced e.m.f. acts to oppose the change of flux that produced it.

mcqs.q: A coil of 200 turns is linked by a flux of 40 mWb, which is reversed in 4 ms. The change of flux is
options: 80 mWb = 0.08 Wb
40 mWb = 0.04 Wb
Zero, because the flux size is the same
mcqs.why: Reversal takes the flux from +40 mWb to -40 mWb, so deltaPhi = 40 - (-40) = 80 mWb = 0.08 Wb, as the worked example shows.

mcqs.q: For the coil of 200 turns with flux reversed in 4 ms, the average induced e.m.f. is
mcqs.why: epsilon = N deltaPhi / delta t = 200 x 0.08 / 0.004 = 200 x 20 = 4000 V. The book's 2000 V wrongly uses a change of only 40 mWb.

mcqs.q: Why is the book's printed answer of 2000 V for the flux-reversal example wrong?
options: It uses too many turns for the coil
It converts milliseconds to seconds incorrectly
It uses a flux change of only 40 mWb, as if the flux fell to zero instead of reversing
It forgets to include the negative sign
mcqs.why: The notes point out the printed answer treats the change as 40 mWb to zero; a true reversal changes the flux by 80 mWb, doubling the e.m.f. to 4000 V.

mcqs.q: Pushing a magnet into a coil quickly gives a bigger galvanometer deflection than a slow push because
options: The magnet becomes stronger when it moves quickly
The coil gains extra turns during a quick push
The resistance of the coil falls during a quick push
The flux changes faster, so the rate of change of flux is greater
mcqs.why: A quick push gives a larger deltaPhi / delta t, and by Faraday's law a larger rate of change of flux induces a larger e.m.f.

mcqs.q: For the same rate of change of flux, adding more turns to a coil
options: Increases the induced e.m.f.
Decreases the induced e.m.f.
Leaves the induced e.m.f. unchanged
Stops the e.m.f. after the first turn
mcqs.why: Epsilon is proportional to N in epsilon = - N deltaPhi / delta t, so more turns give a larger e.m.f. for the same flux change.

mcqs.q: In Faraday's law, deltaPhi / delta t is measured in
options: Wb only
Wb s-1
V per turn only
T s-1
mcqs.why: The notes give deltaPhi / delta t, the rate of change of flux, the unit Wb s-1: flux in webers divided by time in seconds.

mcqs.q: If the flux through a 200-turn coil fell to zero from 40 mWb in 4 ms (not reversed), the e.m.f. would be
mcqs.why: Here deltaPhi = 0.04 Wb, so epsilon = N deltaPhi / delta t = 200 x 0.04 / 0.004 = 200 x 10 = 2000 V, half the reversal value.

lessons.title: Lenz's Law
lessons.notes_html:
Lenz's law gives the direction of the induced e.m.f. and current: the induced current always acts to oppose the change of flux that produced it.

Finding the Direction

When the north pole of a magnet moves toward a coil, the near face of the coil becomes a north pole and repels it. When the magnet moves away, the near face becomes a south pole and attracts it. In each case the induced field fights the motion causing it.

Conservation of Energy

Lenz's law is the law of conservation of energy applied to induction. If the induced current helped the change instead of opposing it, the magnet would speed up with no work done and energy would come from nothing. Because it opposes, work must be done to move the magnet, and that work is exactly the electrical energy produced.

Faraday's lawLenz's law
Gives the size of the e.m.f.Gives the direction of the e.m.f.
ε = - N ΔΦ / ΔtThe minus sign in the law

mcqs.q: Lenz's law gives which property of the induced e.m.f.?
options: Its size in volts
The number of turns needed
Its direction
The frequency of the supply
mcqs.why: The notes contrast the two laws: Faraday's law gives the size of the e.m.f., while Lenz's law gives its direction.

mcqs.q: Lenz's law states that the induced current always acts to
options: Help the change of flux that produced it
Keep the flux permanently at its maximum
Flow in the same direction as the magnet moves
Oppose the change of flux that produced it
mcqs.why: By Lenz's law the induced current always opposes the change of flux that produced it, so its field fights the change.

mcqs.q: When the north pole of a magnet moves toward a coil, the near face of the coil becomes
options: A north pole, and repels the magnet
A south pole, and attracts the magnet
Unmagnetised, with no force on the magnet
A north pole, and attracts the magnet
mcqs.why: The coil's near face becomes a north pole to repel the approaching north pole, opposing the increase of flux, as Lenz's law requires.

mcqs.q: When a magnet moves away from a coil, the near face of the coil becomes
options: A north pole, and repels the magnet away
A south pole, and attracts the magnet back
A south pole, and repels the magnet away
Unmagnetised, so nothing happens
mcqs.why: As flux falls, the induced current makes the near face a south pole that attracts the magnet, opposing its removal and the fall in flux.

mcqs.q: Lenz's law is an application of which conservation law?
options: Conservation of charge
Conservation of magnetic flux
Conservation of energy
Conservation of momentum
mcqs.why: The notes state Lenz's law is the law of conservation of energy applied to electromagnetic induction.

mcqs.q: If the induced current helped the change instead of opposing it, what would go wrong?
options: The galvanometer needle would deflect the wrong way only
The coil would cool down below room temperature
The flux would stay exactly constant forever
The magnet would speed up with no work done and energy would come from nothing
mcqs.why: Helping the change would let the magnet accelerate without work input, creating energy from nothing, which is why the current must oppose.

mcqs.q: Because the induced current opposes the motion of the magnet, the work done moving the magnet becomes
options: Exactly the electrical energy produced
Heat lost in the galvanometer only
Stored permanently in the magnet
Much larger than the electrical energy produced
mcqs.why: The notes say work must be done to move the magnet against the opposition, and that work is exactly the electrical energy produced.

mcqs.q: In Faraday's law, Lenz's law appears as
options: The number of turns N in the formula
The minus sign in epsilon = - N deltaPhi / delta t
The delta t in the denominator
The unit of flux used in the formula
mcqs.why: The negative sign in epsilon = - N deltaPhi / delta t is the mathematical statement of Lenz's law, showing opposition to the change.

mcqs.q: A metal plate swinging in a magnetic field is slowed down. This happens because
options: The field makes the plate heavier as it swings
The plate becomes permanently magnetised and sticks
The induced currents oppose the change that produces them, as Lenz's law states
Air resistance inside the field is much greater
mcqs.why: Currents induced in the plate oppose, by Lenz's law, the flux change caused by its motion, so a force acts against the swinging.

mcqs.q: Which pairing is correct?
options: Faraday's law gives direction, Lenz's law gives size
Both laws give only the size of the e.m.f.
Both laws give only the direction of the e.m.f.
Faraday's law gives size, Lenz's law gives direction
mcqs.why: The comparison in the notes is explicit: Faraday's law gives the size of the induced e.m.f. and Lenz's law gives its direction.

lessons.title: Mutual Induction
lessons.notes_html:
Mutual induction is the induction of an e.m.f. in one coil by a changing current in a nearby second coil. The changing flux from the first coil links the second coil.

Coefficient of Mutual Inductance

εs = - M ΔIp / Δt

  • εs - e.m.f. induced in the secondary coil, unit V
  • M - coefficient of mutual inductance, unit henry (H)
  • ΔIp / Δt - rate of change of current in the primary coil, unit A s-1

One henry of mutual inductance means a current changing at 1 A s-1 in the primary induces 1 V in the secondary. M is largest when the coils face each other and are close, and it depends on their turns, size, distance, position and core. Mutual induction is the working principle of the transformer.

M can also be written as the flux linkage in the secondary divided by the primary current, M = Ns Φs / Ip, which shows why a core that carries more flux raises M.

mcqs.q: Mutual induction is
options: The induction of an e.m.f. in a coil by its own changing current
The induction of an e.m.f. by moving a coil in a steady field
The transfer of charge between two coils joined by a wire
The induction of an e.m.f. in one coil by a changing current in a nearby second coil
mcqs.why: The notes define mutual induction as an e.m.f. induced in one coil by a changing current in a nearby second coil whose flux links it.

mcqs.q: The formula for the e.m.f. induced in the secondary coil by mutual induction is
options: epsilon_s = - M deltaI_p / delta t
epsilon_s = - L deltaI_p / delta t
epsilon_s = M deltaI_p x delta t
epsilon_s = - M / deltaI_p
mcqs.why: The notes give epsilon_s = - M deltaI_p / delta t, where M is the coefficient of mutual inductance and deltaI_p / delta t is in the primary.

mcqs.q: The unit of the coefficient of mutual inductance M is
options: The weber (Wb)
The henry (H)
The tesla (T)
The ohm
mcqs.why: Mutual inductance M is measured in henry, the same unit as self-inductance, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: One henry of mutual inductance means that
options: A steady current of 1 A in the primary induces 1 V in the secondary
A current of 1 A in the secondary induces 1 V in the primary at any rate
A current changing at 1 A s-1 in the primary induces 1 V in the secondary
The primary stores 1 J of energy in its field
mcqs.why: The notes define one henry this way: a rate of change of 1 A s-1 in the primary induces an e.m.f. of 1 V in the secondary.

mcqs.q: Mutual inductance M is largest when the two coils
options: Are far apart and at right angles
Are far apart and face away from each other
Carry steady currents of equal size
Face each other and are close together
mcqs.why: The notes say M is largest when the coils face each other and are close, because then the flux from one links the other most strongly.

mcqs.q: M depends on which set of factors?
options: The turns, size, distance, position and core of the coils
Only the resistance of the secondary coil
Only the frequency of the supply voltage
The colour and insulation of the coil wires
mcqs.why: The notes list turns, size, distance, position and core as the factors on which the coefficient of mutual inductance depends.

mcqs.q: Mutual induction is the working principle of
options: The A.C. generator
The transformer
The choke coil
The moving-coil galvanometer
mcqs.why: A transformer works because a changing primary current induces an e.m.f. in the secondary by mutual induction, as the notes state.

mcqs.q: M can also be written as M = N_s Phi_s / I_p. This shows that M is increased by
options: A larger primary current with the same flux linkage
Fewer turns on the secondary coil
A core that carries more flux to the secondary
A smaller flux linkage in the secondary
mcqs.why: Since M equals flux linkage in the secondary divided by primary current, a core carrying more flux raises Phi_s and so raises M.

mcqs.q: If M = 0.5 H and the primary current changes at 4 A s-1, the e.m.f. induced in the secondary is
options: 8 V
2 V
mcqs.why: epsilon_s = M deltaI_p / delta t = 0.5 x 4 = 2 V, using the magnitude from epsilon_s = - M deltaI_p / delta t in the notes.

mcqs.q: Why must the primary current be changing for mutual induction to occur?
options: Only a changing current gives a changing flux linking the secondary
A steady current produces no magnetic field at all
A steady current flows into the secondary instead
The secondary can only respond to currents above 1 A
mcqs.why: A steady primary current gives a steady flux, and a steady flux induces no e.m.f.; the flux must change to induce an e.m.f. in the secondary.

lessons.title: Self-Induction
lessons.notes_html:
Self-induction is the induction of an e.m.f. in a coil by its own changing current. The changing current changes the flux through the coil itself, and that induces an e.m.f. in the same coil.

Self-Inductance

ε = - L ΔI / Δt

  • L - coefficient of self-inductance, unit henry (H)
  • One henry is the inductance of a coil in which a current change of 1 A s-1 induces an e.m.f. of 1 V: 1 H = 1 V s A-1.
  • L depends on the turns, area and length of the coil and on its core.

By Lenz's law the induced e.m.f. opposes the change, so current grows slowly at switch-on and falls slowly at switch-off, often with a spark. Self-inductance acts like electrical inertia.

Worked Example: Self-Inductance of a Coil

The current in a coil changes by 3 A in 60 ms and an e.m.f. of 10 V is induced in it. Find its self-inductance.

Step 1: Rate of change = 3 / 0.060 = 50 A s-1.

Step 2: From ε = L ΔI / Δt, L = ε / (ΔI / Δt).

Step 3: L = 10 / 50 = 0.2.

Answer: L = 0.2 H.

mcqs.q: Self-induction is
options: The induction of an e.m.f. in a coil by its own changing current
The induction of an e.m.f. in a coil by a nearby coil's changing current
The induction of an e.m.f. by a magnet held still near a coil
The heating of a coil by a steady current
mcqs.why: The notes define self-induction as a coil inducing an e.m.f. in itself when its own current changes and changes the flux through it.

mcqs.q: The formula for the self-induced e.m.f. is
options: epsilon = - M deltaI / delta t with M for the same coil
epsilon = - L deltaI / delta t
epsilon = L deltaI x delta t
epsilon = - deltaI / (L delta t)
mcqs.why: The notes give epsilon = - L deltaI / delta t, where L is the coefficient of self-inductance measured in henry.

mcqs.q: One henry is the inductance of a coil in which
options: A steady current of 1 A stores an e.m.f. of 1 V
A current of 1 A produces a flux of 1 Wb
A current change of 1 A s-1 induces an e.m.f. of 1 V
The resistance to alternating current is 1 ohm
mcqs.why: The notes define 1 H as the inductance where a change of 1 A s-1 induces 1 V, written as 1 H = 1 V s A-1.

mcqs.q: Self-inductance L depends on
options: Only the current flowing in the coil at the time
Only the voltage of the supply connected to it
The resistance of the connecting wires only
The turns, area and length of the coil and on its core
mcqs.why: The notes state L depends on the turns, area and length of the coil and on its core material, not on the current itself.

mcqs.q: The current in a coil changes by 3 A in 60 ms and an e.m.f. of 10 V is induced. The rate of change of current is
options: 5 A s-1
mcqs.why: Rate of change = deltaI / delta t = 3 / 0.060 = 50 A s-1, the first step of the worked example in the notes.

mcqs.q: For that coil (3 A change in 60 ms, 10 V induced), the self-inductance is
options: 2 H
5 H
mcqs.why: L = epsilon / (deltaI / delta t) = 10 / 50 = 0.2 H, from epsilon = L deltaI / delta t as worked in the notes.

mcqs.q: At switch-off, the current in an inductive coil falls slowly and often with a spark because
options: The coil resistance drops suddenly to zero
The supply voltage rises when the switch opens
The self-induced e.m.f. opposes the fall of current, by Lenz's law
The core keeps supplying charge to the coil
mcqs.why: By Lenz's law the induced e.m.f. opposes any change, so at switch-off it tries to keep the current flowing, causing the slow fall and spark.

mcqs.q: Self-inductance is described in the notes as acting like
options: Electrical friction
A permanent battery
A short circuit
Electrical inertia
mcqs.why: Because it resists changes in current, growing and falling slowly, self-inductance acts like inertia for the current: electrical inertia.

mcqs.q: At switch-on, the current in a coil with self-inductance
options: Grows slowly because the induced e.m.f. opposes its growth
Jumps instantly to its final value
Stays at zero until the coil is fully charged
Grows quickly because the induced e.m.f. helps it
mcqs.why: The self-induced e.m.f. opposes the change by Lenz's law, so at switch-on it fights the growth and the current rises slowly.

mcqs.q: A coil has L = 0.2 H. When its current changes at 50 A s-1, the induced e.m.f. is
mcqs.why: epsilon = L deltaI / delta t = 0.2 x 50 = 10 V, the same values as the worked example run in reverse.

lessons.title: Energy Stored in an Inductor
lessons.notes_html:
An inductor stores energy in its magnetic field. To build up the current, the source must do work against the back e.m.f. of the growing current, and that work is stored, not lost.

Deriving the Energy

At an instant when the current is I and growing, the back e.m.f. is L ΔI / Δt, so the power supplied is P = L I ΔI / Δt and the work in a short time is L I ΔI. Adding this work as the current grows from zero to I gives:

U = 1/2 L I2

  • U - magnetic potential energy stored, unit J
  • L - inductance, unit H; I - final current, unit A

When the current falls, the collapsing field returns this energy to the circuit and tries to keep the current flowing. This is why an inductor circuit cannot be switched off instantly without a spark.

Because the energy depends on I2, doubling the current stores four times as much energy, and a larger inductance stores more energy at the same current.

mcqs.q: Where does an inductor store its energy?
options: In its electric field between turns
In its magnetic field
As heat in the coil resistance
In the core as permanent magnetisation only
mcqs.why: The notes state an inductor stores energy in its magnetic field; the work done against the back e.m.f. is stored, not lost.

mcqs.q: The energy stored in an inductor is given by
options: U = L I^2
U = 1/2 L I
mcqs.why: Adding the work L I deltaI as the current grows from zero to I gives U = 1/2 L I^2, with U in joules, L in henry and I in ampere.

mcqs.q: Why must the supply do work when the current in an inductor is building up?
options: It must overcome the weight of the coil
It must charge the plates of the inductor
It must reverse the magnetic field of the Earth
It must work against the back e.m.f. of the growing current
mcqs.why: The growing current induces a back e.m.f.; the source does work against it and that work is stored in the magnetic field.

mcqs.q: An inductor of 0.2 H carries a final current of 5 A. The stored energy is
options: 5 J
1 J
mcqs.why: U = 1/2 L I^2 = 0.5 x 0.2 x 5^2 = 0.5 x 0.2 x 25 = 2.5 J, using the energy formula from the notes.

mcqs.q: If the current in an inductor is doubled, the stored energy becomes
options: Twice as much
Four times as much
Half as much
Eight times as much
mcqs.why: U depends on I^2, so doubling I multiplies U by 2^2 = 4; the notes state doubling the current stores four times as much energy.

mcqs.q: At the same current, a larger inductance stores
options: Less energy
Exactly the same energy
More energy
No energy at all
mcqs.why: U = 1/2 L I^2 is proportional to L, so the notes conclude a larger inductance stores more energy at the same current.

mcqs.q: When the current in an inductor falls, the stored energy
options: Is destroyed completely with no effect
Turns into charge stored on the coil
Stays locked in the field forever
Is returned to the circuit by the collapsing field, which tries to keep the current flowing
mcqs.why: The notes say the collapsing field returns the energy to the circuit and tries to keep the current flowing as it falls.

mcqs.q: Why can an inductor circuit not be switched off instantly without a spark?
options: The stored magnetic energy is returned and keeps the current trying to flow
The switch contacts become magnetised and stick
The inductor resistance becomes infinite at switch-off
The supply voltage doubles at the moment of switching
mcqs.why: Because the field holds stored energy that is returned as the current falls, the current cannot stop instantly and a spark appears.

mcqs.q: During the growth of current, the power supplied at an instant when current is I is
options: P = L I^2 delta t
P = L I deltaI / delta t
P = I / (L delta t)
P = 1/2 L I^2 / delta t
mcqs.why: The back e.m.f. is L deltaI / delta t, so the power supplied against it is P = L I deltaI / delta t, as derived in the notes.

mcqs.q: The unit of the energy stored in an inductor is
options: The henry (H)
The watt (W)
The joule (J)
The volt (V)
mcqs.why: U is magnetic potential energy stored, measured in joules; henry is inductance, watt is power and volt is e.m.f.

lessons.title: A.C. Generator
lessons.notes_html:
An A.C. generator converts mechanical energy into alternating electrical energy by electromagnetic induction.

Construction

A rectangular coil of many turns on a soft iron core rotates between the poles of a strong magnet. Two slip rings turn with the coil, and two fixed carbon brushes press on the rings to carry the current to the external circuit. Carbon is soft, conducts well and does not wear or weld to the rings.

Working

As the coil rotates, the flux through it changes continuously, so an alternating e.m.f. is induced. It is zero when the coil is across the field and maximum when its plane is along the field, reversing every half turn.

ε = N B A ω sin θ

  • ε - induced e.m.f. at an instant, unit V; maximum value εo = N B A ω
  • ω - angular speed, ω = 2 π f, unit rad s-1

Worked Example: Field of a Generator

A generator coil has 150 turns, area 150 cm2 and frequency 60 Hz, and its maximum e.m.f. is 250 V. Find B. (The book's printed answer has a wrong unit; see the answer.)

Step 1: A = 150 cm2 = 0.015 m2; ω = 2 π f = 2 x 3.14 x 60 = 377 rad s-1.

Step 2: B = εo / (N A ω) = 250 / (150 x 0.015 x 377).

Step 3: Denominator = 848.25, so B = 0.295 T.

Answer: B is about 0.3 T. The book prints 0.3 mT, which is 1000 times too small.

mcqs.q: An A.C. generator converts
options: Alternating electrical energy into mechanical energy
Direct current into alternating current only
Mechanical energy into alternating electrical energy
Mechanical energy into direct electrical energy only
mcqs.why: The notes define the A.C. generator as converting mechanical energy into alternating electrical energy by electromagnetic induction.

mcqs.q: In an A.C. generator, the coil is connected to the external circuit through
options: A split-ring commutator and two brushes
Two fixed wires soldered to the coil ends
A transformer linked to the rotating coil
Two slip rings turning with the coil and two fixed carbon brushes
mcqs.why: Slip rings turn with the coil and carbon brushes press on them, carrying the alternating current out without reversing the connections.

mcqs.q: Why is carbon used for the brushes of a generator?
options: It is soft, conducts well and does not wear or weld to the rings
It is an insulator that protects the rings
It is magnetic and strengthens the field
It melts and solders itself to the rings
mcqs.why: The notes give these reasons: carbon is soft, conducts well and does not wear or weld to the slip rings.

mcqs.q: The generator coil is wound on a core of
options: Hard steel
Soft iron
Copper
Wood
mcqs.why: The notes describe a rectangular coil of many turns on a soft iron core rotating between the poles of a strong magnet.

mcqs.q: The induced e.m.f. in a generator is zero when the coil is across the field and maximum when
options: Its plane is across the field
It stops rotating for an instant
Its plane is along the field
The brushes leave the slip rings
mcqs.why: As stated in the notes, the e.m.f. is zero with the coil across the field and maximum when its plane is along the field, reversing every half turn.

mcqs.q: The instantaneous e.m.f. of a generator is given by
options: epsilon = N B A / omega
epsilon = B A omega / N
epsilon = N B A omega cos theta only, with no sine form
epsilon = N B A omega sin theta
mcqs.why: The notes give epsilon = N B A omega sin theta, with maximum value epsilon_o = N B A omega when sin theta = 1.

mcqs.q: The maximum e.m.f. of a generator coil is
options: epsilon_o = N B A omega
epsilon_o = N B A / omega
epsilon_o = B A omega sin theta at theta = 0
epsilon_o = N A omega / B
mcqs.why: Epsilon is greatest when sin theta = 1 in epsilon = N B A omega sin theta, so the peak value is epsilon_o = N B A omega.

mcqs.q: A generator runs at 60 Hz. Its angular speed omega is about
options: 60 rad s-1
377 rad s-1
120 rad s-1
188 rad s-1
mcqs.why: omega = 2 pi f = 2 x 3.14 x 60 = 376.8, about 377 rad s-1, as calculated in the worked example in the notes.

mcqs.q: A generator coil has 150 turns, area 150 cm^2, frequency 60 Hz and maximum e.m.f. 250 V. The field B is about
options: 0.3 mT
3 T
mcqs.why: B = epsilon_o / (N A omega) = 250 / (150 x 0.015 x 377) = 250 / 848.25 = 0.295 T, about 0.3 T. The book's 0.3 mT is 1000 times too small.

mcqs.q: In the generator worked example, the area 150 cm^2 must first be converted to
mcqs.why: 150 cm^2 = 150 x 10^-4 m^2 = 0.015 m^2, the conversion used in step 1 of the worked example before finding B.

lessons.title: A.C. Motor
lessons.notes_html:
An A.C. motor converts alternating electrical energy into mechanical energy.

Construction

PartDetail
StatorFixed part with windings that make a rotating field
RotorTurning part, such as a squirrel cage of bars, on a shaft
ConnectionNo physical electrical link between stator and rotor

A two-phase supply uses two stator windings. The alternating current in the stator makes a field that rotates.

Working

The rotating field induces currents in the rotor conductors. These currents interact with the field and feel a force, giving a torque that drags the rotor around after the field. As the rotor turns, its conductors cut the field and a back e.m.f. is induced in them.

In an induction motor the rotor is a squirrel cage of conducting bars; in a synchronous motor the rotor is a coil or a permanent magnet. In both kinds the rotor is dragged around by the rotating field of the stator.

mcqs.q: An A.C. motor converts
options: Mechanical energy into alternating electrical energy
Direct current into mechanical energy only
Alternating current into direct current
Alternating electrical energy into mechanical energy
mcqs.why: The notes define the A.C. motor as converting alternating electrical energy into mechanical energy, the reverse of the generator.

mcqs.q: The fixed part of an A.C. motor, whose windings make a rotating field, is the
options: Stator
Rotor
Shaft
Squirrel cage
mcqs.why: The construction table in the notes lists the stator as the fixed part with windings that make a rotating field.

mcqs.q: The turning part of an A.C. motor, mounted on a shaft, is the
options: Stator
Rotor
Brush
Slip ring
mcqs.why: The rotor is the turning part on a shaft; in an induction motor it is a squirrel cage of conducting bars, per the notes.

mcqs.q: Between stator and rotor in an A.C. motor there is
options: A pair of carbon brushes and slip rings
A soldered wire connection
No physical electrical link
A commutator joining them
mcqs.why: The construction table states there is no physical electrical link between stator and rotor; the rotor is driven by induction.

mcqs.q: A two-phase supply in an A.C. motor uses
options: Two rotors on one shaft
Two separate magnets outside the motor
Two batteries in the stator
Two stator windings
mcqs.why: The notes state a two-phase supply uses two stator windings, whose alternating currents make the field rotate.

mcqs.q: How does the rotor of an induction motor get its currents?
options: The rotating stator field induces currents in the rotor conductors
Brushes feed current directly into the rotor bars
A battery inside the rotor supplies the current
The shaft generates current by friction
mcqs.why: The rotating field induces currents in the rotor conductors; these interact with the field to give a force and torque, per the notes.

mcqs.q: The torque that turns the rotor comes from
options: The attraction of the stator windings for the shaft
The force on the induced rotor currents interacting with the magnetic field
The heating of the rotor bars by the current
The weight of the squirrel cage bars
mcqs.why: Induced rotor currents interact with the field and feel a force, giving a torque that drags the rotor around after the field.

mcqs.q: In an induction motor the rotor is
options: A coil fed through slip rings only
A permanent magnet only
A squirrel cage of conducting bars
A soft iron disc with no conductors
mcqs.why: The notes state that in an induction motor the rotor is a squirrel cage of conducting bars, while a synchronous motor uses a coil or permanent magnet.

mcqs.q: In a synchronous motor the rotor is
options: A squirrel cage of conducting bars
A plain copper disc
A second stator winding
A coil or a permanent magnet
mcqs.why: The notes contrast the two kinds: induction motor rotors are squirrel cages; synchronous motor rotors are a coil or a permanent magnet.

mcqs.q: As the motor rotor turns, its conductors cut the field and this induces in them
options: A back e.m.f.
A permanent charge
A direct current from the stator
Extra flux in the stator only
mcqs.why: The notes say that as the rotor turns, its conductors cut the field and a back e.m.f. is induced in them, opposing the supply.

lessons.title: Back e.m.f. in a Motor
lessons.notes_html:
Back e.m.f. is the e.m.f. induced in the rotating coil of a motor by its own rotation in the field. By Lenz's law it opposes the applied voltage, so it limits the motor current.

Motor Current

I = (V - εb) / R

  • I - current in the motor, unit A; V - applied voltage, unit V
  • εb - back e.m.f., unit V; R - resistance of the motor circuit, unit ohm

Starting and Running

At start the rotor is still, so εb = 0 and the current is at its largest, I = V / R. This is why a heavy motor starting at home draws a big current, drops the voltage in the house wiring, and makes a bulb dim for a moment. As the motor speeds up, back e.m.f. grows, the current falls to its normal running value, and the bulb brightens again. If the load grows, the motor slows a little, back e.m.f. falls, and the current rises by itself to meet the load.

mcqs.q: Back e.m.f. in a motor is
options: The e.m.f. induced in the rotating coil of a motor by its own rotation in the field
The voltage applied to the motor from the supply
The e.m.f. induced in the stator by the supply
The voltage drop across the house wiring
mcqs.why: The notes define back e.m.f. as the e.m.f. induced in the rotating coil by its own rotation in the field, opposing the applied voltage.

mcqs.q: The motor current is given by
options: I = (V + epsilon_b) / R
I = (V - epsilon_b) / R
I = V / (R - epsilon_b)
I = epsilon_b / (V R)
mcqs.why: Because back e.m.f. opposes the applied voltage, the net voltage is V - epsilon_b, so I = (V - epsilon_b) / R as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: At the moment a motor starts, its back e.m.f. is
options: Maximum, because the current is largest
Equal to the applied voltage
Zero, because the rotor is still
Negative, because the rotor turns backwards
mcqs.why: At start the rotor is still, so no e.m.f. is induced by rotation: epsilon_b = 0 and the current is at its largest, I = V / R.

mcqs.q: A motor with circuit resistance 10 ohm is connected to 220 V. Its starting current is
mcqs.why: At start epsilon_b = 0, so I = V / R = 220 / 10 = 22 A, the largest current the motor draws, from the formula in the notes.

mcqs.q: The same motor running with back e.m.f. 200 V on a 220 V supply with R = 10 ohm takes a current of
options: 2 A
mcqs.why: I = (V - epsilon_b) / R = (220 - 200) / 10 = 20 / 10 = 2 A, much less than the 22 A starting current because back e.m.f. has grown.

mcqs.q: Why does a bulb in a house dim for a moment when a heavy motor starts?
options: The motor sends its back e.m.f. into the bulb
The large starting current drops voltage in the house wiring
The bulb filament cools when any motor starts
The supply frequency falls while the motor starts
mcqs.why: At start back e.m.f. is zero, the motor draws a big current, and that current drops voltage in the house wiring, dimming the bulb briefly.

mcqs.q: As a motor speeds up after starting, the current it takes
options: Rises steadily as back e.m.f. grows
Stays at the starting value
Falls to its normal running value as back e.m.f. grows
Falls to zero and the motor stops
mcqs.why: Speeding up raises the back e.m.f., so (V - epsilon_b) shrinks and the current falls to its normal running value, per the notes.

mcqs.q: If the load on a motor grows, the motor responds by
options: Speeding up, so back e.m.f. rises and current falls
Keeping exactly the same current whatever the load
Switching itself off until the load is removed
Slowing a little, so back e.m.f. falls and current rises by itself to meet the load
mcqs.why: The notes explain: more load slows the motor slightly, back e.m.f. falls, and the current rises by itself to meet the load.

mcqs.q: Back e.m.f. opposes the applied voltage. This is an example of
options: Lenz's law
Faraday's law giving only the size
The transformer turns rule
The resonance condition
mcqs.why: The notes state back e.m.f. opposes the applied voltage by Lenz's law, which is why it limits the motor current.

mcqs.q: In the motor current formula, R stands for
options: The reactance of the motor coil, in ohm
The resistance of the motor circuit, in ohm
The radius of the motor coil, in metres
The rate of rotation of the motor
mcqs.why: The notes define R as the resistance of the motor circuit in ohm, V as applied voltage and epsilon_b as back e.m.f., both in volts.

lessons.title: Eddy Current
lessons.notes_html:
Eddy currents are loops of current induced in a solid piece of metal when the flux through it changes. Like eddies in water, they circulate inside the metal and waste energy as heat.

Advantages and Disadvantages

Useful usesHarmful effects
Induction furnaces for melting metalHeat loss in transformer cores
Induction cookersHeat loss in motors and generators
Electromagnetic brakesLower efficiency of machines
Damping in galvanometersExtra energy wasted as I2 R heat

Reducing Eddy Currents

Cores are laminated: built from thin sheets insulated from each other. Lamination breaks up the paths of the eddy currents and greatly reduces them, while the flux can still pass along the sheets.

Their direction follows Lenz's law, so they oppose the change that produces them, which is also why a metal plate swinging in a field is slowed down.

mcqs.q: Eddy currents are
options: Currents that flow only in the wires of a coil
Loops of current induced in a solid piece of metal when the flux through it changes
Loops of current in water cooling a machine
Steady currents supplied by a battery to a core
mcqs.why: The notes define eddy currents as loops induced inside a solid piece of metal when flux changes, circulating like eddies in water.

mcqs.q: Eddy currents are harmful in transformer cores because they
options: Increase the secondary voltage too much
Magnetise the core permanently
Waste energy as heat
Stop the flux from reaching the secondary
mcqs.why: Eddy currents circulate inside the metal and waste energy as I^2 R heat, causing heat loss in transformer cores, per the notes.

mcqs.q: Which is a useful application of eddy currents?
options: Laminating transformer cores
Insulating motor windings
Reducing the efficiency of generators
Induction furnaces for melting metal
mcqs.why: The table in the notes lists induction furnaces for melting metal, induction cookers, electromagnetic brakes and galvanometer damping as useful uses.

mcqs.q: Electromagnetic brakes work using
options: Eddy currents
Back e.m.f. in a stator
Mutual inductance between coils
Resonance in an LC circuit
mcqs.why: Electromagnetic brakes are listed in the notes among the useful applications of eddy currents, which oppose the motion producing them.

mcqs.q: Eddy currents are reduced in cores by
options: Making the core from one thicker solid block
Laminating the core: building it from thin sheets insulated from each other
Removing all insulation between core parts
Winding the core with thicker copper wire
mcqs.why: Lamination breaks up the paths of the eddy currents and greatly reduces them, while flux can still pass along the sheets.

mcqs.q: Lamination reduces eddy currents greatly, but the magnetic flux
options: Is blocked completely by the insulation
Must flow across the sheets instead
Can still pass along the sheets
Is reduced to zero in the core
mcqs.why: The notes state lamination breaks up eddy current paths while the flux can still pass along the thin sheets of the core.

mcqs.q: The direction of eddy currents follows
options: The direction of the applied voltage only
The right-hand rule for a straight wire only
No law; their direction is random
Lenz's law, so they oppose the change that produces them
mcqs.why: Their direction follows Lenz's law, opposing the change that produces them, which is why a swinging metal plate in a field is slowed.

mcqs.q: A harmful effect of eddy currents in motors and generators is
options: Lower efficiency of the machines
Higher output voltage at no load
Quieter running of the machines
Longer life of the windings
mcqs.why: The notes list heat loss in motors and generators and the resulting lower efficiency among the harmful effects of eddy currents.

mcqs.q: Damping in galvanometers is provided by
options: Slip rings
Eddy currents
Carbon brushes
Laminated windings
mcqs.why: Damping in galvanometers appears in the notes' list of useful eddy current applications; the currents oppose the coil's motion and settle it.

mcqs.q: The energy wasted by eddy currents appears as
options: Light given out by the core
Extra flux in the core
I^2 R heat in the metal
Sound in the windings
mcqs.why: The notes describe the harmful effect as extra energy wasted as I^2 R heat, since the circulating currents flow through the metal's resistance.

lessons.title: Transformer
lessons.notes_html:
A transformer transfers electrical energy from one circuit to another by mutual induction and changes the voltage, without changing the frequency. It works only on A.C., because only a changing flux can induce an e.m.f.; steady D.C. gives a steady flux and no secondary e.m.f., and would overheat the primary.

Working and Turns Ratio

An alternating current in the primary coil makes a changing flux in the laminated soft iron core. The core carries the flux to the secondary coil, where it induces an alternating e.m.f. The soft iron core increases the flux linking both coils.

Vs / Vp = Ns / Np

  • Vs, Vp - secondary and primary voltages; Ns, Np - their numbers of turns
  • For an ideal transformer input power = output power, so Vp Ip = Vs Is.

Step-Up and Step-Down

Step-upStep-down
Ns greater than Np, Vs greater than VpNs less than Np, Vs less than Vp
Secondary current smallerSecondary current larger
Used at power stationsUsed near consumers

For long distance transmission, power is sent at high voltage and small current, which cuts the I2 R loss in the lines. An ideal transformer has no losses: no copper loss, no hysteresis or eddy loss, and no flux leakage. Real losses are cut by thick low resistance windings, a soft core with a narrow hysteresis loop, lamination against eddy currents, and coils wound close together against flux leakage.

Worked Example: Step-Down Transformer

An ideal step-down transformer works on a 2.5 kV line and supplies 80 A. The primary to secondary turns ratio is 20:1. Find the secondary voltage, primary current and output power.

Step 1: Vs = Vp / 20 = 2500 / 20 = 125 V, about 0.13 kV.

Step 2: Ip = Is / 20 = 80 / 20 = 4 A.

Step 3: Output power = Vs Is = 125 x 80 = 10000 W.

Answer: Vs is about 0.13 kV, Ip = 4 A, output power = 10 kW.

Key Points

  • Induced e.m.f. appears only while the flux linked with a coil changes; a still magnet induces nothing.
  • Motional e.m.f.: ε = v B l for motion across the field.
  • Faraday's law: ε = - N ΔΦ / Δt; the e.m.f. depends on the rate of change of flux.
  • Lenz's law gives the direction: the induced current opposes the change, conserving energy.
  • Mutual induction: εs = - M ΔIp / Δt; self-induction: ε = - L ΔI / Δt; unit henry.
  • Energy stored in an inductor: U = 1/2 L I2.
  • A.C. generator: ε = N B A ω sin θ, with slip rings and carbon brushes giving A.C. output.
  • Motor current: I = (V - εb) / R; back e.m.f. is zero at start, so starting current is largest.
  • Eddy currents waste heat in solid cores; lamination reduces them.
  • Transformer: Vs / Vp = Ns / Np, works only on A.C., frequency unchanged.

mcqs.q: A transformer transfers electrical energy between circuits by
options: Self-induction, changing both voltage and frequency
A direct wire connection between the circuits
Mutual induction, changing the voltage without changing the frequency
Motional e.m.f. in a rotating coil
mcqs.why: The notes state a transformer works by mutual induction and changes the voltage, without changing the frequency of the supply.

mcqs.q: A transformer works only on A.C. because
options: D.C. voltage is always too low for a transformer
The core cannot carry any flux from D.C.
D.C. would make the secondary voltage too high
Only a changing flux can induce an e.m.f.; steady D.C. gives a steady flux and no secondary e.m.f.
mcqs.why: Steady D.C. produces a steady flux, which induces nothing in the secondary, and would overheat the primary, as the notes explain.

mcqs.q: The transformer turns ratio is
options: V_s / V_p = N_s / N_p
V_s / V_p = N_p / N_s
V_s x V_p = N_s x N_p
V_s / N_p = V_p / N_s with voltages crossed
mcqs.why: The notes give V_s / V_p = N_s / N_p: the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio for secondary and primary coils.

mcqs.q: For an ideal transformer, input power equals output power, so
options: V_p I_s = V_s I_p in all cases
V_p I_p = V_s I_s
I_p = I_s whatever the turns ratio
V_p = V_s whatever the turns ratio
mcqs.why: An ideal transformer has no losses, so V_p I_p = V_s I_s; stepping voltage up steps current down by the same ratio.

mcqs.q: In a step-up transformer
options: N_s is less than N_p and V_s is greater than V_p
N_s is greater than N_p and the secondary current is larger
N_s is greater than N_p and V_s is greater than V_p, with a smaller secondary current
N_s equals N_p and only the current changes
mcqs.why: The step-up column in the notes: more secondary turns, higher secondary voltage, smaller secondary current; used at power stations.

mcqs.q: Step-down transformers are used
options: At power stations, to raise voltage for transmission
In the middle of long transmission lines only
Only inside generators to raise the output
Near consumers, with N_s less than N_p and a larger secondary current
mcqs.why: The notes place step-down transformers near consumers: fewer secondary turns, lower voltage and larger secondary current.

mcqs.q: Power is transmitted over long distances at high voltage and small current because this
options: Cuts the I^2 R loss in the lines
Increases the frequency of the supply
Removes the need for transformers
Makes the line resistance zero
mcqs.why: Line loss is I^2 R, so a small current at high voltage greatly reduces wasted heat during long-distance transmission.

mcqs.q: An ideal step-down transformer works on a 2.5 kV line, supplies 80 A, with turns ratio 20:1. The secondary voltage is
options: 250 V, about 0.25 kV
125 V, about 0.13 kV
50 V, about 0.05 kV
500 V, about 0.5 kV
mcqs.why: V_s = V_p / 20 = 2500 / 20 = 125 V, about 0.13 kV, from V_s / V_p = N_s / N_p with ratio 20:1, as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: For that same transformer, the primary current and output power are
options: I_p = 40 A and output power = 10 kW
I_p = 4 A and output power = 1 kW
I_p = 4 A and output power = 10 kW
I_p = 1600 A and output power = 200 kW
mcqs.why: I_p = I_s / 20 = 80 / 20 = 4 A. Output power = V_s I_s = 125 x 80 = 10000 W = 10 kW, matching the worked example.

mcqs.q: Real transformer losses are reduced by laminating the core. This acts against
options: Copper loss in the windings
Flux leakage between the coils
Hysteresis loss in the core
Eddy current loss
mcqs.why: The notes match each remedy to its loss: lamination fights eddy currents, thick low-resistance windings fight copper loss, coils close together fight flux leakage.

lessons.title: Alternating Current
lessons.notes_html:
An alternating current (A.C.) is a current whose magnitude changes continuously and whose direction reverses periodically. An alternating voltage varies in the same way. A steady current that flows in one direction only is direct current (D.C.).

Mathematical and Graphical Form

I = I0 sin(ω t)

  • I — instantaneous current at time t; I0 — peak current, the maximum value; ω — angular frequency, unit rad s-1

V = V0 sin(ω t)

  • V — instantaneous voltage; V0 — peak voltage; t — time, unit s

ω = 2 π f

  • f — frequency of the supply, unit Hz; one complete cycle takes period T = 1 / f

Graphically both current and voltage are sine waves against time: starting from zero, rising to a positive peak, falling through zero to an equal negative peak, and returning to zero in one cycle.

Mean, Peak and R.M.S. Values

The mean value of current over one complete cycle is zero, because the positive half cycle cancels the negative half cycle. That is why we use the mean of I2, which is never negative. The root mean square (r.m.s.) value is the effective value: the D.C. value that gives the same heating effect in a resistor.

Irms = I0 / √2 = 0.707 I0

  • Irms — r.m.s. current, unit A; 0.707 is 70.7 percent of the peak value

Vrms = V0 / √2 = 0.707 V0

  • Vrms — r.m.s. voltage, unit V

The 220 V marked on a supply is its r.m.s. value. Its peak is √2 x 220 V, about 311 V, so 220 V A.C. gives a stronger effect than 220 V D.C. A.C. and D.C. become equal in effect at the r.m.s. value. If the initial phase is π / 2, one cycle completes at phase 5π / 2.

Worked Example: Peak and Instantaneous Current

The r.m.s. value of an alternating current is 5 A and its frequency is 50 Hz. Calculate the peak current and the value of the current after 0.002 s.

Step 1: Peak current I0 = √2 x Irms = 1.414 x 5 A = 7.07 A, about 7 A.

Step 2: Angular frequency ω = 2 π f = 2 x 3.14 x 50 = 314 rad s-1.

Step 3: At t = 0.002 s, phase ω t = 314 x 0.002 = 0.628 rad, which is 36 degrees.

Step 4: Instantaneous current i = I0 sin(ω t) = 7.07 x sin 36 degrees = 7.07 x 0.588 = 4.2 A.

Answer: Peak current is about 7 A and the current after 0.002 s is about 4.2 A. (The book printed answer 4.4 A is wrong; the correct value is 4.1 A with the rounded peak 7 A, or 4.2 A with 7.07 A.)

mcqs.q: An alternating current is a current whose
options: Magnitude changes continuously and direction reverses periodically
Magnitude is constant and direction never changes
Direction reverses but magnitude stays constant
Magnitude changes but direction never reverses
mcqs.why: The notes define A.C. as a current whose magnitude changes continuously and whose direction reverses periodically; D.C. flows one way only.

mcqs.q: The instantaneous alternating current is written as
options: I = I_0 cos(omega / t)
I = I_0 sin(omega t)
I = I_rms sin(omega / t)
I = omega sin(I_0 t)
mcqs.why: The notes give I = I_0 sin(omega t), where I_0 is the peak current and omega is the angular frequency in rad s-1.

mcqs.q: The angular frequency omega is related to frequency f by
options: omega = f / (2 pi)
omega = 2 pi / f
omega = 2 pi f
omega = pi f / 2
mcqs.why: The notes give omega = 2 pi f, with f in hertz; one complete cycle takes the period T = 1 / f.

mcqs.q: The mean value of an alternating current over one complete cycle is
options: Equal to the peak value I_0
Equal to 0.707 times the peak value
Equal to half the peak value
Zero, because the positive half cycle cancels the negative half cycle
mcqs.why: Over a full cycle the positive half cancels the negative half, giving a mean of zero, which is why the mean of I^2 is used instead.

mcqs.q: The r.m.s. value of an alternating current is
options: I_rms = I_0 x sqrt(2) = 1.414 I_0
I_rms = I_0, the same as the peak
mcqs.why: The notes give I_rms = I_0 / sqrt(2) = 0.707 I_0; the r.m.s. value is 70.7 percent of the peak value.

mcqs.q: The r.m.s. value is called the effective value because it is
options: The average of the positive half cycle only
The D.C. value that gives the same heating effect in a resistor
The value shown by a galvanometer at its peak
The D.C. value that gives twice the heating effect
mcqs.why: By definition in the notes, the r.m.s. value is the D.C. value producing the same heating effect in a resistor as the A.C.

mcqs.q: The 220 V marked on a supply is its r.m.s. value. Its peak value is about
mcqs.why: Peak = sqrt(2) x V_rms = 1.414 x 220 = 311.1 V, about 311 V, so 220 V A.C. peaks higher than 220 V D.C., as the notes state.

mcqs.q: An alternating current has r.m.s. value 5 A at 50 Hz. Its peak current is about
options: 5 A
mcqs.why: I_0 = sqrt(2) x I_rms = 1.414 x 5 = 7.07 A, about 7 A, from the worked example in the notes.

mcqs.q: For that 50 Hz current, the angular frequency and the current after 0.002 s are
options: omega = 314 rad s-1 and i is about 4.2 A
omega = 100 rad s-1 and i is about 7 A
omega = 314 rad s-1 and i is about 7.07 A
omega = 50 rad s-1 and i is about 2.5 A
mcqs.why: omega = 2 pi f = 2 x 3.14 x 50 = 314 rad s-1. Phase = 314 x 0.002 = 0.628 rad = 36 degrees, so i = 7.07 x sin 36 degrees = 7.07 x 0.588 = 4.2 A.

mcqs.q: The period of a 50 Hz alternating current is
mcqs.why: T = 1 / f = 1 / 50 = 0.02 s. One complete cycle of a 50 Hz supply takes one fiftieth of a second, from T = 1 / f in the notes.

lessons.title: A.C. Circuit and A.C. through a Resistor
lessons.notes_html:
An A.C. circuit is a circuit connected to an alternating supply. Its behaviour depends on the phase relation between voltage and current, shown clearly on a phasor diagram.

Phase, Phasor and Phasor Diagram

The phase of an alternating quantity is the angle ω t, plus any initial phase, which fixes its position in the cycle. A phasor is a rotating vector whose length gives the peak value and whose angle gives the phase. A phasor diagram shows several phasors together, so phase differences can be read at a glance. If current reaches its peak after voltage, it lags; if it reaches its peak before voltage, it leads.

A.C. through a Resistor

When an A.C. voltage is applied across a resistor R, voltage and current are in phase: they rise, peak and fall together, with no phase difference.

I = V / R

  • I — current through the resistor, unit A; V — voltage across it, unit V; R — resistance, unit Ω

The instantaneous power is p = V I. Averaged over a complete cycle, all the power is dissipated as heat in the resistor.

P = Vrms Irms

  • P — average power, unit W; this is the average power dissipation across a resistor

P = Irms2 R

  • Power can also be written as P = Vrms2 / R; use whichever form fits the data given

Worked Example: Heating in a Resistor

An alternating current flows through a resistor of 10 Ω and produces heat at the rate of 360 W. Calculate the effective value of current and voltage.

Step 1: Power in a resistor is P = Irms2 R.

Step 2: Irms = √(P / R) = √(360 / 10) = √36 = 6 A.

Step 3: Effective voltage Vrms = Irms R = 6 x 10 = 60 V.

Answer: The effective current is 6 A and the effective voltage is 60 V.

mcqs.q: The phase of an alternating quantity is
options: The peak value of the quantity
The angle omega t, plus any initial phase, fixing its position in the cycle
The frequency of the supply in hertz
The length of its phasor only
mcqs.why: The notes define phase as the angle omega t plus any initial phase, which fixes where the quantity is in its cycle.

mcqs.q: A phasor is
options: A fixed arrow showing only the r.m.s. value
A graph of voltage against current
A rotating vector whose length gives the peak value and whose angle gives the phase
A resistor drawn in a circuit diagram
mcqs.why: The notes define a phasor as a rotating vector: length gives peak value, angle gives phase, and phasor diagrams show phase differences at a glance.

mcqs.q: If a current reaches its peak after the voltage, the current is said to
options: Lead the voltage
Be in phase with the voltage
Cancel the voltage
Lag the voltage
mcqs.why: The notes state: if current reaches its peak after voltage, it lags; if it reaches its peak before voltage, it leads.

mcqs.q: When A.C. passes through a resistor, voltage and current are
options: In phase: they rise, peak and fall together
90 degrees out of phase
In opposite phase, differing by 180 degrees
Out of phase by 45 degrees
mcqs.why: For a resistor the notes state voltage and current are in phase with no phase difference, and I = V / R at every instant.

mcqs.q: The average power dissipated in a resistor on A.C. is
options: P = V_rms I_rms
Zero, because the current reverses
P = V_rms / I_rms
mcqs.why: Averaged over a complete cycle, all the power is dissipated as heat, giving P = V_rms I_rms, also written I_rms^2 R or V_rms^2 / R.

mcqs.q: An alternating current through a 10 ohm resistor produces heat at 360 W. The effective current is
options: 6 A
mcqs.why: P = I_rms^2 R, so I_rms = sqrt(P / R) = sqrt(360 / 10) = sqrt(36) = 6 A, from the worked example in the notes.

mcqs.q: For that resistor, the effective voltage across it is
mcqs.why: V_rms = I_rms R = 6 x 10 = 60 V. Check: P = V_rms I_rms = 60 x 6 = 360 W, matching the worked example.

mcqs.q: Power in a resistor can also be written as
options: P = V_rms^2 / R
P = R / V_rms^2
P = V_rms^2 R^2
P = I_rms / R^2
mcqs.why: The notes give the three equivalent forms P = V_rms I_rms = I_rms^2 R = V_rms^2 / R, using whichever fits the data given.

mcqs.q: The instantaneous power in a resistor circuit is
options: p = V / I
p = V I
p = I / V
p = V I / 2 at every instant
