mcqs.why: The notes give the instantaneous power as p = V I; averaged over a complete cycle in a resistor it becomes P = V_rms I_rms.

mcqs.q: A phasor diagram is useful in an A.C. circuit because it shows
options: The exact resistance of every component
The heating produced in each part
Several phasors together, so phase differences can be read at a glance
The frequency of the supply directly
mcqs.why: The notes state a phasor diagram shows several phasors together so that phase differences between voltage and current can be read at a glance.

lessons.title: A.C. through a Capacitor
lessons.notes_html:
When an A.C. voltage is applied across a capacitor, the current leads the voltage by 90 degrees, that is by π / 2 or a quarter cycle.

Why the Current Leads

Current must flow first to build up charge on the plates. So the current reaches its peak a quarter cycle before the voltage across the capacitor reaches its peak. This is the cause of current leading in a capacitive circuit.

Capacitive Reactance

The opposition offered by a capacitor is the capacitive reactance. It falls as frequency rises, so a capacitor works best at high frequency and blocks steady D.C.

XC = 1 / (2 π f C)

  • XC — capacitive reactance, unit Ω; f — frequency, unit Hz; C — capacitance, unit F

I = V / XC

  • I — r.m.s. current, unit A; V — r.m.s. voltage across the capacitor, unit V

Power in a Capacitor

Energy is stored in the electric field of the capacitor in one quarter cycle and returned to the source in the next. The average power over a complete cycle is zero: an ideal capacitor dissipates no power.

Worked Example: Current through a Capacitor

A capacitor of capacitance 6 µF is connected across an A.C. source of 220 V. Calculate the current through the capacitor if the frequency of the source is 50 Hz.

Step 1: XC = 1 / (2 π f C) = 1 / (2 x 3.14 x 50 x 6 x 10-6).

Step 2: Denominator = 1.885 x 10-3, so XC = 1 / (1.885 x 10-3) = 530.5 Ω.

Step 3: Current I = V / XC = 220 / 530.5 = 0.415 A.

Answer: The current through the capacitor is about 0.4 A.

mcqs.q: When A.C. passes through a capacitor, the current
options: Lags the voltage by 90 degrees
Is exactly in phase with the voltage
Leads the voltage by 90 degrees, that is pi / 2 or a quarter cycle
Leads the voltage by 180 degrees
mcqs.why: The notes state the current leads the voltage by 90 degrees in a capacitor, because charge must build up before voltage reaches its peak.

mcqs.q: The current leads in a capacitor because
options: The capacitor stores magnetic energy first
The plates resist the flow of current at the start
The voltage is generated inside the capacitor
Current must flow first to build up charge on the plates
mcqs.why: Current flows first to charge the plates, so current peaks a quarter cycle before the voltage across the capacitor peaks.

mcqs.q: The capacitive reactance is given by
options: X_C = 1 / (2 pi f C)
X_C = 2 pi f C
X_C = 1 / (2 pi f / C)
X_C = 2 pi f / C
mcqs.why: The notes give X_C = 1 / (2 pi f C), in ohm, with f in hertz and C in farad; reactance falls as frequency rises.

mcqs.q: As the frequency of the supply increases, the capacitive reactance
options: Rises, so a capacitor blocks high frequency
Falls, so a capacitor works best at high frequency
Stays exactly the same
Falls to zero only at zero frequency
mcqs.why: X_C = 1 / (2 pi f C) is inversely proportional to f, so higher frequency means lower reactance; a capacitor blocks steady D.C.

mcqs.q: A capacitor blocks steady D.C. because
options: Its plates melt at zero frequency
D.C. cannot produce any charge on plates
At zero frequency its reactance X_C is effectively infinite
Its capacitance becomes zero for D.C.
mcqs.why: For D.C., f = 0, so X_C = 1 / (2 pi f C) becomes infinitely large; the notes state a capacitor blocks steady D.C.

mcqs.q: A 6 microfarad capacitor is connected across 220 V at 50 Hz. Its reactance is about
options: 53 ohm
1061 ohm
mcqs.why: X_C = 1 / (2 pi f C) = 1 / (2 x 3.14 x 50 x 6 x 10^-6) = 1 / (1.885 x 10^-3) = 530.5 ohm, from the worked example.

mcqs.q: The current through that 6 microfarad capacitor (220 V, 50 Hz, X_C = 530.5 ohm) is about
options: 4 A
mcqs.why: I = V / X_C = 220 / 530.5 = 0.415 A, about 0.4 A, using I = V / X_C with r.m.s. values as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: If the frequency for that capacitor were doubled to 100 Hz, its reactance would become about
options: 1061 ohm, double the 50 Hz value
265 ohm, half of 530.5 ohm
530.5 ohm, unchanged
132 ohm, a quarter of the 50 Hz value
mcqs.why: X_C = 1 / (2 pi f C) = 1 / (2 x 3.14 x 100 x 6 x 10^-6) = 265.3 ohm. Doubling f halves X_C because X_C varies as 1 / f.

mcqs.q: The average power over a complete cycle in an ideal capacitor is
options: Equal to V_rms I_rms
Equal to half of V_rms I_rms
Zero: an ideal capacitor dissipates no power
Maximum at the peak of the voltage
mcqs.why: Energy stored in the electric field in one quarter cycle is returned in the next, so the average power over a cycle is zero.

mcqs.q: In a capacitor, energy is stored in
options: The magnetic field around its leads
The resistance of its plates as heat
The supply, and never in the capacitor
The electric field of the capacitor
mcqs.why: The notes state energy is stored in the electric field of the capacitor in one quarter cycle and returned to the source in the next.

lessons.title: A.C. through an Inductor
lessons.notes_html:
When an ideal inductor is connected across an A.C. source, the current lags the voltage by 90 degrees, that is by π / 2.

Instantaneous Values

If the applied voltage is V = V0 sin(ω t), the current is i = (V0 / XL) sin(ω t - π / 2). The current reaches its peak a quarter cycle after the voltage.

Inductive Reactance

The opposition offered by an inductor is the inductive reactance. It rises directly with frequency: if frequency increases, reactance increases and current decreases.

XL = 2 π f L

  • XL — inductive reactance, unit Ω; f — frequency, unit Hz; L — inductance, unit H

I = V / XL

  • I — r.m.s. current, unit A; V — r.m.s. voltage across the inductor, unit V

Power in an Inductor

Energy is stored in the magnetic field of the inductor and then returned to the source. The average power dissipated over a complete cycle is zero. In a pure LC circuit the power dissipation is also zero.

Worked Example: Current through an Inductor

An inductor of inductance 0.6 H is connected across an A.C. source of 220 V. Calculate the current through the inductor if the frequency of the source is 50 Hz.

Step 1: XL = 2 π f L = 2 x 3.14 x 50 x 0.6 = 188.5 Ω.

Step 2: Current I = V / XL = 220 / 188.5 = 1.167 A.

Answer: The current through the inductor is about 1.2 A.

mcqs.q: When A.C. passes through an ideal inductor, the current
options: Leads the voltage by 90 degrees
Is exactly in phase with the voltage
Lags the voltage by 180 degrees
Lags the voltage by 90 degrees, that is pi / 2
mcqs.why: The notes state the current lags the voltage by 90 degrees in an inductor, reaching its peak a quarter cycle after the voltage.

mcqs.q: If the applied voltage is V = V_0 sin(omega t), the current through an inductor is
options: i = (V_0 / X_L) sin(omega t - pi / 2)
i = (V_0 / X_L) sin(omega t + pi / 2)
i = (V_0 X_L) sin(omega t)
i = (V_0 / X_L) sin(omega t) with no phase shift
mcqs.why: The minus pi / 2 in the notes' expression shows the current lagging the voltage by a quarter cycle in a pure inductor.

mcqs.q: The inductive reactance is given by
options: X_L = 1 / (2 pi f L)
X_L = 2 pi f L
X_L = 2 pi f / L
X_L = L / (2 pi f)
mcqs.why: The notes give X_L = 2 pi f L, in ohm, with f in hertz and L in henry; the reactance rises directly with frequency.

mcqs.q: As frequency increases for an inductor, the reactance and current
options: Reactance decreases and current increases
Both reactance and current increase
Reactance increases and current decreases
Reactance increases and current stays the same
mcqs.why: X_L = 2 pi f L rises with f, and since I = V / X_L, a larger reactance means a smaller current, as the notes state.

mcqs.q: An inductor of 0.6 H is connected across 220 V at 50 Hz. Its reactance is
options: 377 ohm
mcqs.why: X_L = 2 pi f L = 2 x 3.14 x 50 x 0.6 = 188.4, about 188.5 ohm, from the worked example in the notes.

mcqs.q: The current through that 0.6 H inductor (220 V, X_L = 188.5 ohm) is about
mcqs.why: I = V / X_L = 220 / 188.5 = 1.167 A, about 1.2 A, using r.m.s. values as in the worked example in the notes.

mcqs.q: The average power dissipated over a complete cycle in an ideal inductor is
options: V_rms I_rms
Zero
Half of V_rms I_rms
I_rms^2 X_L
mcqs.why: Energy stored in the magnetic field is returned to the source, so the average power over a complete cycle is zero for a pure inductor.

mcqs.q: In an inductor, energy is stored in and returned from
options: Its electric field
Heat in its winding resistance
Its magnetic field
Charge on its end plates
mcqs.why: The notes state energy is stored in the magnetic field of the inductor and then returned to the source, giving zero average power.

mcqs.q: In a pure LC circuit, the power dissipation is
options: Double that of a resistor circuit
Equal to V_rms I_rms
Small but always positive
Also zero
mcqs.why: The notes add that in a pure LC circuit the power dissipation is also zero, because both L and C only store and return energy.

mcqs.q: The current through an inductor is calculated from the r.m.s. voltage by
options: I = V / X_L
I = V X_L
I = X_L / V
I = V / (2 pi X_L)
mcqs.why: The notes give I = V / X_L, with V the r.m.s. voltage across the inductor and I the r.m.s. current, both in standard units.

lessons.title: Impedance
lessons.notes_html:
Impedance is the total opposition offered by an A.C. circuit to alternating current. It combines resistance with reactance, and its unit is the ohm (Ω).

Impedance of a Series RLC Circuit

In a series RLC circuit the voltage across R is in phase with the current, the voltage across L leads the current by 90 degrees, and the voltage across C lags by 90 degrees. So VL and VC are opposite to each other: their phase difference is π. Adding the phasors gives the total voltage and hence the impedance.

Z = √(R2 + (XL - XC)2)

  • Z — impedance, unit Ω; R — resistance, unit Ω; XL and XC — reactances, unit Ω

Z = V / I

  • V — r.m.s. supply voltage, unit V; I — r.m.s. circuit current, unit A

At resonance XL = XC, so the net reactance is zero and Z = R, its minimum value. Impedance is the key quantity in every series A.C. circuit in this unit: once Z is known, the current and the phase angle follow from it.

mcqs.q: Impedance is
options: The total opposition offered by an A.C. circuit to alternating current
The opposition offered by a resistor only
The sum of the voltages in an A.C. circuit
The power factor of an A.C. circuit
mcqs.why: The notes define impedance as the total opposition combining resistance with reactance, measured in ohm.

mcqs.q: The impedance of a series RLC circuit is
options: Z = R + X_L + X_C
Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2)
Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L + X_C)^2)
Z = (X_L - X_C) / R
mcqs.why: V_L and V_C are opposite in phase, so their reactances subtract; adding phasors gives Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2) in the notes.

mcqs.q: In a series RLC circuit, the phase difference between V_L and V_C is
options: Zero, because they are in phase
Pi / 2, because they are at right angles
Pi (180 degrees), because they are opposite to each other
Pi / 4, because they partly cancel
mcqs.why: V_L leads the current by 90 degrees and V_C lags by 90 degrees, so they differ by 180 degrees, that is pi, and partly cancel.

mcqs.q: Impedance is related to voltage and current by
options: Z = V I
Z = I / V
Z = V^2 / I
Z = V / I
mcqs.why: The notes give Z = V / I, with V the r.m.s. supply voltage and I the r.m.s. circuit current, giving Z in ohm.

mcqs.q: A series RLC circuit has R = 6 ohm, X_L = 10 ohm and X_C = 2 ohm. Its impedance is
options: 10 ohm
18 ohm
14 ohm
8 ohm
mcqs.why: Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2) = sqrt(6^2 + (10 - 2)^2) = sqrt(36 + 64) = sqrt(100) = 10 ohm, using the impedance formula.

mcqs.q: With a supply of 100 V, the current in that circuit (Z = 10 ohm) is
options: 1 A
6 A
mcqs.why: I = V / Z = 100 / 10 = 10 A, from Z = V / I rearranged, using r.m.s. values as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: At resonance in a series RLC circuit, the impedance is
options: Maximum and equal to X_L + X_C
Zero, because all opposition disappears
Minimum and equal to R, because X_L = X_C
Equal to sqrt(R^2 + X_L^2) as usual
mcqs.why: At resonance X_L = X_C, the net reactance is zero and Z = sqrt(R^2 + 0) = R, its minimum value, as the notes state.

mcqs.q: In the series RLC circuit, the voltage across R is
options: Leading the current by 90 degrees
Lagging the current by 90 degrees
Opposite in phase to the current
In phase with the current
mcqs.why: The notes state the voltage across R is in phase with the current, while V_L leads by 90 degrees and V_C lags by 90 degrees.

mcqs.q: Once the impedance Z of a series A.C. circuit is known, the notes say we can find from it
options: The current and the phase angle
The frequency and the capacitance directly
The inductance and the resistance separately
The peak voltage of the supply only
mcqs.why: Impedance is the key quantity: once Z is known, the current follows from I = V / Z and the phase angle follows from the phasor diagram.

mcqs.q: The unit of impedance is
options: The henry
The ohm
The farad
The volt-ampere
mcqs.why: Impedance combines resistance and reactance, both in ohm, so its unit is the ohm, as stated in the notes.

lessons.title: A.C. through RC Series Circuit
lessons.notes_html:
In an RC series circuit a resistor and a capacitor carry the same current. The voltage across R is in phase with the current, while the voltage across C lags the current by 90 degrees, so R and XC act at right angles in the phasor diagram.

Impedance of the RC Circuit

Z = √(R2 + XC2)

  • Z — impedance, unit Ω; R — resistance, unit Ω; XC — capacitive reactance, unit Ω

Phase Angle

The current leads the applied voltage by the phase angle phi. From the phasor diagram the tangent of this angle is the ratio of reactance to resistance.

tan Φ = XC / R

  • Φ — phase angle by which current leads voltage; XC — capacitive reactance; R — resistance

Φ = tan-1(XC / R)

  • Find XC first from XC = 1 / (2 π f C), then use this relation for the angle

Because the capacitor dominates the phase behaviour, the RC circuit is a leading circuit: raise the frequency and XC falls, so Z falls and the current rises.

mcqs.q: In an RC series circuit, the resistor and capacitor
options: Carry currents 90 degrees apart in separate branches
Carry the same current
Have the same voltage at every instant
Share the current equally between them
mcqs.why: The notes state that in an RC series circuit a resistor and a capacitor carry the same current, being in series.

mcqs.q: The impedance of an RC series circuit is
options: Z = R + X_C
Z = sqrt(R^2 - X_C^2)
Z = sqrt(R^2 + X_C^2)
Z = sqrt(X_C^2 / R^2)
mcqs.why: V_R is in phase with the current and V_C lags by 90 degrees, so they act at right angles, giving Z = sqrt(R^2 + X_C^2).

mcqs.q: In an RC series circuit, the current relative to the applied voltage
options: Lags it by the phase angle phi
Is exactly in phase with it
Leads it by exactly 180 degrees
Leads it by the phase angle phi
mcqs.why: Because the capacitor dominates the phase behaviour, the RC circuit is a leading circuit: the current leads the applied voltage.

mcqs.q: The phase angle in an RC series circuit is found from
options: tan phi = X_C / R, so phi = tan^-1(X_C / R)
tan phi = R / X_C in all cases
sin phi = X_C / R
tan phi = X_C x R
mcqs.why: From the phasor diagram the tangent of the lead angle is reactance over resistance: tan phi = X_C / R, as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: An RC circuit has R = 3 ohm and X_C = 4 ohm. Its impedance and phase angle are
options: Z = 7 ohm and phi is about 37 degrees
Z = 5 ohm and phi is about 53 degrees
Z = 5 ohm and phi is about 37 degrees
Z = 1 ohm and phi is about 53 degrees
mcqs.why: Z = sqrt(R^2 + X_C^2) = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(25) = 5 ohm. tan phi = X_C / R = 4 / 3 = 1.333, so phi = tan^-1(1.333) = about 53 degrees, current leading.

mcqs.q: With a 50 V supply, the current in that RC circuit (Z = 5 ohm) is
options: 2 A
5 A
mcqs.why: I = V / Z = 50 / 5 = 10 A, using the impedance found from Z = sqrt(R^2 + X_C^2) for the RC series circuit.

mcqs.q: To find the phase angle of an RC circuit, the notes say you must first find
options: X_L, from X_L = 2 pi f L
The power factor, from cos phi
The resonance frequency of the circuit
X_C, from X_C = 1 / (2 pi f C)
mcqs.why: The notes instruct: find X_C first from X_C = 1 / (2 pi f C), then use tan phi = X_C / R for the angle.

mcqs.q: In an RC circuit, raising the frequency makes X_C fall, so
options: Z falls and the current rises
Z rises and the current falls
Z falls and the current falls
Z and the current both stay the same
mcqs.why: Higher f lowers X_C = 1 / (2 pi f C); with Z = sqrt(R^2 + X_C^2) smaller, I = V / Z rises, as the notes state.

mcqs.q: The voltage across the capacitor in an RC series circuit
options: Leads the current by 90 degrees
Lags the current by 90 degrees
Is in phase with the current
Leads the applied voltage by 90 degrees
mcqs.why: The notes state V_C lags the current by 90 degrees while V_R is in phase with it, so R and X_C act at right angles in the diagram.

mcqs.q: An RC series circuit is called a leading circuit because
options: Its voltage leads the current in the resistor
It is always used before other circuits
Its current leads the applied voltage
Its capacitor is placed first in the diagram
mcqs.why: The notes call the RC circuit a leading circuit because the capacitor makes the current lead the applied voltage by angle phi.

lessons.title: A.C. through RL Series Circuit
lessons.notes_html:
In an RL series circuit the same current flows through the resistor and the inductor. The voltage across R is in phase with the current, while the voltage across L leads the current by 90 degrees.

Impedance of the RL Circuit

The total voltage is the phasor sum of the two voltages, V = I √(R2 + XL2), which gives the impedance directly.

Z = √(R2 + XL2)

  • Z — impedance, unit Ω; R — resistance, unit Ω; XL — inductive reactance, unit Ω

Phase Angle

The current lags the applied voltage by the phase angle phi, found from the phasor diagram.

tan Φ = XL / R

  • Φ — phase angle by which current lags voltage; XL — inductive reactance; R — resistance

As frequency increases, XL = 2 π f L increases, so Z increases and the current decreases. The RL circuit is therefore a lagging circuit, the opposite of the RC circuit.

mcqs.q: In an RL series circuit, the same current flows through
options: The resistor only, bypassing the inductor
Two parallel branches of the circuit
The resistor and the inductor
The inductor only at high frequency
mcqs.why: The notes state that in an RL series circuit the same current flows through the resistor and the inductor, since they are in series.

mcqs.q: The impedance of an RL series circuit is
options: Z = R + X_L
Z = sqrt(R^2 - X_L^2)
Z = sqrt(R^2 + X_C^2)
Z = sqrt(R^2 + X_L^2)
mcqs.why: The total voltage is the phasor sum V = I sqrt(R^2 + X_L^2), which gives Z = sqrt(R^2 + X_L^2) directly, per the notes.

mcqs.q: In an RL series circuit, the current relative to the applied voltage
options: Lags it by the phase angle phi
Leads it by the phase angle phi
Is exactly in phase with it
Lags it by exactly 180 degrees
mcqs.why: The RL circuit is a lagging circuit, the opposite of the RC circuit: its current lags the applied voltage by angle phi.

mcqs.q: The phase angle in an RL series circuit is found from
options: tan phi = R / X_L in all cases
tan phi = X_L / R
tan phi = X_C / R
sin phi = X_L x R
mcqs.why: From the phasor diagram in the notes, tan phi = X_L / R, where phi is the angle by which current lags voltage.

mcqs.q: An RL circuit has R = 6 ohm and X_L = 8 ohm. Its impedance and phase angle are
options: Z = 14 ohm and phi is about 37 degrees
Z = 10 ohm and phi is about 37 degrees
Z = 10 ohm and phi is about 53 degrees
Z = 2 ohm and phi is about 53 degrees
mcqs.why: Z = sqrt(R^2 + X_L^2) = sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = sqrt(100) = 10 ohm. tan phi = X_L / R = 8 / 6 = 1.333, so phi = about 53 degrees, current lagging.

mcqs.q: With a 200 V supply, the current in that RL circuit (Z = 10 ohm) is
options: 2 A
mcqs.why: I = V / Z = 200 / 10 = 20 A, using the impedance Z = sqrt(R^2 + X_L^2) = 10 ohm for this RL circuit.

mcqs.q: The voltage across the inductor in an RL series circuit
options: Leads the current by 90 degrees
Lags the current by 90 degrees
Is in phase with the current
Lags the applied voltage by 90 degrees
mcqs.why: The notes state V_L leads the current by 90 degrees while V_R is in phase with it, so the two voltages add as phasors at right angles.

mcqs.q: As frequency increases in an RL circuit, X_L increases, so
options: Z decreases and the current increases
Z increases and the current decreases
Z increases and the current increases
Z and current both stay unchanged
mcqs.why: X_L = 2 pi f L rises with f, so Z = sqrt(R^2 + X_L^2) rises and I = V / Z falls, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: The RL circuit is the opposite of the RC circuit because
options: It contains no resistance at all
Its impedance is always smaller
Its current lags the voltage, while the RC current leads it
It works only on direct current
mcqs.why: The notes call the RL circuit a lagging circuit, the opposite of the RC leading circuit, because of the inductor's lagging effect.

mcqs.q: The total voltage in an RL series circuit is given by the phasor sum
options: V = I (R + X_L)
V = I sqrt(R^2 - X_L^2)
V = sqrt(R + X_L) / I
V = I sqrt(R^2 + X_L^2)
mcqs.why: Adding V_R and V_L as phasors at right angles gives V = I sqrt(R^2 + X_L^2), from which the impedance follows directly.

lessons.title: Power in an A.C. Circuit
lessons.notes_html:
The instantaneous power in an A.C. circuit is p = V I, but only part of it is useful on average, because voltage and current may not be in phase.

Average Power and Power Factor

P = Vrms Irms cos Φ

  • P — true or real power, unit W; Vrms Irms — apparent power, unit volt-ampere; Φ — phase angle between voltage and current

The power factor is the ratio of true power to apparent power. It tells what fraction of the apparent power is actually consumed.

Power factor = cos Φ

  • Power factor is 1 for a pure resistor, 0 for a pure inductor or capacitor, and R / Z for a series RLC circuit

Average power dissipation across a resistor alone is Vrms Irms, because there Φ = 0 and cos Φ = 1. In pure L, C or LC circuits the average power is zero, because energy is only stored and returned, never consumed.

mcqs.q: The average (true) power in an A.C. circuit is
options: P = V_rms I_rms in every circuit
P = V_rms I_rms sin phi
P = V_0 I_0 cos phi
P = V_rms I_rms cos phi
mcqs.why: Only part of the apparent power is useful when V and I are out of phase, so P = V_rms I_rms cos phi, as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: The product V_rms I_rms is called the
options: Apparent power, measured in volt-ampere
True power, measured in watt
Reactive power, measured in ohm
Power factor, which has no unit name here
mcqs.why: The notes distinguish true power in watt from apparent power V_rms I_rms, measured in volt-ampere.

mcqs.q: The power factor is defined as
options: The ratio of apparent power to true power
The ratio of true power to apparent power, equal to cos phi
The product of voltage and current
The phase angle itself in degrees
mcqs.why: Power factor = true power / apparent power = cos phi; it tells what fraction of the apparent power is actually consumed.

mcqs.q: The power factor of a pure resistor is
mcqs.why: For a pure resistor phi = 0 and cos phi = 1, so the power factor is 1 and P = V_rms I_rms, per the notes.

mcqs.q: The power factor of a pure inductor or a pure capacitor is
mcqs.why: For pure L or C, phi = 90 degrees and cos phi = 0, so the power factor is 0 and no average power is consumed.

mcqs.q: For a series RLC circuit, the power factor can be written as
options: R / Z
Z / R
X_L / Z in all cases
R x Z
mcqs.why: The notes give power factor = cos phi = R / Z for a series RLC circuit, since R is the adjacent side in the impedance phasor triangle.

mcqs.q: A circuit has V_rms = 100 V, I_rms = 2 A and cos phi = 0.5. Its true power is
mcqs.why: P = V_rms I_rms cos phi = 100 x 2 x 0.5 = 100 W. The apparent power is 100 x 2 = 200 volt-ampere, and only half is consumed.

mcqs.q: A series circuit has R = 3 ohm and Z = 5 ohm. Its power factor is
mcqs.why: Power factor = cos phi = R / Z = 3 / 5 = 0.6, using the series RLC relation given in the notes.

mcqs.q: In pure L, C or LC circuits, the average power is zero because
options: No current ever flows in them
The voltage is always zero in them
Their resistance is infinite
Energy is only stored and returned, never consumed
mcqs.why: The notes explain that in pure reactive circuits energy is stored in fields and returned to the source, never consumed as heat.

mcqs.q: The instantaneous power in an A.C. circuit is
options: p = V I
p = V / I
p = cos phi always
p = V_rms I_rms at every instant
mcqs.why: The notes give instantaneous power p = V I, but only the part V_rms I_rms cos phi is useful on average when phase differs.

lessons.title: Choke Coil
lessons.notes_html:
A choke coil is an inductor, usually wound on a laminated iron core, used to control current in an A.C. circuit. Ideally it dissipates no power.

Function of a Choke

Its reactance XL = ω L limits the current without wasting energy as heat, unlike a resistor, which would consume power all the time. This makes the choke the better current controller for A.C.

Why a Choke Cannot Control D.C.

For D.C. the frequency is zero, so ω = 0 and XL = 0. The choke then offers only the small resistance of its winding, so it cannot limit a direct current the way it limits an alternating current.

Applications

The common application is in fluorescent tube circuits, where the choke limits the current through the tube. Chokes are also used in radio circuits to block high-frequency currents while passing low-frequency or direct currents.

mcqs.q: A choke coil is
options: An inductor, usually wound on a laminated iron core, used to control current in an A.C. circuit
A resistor used to waste power as heat
A capacitor used to block alternating current
A transformer used to change voltage
mcqs.why: The notes define a choke coil this way and add that ideally it dissipates no power while controlling the current.

mcqs.q: A choke limits A.C. by means of its
options: Large winding resistance
Reactance X_L = omega L
Capacitance to the core
Back e.m.f. from a battery
mcqs.why: Its reactance X_L = omega L limits the current without wasting energy as heat, unlike a resistor, per the notes.

mcqs.q: A choke is a better A.C. current controller than a resistor because
options: It raises the supply voltage as it limits current
It stores the current and releases it later
It limits current without consuming power all the time, while a resistor would waste power as heat
It changes the frequency of the supply
mcqs.why: The notes contrast the two: a resistor consumes power continuously, but an ideal choke limits current by reactance with no power loss.

mcqs.q: A choke cannot control direct current because for D.C.
options: The inductance becomes infinite
The core becomes a permanent magnet
The current reverses too quickly
Frequency is zero, so omega = 0 and X_L = 0
mcqs.why: X_L = omega L = 2 pi f L; for D.C. f = 0, so X_L = 0 x L = 0, leaving only the small winding resistance, per the notes.

mcqs.q: For D.C., a choke offers only
options: The small resistance of its winding
An infinite reactance
The same reactance as at 50 Hz
A capacitive reactance instead
mcqs.why: With X_L = 0 at zero frequency, the notes say the choke then offers only the small resistance of its winding to direct current.

mcqs.q: The common application of a choke coil given in the notes is in
options: Radio receivers, where it detects the signal
Fluorescent tube circuits, where it limits the current through the tube
Generators, where it acts as the rotor
Motors, where it replaces the stator
mcqs.why: The notes name fluorescent tube circuits as the common application, with the choke limiting the current through the tube.

mcqs.q: Chokes are also used in radio circuits to
options: Block low-frequency currents while passing high-frequency ones
Convert radio waves into sound directly
Block high-frequency currents while passing low-frequency or direct currents
Raise the frequency of all currents
mcqs.why: Since X_L rises with frequency, a choke opposes high frequencies most; the notes state this radio use of chokes.

mcqs.q: Ideally, a choke coil dissipates
options: As much power as a resistor of the same reactance
Half the power supplied to it
Power only at switch-on
No power
mcqs.why: Like a pure inductor, an ideal choke stores and returns energy, so ideally it dissipates no power, as the notes state.

mcqs.q: The core of a choke coil is usually
options: Laminated iron
Solid copper
Solid hard steel in one block
Plastic, to block the flux
mcqs.why: The notes describe the choke as wound on a laminated iron core; lamination also reduces eddy currents in the core.

mcqs.q: If the frequency of the A.C. through a choke is increased, its limiting effect
options: Decreases, because X_L falls with frequency
Increases, because X_L = omega L increases
Stays the same at all frequencies
Becomes zero at high frequency
mcqs.why: X_L = omega L = 2 pi f L grows with frequency, so the choke opposes and limits the current more at higher frequency.

lessons.title: Resonance in an RLC Series Circuit
lessons.notes_html:
Resonance in a series RLC circuit occurs when the inductive reactance equals the capacitive reactance. The two reactances cancel, and the circuit behaves like a pure resistor.

Condition and Effects of Resonance

XL = XC

  • At this condition Z = √(R2 + (XL - XC)2) becomes minimum and equal to R

Because impedance is minimum, the amplitude of the current is maximum at resonance, I0 = V0 / R, and the power factor becomes 1.

Resonance Frequency

Setting ω L = 1 / (ω C) gives ω2 = 1 / (L C), from which the resonance frequency follows.

f = 1 / (2 π √(L C))

  • f — resonance frequency, unit Hz; L — inductance, unit H; C — capacitance, unit F

The sharp current peak at f0 is how series resonance is observed and used, for example in tuning a radio receiver to one station.

mcqs.q: Resonance in a series RLC circuit occurs when
options: The resistance equals the inductive reactance
The inductive reactance equals the capacitive reactance, X_L = X_C
The inductive reactance is twice the capacitive reactance
Both reactances are zero
mcqs.why: The notes define series resonance by X_L = X_C; the two reactances cancel and the circuit behaves like a pure resistor.

mcqs.q: At series resonance, the circuit behaves like
options: A pure inductor
A pure capacitor
A pure resistor
An open circuit
mcqs.why: With X_L and X_C cancelling, only R remains effective, so the notes say the circuit behaves like a pure resistor at resonance.

mcqs.q: At series resonance the impedance is
options: Maximum and equal to R
Minimum and equal to zero
Equal to X_L + X_C
Minimum and equal to R
mcqs.why: Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2) becomes sqrt(R^2 + 0) = R, its minimum value, when X_L = X_C at resonance.

mcqs.q: At series resonance the current is
options: Maximum, with I_0 = V_0 / R
Minimum, close to zero
Equal to V_0 / X_L
The same as at all other frequencies
mcqs.why: Minimum impedance means maximum current; the notes give the resonant peak current amplitude as I_0 = V_0 / R.

mcqs.q: The power factor at series resonance is
options: Equal to X_L / R
mcqs.why: At resonance the circuit is purely resistive in behaviour, so phi = 0 and the power factor cos phi becomes 1, per the notes.

mcqs.q: The resonance frequency of a series RLC circuit is
options: f = 2 pi sqrt(L C)
f = 1 / (2 pi L C)
f = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(L C))
f = sqrt(L C) / (2 pi)
mcqs.why: Setting omega L = 1 / (omega C) gives omega^2 = 1 / (L C), from which f = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(L C)) follows, as in the notes.

mcqs.q: For L = 0.1 H and C = 10 microfarad, the resonance frequency is about
options: 50 Hz
159 Hz

mcqs.q: The resonance condition is derived by setting
options: omega L = 1 / (omega C)
omega L = omega C
L = C in value
omega = L C
mcqs.why: X_L = omega L and X_C = 1 / (omega C); equating them gives omega L = 1 / (omega C), hence omega^2 = 1 / (L C), per the notes.

mcqs.q: Series resonance is used in
options: Blocking all radio stations at once
Tuning a radio receiver to one station
Controlling current in a fluorescent tube
Detecting buried metal directly
mcqs.why: The sharp current peak at f_0 lets a receiver select one station's frequency, the application named in the notes.

mcqs.q: How is series resonance observed as frequency is varied?
options: By the current falling to zero at f_0
By the impedance reaching its maximum at f_0
By the sharp peak in current at f_0
By the voltage disappearing at f_0
mcqs.why: The notes describe the sharp current peak at f_0 as how series resonance is observed and used in practice.

lessons.title: Resonance in an LC Parallel Circuit
lessons.notes_html:
In a parallel LC circuit the inductor and capacitor are connected across the same A.C. source. Resonance here gives the opposite result to the series case: minimum supply current and maximum impedance.

How the Net Current Becomes Zero

At resonance the currents through the inductor and the capacitor are equal in magnitude but opposite in phase, so they cancel each other. The net current drawn from the source therefore becomes zero in an ideal circuit, and falls to a very small minimum in a real circuit. The parallel circuit then behaves like a very high impedance.

Resonance Frequency and Observation

The resonance frequency is the same as for the series circuit.

f = 1 / (2 π √(L C))

  • f — resonance frequency, unit Hz; L — inductance, unit H; C — capacitance, unit F

Resonance in the parallel circuit is observed by the minimum in the supply current, or the maximum in the impedance, as the frequency is varied through f0. In an RLC parallel circuit the resonance phenomenon is likewise observed when the net current in the circuit is minimum.

mcqs.q: In a parallel LC circuit, the inductor and capacitor are
options: Connected in series with the source
Connected only to each other, with no source
Connected across the same A.C. source
Connected across a D.C. source only
mcqs.why: The notes define the parallel LC circuit by L and C connected across the same A.C. source, in parallel branches.

mcqs.q: At parallel resonance, the result is the opposite of the series case:
options: Maximum supply current and minimum impedance
Maximum supply current and maximum impedance
Zero impedance and maximum current
Minimum supply current and maximum impedance
mcqs.why: The notes stress this contrast: parallel resonance gives minimum supply current and maximum impedance, unlike series resonance.

mcqs.q: At parallel resonance the net current from the source becomes zero in an ideal circuit because
options: The inductor and capacitor currents are equal in magnitude but opposite in phase, so they cancel
Both branch currents fall to zero individually
The source voltage falls to zero at resonance
The capacitor blocks the inductor completely
mcqs.why: Equal and opposite branch currents cancel each other, so the net current drawn from the source becomes zero ideally, per the notes.

mcqs.q: In a real parallel LC circuit at resonance, the supply current
options: Rises to its largest possible value
Falls to a very small minimum, not exactly zero
Stays exactly at zero for all frequencies
Becomes equal to the capacitor current
mcqs.why: The notes qualify the ideal result: in a real circuit the supply current falls to a very small minimum at parallel resonance.

mcqs.q: At parallel resonance the circuit behaves like
options: A pure resistor of low value
A short circuit
A very high impedance
A pure capacitor
mcqs.why: With the supply current at a minimum for the applied voltage, the notes say the parallel circuit behaves like a very high impedance.

mcqs.q: The resonance frequency of the parallel LC circuit is
options: Double the series resonance frequency
Half the series resonance frequency
f = 2 pi sqrt(L C), unlike the series case
The same as for the series circuit: f = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(L C))
mcqs.why: The notes state the resonance frequency is the same formula in both cases: f = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(L C)).

mcqs.q: For L = 0.5 H and C = 8 microfarad, the parallel resonance frequency is about
options: 159 Hz
796 Hz

mcqs.q: Parallel resonance is observed by
options: The maximum in the supply current as frequency passes through f_0
The minimum in the supply current, or the maximum in the impedance, as frequency passes through f_0
The disappearance of the capacitor current at f_0
A spark at the source terminals at f_0
mcqs.why: The notes say parallel resonance is observed by the minimum supply current or maximum impedance as frequency is varied through f_0.

mcqs.q: In an RLC parallel circuit, resonance is likewise observed when
options: The net current in the circuit is maximum
The resistance is maximum
The net current in the circuit is minimum
The capacitor current is maximum
mcqs.why: The notes add that in an RLC parallel circuit the resonance phenomenon is observed when the net current is minimum.

mcqs.q: Which pairing correctly contrasts the two resonances?
options: Series: current minimum; parallel: current maximum
Both give maximum current and minimum impedance
Both give minimum current and maximum impedance
Series: current maximum and impedance minimum; parallel: current minimum and impedance maximum
mcqs.why: This is the central contrast of the two lessons: series resonance maximises current, parallel resonance minimises the supply current.

lessons.title: Metal Detector and Maximum Power Transfer
lessons.notes_html:
This lesson covers two applications of resonance and impedance: detecting metal, and matching a load to a source for best power transfer.

Metal Detector

A metal detector is an electronic instrument used to detect metal and metallic objects, including buried metals. It works on a resonant LC circuit: its search coil forms part of a circuit tuned to resonance. When a metallic object comes near the coil, eddy currents induced in the metal change the effective inductance of the coil and disturb the resonance. The detector senses this change and gives an audible or visible signal, revealing the presence of metal without digging.

Maximum Power Transfer

By the maximum power transfer theorem, an A.C. source transfers its maximum power to a load when the impedance of the load equals the impedance of the source.

Zload = Zsource

  • Zload — impedance of the load, unit Ω; Zsource — impedance of the source, unit Ω; matching the two gives maximum power transfer

Matching matters wherever a source feeds a load, such as an amplifier feeding a loudspeaker: a badly matched load receives far less than the maximum possible power.

mcqs.q: A metal detector works on the principle of
options: A transformer whose voltage is changed by metal
A choke coil blocking direct current
Back e.m.f. in a rotating motor coil
A resonant LC circuit whose resonance is disturbed by nearby metal
mcqs.why: The notes state the detector's search coil forms part of a circuit tuned to resonance, which nearby metal disturbs.

mcqs.q: In a metal detector, the part that forms part of the resonant circuit is the
options: Search coil
Battery pack
Loudspeaker
Display screen
mcqs.why: The notes say its search coil forms part of a circuit tuned to resonance; metal near the coil disturbs that resonance.

mcqs.q: When a metallic object comes near the search coil, the detector responds because
options: The metal reflects the sound waves of the detector
Eddy currents induced in the metal change the effective inductance of the coil and disturb the resonance
The metal charges the coil with static electricity
The metal increases the battery voltage
mcqs.why: Eddy currents in the metal change the coil's effective inductance, disturbing resonance; the detector senses this, per the notes.

mcqs.q: When the resonance is disturbed by metal, the detector gives
options: A printed map of the buried object
A shock to warn the operator
An audible or visible signal
No signal until the object is dug up
mcqs.why: The notes say the detector senses the change and gives an audible or visible signal, revealing metal without digging.

mcqs.q: A metal detector can detect
options: Only iron objects on the surface
Only gold and silver objects
Plastic and wooden objects underground
Metal and metallic objects, including buried metals
mcqs.why: The notes define it as an instrument to detect metal and metallic objects, including buried metals, without digging.

mcqs.q: By the maximum power transfer theorem, an A.C. source transfers maximum power to a load when
options: The impedance of the load equals the impedance of the source
The impedance of the load is zero
The impedance of the load is as large as possible
The impedance of the source is zero
mcqs.why: The theorem in the notes: maximum power transfers when Z_load = Z_source; matching the two gives maximum power transfer.

mcqs.q: The maximum power transfer condition is written as
options: Z_load = 2 x Z_source
Z_load = Z_source
Z_load + Z_source = 0
Z_load = 1 / Z_source
mcqs.why: The notes write the matching condition directly as Z_load = Z_source, both impedances measured in ohm.

mcqs.q: Matching matters, for example, where
options: A choke feeds a fluorescent tube
A generator feeds its own slip rings
An amplifier feeds a loudspeaker
A capacitor blocks a D.C. supply
mcqs.why: The notes give the amplifier and loudspeaker as the example: a badly matched load receives far less than the maximum power.

mcqs.q: A badly matched load receives
options: Exactly the maximum possible power
More than the maximum possible power
No power at all in every case
Far less than the maximum possible power
mcqs.why: The notes state a badly matched load receives far less than the maximum possible power, which is why matching matters.

mcqs.q: This lesson covers metal detection and maximum power transfer as applications of
options: Resonance and impedance
Self-induction and back e.m.f.
Eddy currents and lamination only
Modulation and demodulation
mcqs.why: The lesson introduction states these are two applications of resonance and impedance: detecting metal, and matching a load to a source.

lessons.title: Electromagnetic Waves
lessons.notes_html:
Electromagnetic waves are waves of oscillating electric and magnetic fields at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel. They need no medium and travel through free space at the speed of light.

Maxwell Prediction

The propagation of electromagnetic waves was predicted by Maxwell. He showed that a changing electric field produces a magnetic field and a changing magnetic field produces an electric field, so the two sustain each other and travel through space as a wave. He calculated their speed and found it equal to the speed of light, and predicted that light itself is an electromagnetic wave.

c = 1 / √(ε0 µ0)

  • c — speed of electromagnetic waves in free space, 3 x 108 m s-1; ε0 — permittivity of free space; µ0 — permeability of free space

c = f λ

  • f — frequency, unit Hz; λ — wavelength, unit m; the speed can also be found from frequency and wavelength

Electromagnetic waves transport energy, momentum and information, but they do not transport charges.

The Electromagnetic Spectrum

The electromagnetic spectrum is all electromagnetic waves arranged in order of wavelength, from longest to shortest: radio waves for broadcasting, microwaves for radar and cooking, infrared felt as heat, visible light from red to violet, ultraviolet for sterilisation, X-rays for medical imaging, and gamma rays, the shortest and most penetrating, from radioactive nuclei. All travel at 3 x 108 m s-1 in free space and differ only in wavelength and frequency.

mcqs.q: Electromagnetic waves consist of
options: Oscillating electric and magnetic fields at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel
Oscillating electric fields only, along the direction of travel
Moving charges travelling through free space
Pressure oscillations in a material medium
mcqs.why: The notes define them as waves of oscillating electric and magnetic fields at right angles to each other and to the travel direction.

mcqs.q: Electromagnetic waves need no medium and travel through free space at
options: The speed of sound in air
The speed of light, 3 x 10^8 m s-1
A speed depending on their colour only in vacuum
Half the speed of light
mcqs.why: The notes state they travel through free space at the speed of light, c = 3 x 10^8 m s-1, the same for all of them.

mcqs.q: The propagation of electromagnetic waves was predicted by
options: Faraday
Lenz
Maxwell
Hertz, as a pure guess with no calculation
mcqs.why: The notes credit Maxwell, who showed changing electric and magnetic fields sustain each other and travel through space as a wave.

mcqs.q: Maxwell showed that a changing electric field produces a magnetic field and a changing magnetic field produces
options: A steady current in a wire
A permanent magnet
Heat in the surrounding space
An electric field, so the two sustain each other as a wave
mcqs.why: This mutual production is Maxwell's key idea in the notes: the two fields sustain each other and travel through space as a wave.

mcqs.q: Maxwell calculated the speed of electromagnetic waves and found it
options: Equal to the speed of light, predicting that light itself is an electromagnetic wave
Equal to the speed of sound in air
Much slower than the speed of light
Different for every colour in free space
mcqs.why: Finding the speed equal to light's speed led Maxwell to predict that light itself is an electromagnetic wave, per the notes.

mcqs.q: The speed of electromagnetic waves in free space is given by
options: c = sqrt(epsilon_0 mu_0)
c = 1 / sqrt(epsilon_0 mu_0)
c = epsilon_0 / mu_0
c = 1 / (epsilon_0 mu_0)
mcqs.why: The notes give c = 1 / sqrt(epsilon_0 mu_0), where epsilon_0 is the permittivity and mu_0 the permeability of free space.

mcqs.q: The speed, frequency and wavelength of an electromagnetic wave are related by
options: c = f / lambda
c = lambda / f
c = f lambda
c = f lambda^2
mcqs.why: The notes give c = f lambda, with f in hertz and lambda in metres; the speed can be found from frequency and wavelength.

mcqs.q: An electromagnetic wave has frequency 1 x 10^8 Hz. Its wavelength in free space is
options: 3 m
mcqs.why: lambda = c / f = (3 x 10^8) / (1 x 10^8) = 3 m, using c = f lambda from the notes with c = 3 x 10^8 m s-1.

mcqs.q: Electromagnetic waves transport energy, momentum and information, but they do not transport
options: Charges
Energy
Momentum
Information
mcqs.why: The notes state this explicitly: electromagnetic waves carry energy, momentum and information, but no charges travel with them.

mcqs.q: In the electromagnetic spectrum, the waves with the shortest wavelength and most penetrating power are
options: Radio waves, used for broadcasting
Gamma rays, from radioactive nuclei
Microwaves, used for radar and cooking
Infrared, felt as heat
mcqs.why: The spectrum in the notes runs from radio waves (longest) down to gamma rays, the shortest and most penetrating, from radioactive nuclei.

lessons.title: Generation, Transmission and Reception of Electromagnetic Waves
lessons.notes_html:
Electromagnetic waves are generated by oscillating charges, sent out by a transmitting antenna, and picked up by a receiving antenna. Information is carried by modulation.

Generation and Transmission

A transmitting antenna is fed with a rapidly oscillating current. The oscillating charges produce changing electric and magnetic fields around the antenna, and these fields detach and propagate away through space as electromagnetic waves carrying the signal.

Reception

When a wave reaches a receiving antenna, its oscillating electric field drives the free electrons in the antenna to oscillate with the same frequency. This produces an alternating current in the antenna, which is the received signal; tuning selects the wanted frequency from it.

Modulation and Demodulation

Modulation is the process in which a low-frequency audio signal is superimposed on a high-frequency radio carrier wave, so the signal can be transmitted over long distances. Demodulation is the reverse process in the receiver: the audio signal is separated from the carrier so the original sound is recovered.

ProcessWhereWhat happens
ModulationTransmitterAudio signal put on carrier wave
DemodulationReceiverAudio signal taken off carrier wave

mcqs.q: Electromagnetic waves are generated by
options: Steady charges at rest
Oscillating charges
A steady current in a wire
Permanent magnets held still
mcqs.why: The notes state electromagnetic waves are generated by oscillating charges, sent out by a transmitting antenna.

mcqs.q: A transmitting antenna is fed with
options: A steady direct current
A slowly changing battery voltage
A rapidly oscillating current
No current; it works by magnetism alone
mcqs.why: The notes describe the transmitting antenna fed with a rapidly oscillating current, producing the fields that detach as waves.

mcqs.q: The fields produced around a transmitting antenna
options: Stay attached to the antenna and fade at its surface
Travel only along the connecting wires
Move into the ground and are lost
Detach and propagate away through space as electromagnetic waves carrying the signal
mcqs.why: Changing electric and magnetic fields around the antenna detach and propagate away through space as waves carrying the signal.

mcqs.q: When a wave reaches a receiving antenna, its oscillating electric field
options: Drives the free electrons in the antenna to oscillate with the same frequency
Heats the antenna until it glows
Charges the antenna permanently positive
Stops at the surface with no effect inside
mcqs.why: The notes explain reception this way: the wave's field drives free electrons to oscillate at the same frequency, producing the received signal.

mcqs.q: The alternating current produced in a receiving antenna is
options: Sent back out as a stronger wave
The received signal, from which tuning selects the wanted frequency
Used only to power the receiver battery
Discarded, since the sound is in the antenna metal
mcqs.why: The induced alternating current is the received signal; the notes add that tuning selects the wanted frequency from it.

mcqs.q: Modulation is the process in which
options: An audio signal is separated from a carrier wave
A carrier wave is generated by a battery
A low-frequency audio signal is superimposed on a high-frequency radio carrier wave
Two audio signals are mixed in a loudspeaker
mcqs.why: The notes define modulation as putting the low-frequency audio signal on a high-frequency carrier so it can be transmitted far.

mcqs.q: Modulation is carried out at the
options: Receiver
Loudspeaker
Receiving antenna only
Transmitter
mcqs.why: The table in the notes places modulation at the transmitter, where the audio signal is put on the carrier wave.

mcqs.q: Demodulation is
options: The reverse of modulation: separating the audio signal from the carrier in the receiver
Putting the audio signal onto a carrier wave
Amplifying the carrier wave at the transmitter
Selecting the wanted station frequency
mcqs.why: The notes define demodulation as the reverse process in the receiver, where the audio signal is taken off the carrier.

mcqs.q: Demodulation takes place in the
options: Transmitter
Receiver
Transmitting antenna
Broadcast studio microphone only
mcqs.why: The process table in the notes places demodulation in the receiver, recovering the original sound from the carrier wave.

mcqs.q: Why is the audio signal put on a high-frequency carrier for transmission?
options: So the sound becomes louder at the source
So the carrier can be heard directly as sound
So the signal can be transmitted over long distances
So no antenna is needed at the receiver
mcqs.why: The notes give this purpose for modulation: the carrier carries the audio signal over long distances through space.

lessons.title: Electrocardiography
lessons.notes_html:
Electrocardiography is the technique, and the instrument, that records the voltage pulses associated with the action of the heart. The record itself is called the electrocardiogram (E.C.G.).

Working Principle

Each heartbeat is triggered by a small electrical pulse travelling through the heart muscle. Electrodes placed on the skin pick up these pulses, and the instrument amplifies them and traces them on paper as the electrocardiogram.

Function

Doctors read the trace to study the rhythm and working of the heart and to detect heart disease. Electrocardiography is thus the technique and instrument, while the electrocardiogram is the traced record it produces.

Note on the source: the exercise page printed p.196 is missing from the source scan, so any numerical problems of Unit 15 beyond Q4 cannot be verified and are not included in these notes; nothing has been invented to fill the gap.

Key Points

  • A.C. reverses periodically; I = I0 sin(ω t) with ω = 2 π f, mean over a cycle zero
  • R.M.S. value is the effective value: Irms = 0.707 I0, Vrms = 0.707 V0
  • Resistor: V and I in phase, P = Vrms Irms; capacitor: I leads V by 90 degrees, XC = 1 / (2 π f C); inductor: I lags V by 90 degrees, XL = 2 π f L; average power in pure L or C is zero
  • Impedance Z = √(R2 + (XL - XC)2), unit ohm; RC: Z = √(R2 + XC2), current leads; RL: Z = √(R2 + XL2), current lags
  • Average power P = Vrms Irms cos Φ; power factor = cos Φ = R / Z
  • A choke controls A.C. by reactance without wasting power, but cannot control D.C. because XL = 0 at zero frequency
  • Series resonance: XL = XC, Z minimum = R, current maximum; parallel resonance: supply current minimum, impedance maximum; f = 1 / (2 π √(L C)) in both
  • Maximum power transfers when load impedance equals source impedance; a metal detector uses a resonant LC circuit disturbed by nearby metal
  • Electromagnetic waves travel at c = 1 / √(ε0 µ0) = 3 x 108 m s-1, carry energy and information but no charge, and are sent and received by antennas using modulation and demodulation
  • Electrocardiography records heart pulses as an electrocardiogram for studying the working of the heart

mcqs.q: Electrocardiography is
options: The traced record produced by the heart instrument
A method of detecting buried metal objects
The technique, and the instrument, that records the voltage pulses associated with the action of the heart
A technique for tuning a radio receiver
mcqs.why: The notes define electrocardiography as the technique and instrument recording the heart's voltage pulses; the record itself has a different name.

mcqs.q: The record produced by electrocardiography is called
options: The electrocardiography (E.C.G.)
The electromyogram trace
The resonance curve of the heart
The electrocardiogram (E.C.G.)
mcqs.why: The notes distinguish the two terms: electrocardiography is the technique and instrument, while the electrocardiogram is the traced record it produces.

mcqs.q: Each heartbeat is triggered by
options: A small electrical pulse travelling through the heart muscle
A pulse of blood pressure from the lungs
A signal sent from the skin electrodes
A vibration of the chest wall
mcqs.why: The working principle in the notes: each heartbeat is triggered by a small electrical pulse travelling through the heart muscle.

mcqs.q: The heart's electrical pulses are picked up by
options: A search coil held near the chest
Electrodes placed on the skin
Slip rings and carbon brushes
A choke coil in the instrument
mcqs.why: The notes state electrodes placed on the skin pick up the pulses from each heartbeat for the instrument to record.

mcqs.q: After the electrodes pick up the pulses, the instrument
options: Stores them as sound in the electrodes
Sends them back into the heart muscle
Amplifies them and traces them on paper as the electrocardiogram
Converts them into a magnetic field plot only
mcqs.why: The notes describe the instrument amplifying the small pulses and tracing them on paper as the electrocardiogram.

mcqs.q: Doctors read the E.C.G. trace to
options: Measure the blood pressure in the arteries directly
Detect metal objects inside the body
Tune the heart to a resonance frequency
Study the rhythm and working of the heart and detect heart disease
mcqs.why: The stated function in the notes is that doctors read the trace to study the heart's rhythm and working and to detect heart disease.

mcqs.q: From the unit key points: the r.m.s. value of a current with peak value 20 A is
mcqs.why: I_rms = 0.707 I_0 = 0.707 x 20 = 14.14 A, using the key-point relation I_rms = 0.707 I_0 given in this lesson's notes.

mcqs.q: From the unit key points: a choke cannot control D.C. because at zero frequency
options: X_C = 0, so it blocks direct current
X_L = 0, so it offers no reactance to direct current
The impedance becomes infinite
The power factor becomes 1
mcqs.why: The key points state a choke controls A.C. by reactance but cannot control D.C. because X_L = 0 at zero frequency.

mcqs.q: From the unit key points: at series resonance, with R = 5 ohm, the impedance is
options: Zero, because the reactances cancel
10 ohm, double the resistance
5 ohm, its minimum value
Maximum, equal to X_L + X_C
mcqs.why: Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2) = sqrt(5^2 + 0) = 5 ohm at resonance, since X_L = X_C; the key points give Z minimum = R.

mcqs.q: From the unit key points: electromagnetic waves carry energy and information but no charge, and travel in free space at
options: c = 3 x 10^6 m s-1 in free space
A speed equal to the speed of sound
Different speeds for each kind of wave in free space
c = 1 / sqrt(epsilon_0 mu_0) = 3 x 10^8 m s-1
mcqs.why: The key points give c = 1 / sqrt(epsilon_0 mu_0) = 3 x 10^8 m s-1 for all electromagnetic waves in free space.

lessons.title: Classification of Solids
lessons.notes_html:
Solids have a definite shape and volume because their atoms, molecules or ions are held by strong forces in fixed positions. They only vibrate about their mean positions and cannot move freely past one another. When temperature increases, the distance between the molecules of a crystal increases. Solids are classified by the arrangement of their particles.

Three Classes of Solids

ClassArrangementMeltingExamples
CrystallineRegular repeating patternSharp melting pointSodium chloride, diamond, copper
AmorphousDisordered, like frozen liquidSoftens over a rangeGlass, pitch
PolymericLong chains, partly orderedGenerally low melting pointWool, rubber, plastics

Crystalline Solids

In a crystal the particles are arranged in a regular, repeating three-dimensional pattern called a crystal lattice. Every particle sits at a fixed lattice site, which is why crystals have flat faces and sharp melting points.

Amorphous and Polymeric Solids

Amorphous solids have no regular arrangement; frozen amorphous material has the same disordered structure as a liquid, so it softens gradually with no sharp melting point. They are also called glassy solids because glass is their commonest example. A polymer such as wool is a polymeric solid of long chain molecules, only partly ordered, so it is called poor crystalline: neither fully crystalline nor fully amorphous. Amorphous and glassy solids have low melting points compared with crystals.

mcqs.q: Why do solids have a definite shape and volume?
options: Their particles move freely past one another like a liquid
Their atoms, molecules or ions are held by strong forces in fixed positions and only vibrate about their mean positions
Their particles are far apart and expand to fill any container
There are no forces holding their particles together
mcqs.why: In a solid the particles are held by strong forces in fixed positions. They can only vibrate about their mean positions and cannot move freely past one another, so shape and volume stay definite.

mcqs.q: What happens to the distance between the molecules of a crystal when its temperature increases?
options: The distance between the molecules decreases
The distance between the molecules stays exactly the same
The distance between the molecules increases
The molecules leave their lattice sites and flow away
mcqs.why: The notes state that when temperature increases, the distance between the molecules of a crystal increases, which is why solids expand slightly on heating.

mcqs.q: How are the particles arranged in a crystalline solid?
options: In a disordered way, like a frozen liquid
In long chains that are only partly ordered
Completely at random with large empty spaces
In a regular repeating pattern
mcqs.why: Crystalline solids have a regular repeating pattern of particles. Amorphous solids are disordered, and polymeric solids are long chains that are only partly ordered.

mcqs.q: How does a crystalline solid melt?
options: At a sharp melting point
It softens gradually over a range of temperature
It has no melting point at all
It melts only at a generally low temperature with no fixed point
mcqs.why: Crystals melt at a sharp melting point because every particle sits at a fixed lattice site in a regular pattern, so the whole structure breaks down at one definite temperature.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a crystalline solid?
options: Glass
Sodium chloride
Pitch
Wool
mcqs.why: Sodium chloride is listed with diamond and copper as a crystalline solid. Glass and pitch are amorphous, while wool is a polymeric solid.

mcqs.q: How are the particles arranged in an amorphous solid?
options: In a regular repeating three-dimensional lattice
In long ordered chains only
In a disordered way, with the same structure as a frozen liquid
In fixed lattice sites with flat faces
mcqs.why: Amorphous solids have no regular arrangement. Frozen amorphous material has the same disordered structure as a liquid, so it is like a frozen liquid rather than a lattice.

mcqs.q: Why are amorphous solids also called glassy solids?
options: Because they are fully crystalline like glass crystals
Because they have sharp melting points like glass
Because they are made only of long chain molecules
Because glass is their commonest example
mcqs.why: Amorphous solids are also called glassy solids because glass is their commonest example. They soften gradually and have no sharp melting point, unlike crystals.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an amorphous solid?
options: Pitch
Diamond
Copper
Sodium chloride
mcqs.why: Pitch is listed with glass as an amorphous solid that softens over a range. Diamond, copper and sodium chloride are all crystalline solids with sharp melting points.

mcqs.q: What is the structure of a polymeric solid?
options: A fully regular repeating lattice
Long chain molecules that are only partly ordered
A completely disordered frozen liquid structure
Single atoms held at fixed lattice sites
mcqs.why: A polymeric solid is made of long chain molecules and is only partly ordered, so it is neither fully crystalline nor fully amorphous.

mcqs.q: Why is a polymer such as wool called poor crystalline?
options: It has a perfectly regular lattice but a low density
It is completely disordered like glass
Its long chain molecules are only partly ordered, so it is neither fully crystalline nor fully amorphous
It melts at a sharp point like a true crystal
mcqs.why: Wool is a polymeric solid of long chain molecules, only partly ordered. Because it is neither fully crystalline nor fully amorphous, it is called poor crystalline.

lessons.title: Mechanical Properties of Solids
lessons.notes_html:
The mechanical properties of solids describe how they respond to applied forces. The force that produces a change in a body is the deforming force.

Main Mechanical Properties

  • Elasticity — the property of regaining the original shape and position after the deforming force is removed, as in a steel spring
  • Plasticity — permanent deformation that stays after the force is removed, as in a bent copper wire
  • Ductility — the ability to be drawn into wires, as in copper and aluminium
  • Brittleness — breaking with almost no deformation, as in glass
  • Strength — the ability to bear large loads, as in a steel column; hardness — resistance to scratching, as in diamond

Stress and Strain

Stress is the internal restoring force per unit area set up inside a deformed solid. It differs from pressure: pressure is exerted by a fluid equally in all directions, while stress can be tensile, compressive or shearing.

Stress = F / A

  • F — deforming force, unit N; A — area over which it acts, unit m2; stress unit is N m-2, the pascal (Pa)

Strain is the fractional deformation produced. It has no unit and no dimension, while the modulus of elasticity is dimensionally equal to stress.

KindStressStrain
TensilePulling force on a wireChange in length / original length
CompressiveSqueezing force on a columnFractional decrease in length or volume
ShearTangential force on faces, as in a rivetAngle through which a layer is displaced

mcqs.q: What is a deforming force?
options: The internal restoring force per unit area in a body
The force that always breaks a body apart
The force that produces a change in a body
The fractional change produced in a body
mcqs.why: The mechanical properties describe how solids respond to applied forces, and the force that produces a change in a body is called the deforming force.

mcqs.q: What is elasticity?
options: Permanent deformation that stays after the force is removed
The ability to be drawn into wires
Breaking with almost no deformation
The property of regaining the original shape and position after the deforming force is removed, as in a steel spring
mcqs.why: Elasticity is regaining the original shape and position once the deforming force is removed, shown by a steel spring. Staying deformed is plasticity, not elasticity.

mcqs.q: What is plasticity?
options: Permanent deformation that stays after the force is removed, as in a bent copper wire
Regaining the original shape after the force is removed
The ability to bear very large loads
Resistance to scratching
mcqs.why: Plasticity means the deformation is permanent and stays after the force is removed, as in a bent copper wire. A body that regains its shape shows elasticity instead.

mcqs.q: What is ductility?
options: Breaking with almost no deformation, as in glass
The ability to be drawn into wires, as in copper and aluminium
Regaining the original shape, as in a steel spring
Resistance to scratching, as in diamond
mcqs.why: Ductility is the ability of a material to be drawn into wires. Copper and aluminium are the examples given, while glass is brittle and diamond is hard.

mcqs.q: What is brittleness?
options: Being drawn into thin wires
Bearing large loads without breaking
Breaking with almost no deformation, as in glass
Keeping a permanent bend after the force is removed
mcqs.why: A brittle material breaks with almost no deformation, as glass does. It does not stretch, bend permanently or get drawn into wires before it breaks.

mcqs.q: What does hardness mean for a solid?
options: The ability to bear large loads, as in a steel column
The ability to be drawn into wires
Regaining the original shape after deformation
Resistance to scratching, as in diamond
mcqs.why: Hardness is resistance to scratching, shown by diamond. The ability to bear large loads is strength, shown by a steel column, which is a different property.

mcqs.q: How does stress differ from pressure?
options: Pressure is exerted by a fluid equally in all directions, while stress can be tensile, compressive or shearing
Stress is exerted by a fluid, while pressure acts only on solids
Stress and pressure are exactly the same in every way
Pressure has no unit, while stress is measured in pascals
mcqs.why: Stress is the internal restoring force per unit area in a deformed solid. Pressure is exerted by a fluid equally in all directions, but stress can be tensile, compressive or shearing.

mcqs.q: A force of 500 N acts on an area of 0.01 m2. What is the stress?
options: 50 Pa
mcqs.why: Stress = F / A. Substituting: stress = 500 / 0.01 = 50000 Pa = 5 x 10^4 Pa. The unit of stress is the pascal, the same as N m-2.

mcqs.q: A wire of original length 2 m increases in length by 2 mm. What is the tensile strain?
options: 2 x 10^-3, with no unit
1 x 10^-3, with no unit
1 m
mcqs.why: Tensile strain = change in length / original length = 0.002 / 2 = 1 x 10^-3. Strain is a fractional deformation, so it has no unit and no dimension.

mcqs.q: What is shear strain?
options: The change in length divided by the original length
The fractional decrease in volume of a column
The restoring force per unit area on a face
The angle through which a layer is displaced, produced by a tangential force on the faces, as in a rivet
mcqs.why: Shear stress comes from a tangential force on the faces, as in a rivet, and shear strain is the angle through which a layer is displaced. Change in length over original length is tensile strain.

lessons.title: Hooke's Law and Elastic Moduli
lessons.notes_html:
Hooke's law states that within the elastic limit, the stress applied to a body is directly proportional to the strain produced in it. If the applied stress is increased within this limit, the ratio of stress to strain stays constant.

Modulus of Elasticity

The constant ratio is the modulus of elasticity, also called the co-efficient of elasticity. A larger modulus means a stiffer material.

Modulus = stress / strain

  • Modulus unit is the pascal (Pa), the same as stress, because strain has no unit

Three Kinds of Modulus

Y = tensile stress / tensile strain

  • Y — Young's modulus, for a change in length, unit Pa

K = volumetric stress / volumetric strain

  • K — bulk modulus, for a change in volume under uniform pressure, unit Pa

G = shearing stress / shear strain

  • G — shear modulus, for a change in shape, unit Pa

Each modulus is a property of the material, not of the size of the specimen. Iron, with Y about 1.9 x 1011 Pa, is more elastic than rubber: a given stress produces a far smaller strain in iron, even though rubber stretches further.

Worked Example: Stress, Strain and Young's Modulus

An iron rod 4 m long and 0.5 cm2 in cross section stretches by 0.5 mm when a mass of 115 kg is hung from its lower end. Compute stress, strain and Young's modulus.

Step 1: Force F = m g = 115 x 9.8 = 1127 N.

Step 2: Area A = 0.5 cm2 = 0.5 x 10-4 m2 = 5 x 10-5 m2.

Step 3: Stress = F / A = 1127 / (5 x 10-5) = 2.254 x 107 Pa.

Step 4: Strain = change in length / original length = (0.5 x 10-3) / 4 = 1.25 x 10-4.

Step 5: Y = stress / strain = (2.254 x 107) / (1.25 x 10-4) = 1.8 x 1011 Pa.

Answer: Stress is 2.254 x 107 Pa, strain is 1.25 x 10-4 and Young's modulus is 1.8 x 1011 Pa. (The book printed the stress as 2.254 x 1011 Pa, which is wrong; the correct value is 2.254 x 107 Pa.)

mcqs.q: What does Hooke's law state?
options: Stress is inversely proportional to strain at all deformations
Stress stays constant however large the strain becomes
Strain is proportional to the square of the stress
Within the elastic limit, the stress applied to a body is directly proportional to the strain produced in it
mcqs.why: Hooke's law says that within the elastic limit stress is directly proportional to strain, so the ratio of stress to strain stays constant while the stress stays within this limit.

mcqs.q: What is the modulus of elasticity?
options: The constant ratio of stress to strain, also called the co-efficient of elasticity
The maximum stress a material can bear before breaking
The product of stress and strain
The force needed to break a specimen of the material
mcqs.why: Modulus = stress / strain. It is the constant ratio given by Hooke's law within the elastic limit, and a larger modulus means a stiffer material.

mcqs.q: What is the unit of the modulus of elasticity?
options: The newton (N)
The pascal (Pa), the same as stress, because strain has no unit
No unit at all, like strain
Joules per cubic metre
mcqs.why: Modulus = stress / strain. Since strain has no unit, the modulus takes the unit of stress, which is the pascal. Each modulus is a property of the material, not of the size of the specimen.

mcqs.q: What is Young's modulus Y?
options: Volumetric stress divided by volumetric strain
Shearing stress divided by shear strain
Tensile stress divided by tensile strain, for a change in length
Tensile strain divided by tensile stress
mcqs.why: Young's modulus Y = tensile stress / tensile strain and applies to a change in length. Bulk modulus K covers volume change and shear modulus G covers change of shape.

mcqs.q: What is the bulk modulus K?
options: Tensile stress divided by tensile strain
Shearing stress divided by shear strain
Pressure multiplied by the change in volume
Volumetric stress divided by volumetric strain, for a change in volume under uniform pressure
mcqs.why: The bulk modulus K = volumetric stress / volumetric strain. It describes a change in volume under uniform pressure, and its unit is the pascal like the other moduli.

mcqs.q: What is the shear modulus G?
options: Shearing stress divided by shear strain, for a change in shape
Tensile stress divided by tensile strain
Volumetric stress divided by volumetric strain
Shear strain divided by shearing stress
mcqs.why: The shear modulus G = shearing stress / shear strain and applies to a change in shape. Young's modulus covers length change and bulk modulus covers volume change.

mcqs.q: Why is iron described as more elastic than rubber?
options: Iron stretches further than rubber under the same stress
Iron has Y about 1.9 x 10^11 Pa, so a given stress produces a far smaller strain in iron, even though rubber stretches further
Rubber has a larger Young's modulus than iron
Iron has no elastic limit, unlike rubber
mcqs.why: Elasticity here means a large modulus: with Y about 1.9 x 10^11 Pa, a given stress produces a far smaller strain in iron than in rubber, even though rubber can stretch much further before breaking.

mcqs.q: An iron rod 4 m long stretches by 0.5 mm under a load. What is the strain?
mcqs.why: Strain = change in length / original length = (0.5 x 10^-3) / 4 = 1.25 x 10^-4. Strain is a ratio of lengths, so it has no unit.

mcqs.q: In the same example, a mass of 115 kg hangs from a rod of cross section 0.5 cm2. What is the stress?
mcqs.why: Force F = m g = 115 x 9.8 = 1127 N. Area A = 0.5 cm2 = 5 x 10^-5 m2. Stress = F / A = 1127 / (5 x 10^-5) = 2.254 x 10^7 Pa. The book value of 10^11 Pa for stress is wrong.

mcqs.q: Using stress 2.254 x 10^7 Pa and strain 1.25 x 10^-4 for the iron rod, what is Young's modulus?
mcqs.why: Y = stress / strain = (2.254 x 10^7) / (1.25 x 10^-4) = 1.8032 x 10^11 Pa, about 1.8 x 10^11 Pa. This is close to the standard value for iron of about 1.9 x 10^11 Pa.

lessons.title: Elastic Limit, Yield Strength and Strain Energy
lessons.notes_html:
Beyond small deformations a solid stops obeying Hooke's law. The stress-strain curve shows each stage from elastic behaviour to breaking.

Key Points on the Curve

  • Elastic limit — maximum stress up to which the body regains its original shape completely when the force is removed
  • Yield point — stress beyond which a small increase in stress produces a large increase in strain and the material begins to flow; this stress is the yield strength
  • Ultimate strength — maximum stress the material can bear, the highest point of the curve, before it necks down and breaks
  • Breaking point — stress at which the material finally breaks apart; between yield and breaking the deformation is permanent and plastic

A substance permanently deformed by applied stress is plastic. A brittle substance, such as glass or cast iron, breaks just after crossing the elastic limit with almost no plastic deformation, and brittle materials are very strong in compression. A ductile substance, such as copper, undergoes large permanent deformation before breaking and can be drawn into wires.

Strain Energy

Strain energy is the potential energy stored in a body deformed within the elastic limit, released when the force is removed. For a wire stretched by force F through extension x, the work done is (1 / 2) F x.

Energy / volume = (1 / 2) stress x strain

  • Strain energy per unit volume, unit J m-3; for a linear material it also equals (1 / 2) x stress2 / Y

Worked Example: Strain Energy per Unit Volume

A metallic wire of length 15 m is stretched 6 x 10-9 m by an applied stress of 5 x 108 N m-2. Calculate the strain energy per unit volume.

Step 1: Strain = change in length / original length = (6 x 10-9) / 15 = 4 x 10-10.

Step 2: Energy per unit volume = (1 / 2) x stress x strain = 0.5 x (5 x 108) x (4 x 10-10).

Step 3: Multiply: 0.5 x 5 x 4 = 10, and 108 x 10-10 = 10-2, giving 10 x 10-2 = 0.1.

Answer: The strain energy per unit volume is 0.1 J m-3. (The book prints 0.1 J; per unit volume the unit is J m-3.)

Worked Example: Extension of a Steel Column

A solid cylindrical steel column is 6 m long and 10 cm in diameter. What will be its increase in length when carrying a load of 2 x 105 kg? Young's modulus for steel is 1.9 x 1011 Pa.

Step 1: Load F = m g = 2 x 105 x 9.8 = 1.96 x 106 N.

Step 2: Radius r = 0.05 m, so A = π r2 = 3.14 x (0.05)2 = 7.854 x 10-3 m2.

Step 3: Increase in length = F L / (A Y) = (1.96 x 106 x 6) / (7.854 x 10-3 x 1.9 x 1011).

Step 4: Numerator = 1.176 x 107; denominator = 1.4923 x 109; ratio = 7.88 x 10-3 m.

Answer: The column increases in length by 7.88 mm.

mcqs.q: What is the elastic limit on the stress-strain curve?
options: The maximum stress up to which the body regains its original shape completely when the force is removed
The maximum stress the material can bear before it necks down
The stress at which the material finally breaks apart
The stress at which the material begins to flow
mcqs.why: Up to the elastic limit the body regains its original shape completely when the force is removed. Beyond it, deformation becomes permanent and Hooke's law no longer holds.

mcqs.q: What happens at the yield point?
options: The material finally breaks apart
A small increase in stress produces a large increase in strain and the material begins to flow; this stress is the yield strength
The body regains its original shape completely
The stress reaches its highest possible value
mcqs.why: At the yield point a small increase in stress produces a large increase in strain and the material begins to flow. The stress at this point is called the yield strength.

mcqs.q: What is the ultimate strength of a material?
options: The stress at which the material finally breaks apart
The maximum stress for complete recovery of shape
The maximum stress the material can bear, the highest point of the curve, before it necks down and breaks
The stress at which the material begins to flow
mcqs.why: Ultimate strength is the maximum stress the material can bear and is the highest point of the stress-strain curve. After it, the material necks down and then reaches the breaking point.

mcqs.q: Between the yield point and the breaking point, the deformation of a material is:
options: Fully elastic and recoverable
Zero, because the material cannot deform
Reversed when the force is removed
Permanent and plastic
