mcqs.why: The breaking point is the stress at which the material finally breaks apart. Between yield and breaking the deformation is permanent and plastic, and a substance deformed this way is called plastic.

mcqs.q: How does a brittle substance such as glass or cast iron behave?
options: It breaks just after crossing the elastic limit with almost no plastic deformation, and brittle materials are very strong in compression
It undergoes large permanent deformation before breaking
It can be drawn into wires easily
It flows like a liquid after the yield point
mcqs.why: A brittle substance breaks just after crossing the elastic limit with almost no plastic deformation. Glass and cast iron are examples, and brittle materials are very strong in compression.

mcqs.q: How does a ductile substance such as copper behave?
options: It breaks just after the elastic limit with almost no deformation
It undergoes large permanent deformation before breaking and can be drawn into wires
It regains its shape completely at every stress
It breaks only in compression, never in tension
mcqs.why: A ductile substance undergoes large permanent deformation before breaking, which is why copper can be drawn into wires. This is the opposite of brittle behaviour.

mcqs.q: What is strain energy?
options: The heat produced when a material breaks
The kinetic energy of a falling load
The potential energy stored in a body deformed within the elastic limit, released when the force is removed
The energy needed to melt a solid
mcqs.why: Strain energy is stored as potential energy when a body is deformed within the elastic limit and is released when the force is removed. For a wire stretched by force F through extension x, the work done is (1/2) F x.

mcqs.q: What is the strain energy per unit volume of a stretched wire?
options: Stress x strain, with unit Pa
(1/2) x stress / strain, with unit J
Stress^2 x strain, with unit N
(1/2) x stress x strain, which also equals (1/2) x stress^2 / Y, with unit J m-3
mcqs.why: Energy per unit volume = (1/2) x stress x strain. For a linear material this also equals (1/2) x stress^2 / Y, and its unit is joules per cubic metre, J m-3.

mcqs.q: A wire 15 m long is stretched by 6 x 10^-9 m under a stress of 5 x 10^8 N m-2. What is the strain energy per unit volume?
mcqs.why: Strain = (6 x 10^-9) / 15 = 4 x 10^-10. Energy per unit volume = (1/2) x stress x strain = 0.5 x (5 x 10^8) x (4 x 10^-10) = 0.5 x 0.2 = 0.1 J m-3.

mcqs.q: A steel column 6 m long and 10 cm in diameter carries a load of 2 x 10^5 kg. Young's modulus for steel is 1.9 x 10^11 Pa. What is its increase in length?
options: 7.88 x 10^-2 m, that is 78.8 mm
7.88 x 10^-3 m, that is 7.88 mm
1.96 x 10^-3 m, that is 1.96 mm

lessons.title: Electrical Properties of Solids
lessons.notes_html:
Band theory explains electrical behaviour: when many atoms combine in a solid, their energy levels spread into allowed energy bands separated by forbidden gaps.

Valence Band, Conduction Band and Forbidden Gap

The valence band is the highest band filled, or partly filled, with electrons at ordinary temperatures; its electrons are bound to their atoms. The conduction band is the next higher band, normally empty in insulators and semiconductors; electrons reaching it move freely and conduct. The forbidden gap is the energy range between them where no electron states exist.

TypeBand pictureConductivity (Ω m)-1
InsulatorFull valence band, large gap of several eV10-11 to 10-19
SemiconductorSmall gap, up to about 1 eVBetween insulator and conductor
ConductorValence band partly filled, or bands overlap102 to 108

A conductor has a partially filled valence band, so electrons move freely. In a semiconductor a few electrons gain enough thermal energy to cross the small gap, so conduction increases when temperature is increased. In an insulator the gap is too large for electrons to cross, so almost no current flows.

Worked Example: Change in Volume under Pressure

Calculate the change in volume of a copper cube 40 mm on each edge when subjected to a pressure of 2 MPa. The bulk modulus for copper is 125 GPa.

Step 1: Volume V = (40 x 10-3)3 = 6.4 x 10-5 m3.

Step 2: From K = stress / strain, change in volume = V x pressure / K.

Step 3: Change = (6.4 x 10-5 x 2 x 106) / (125 x 109) = 6.4 x 10-5 x 1.6 x 10-5.

Step 4: Change = 1.024 x 10-9 m3, about 1 x 10-9 m3.

Answer: The volume decreases by about 1 x 10-9 m3, that is 1 mm3.

Worked Example: Angle of Shear

Two parallel and opposite forces, each 4000 N, are applied tangentially to the upper and lower faces of a cubical metal block 25 cm on a side. Find the angle of shear. The shearing modulus is 80 GPa.

Step 1: Area of a face A = 0.25 x 0.25 = 0.0625 m2.

Step 2: Shearing stress = F / A = 4000 / 0.0625 = 6.4 x 104 Pa.

Step 3: Angle of shear = shearing stress / shearing modulus = (6.4 x 104) / (80 x 109) = 8 x 10-7 rad.

Answer: The angle of shear is 8 x 10-7 rad. (The book printed answer 8 x 10-5 rad is wrong; the correct value is 8 x 10-7 rad.)

mcqs.q: What is the valence band in a solid?
options: The next higher band above the conduction band, always full
The highest band filled, or partly filled, with electrons at ordinary temperatures; its electrons are bound to their atoms
The energy range where no electron states exist
A band that is always empty in every solid
mcqs.why: In band theory the valence band is the highest band filled, or partly filled, at ordinary temperatures, and its electrons are bound to their atoms. The next higher band is the conduction band.

mcqs.q: What is the conduction band?
options: The highest filled band whose electrons are bound to atoms
The forbidden energy range between two bands
The next higher band above the valence band, normally empty in insulators and semiconductors; electrons reaching it move freely and conduct
A band found only in metals at high temperature
mcqs.why: The conduction band is the next higher band above the valence band. It is normally empty in insulators and semiconductors, and electrons that reach it move freely and conduct.

mcqs.q: What is the forbidden gap?
options: The width of the valence band in a conductor
The energy of a free electron in the conduction band
The overlap region of two bands in a metal
The energy range between the valence band and the conduction band where no electron states exist
mcqs.why: The forbidden gap is the energy range between the valence and conduction bands where no electron states exist. Its size decides whether a solid is an insulator, semiconductor or conductor.

mcqs.q: What is the band picture of an insulator?
options: A full valence band with a large forbidden gap of several eV, and conductivity of 10^-11 to 10^-19 (ohm m)^-1
A partly filled valence band with overlapping bands
A small gap of about 1 eV that electrons cross easily
No valence band at all
mcqs.why: An insulator has a full valence band and a large gap of several eV that electrons cannot cross, so almost no current flows and conductivity is only 10^-11 to 10^-19 (ohm m)^-1.

mcqs.q: How does the conduction of a semiconductor change with temperature?
options: It decreases when temperature is increased
It increases when temperature is increased, because more electrons gain enough thermal energy to cross the small gap
It stays exactly the same at all temperatures
It becomes zero when temperature is increased
mcqs.why: A semiconductor has a small gap, up to about 1 eV. As temperature rises, more electrons gain enough thermal energy to cross the gap, so conduction increases with temperature.

mcqs.q: What is the band picture and conductivity of a conductor?
options: A full valence band with a gap of several eV
A small gap of about 1 eV and very low conductivity
The valence band is partly filled, or the bands overlap, and conductivity is 10^2 to 10^8 (ohm m)^-1
An empty valence band with a large forbidden gap
mcqs.why: A conductor has a partially filled valence band, or overlapping bands, so electrons move freely. Its conductivity is high, from 10^2 to 10^8 (ohm m)^-1, far above insulators and semiconductors.

mcqs.q: What is the volume of a copper cube 40 mm on each edge?
mcqs.why: Each edge is 40 mm = 40 x 10^-3 m. Volume V = (40 x 10^-3)^3 = 64000 x 10^-9 = 6.4 x 10^-5 m3. This volume is used with the bulk modulus to find the change in volume under pressure.

mcqs.q: The copper cube of volume 6.4 x 10^-5 m3 is subjected to a pressure of 2 MPa. The bulk modulus of copper is 125 GPa. What is the change in volume?
options: About 1 x 10^-9 m3, that is 1 mm3, a decrease
About 1 x 10^-6 m3, that is 1000 mm3
About 1 x 10^-12 m3
About 6.4 x 10^-5 m3, the whole volume
mcqs.why: Change in volume = V x pressure / K = (6.4 x 10^-5 x 2 x 10^6) / (125 x 10^9) = 6.4 x 10^-5 x 1.6 x 10^-5 = 1.024 x 10^-9 m3, about 1 x 10^-9 m3 = 1 mm3. The volume decreases under pressure.

mcqs.q: Two opposite forces of 4000 N are applied tangentially to the faces of a cubical block 25 cm on a side. What is the shearing stress?
mcqs.why: Area of a face A = 0.25 x 0.25 = 0.0625 m2. Shearing stress = F / A = 4000 / 0.0625 = 64000 Pa = 6.4 x 10^4 Pa.

mcqs.q: For the same block, the shearing modulus is 80 GPa. What is the angle of shear?
options: 8 x 10^-5 rad
8 x 10^-9 rad
8 x 10^-7 rad
mcqs.why: Angle of shear = shearing stress / shearing modulus = (6.4 x 10^4) / (80 x 10^9) = 8 x 10^-7 rad. The book value of 8 x 10^-5 rad is wrong; the correct value is 8 x 10^-7 rad.

lessons.title: Superconductors
lessons.notes_html:
A superconductor is a conductor whose resistance drops to zero when it is cooled below its critical temperature.

Graph of Superconductivity

For an ordinary conductor, resistance falls gradually as temperature falls. For a superconductor, the resistance against temperature curve drops suddenly to zero at the critical temperature and stays zero below it. Below this temperature the material also expels magnetic fields from its interior, the Meissner effect.

Mercury was the first superconductor discovered, with a critical temperature of about 4.2 K. Mercury, aluminium and zinc show superconductivity; copper does not exhibit superconductivity. Zero resistance means current can flow without energy loss as heat, which is why superconductors are so valuable.

mcqs.q: What is a superconductor?
options: A conductor whose resistance rises sharply when cooled
An insulator that conducts only at room temperature
A conductor whose resistance drops to zero when it is cooled below its critical temperature
A semiconductor with a very small forbidden gap
mcqs.why: A superconductor is a conductor whose resistance drops to zero when cooled below its critical temperature, and it stays zero below that temperature.

mcqs.q: How does the resistance-temperature curve of a superconductor differ from that of an ordinary conductor?
options: Both fall gradually to zero at absolute zero
A superconductor's resistance falls gradually, while an ordinary conductor's drops suddenly
Both rise suddenly at the critical temperature
An ordinary conductor's resistance falls gradually, while a superconductor's resistance drops suddenly to zero at the critical temperature
mcqs.why: For an ordinary conductor resistance falls gradually as temperature falls. For a superconductor the curve drops suddenly to zero at the critical temperature Tc and stays zero below it.

mcqs.q: What is the Meissner effect?
options: Below the critical temperature the superconductor expels magnetic fields from its interior
The superconductor attracts magnetic fields into its interior
The resistance of a superconductor rises in a magnetic field
A superconductor produces its own permanent magnetic field when heated
mcqs.why: Below its critical temperature a superconductor also expels magnetic fields from its interior. This expulsion of magnetic field is called the Meissner effect.

mcqs.q: Which was the first superconductor discovered, and what is its critical temperature?
options: Copper, with a critical temperature of about 4.2 K
Mercury, with a critical temperature of about 4.2 K
Mercury, with a critical temperature of about 42 K
Aluminium, with a critical temperature of about 0.42 K
mcqs.why: Mercury was the first superconductor discovered, with a critical temperature of about 4.2 K. Below 4.2 K its resistance is zero.

mcqs.q: Which of these metals shows superconductivity?
options: Copper
Iron at room temperature
Aluminium
Brass
mcqs.why: Mercury, aluminium and zinc show superconductivity when cooled below their critical temperatures. Copper does not exhibit superconductivity.

mcqs.q: Which of these metals also shows superconductivity?
options: Copper
Silver at room temperature
Steel at room temperature
Zinc
mcqs.why: Zinc is named with mercury and aluminium as a metal that shows superconductivity below its critical temperature. Copper is the clear example of a metal that does not superconduct.

mcqs.q: Which statement about copper is correct?
options: Copper does not exhibit superconductivity
Copper was the first superconductor discovered
Copper has a critical temperature of about 4.2 K
Copper expels magnetic fields below 4.2 K
mcqs.why: The notes state clearly that copper does not exhibit superconductivity, unlike mercury, aluminium and zinc. Mercury, not copper, was the first superconductor, with Tc about 4.2 K.

mcqs.q: What does zero resistance in a superconductor mean for electric current?
options: Current cannot flow at all
Current can flow without energy loss as heat
Current flows only in short pulses
Current produces more heat than in a normal conductor
mcqs.why: Zero resistance means no energy is wasted as heat when current flows, so current can flow without energy loss as heat. This is why superconductors are so valuable.

mcqs.q: Below the critical temperature, the resistance of a superconductor is:
options: Small but steadily increasing
Equal to its room-temperature value
Zero, and it stays zero
Negative
mcqs.why: On the resistance-temperature graph, R = 0 below Tc. Once the temperature falls below the critical temperature, the resistance drops suddenly to zero and stays zero.

mcqs.q: What is the critical temperature Tc of a superconductor?
options: The temperature at which it melts
The temperature at which its resistance is maximum
The temperature at which it becomes an insulator
The temperature at which its resistance drops suddenly to zero on cooling
mcqs.why: The critical temperature Tc is the temperature at which the resistance of the material drops suddenly to zero as it is cooled. Below Tc the material is superconducting and also shows the Meissner effect.

lessons.title: Magnetic Properties of Solids
lessons.notes_html:
The magnetic properties of solids come from the magnetic moment of their atoms. An electron produces a magnetic moment in two ways: its orbital motion around the nucleus acts like a tiny current loop, and its spin about its own axis gives an intrinsic moment. The moment of an atom is the sum of all its electrons' moments.

Three Classes of Magnetic Solids

ClassAtomic momentBehaviourRelative permeability
DiamagneticZero, paired electrons cancelWeakly repelled, induced field opposite to applied fieldLess than 1, e.g. 0.9999
ParamagneticSmall permanent moment, random directionsWeakly attractedSlightly more than 1, e.g. 1.001
FerromagneticMoments co-operate in domainsStrongly magnetised, stays magnetisedVery large, 102 to 104 for iron

Diamagnetic examples are bismuth and copper; brass is not a strongly magnetic substance. Paramagnetic examples are aluminium and platinum. Ferromagnetic examples are iron, nickel and cobalt, whose atoms co-operate to give a strong magnetic moment.

Domains and Curie Temperature

Domains are small regions inside a ferromagnetic material where all atomic moments align in one direction. In an unmagnetised specimen the domains cancel out; an applied field makes well-aligned domains grow, producing strong magnetisation. The Curie temperature is the temperature at which a ferromagnetic substance becomes paramagnetic, because thermal motion destroys the domain alignment.

mcqs.q: In what two ways does an electron produce a magnetic moment?
options: By vibrating about its mean position and by colliding with other electrons
By moving through the conduction band and by crossing the forbidden gap
By orbiting the nucleus only, with no effect from spin
By its orbital motion around the nucleus, which acts like a tiny current loop, and by its spin about its own axis
mcqs.why: An electron produces a magnetic moment in two ways: its orbital motion around the nucleus acts like a tiny current loop, and its spin about its own axis gives an intrinsic moment.

mcqs.q: What is the magnetic moment of an atom?
options: The sum of all its electrons' moments
The moment of its nucleus alone
The moment of its outermost electron only
Always zero for every atom
mcqs.why: The moment of an atom is the sum of all its electrons' orbital and spin moments. In diamagnetic atoms these moments cancel in pairs, while in ferromagnetic atoms they co-operate.

mcqs.q: What is the atomic moment of a diamagnetic solid?
options: Large, because all moments align in domains
Zero, because the electrons are paired and their moments cancel
Small and permanent, pointing in random directions
Very large, giving strong magnetisation
mcqs.why: Diamagnetic solids have zero atomic moment because their electrons are paired and the moments cancel. They are only weakly repelled by a magnet.

mcqs.q: How does a diamagnetic material behave in a magnetic field?
options: It is strongly attracted and stays magnetised, with permeability 10^2 to 10^4
It is weakly attracted, with permeability slightly more than 1, e.g. 1.001
It is weakly repelled, its induced field is opposite to the applied field, and its relative permeability is less than 1, e.g. 0.9999
It is completely unaffected and its permeability is exactly zero
mcqs.why: Diamagnetic materials are weakly repelled, the induced field opposes the applied field, and relative permeability is less than 1, for example 0.9999. Bismuth and copper are examples.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a diamagnetic material?
options: Aluminium
Iron
Nickel
Bismuth
mcqs.why: Bismuth and copper are diamagnetic examples. Aluminium is paramagnetic, while iron and nickel are ferromagnetic with domains and very large permeability.

mcqs.q: How does a paramagnetic material behave?
options: It has a small permanent moment in random directions, is weakly attracted, and its relative permeability is slightly more than 1, e.g. 1.001
It has zero moment and is weakly repelled, with permeability less than 1
It is strongly magnetised in domains, with permeability 10^2 to 10^4
It loses all magnetism at the Curie temperature
mcqs.why: Paramagnetic atoms have a small permanent moment pointing in random directions. The material is weakly attracted and its relative permeability is slightly more than 1, e.g. 1.001. Aluminium and platinum are examples.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a paramagnetic material?
options: Bismuth
Platinum
Cobalt
Copper
mcqs.why: Platinum is listed with aluminium as a paramagnetic material. Bismuth and copper are diamagnetic, while cobalt is ferromagnetic.

mcqs.q: How does a ferromagnetic material behave?
options: It is weakly repelled with permeability less than 1
It is weakly attracted with permeability about 1.001
Its moments co-operate in domains, it is strongly magnetised and stays magnetised, with relative permeability very large, 10^2 to 10^4 for iron
Its atomic moments always cancel to zero
mcqs.why: In ferromagnetic materials such as iron, nickel and cobalt the atomic moments co-operate to give a strong magnetic moment. The material is strongly magnetised, stays magnetised, and iron has relative permeability of 10^2 to 10^4.

mcqs.q: What are domains in a ferromagnetic material?
options: Regions where atomic moments point in completely random directions
Layers on the surface where no magnetism exists
Gaps between atoms in the crystal lattice
Small regions inside the material where all atomic moments align in one direction
mcqs.why: Domains are small regions inside a ferromagnetic material where all atomic moments align in one direction. In an unmagnetised specimen the domains cancel out; an applied field makes well-aligned domains grow, producing strong magnetisation.

mcqs.q: What is the Curie temperature?
options: The temperature at which a ferromagnetic substance becomes paramagnetic, because thermal motion destroys the domain alignment
The temperature at which a superconductor loses its resistance
The temperature at which a paramagnetic substance becomes ferromagnetic
The temperature at which a diamagnetic substance melts
mcqs.why: Above the Curie temperature, thermal motion destroys the domain alignment, so a ferromagnetic substance becomes paramagnetic. Below it, the domains can align and give strong magnetisation.

lessons.title: Hysteresis and Hysteresis Loop
lessons.notes_html:
Hysteresis is the lagging of the magnetic flux density B behind the magnetising force H when a ferromagnetic material is taken through a cycle of magnetisation and demagnetisation.

The Hysteresis Loop

Starting unmagnetised, B rises with H to saturation. When H falls to zero, B keeps a residual value. A reverse field is needed to bring B to zero, and the cycle then repeats in the opposite direction, tracing the closed hysteresis loop of B against H.

Retentivity, Coercive Force and Loss

  • Residual flux density or retentivity — the value of B remaining when H is reduced to zero, the intercept on the B axis
  • Coercive force — the reverse magnetising force needed to reduce the residual B to zero, the intercept on the H axis; large for hard magnetic materials used as permanent magnets, small for soft materials
  • Hysteresis loss — energy wasted as heat per cycle, proportional to the area of the loop; a small loop area means small energy dissipation, so soft iron suits transformer cores
PropertySoft magnetic materialHard magnetic material
Loop areaSmall, low lossLarge, high loss
Coercive forceSmallLarge
UseTransformer cores, electromagnetsPermanent magnets

Key Points

  • Solids keep definite shape and volume; they are crystalline (regular lattice, sharp melting point), amorphous or glassy (disordered, softens gradually) or polymeric (long chains, poor crystalline)
  • Stress = F / A, unit Pa; strain is fractional deformation with no unit; tensile, compressive and shear kinds exist for both
  • Hooke's law: within the elastic limit stress is proportional to strain; modulus = stress / strain — Young's modulus Y, bulk modulus K, shear modulus G
  • Elastic limit, yield strength, ultimate strength and breaking point mark the stress-strain curve; brittle solids break just past the elastic limit, ductile solids deform greatly first
  • Strain energy per unit volume = (1 / 2) x stress x strain = (1 / 2) x stress2 / Y
  • Band theory: insulators have a large forbidden gap, semiconductors a small gap of about 1 eV with conduction rising with temperature, conductors a partly filled or overlapping band; conductivity of conductors is 102 to 108 (Ω m)-1
  • A superconductor has zero resistance below its critical temperature, e.g. mercury at about 4.2 K; copper does not superconduct
  • Diamagnetic materials have zero atomic moment and permeability less than 1; paramagnetic have small random moments; ferromagnetic have domains, very large permeability, and become paramagnetic above the Curie temperature
  • Hysteresis is B lagging H; retentivity is B at H = 0, coercive force is the reverse H that makes B zero, and loop area gives the hysteresis loss

mcqs.q: What is hysteresis?
options: The lagging of the magnetic flux density B behind the magnetising force H when a ferromagnetic material is taken through a cycle of magnetisation and demagnetisation
The complete loss of magnetism when a field is removed
The rise of B above saturation in a strong field
The heating of a superconductor below its critical temperature
mcqs.why: Hysteresis is the lagging of B behind H during a full cycle of magnetisation and demagnetisation. It is shown by the closed hysteresis loop of B against H.

mcqs.q: What happens when an unmagnetised ferromagnetic specimen is magnetised by increasing H?
options: B falls to zero immediately
B rises with H until it reaches saturation
B stays zero however large H becomes
B becomes negative at once
mcqs.why: Starting unmagnetised, B rises with H to saturation. When H then falls to zero, B keeps a residual value instead of returning to zero, which is the lag called hysteresis.

mcqs.q: What is retentivity (residual flux density)?
options: The reverse magnetising force needed to reduce B to zero
The area enclosed by the hysteresis loop
The value of B remaining when H is reduced to zero, the intercept on the B axis
The maximum value of B at saturation
mcqs.why: Retentivity is the residual flux density: the value of B remaining when H is reduced to zero. On the loop it is the intercept on the B axis.

mcqs.q: What is the coercive force?
options: The value of B remaining when H is zero
The forward field needed to reach saturation
The energy lost as heat in one cycle
The reverse magnetising force needed to reduce the residual B to zero, the intercept on the H axis
mcqs.why: The coercive force is the reverse H needed to bring the residual B to zero, the intercept on the H axis. It is large for hard magnetic materials and small for soft materials.

mcqs.q: What does the area of the hysteresis loop represent?
options: The hysteresis loss, the energy wasted as heat per cycle; the loss is proportional to the loop area
The retentivity of the material
The coercive force of the material
The maximum flux density at saturation
mcqs.why: Hysteresis loss is the energy wasted as heat per cycle and is proportional to the area of the loop. A small loop area means small energy dissipation.

mcqs.q: What are the properties of a soft magnetic material?
options: Large loop area with high loss, and a large coercive force
Small loop area with low loss, and a small coercive force
Zero retentivity and zero permeability
Large loop area but no energy loss
mcqs.why: Soft magnetic materials have a small loop area, so the hysteresis loss is low, and a small coercive force, so they are easily magnetised and demagnetised.

mcqs.q: What are soft magnetic materials used for?
options: Permanent magnets
Cutting tools and springs
Transformer cores and electromagnets
Semiconductor diodes
mcqs.why: Soft magnetic materials are used for transformer cores and electromagnets because their small loop area gives low loss and their small coercive force lets the magnetism reverse easily.

mcqs.q: Why does soft iron suit transformer cores?
options: Its large coercive force keeps the magnetism fixed
Its large loop area stores more energy in the core
It has zero permeability, so no flux is lost
Its small loop area means small energy dissipation as heat per cycle
mcqs.why: A small loop area means small energy dissipation, so soft iron suits transformer cores where the magnetisation reverses every cycle and hysteresis loss must stay low.

mcqs.q: What are the properties and use of a hard magnetic material?
options: Large loop area with high loss and a large coercive force; used for permanent magnets
Small loop area and small coercive force; used for transformer cores
Zero coercive force; used for electromagnets
Small loop area and large retentivity only; used in motors
mcqs.why: Hard magnetic materials have a large loop area, high loss and a large coercive force, so once magnetised they stay magnetised. That is why they are used as permanent magnets.

mcqs.q: The hysteresis loop is a closed graph plotted between which two quantities?
options: Stress against strain
Magnetic flux density B against magnetising force H
Resistance against temperature
Current against voltage
mcqs.why: The hysteresis loop is the closed curve of B against H traced as the material goes through a cycle of magnetisation and demagnetisation in both directions. Retentivity is read on the B axis and coercive force on the H axis.

lessons.title: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Semiconductors
lessons.notes_html:
A semiconductor is a material whose conductivity lies between a conductor and an insulator. Silicon and germanium are the main examples. At 0 K no covalent bonds are broken, so a semiconductor behaves as an insulator. As temperature rises, more bonds break and conductivity increases.

Intrinsic Semiconductor

An intrinsic semiconductor is an extremely pure crystal. Its carriers come only from thermal breaking of covalent bonds. Each broken bond gives one free electron and one hole, so electrons and holes are equal in number. Its conductivity is low.

Extrinsic Semiconductor and Doping

Doping is adding a small, controlled amount of impurity to a pure crystal, about 1 part in 106. The result is an extrinsic semiconductor with much higher and controllable conductivity. A hole is the vacancy left when an electron breaks free. It behaves like a positive charge and moves opposite to electrons.

FeatureN-typeP-type
DopantPentavalent, e.g. phosphorus, arsenicTrivalent, e.g. boron, indium
Majority carriersElectronsHoles
Minority carriersHolesElectrons

In N-type material each pentavalent atom gives one free electron. In P-type material each trivalent atom leaves one hole.

mcqs.q: What is a semiconductor?
options: A material with conductivity higher than every metal
A material that never conducts at any temperature
A material whose conductivity lies between a conductor and an insulator; silicon and germanium are the main examples
A pure metal with a partly filled valence band
mcqs.why: A semiconductor has conductivity between a conductor and an insulator. Silicon and germanium are the main examples used in electronics.

mcqs.q: How does a semiconductor behave at 0 K?
options: It behaves as a superconductor
It conducts better than at room temperature
All its covalent bonds are broken
It behaves as an insulator, because no covalent bonds are broken
mcqs.why: At 0 K no covalent bonds are broken, so there are no free carriers and a semiconductor behaves as an insulator. As temperature rises, more bonds break and conductivity increases.

mcqs.q: What happens to the conductivity of a semiconductor as temperature rises?
options: It increases, because more covalent bonds break and give more carriers
It decreases, because bonds join together
It stays exactly the same
It falls to zero at high temperature
mcqs.why: As temperature rises, more covalent bonds break, giving more free electrons and holes, so the conductivity of a semiconductor increases with temperature.

mcqs.q: What is an intrinsic semiconductor?
options: A crystal doped with pentavalent impurity atoms
An extremely pure crystal whose carriers come only from thermal breaking of covalent bonds
A crystal doped with trivalent impurity atoms
A crystal with far more electrons than holes
mcqs.why: An intrinsic semiconductor is an extremely pure crystal. Its carriers come only from thermal breaking of covalent bonds, and its conductivity is low.

mcqs.q: In an intrinsic semiconductor, how do the numbers of electrons and holes compare?
options: Electrons are far more numerous than holes
Holes are far more numerous than electrons
They are equal in number, because each broken bond gives one free electron and one hole
There are holes but no free electrons
mcqs.why: Each broken covalent bond gives one free electron and one hole, so in an intrinsic semiconductor electrons and holes are equal in number.

mcqs.q: What is a hole in a semiconductor?
options: A free electron trapped inside the nucleus
A pentavalent impurity atom
An empty conduction band in an insulator
The vacancy left when an electron breaks free; it behaves like a positive charge and moves opposite to electrons
mcqs.why: A hole is the vacancy left when an electron breaks free from a covalent bond. It behaves like a positive charge and moves in the opposite direction to electrons.

mcqs.q: What is doping?
options: Adding a small, controlled amount of impurity to a pure crystal, about 1 part in 10^6
Heating a pure crystal until its bonds break
Joining P-type and N-type material in one crystal
Removing all impurities from a crystal
mcqs.why: Doping is adding a small, controlled amount of impurity, about 1 part in 10^6, to a pure crystal. The result is an extrinsic semiconductor.

mcqs.q: What is an extrinsic semiconductor?
options: An extremely pure crystal with low conductivity
A doped semiconductor with much higher and controllable conductivity than a pure crystal
A semiconductor that conducts only at 0 K
A crystal in which electrons and holes must be equal
mcqs.why: Doping produces an extrinsic semiconductor whose conductivity is much higher than that of the pure crystal and can be controlled by the amount and type of impurity added.

mcqs.q: What are the dopant and majority carriers in N-type material?
options: Trivalent dopant, e.g. boron or indium; holes are the majority carriers
Pentavalent dopant; holes are the majority carriers and electrons the minority
Pentavalent dopant, e.g. phosphorus or arsenic; electrons are the majority carriers and holes the minority carriers
Trivalent dopant; electrons are the majority carriers
mcqs.why: In N-type material each pentavalent atom, such as phosphorus or arsenic, gives one free electron, so electrons are the majority carriers and holes are the minority carriers.

mcqs.q: What are the dopant and majority carriers in P-type material?
options: Pentavalent dopant, e.g. phosphorus or arsenic; electrons are the majority carriers
Trivalent dopant; electrons are the majority carriers and holes the minority
Pentavalent dopant; holes are the majority carriers
Trivalent dopant, e.g. boron or indium; holes are the majority carriers and electrons the minority carriers
mcqs.why: In P-type material each trivalent atom, such as boron or indium, leaves one hole, so holes are the majority carriers and electrons are the minority carriers.

lessons.title: The PN Junction
lessons.notes_html:
A PN junction is formed by joining P-type and N-type material in a single crystal, for example by growing one part doped pentavalent and the adjoining part doped trivalent. Joining them gives a diode, a device that conducts mainly in one direction.

Diffusion and Depletion Region

Diffusion is movement from higher to lower concentration. Electrons diffuse from N to P and holes diffuse from P to N. Near the junction they recombine, leaving uncovered fixed ions: positive ions on the N side and negative ions on the P side.

The depletion region is the thin layer on both sides of the junction depleted of mobile carriers. It carries no mobile charge, only fixed ions. These ions set up a potential barrier across the junction, about 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium, which stops further diffusion.

mcqs.q: How is a PN junction formed?
options: By soldering two separate metal wires together
By placing a P-type and an N-type block side by side with an air gap
By doping a whole crystal with only one type of impurity
By joining P-type and N-type material in a single crystal, for example by growing one part doped pentavalent and the adjoining part doped trivalent
mcqs.why: A PN junction is formed by joining P-type and N-type material in a single crystal, for example by growing one part doped pentavalent and the adjoining part doped trivalent.

mcqs.q: What device does joining P-type and N-type material give, and how does it conduct?
options: A diode, a device that conducts mainly in one direction
A transistor, which amplifies current in both directions
A resistor, which conducts equally in both directions
A capacitor, which blocks current in both directions
mcqs.why: Joining P-type and N-type material gives a diode. Because of the junction barrier, a diode conducts mainly in one direction, which is the basis of rectification.

mcqs.q: What is diffusion at a PN junction?
options: Movement from lower to higher concentration driven by a battery
Movement from higher to lower concentration: electrons diffuse from N to P and holes diffuse from P to N
Electrons diffuse from P to N and holes from N to P
The flow of current through an external load resistor
mcqs.why: Diffusion is movement from higher to lower concentration. At the junction, electrons diffuse from the N side, where they are numerous, to the P side, and holes diffuse from P to N.

mcqs.q: What is left behind near the junction when electrons and holes recombine?
options: Positive ions on the P side and negative ions on the N side
Free electrons on both sides of the junction
Uncovered fixed ions: positive ions on the N side and negative ions on the P side
Neutral atoms with no charge anywhere
mcqs.why: Near the junction the diffused carriers recombine, leaving uncovered fixed ions: positive ions on the N side and negative ions on the P side. These ions set up the potential barrier.

mcqs.q: What is the depletion region?
options: A thick region full of free electrons and holes
The metal contact at the end of the diode
A region where the doping is heaviest
The thin layer on both sides of the junction depleted of mobile carriers
mcqs.why: The depletion region is the thin layer on both sides of the junction that has been depleted of mobile carriers by diffusion and recombination. It contains only fixed ions.

mcqs.q: What charge carriers are present in the depletion region?
options: No mobile charge, only fixed ions
Large numbers of free electrons only
Large numbers of holes only
Equal free electrons and holes moving freely
mcqs.why: The depletion region carries no mobile charge, only fixed ions: positive ions on the N side and negative ions on the P side. These fixed ions create the potential barrier.

mcqs.q: What is the potential barrier across a silicon PN junction?
options: About 0.3 V
About 0.7 V
About 7 V
About 0.07 V
mcqs.why: The fixed ions in the depletion region set up a potential barrier of about 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium. The barrier stops further diffusion across the junction.

mcqs.q: What is the potential barrier across a germanium PN junction?
options: About 0.7 V
About 3 V
About 0.3 V
About 0.03 V
mcqs.why: The potential barrier is about 0.3 V for germanium and 0.7 V for silicon. These are also the knee voltages above which forward current rises steeply.

mcqs.q: What does the potential barrier do at the junction?
options: It pushes more electrons from P to N
It removes the depletion region completely
It makes the diode conduct equally in both directions
It stops further diffusion of electrons and holes across the junction
mcqs.why: The potential barrier set up by the fixed ions opposes the diffusion of majority carriers, so it stops further diffusion and the junction reaches equilibrium.

mcqs.q: On which side of the junction are the positive fixed ions found?
options: On the N side of the junction
On the P side of the junction
Equally on both sides, with no separation
Only in the metal contacts
mcqs.why: When electrons leave the N side by diffusion, they leave behind uncovered positive fixed ions on the N side. Holes leaving the P side leave negative fixed ions on the P side.

lessons.title: Biasing of PN Junction
lessons.notes_html:
Biasing means applying an external voltage across the PN junction. The way it is connected decides whether current flows easily or is almost blocked.

Forward Bias

In forward bias the P side goes to the positive terminal and the N side to the negative terminal. Carriers are pushed towards the junction, the depletion region narrows and the barrier falls. Above the knee voltage, 0.3 V for germanium and 0.7 V for silicon, current rises steeply.

Reverse Bias

In reverse bias the P side goes to the negative terminal and the N side to the positive terminal. Carriers are pulled away, the depletion region widens and the barrier rises. Only a tiny reverse saturation current flows until breakdown, where current rises suddenly.

Worked Example: Resistance of a Diode

A silicon diode has 0.5 A of current through it with a 0.8 V drop across its terminals. Find its resistance.

Step 1: Use resistance equals voltage divided by current.

R = V / I

  • R - resistance, unit ohm; V - voltage drop; I - current

Step 2: Put V = 0.8 V and I = 0.5 A. R = 0.8 / 0.5 = 1.6 ohm.

Answer: 1.6 ohm.

mcqs.q: What does biasing a PN junction mean?
options: Applying an external voltage across the PN junction
Adding impurity atoms to the crystal
Heating the junction until carriers are produced
Joining two junctions to make a transistor
mcqs.why: Biasing means applying an external voltage across the PN junction. The way it is connected, forward or reverse, decides whether current flows easily or is almost blocked.

mcqs.q: How is a PN junction connected in forward bias?
options: The P side goes to the negative terminal and the N side to the positive terminal
The P side goes to the positive terminal and the N side to the negative terminal
Both sides go to the positive terminal
Both sides go to the negative terminal
mcqs.why: In forward bias the P side is connected to the positive terminal and the N side to the negative terminal, so carriers are pushed towards the junction and current can flow.

mcqs.q: What happens to the depletion region and barrier in forward bias?
options: Carriers are pulled away, the depletion region widens and the barrier rises
The depletion region stays the same width and the barrier is unchanged
Carriers are pushed towards the junction, the depletion region narrows and the barrier falls
The depletion region widens and the barrier falls
mcqs.why: In forward bias carriers are pushed towards the junction, the depletion region narrows and the barrier falls, so above the knee voltage the current rises steeply.

mcqs.q: Above which voltage does forward current rise steeply for silicon and for germanium?
options: 0.3 V for silicon and 0.7 V for germanium
7 V for silicon and 3 V for germanium
0.07 V for silicon and 0.03 V for germanium
0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium, the knee voltages
mcqs.why: Above the knee voltage, 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium, the barrier is overcome and forward current rises steeply. These match the barrier voltages of the two materials.

mcqs.q: How is a PN junction connected in reverse bias?
options: The P side goes to the negative terminal and the N side to the positive terminal
The P side goes to the positive terminal and the N side to the negative terminal
Both sides are left unconnected
The P side goes to the positive terminal and the N side is earthed
mcqs.why: In reverse bias the P side goes to the negative terminal and the N side to the positive terminal, so carriers are pulled away from the junction and current is almost blocked.

mcqs.q: What happens to the depletion region and barrier in reverse bias?
options: Carriers are pushed in, the depletion region narrows and the barrier falls
Carriers are pulled away, the depletion region widens and the barrier rises
The depletion region disappears completely
The barrier falls to zero and current rises steeply
mcqs.why: In reverse bias carriers are pulled away from the junction, so the depletion region widens and the barrier rises. Only a tiny reverse saturation current flows.

mcqs.q: What current flows in reverse bias before breakdown?
options: A large forward current
A current equal to the forward current at the knee voltage
Only a tiny reverse saturation current
No current at all under any reverse voltage, even at breakdown
mcqs.why: In reverse bias only a tiny reverse saturation current flows, until breakdown is reached, where the current rises suddenly.

mcqs.q: What happens at breakdown in reverse bias?
options: The current falls exactly to zero
The depletion region narrows to nothing
The diode starts conducting in forward bias by itself
The current rises suddenly
mcqs.why: Reverse current stays tiny until breakdown, where the current rises suddenly. This sharp rise at breakdown is different from the steep rise above the knee voltage in forward bias.

mcqs.q: A silicon diode has 0.5 A of current through it with a 0.8 V drop across its terminals. What is its resistance?
options: 1.6 ohm
16 ohm
0.4 ohm
mcqs.why: Resistance = voltage / current, R = V / I. Substituting: R = 0.8 / 0.5 = 1.6 ohm. Dividing the other way, 0.5 / 0.8 = 0.625, would give the wrong value.

mcqs.q: Which bias makes a diode conduct easily?
options: Reverse bias, at any reverse voltage
Forward bias, once the voltage passes the knee voltage
Reverse bias, but only just below breakdown
No bias at all, with both terminals unconnected
mcqs.why: A diode conducts easily only in forward bias, where the depletion region narrows and the barrier falls. In reverse bias the barrier rises and only a tiny saturation current flows.

lessons.title: Rectification
lessons.notes_html:
Rectification is the conversion of alternating current into direct current using a diode. A diode offers low resistance in forward bias and very high resistance in reverse bias, so it passes one half of the A.C. wave and blocks the other.

Half-Wave and Full-Wave

FeatureHalf-waveFull-wave bridge
Diodes usedOneFour
Half cycles usedOne onlyBoth
OutputPulsating D.C. with gapsContinuous pulsating D.C., no gaps
Average currentLowerTwice the half-wave value

In a bridge rectifier four diodes form a bridge. In each half cycle a different pair is forward biased, so current always flows through the load in the same direction.

Full-wave rectification can also use two diodes with a centre-tapped transformer.

mcqs.q: What is rectification?
options: The conversion of direct current into alternating current
The conversion of alternating current into direct current using a diode
The amplification of an alternating signal by a transistor
The storage of charge in a capacitor
mcqs.why: Rectification is the conversion of A.C. into D.C. using a diode. It works because a diode passes one half of the A.C. wave and blocks the other.

mcqs.q: Why can a diode act as a rectifier?
options: It offers the same resistance in both directions
It stores charge and releases it in the next half cycle
It offers low resistance in forward bias and very high resistance in reverse bias, so it passes one half of the A.C. wave and blocks the other
It amplifies both halves of the A.C. wave equally
mcqs.why: A diode offers low resistance in forward bias and very high resistance in reverse bias. So during one half cycle it conducts and during the other it blocks, giving pulsating D.C.

mcqs.q: How many diodes are used in a half-wave rectifier, and how much of the wave is used?
options: Four diodes, and both half cycles are used
Two diodes, and both half cycles are used
One diode, and both half cycles are used
One diode, and only one half cycle is used
mcqs.why: A half-wave rectifier uses one diode and uses one half cycle only. The other half cycle is blocked, so the output is pulsating D.C. with gaps.

mcqs.q: What is the output of a half-wave rectifier?
options: Pulsating D.C. with gaps
Continuous pulsating D.C. with no gaps
Pure steady D.C. with no pulses
Alternating current of half the frequency
mcqs.why: Because only one half cycle passes and the other is blocked, the half-wave output is pulsating D.C. with gaps where the blocked half cycles would have been.

mcqs.q: How many diodes are used in a full-wave bridge rectifier?
options: One diode
Four diodes forming a bridge
Two diodes
Three diodes
mcqs.why: In a bridge rectifier four diodes form a bridge. In each half cycle a different pair is forward biased, so both half cycles are used. Full-wave rectification can also use two diodes with a centre-tapped transformer, but that is not the bridge circuit.

mcqs.q: How does a bridge rectifier keep the load current in the same direction?
options: The same pair of diodes conducts in both half cycles
The load is reversed in every half cycle
In each half cycle a different pair of diodes is forward biased, so current always flows through the load in the same direction
Only one diode ever conducts in the bridge
mcqs.why: In the bridge, each half cycle forward-biases a different pair of the four diodes. Whichever pair conducts, the current is routed through the load in the same direction, giving full-wave output.

mcqs.q: What is the output of a full-wave rectifier?
options: Pulsating D.C. with gaps
Alternating current in both directions
Steady D.C. equal to the peak A.C. value
Continuous pulsating D.C., with no gaps
mcqs.why: A full-wave rectifier uses both half cycles, so the output is continuous pulsating D.C. with no gaps, unlike the half-wave output which has gaps.

mcqs.q: How does the average current of a full-wave rectifier compare with that of a half-wave rectifier?
options: It is twice the half-wave value
It is half the half-wave value
It is exactly equal to the half-wave value
It is four times the half-wave value
mcqs.why: Because the full-wave rectifier uses both half cycles while the half-wave rectifier uses only one, the average current of the full-wave rectifier is twice the half-wave value.

mcqs.q: Besides the bridge, how else can full-wave rectification be done?
options: With one diode and a plain transformer
With two diodes and a centre-tapped transformer
With four diodes and no transformer action at all
With a single transistor used as a switch
mcqs.why: Full-wave rectification can also use two diodes with a centre-tapped transformer. The bridge method instead uses four diodes forming a bridge.

mcqs.q: In a bridge rectifier, how many diodes are forward biased during one half cycle?
options: All four diodes at the same time
Only one diode in each half cycle
A pair of diodes (two), with the other pair taking over in the next half cycle
Three diodes in each half cycle
mcqs.why: In each half cycle a different pair of the four bridge diodes is forward biased. The pairs alternate, so current flows through the load in the same direction in both half cycles.

lessons.title: Transistor
lessons.notes_html:
A transistor is a device of two PN junctions with three electrodes: emitter, base and collector. The name comes from transfer of resistance: a small change in the low-resistance input circuit controls a large change in the high-resistance output circuit.

Structure

In an NPN transistor a thin P-type base lies between N-type emitter and collector. In a PNP transistor the types are reversed. The emitter is heavily doped and injects carriers. The base is very thin, about 10-6 m, and lightly doped, so most carriers cross it without recombining. The collector is the widest region, so it can collect carriers and dissipate heat and withstand a larger reverse voltage.

The input resistance is low because the emitter-base junction is forward biased. The output resistance is high because the collector-base junction is reverse biased. This transfer from low to high resistance is the basis of amplification.

mcqs.q: What is a transistor?
options: A device of one PN junction with two electrodes
A device of three PN junctions with two electrodes
A device of two PN junctions with three electrodes: emitter, base and collector
A single crystal with no junctions and four electrodes
mcqs.why: A transistor is made of two PN junctions and has three electrodes: the emitter, the base and the collector. A single PN junction gives a diode, not a transistor.

mcqs.q: Where does the name transistor come from?
options: From the transfer of charge between two metal plates
From the names of its three electrodes
From its use as a transformer for alternating current
From transfer of resistance: a small change in the low-resistance input circuit controls a large change in the high-resistance output circuit
mcqs.why: The name comes from transfer of resistance. The input circuit has low resistance and the output circuit has high resistance, and a small input change controls a large output change.

mcqs.q: What is the structure of an NPN transistor?
options: A thin P-type base lies between an N-type emitter and an N-type collector
A thin N-type base lies between a P-type emitter and a P-type collector
An N-type base lies between two P-type bases
A P-type collector lies between two N-type emitters
mcqs.why: In an NPN transistor a thin P-type base lies between the N-type emitter and the N-type collector. In a PNP transistor the types are reversed.

mcqs.q: How does a PNP transistor differ from an NPN transistor?
options: It has four electrodes instead of three
The types are reversed: an N-type base lies between P-type emitter and collector regions
It has no base region
It has only one PN junction
mcqs.why: In a PNP transistor the semiconductor types are reversed compared with NPN: the emitter and collector are P-type and the thin base between them is N-type. Both types still have two junctions and three electrodes.

mcqs.q: What is special about the emitter of a transistor?
options: It is the widest region and dissipates the most heat
It is very thin and lightly doped
It is heavily doped and injects carriers
It is reverse biased and collects carriers
mcqs.why: The emitter is heavily doped so that it can inject large numbers of carriers into the base. The base is thin and lightly doped, while the collector is the widest region.

mcqs.q: What is special about the base of a transistor?
options: It is the widest and most heavily doped region
It is about 10^-2 m thick and heavily doped
It collects carriers and dissipates heat
It is very thin, about 10^-6 m, and lightly doped, so most carriers cross it without recombining
mcqs.why: The base is very thin, about 10^-6 m, and lightly doped. Because of this, most carriers injected by the emitter cross the base without recombining and reach the collector.

mcqs.q: What is special about the collector of a transistor?
options: It is the widest region, so it can collect carriers, dissipate heat and withstand a larger reverse voltage
It is the thinnest region and injects carriers
It is lightly doped and forward biased
It is heavily doped and only 10^-6 m thick
mcqs.why: The collector is the widest region of the transistor. Its size lets it collect carriers, dissipate heat and withstand the larger reverse voltage at the collector-base junction.

mcqs.q: Why is the input resistance of a transistor low?
options: Because the collector-base junction is reverse biased
Because the emitter-base junction is forward biased
Because the base is heavily doped
Because the collector is the widest region
mcqs.why: The input resistance is low because the emitter-base junction is forward biased, and a forward-biased junction offers low resistance. The output resistance is high for the opposite reason.

mcqs.q: Why is the output resistance of a transistor high?
options: Because the emitter-base junction is forward biased
Because the emitter is heavily doped
Because the collector-base junction is reverse biased
Because the base is very thin
mcqs.why: The output resistance is high because the collector-base junction is reverse biased, and a reverse-biased junction offers high resistance. This transfer from low input resistance to high output resistance is the basis of amplification.

mcqs.q: What is the basis of amplification in a transistor?
options: The transfer of carriers from collector to emitter
The widening of the depletion region in forward bias
The use of four diodes in a bridge
The transfer from the low-resistance input circuit to the high-resistance output circuit
mcqs.why: A small change in the low-resistance emitter-base input circuit controls a large change in the high-resistance collector output circuit. This transfer of resistance is the basis of amplification.

lessons.title: Transistor Configurations
lessons.notes_html:
The three transistor configurations are named by the terminal common to input and output circuits.

ConfigurationCurrent gainInput resistanceOutput resistanceMain use
Common basealpha, slightly less than 1LowHighHigh-frequency circuits
Common emitterbeta, highModerateModerateMost amplifiers
Common collectorNear betaHighLowImpedance matching

The common emitter configuration is mostly used because it gives both high current gain and high voltage gain, so its power gain is the largest. It also reverses the phase of the signal by 180 degrees.

Worked Example: Currents from Beta

The current gain beta of a transistor is 200. If the base current is 0.2 mA, find (i) the collector current (ii) the emitter current (iii) alpha.

Step 1: Collector current is beta times base current.

Step 2: (i) IC = 200 x 0.2 mA = 40 mA.

Step 3: (ii) Emitter current is the sum of collector and base currents: 40 + 0.2 = 40.2 mA.

Step 4: (iii) alpha = beta / (beta + 1) = 200 / 201 = 0.995.

Answer: (i) 40 mA, (ii) 40.2 mA, (iii) 0.995.

mcqs.q: How are the three transistor configurations named?
options: By the type of doping in the emitter
By the number of PN junctions used
By the size of the collector region
By the terminal common to the input and output circuits
mcqs.why: The three configurations, common base, common emitter and common collector, are named by which terminal is common to both the input and the output circuits.

mcqs.q: What are the features of the common base configuration?
options: Current gain alpha, slightly less than 1; low input resistance; high output resistance; used in high-frequency circuits
Current gain beta, high; moderate resistances; used in most amplifiers
Gain near beta; high input resistance; low output resistance; used for impedance matching
Current gain greater than 200; used as a switch only
mcqs.why: In common base the current gain is alpha, slightly less than 1, with low input resistance and high output resistance. It is used in high-frequency circuits.

mcqs.q: What are the features of the common emitter configuration?
options: Current gain alpha, slightly less than 1; used in high-frequency circuits
Current gain beta, high; moderate input and output resistance; used in most amplifiers
Gain near beta; high input and low output resistance; used for impedance matching
No current gain at all; used only for rectification
mcqs.why: In common emitter the current gain is beta, which is high, and the input and output resistances are moderate. It is the configuration used in most amplifiers.

mcqs.q: What are the features of the common collector configuration?
options: Current gain alpha below 1; low input resistance; used in high-frequency circuits
Current gain beta; moderate resistances; used in most amplifiers
Current gain near beta; high input resistance; low output resistance; used for impedance matching
High voltage gain; used where phase reversal is needed
mcqs.why: In common collector the current gain is near beta, the input resistance is high and the output resistance is low, which makes it suitable for impedance matching.

mcqs.q: Why is the common emitter configuration mostly used?
options: It gives the lowest power gain of the three configurations
It is the only configuration that works at high frequency
It has the highest input resistance of the three
It gives both high current gain and high voltage gain, so its power gain is the largest
mcqs.why: The common emitter configuration is mostly used because it gives both high current gain and high voltage gain, so its power gain is the largest of the three configurations.

mcqs.q: What does the common emitter configuration do to the phase of the signal?
options: It reverses the phase of the signal by 180 degrees
It keeps the phase exactly the same
It shifts the phase by 90 degrees
It reverses the phase by 360 degrees
mcqs.why: A common emitter amplifier reverses the phase of the signal by 180 degrees, so the output signal is inverted compared with the input signal.

mcqs.q: The current gain beta of a transistor is 200 and the base current is 0.2 mA. What is the collector current?
options: 4 mA
40 mA
400 mA
mcqs.why: Collector current = beta x base current. Substituting: I_C = 200 x 0.2 mA = 40 mA. The value 40.2 mA is the emitter current, not the collector current.

mcqs.q: With collector current 40 mA and base current 0.2 mA, what is the emitter current?
options: 40 mA
0.2 mA
mcqs.why: Emitter current is the sum of collector and base currents: I_E = I_C + I_B = 40 + 0.2 = 40.2 mA. The emitter current is always the largest of the three currents.

mcqs.q: For a transistor with beta = 200, what is alpha?
mcqs.why: alpha = beta / (beta + 1) = 200 / 201 = 0.995. Alpha is always slightly less than 1 because the collector current is slightly less than the emitter current.

mcqs.q: Which configuration is used for high-frequency circuits?
options: Common base
Common emitter
Common collector
Common emitter with a bridge rectifier
mcqs.why: The common base configuration, with current gain alpha slightly less than 1, low input resistance and high output resistance, is used in high-frequency circuits. Common collector is used for impedance matching.

lessons.title: Operation of a Transistor
lessons.notes_html:
A transistor operates only when the emitter-base junction is forward biased and the collector-base junction is reverse biased. For an NPN transistor the emitter is negative with respect to the base and the collector is positive with respect to the base.

Current Relations

The emitter injects a large number of carriers into the thin base. Most cross into the collector; only a small part becomes base current. Hence emitter current is the sum of the other two:

IE = IC + IB

  • IE - emitter current; IC - collector current; IB - base current, all in A or mA

alpha = IC / IE

  • alpha - common-base current gain, always less than 1 because IC is slightly less than IE

beta = IC / IB

  • beta - common-emitter current gain, typically 100 or more because IB is very small; beta is always much larger than alpha

Worked Example: Alpha, Beta and Currents

A transistor has alpha = 0.995. If the emitter current is 80 mA, find (i) the collector current (ii) the base current (iii) beta.

Step 1: (i) IC = alpha x IE = 0.995 x 80 mA = 79.6 mA.

Step 2: (ii) IB = IE - IC = 80 - 79.6 = 0.4 mA.

Step 3: (iii) beta = alpha / (1 - alpha) = 0.995 / 0.005 = 199.

Answer: (i) 79.6 mA, (ii) 0.4 mA, (iii) 199.

mcqs.q: What biasing is needed for a transistor to operate?
options: The emitter-base junction is forward biased and the collector-base junction is reverse biased
Both junctions are forward biased
Both junctions are reverse biased
The emitter-base junction is reverse biased and the collector-base junction is forward biased
mcqs.why: A transistor operates only when the emitter-base junction is forward biased and the collector-base junction is reverse biased. This is the biasing of the active region.

mcqs.q: For an NPN transistor in operation, what are the polarities of emitter and collector with respect to the base?
options: The emitter is positive and the collector is negative with respect to the base
The emitter is negative with respect to the base and the collector is positive with respect to the base
Both emitter and collector are negative with respect to the base
Both emitter and collector are positive with respect to the base
mcqs.why: For an NPN transistor the emitter is negative with respect to the base, so the emitter-base junction is forward biased, and the collector is positive with respect to the base, so the collector-base junction is reverse biased.

mcqs.q: What is the relation between the three transistor currents?
options: I_C = I_E + I_B
I_B = I_C + I_E
I_E = I_C + I_B
I_E = I_C - I_B
mcqs.why: The emitter injects the total current, which splits into collector current and base current, so emitter current is the sum of the other two: I_E = I_C + I_B.

mcqs.q: What is alpha, and why is it always less than 1?
options: alpha = I_C / I_B; it is large because I_B is very small
alpha = I_E / I_C; it is less than 1 because I_E is the smallest current
alpha = I_B / I_E; it equals 1 for every transistor
alpha = I_C / I_E, the common-base current gain; it is less than 1 because I_C is slightly less than I_E
mcqs.why: alpha = I_C / I_E is the common-base current gain. Since a small part of the emitter current becomes base current, I_C is slightly less than I_E, so alpha is always less than 1.

mcqs.q: What is beta, and why is it large?
options: beta = I_C / I_B, the common-emitter current gain; it is typically 100 or more because I_B is very small, and beta is always much larger than alpha
beta = I_C / I_E; it is always less than 1
beta = I_E / I_B; it is small because I_E is large
beta = I_B / I_C; it is typically about 0.01
mcqs.why: beta = I_C / I_B is the common-emitter current gain. Because the base current is very small compared with the collector current, beta is typically 100 or more, much larger than alpha.

mcqs.q: Why is the base current so small in an operating transistor?
options: Most carriers injected by the emitter recombine in the base
The emitter injects many carriers into the thin base, most cross into the collector, and only a small part becomes base current
The collector repels most carriers back into the emitter
The base is heavily doped and blocks the carriers
mcqs.why: The base is thin and lightly doped, so most carriers injected by the emitter cross it into the collector without recombining. Only a small part becomes base current, which is why beta is large.

mcqs.q: A transistor has alpha = 0.995 and emitter current 80 mA. What is the collector current?
options: 80 mA
0.4 mA
76 mA
mcqs.why: Collector current = alpha x emitter current. Substituting: I_C = 0.995 x 80 mA = 79.6 mA. The collector current is slightly less than the emitter current.

mcqs.q: For the same transistor, with I_E = 80 mA and I_C = 79.6 mA, what is the base current?
options: 4 mA
0.4 mA
mcqs.why: Base current = emitter current - collector current: I_B = I_E - I_C = 80 - 79.6 = 0.4 mA. This small base current is what controls the large collector current.

mcqs.q: For a transistor with alpha = 0.995, what is beta?
mcqs.why: beta = alpha / (1 - alpha) = 0.995 / (1 - 0.995) = 0.995 / 0.005 = 199. As alpha gets closer to 1, beta becomes very large.

mcqs.q: Which transistor current is the largest?
options: The collector current, because alpha is less than 1
The emitter current, because it is the sum of collector and base currents
The base current, because it controls the transistor
All three currents are always equal
mcqs.why: Since I_E = I_C + I_B, the emitter current is the largest. The collector current is slightly smaller, and the base current is by far the smallest.

lessons.title: Transistor as an Amplifier
lessons.notes_html:
Amplification is converting a small input A.C. signal into a large output A.C. signal. In a common emitter amplifier the signal is applied to the forward-biased emitter-base circuit. A small change in base current gives a much larger change in collector current, beta times as large, which flows through the load resistor and gives a large output voltage.

Av = beta x Rout / Rin

  • Av - voltage gain; Rout - output resistance; Rin - input resistance

The flow of carriers is controlled by the base: the small base current controls the large collector current.

Worked Example: Output Voltage of an Amplifier

The input resistance in the common emitter amplifier circuit of a transistor is 2k ohm. The output resistance is 8k ohm. What is the output voltage for an input voltage of 6 mV if the current gain is 100?

Step 1: Voltage gain = beta x output resistance / input resistance.

Step 2: Voltage gain = 100 x 8 / 2 = 100 x 4 = 400.

Step 3: Output voltage = voltage gain x input voltage = 400 x 6 mV = 2400 mV.

Answer: 2.4 V.

mcqs.q: What is amplification?
options: Converting alternating current into direct current
Converting a small input A.C. signal into a large output A.C. signal
Converting a large signal into a smaller one for safety
Storing an A.C. signal in a capacitor
mcqs.why: Amplification is converting a small input A.C. signal into a large output A.C. signal. In a transistor amplifier this happens because a small base current controls a large collector current.

mcqs.q: In a common emitter amplifier, where is the input signal applied?
options: To the reverse-biased collector-base circuit only
Across the load resistor in the collector circuit
To the forward-biased emitter-base circuit
Between the collector and the emitter with the base unconnected
mcqs.why: In a common emitter amplifier the signal is applied to the forward-biased emitter-base circuit. The resulting change in collector current then flows through the load resistor to give the output.

mcqs.q: How is the output of a common emitter amplifier obtained?
options: The base current flows through the load resistor and gives the output
The input voltage is passed unchanged through the collector
The emitter current charges a capacitor that gives the output
The change in collector current flows through the load resistor and gives a large output voltage
mcqs.why: A small change in base current gives a much larger change in collector current, beta times as large. This current flows through the load resistor and produces a large output voltage.

mcqs.q: What is the formula for the voltage gain of a transistor amplifier?
options: A_v = beta x R_out / R_in
A_v = beta x R_in / R_out
A_v = R_out / (beta x R_in)
A_v = beta + R_out / R_in
mcqs.why: Voltage gain A_v = beta x R_out / R_in, where R_out is the output resistance and R_in is the input resistance. A larger beta or a larger ratio R_out / R_in gives a larger voltage gain.

mcqs.q: How does the base control the flow of carriers in an amplifier?
options: The large collector current controls the small base current
The small base current controls the large collector current
The base stops all carriers until saturation is reached
The base current and collector current are always equal
mcqs.why: The flow of carriers is controlled by the base: the small base current controls the large collector current, which is beta times as large. This control is what makes amplification possible.

mcqs.q: In an amplifier, how does a change in collector current compare with the change in base current that causes it?
options: The change in collector current is alpha times the change in base current, so it is smaller
The two changes are exactly equal
The change in collector current is beta times as large as the change in base current
The change in collector current is beta times smaller than the base change
mcqs.why: Because beta = I_C / I_B, a small change in base current gives a change in collector current that is beta times as large. Flowing through the load resistor, this gives a large output voltage.

mcqs.q: An amplifier has input resistance 2k ohm and output resistance 8k ohm. What is the ratio R_out / R_in?
mcqs.why: R_out / R_in = 8k ohm / 2k ohm = 8 / 2 = 4. This ratio is multiplied by beta to get the voltage gain of the amplifier.

mcqs.q: For the same amplifier, the current gain is 100. What is the voltage gain?
mcqs.why: Voltage gain = beta x R_out / R_in = 100 x 8 / 2 = 100 x 4 = 400. The output voltage is therefore 400 times the input voltage.

mcqs.q: With voltage gain 400, what is the output voltage for an input voltage of 6 mV?
options: 240 mV, that is 0.24 V
2400 mV, that is 2.4 V
66 mV
mcqs.why: Output voltage = voltage gain x input voltage = 400 x 6 mV = 2400 mV. Converting: 2400 mV = 2.4 V, so a 6 mV input becomes a 2.4 V output.

mcqs.q: Why does a common emitter amplifier give a large output voltage from a small input?
options: The input voltage is multiplied by the depletion region barrier
The load resistor adds energy from the A.C. supply
A small base current change produces a collector current change beta times larger, which develops a large voltage across the load resistor
The emitter-base junction steps up the voltage like a transformer
mcqs.why: The small input signal changes the base current slightly; the collector current changes beta times as much, and this large current change through the load resistor gives a large output voltage. The gain is A_v = beta x R_out / R_in.

lessons.title: Transistor as a Switch
lessons.notes_html:
A transistor works as a switch when it operates only in cutoff and saturation. A small base signal can then switch a larger load current on and off automatically.

Cutoff, Active and Saturation Regions

In cutoff the emitter-base junction is not forward biased. Base current and collector current are both zero, so the transistor acts as an open switch and the load is OFF.

IC = 0

  • Cutoff condition: collector current is zero when the transistor is fully off

In saturation the junction is forward biased strongly, collector current is at its maximum, and the transistor acts as a closed switch, so the load is ON. In the active region between them, emitter-base is forward biased and collector-base is reverse biased, collector current is proportional to base current, and the transistor works as an amplifier. Working in the active region comes after cutoff and before saturation as base current increases.

Key Points

  • Intrinsic semiconductor: pure crystal, equal electrons and holes; extrinsic: doped, much higher conductivity.
  • N-type uses pentavalent doping, electrons majority; P-type uses trivalent doping, holes majority.
  • PN junction forms a depletion region with no mobile carriers and a barrier of 0.7 V for silicon, 0.3 V for germanium.
  • Forward bias narrows the depletion region; reverse bias widens it.
  • Rectification converts A.C. to D.C.; a bridge rectifier uses four diodes and uses both half cycles.
  • Transistor currents obey IE = IC + IB, with alpha = IC/IE less than 1 and beta = IC/IB large.
  • For operation, emitter-base is forward biased and collector-base is reverse biased; the base is thin and lightly doped.
  • Common emitter gives the largest power gain and is the most used configuration.
  • Cutoff acts as an open switch, saturation as a closed switch, and the active region gives amplification.

mcqs.q: When does a transistor work as a switch?
options: When it operates only in the active region
When it operates in the active region and cutoff only
When it operates only in cutoff and saturation
When both its junctions are reverse biased at all times
mcqs.why: A transistor works as a switch when it operates only in cutoff and saturation, the two fully OFF and fully ON states. In the active region between them it works as an amplifier instead.

mcqs.q: What is the cutoff condition of a transistor switch?
options: The junction is forward biased strongly and collector current is maximum
The collector-base junction is forward biased and the load is ON
The base current is at its largest value
The emitter-base junction is not forward biased, so base current and collector current are both zero
mcqs.why: In cutoff the emitter-base junction is not forward biased. Base current and collector current are both zero, I_C = 0, so the transistor is fully off.

mcqs.q: In cutoff, how does the transistor act and what is the state of the load?
options: It acts as an open switch and the load is OFF
It acts as a closed switch and the load is ON
It acts as an amplifier and the load signal is largest
It acts as a rectifier and the load gets D.C.
mcqs.why: In cutoff, I_C = 0, so no current reaches the load. The transistor acts as an open switch and the load is OFF.

mcqs.q: What happens in saturation in a transistor switch?
options: Collector current falls to zero and the load is OFF
The junction is forward biased strongly, collector current is at its maximum, and the transistor acts as a closed switch, so the load is ON
The emitter-base junction is not forward biased
Collector current is proportional to base current as in an amplifier
mcqs.why: In saturation the junction is forward biased strongly and collector current is at its maximum. The transistor acts as a closed switch, so the load is ON.

mcqs.q: What are the biasing and behaviour of a transistor in the active region?
options: Emitter-base is not forward biased and collector current is zero
The junction is forward biased strongly and collector current is maximum
Emitter-base is forward biased and collector-base is reverse biased; collector current is proportional to base current, and the transistor works as an amplifier
Both junctions are forward biased and the load is fully ON
mcqs.why: In the active region the emitter-base junction is forward biased and the collector-base junction is reverse biased. Collector current is proportional to base current, so the transistor works as an amplifier.

mcqs.q: As base current increases from zero, in what order does a transistor pass through its regions?
options: Saturation first, then the active region, then cutoff
Active region first, then cutoff, then saturation
Cutoff first, then saturation, with no active region
Cutoff first, then the active region, then saturation
mcqs.why: Working in the active region comes after cutoff and before saturation as base current increases. A switch uses only the two end states, cutoff and saturation.

mcqs.q: How can a small base signal switch a load with a transistor?
options: A small base signal can switch a larger load current on and off automatically by driving the transistor between cutoff and saturation
The base signal must be larger than the load current
The base signal rectifies the load current like a diode bridge
The load current flows through the base circuit itself
mcqs.why: Because the small base current controls the large collector current, a small base signal can switch a larger load current on and off automatically: cutoff turns it off and saturation turns it on.

mcqs.q: In cutoff, what is the value of the collector current?
options: I_C is at its maximum value
I_C = 0
I_C equals the emitter current
I_C equals beta times the load current
mcqs.why: The cutoff condition is that the collector current is zero when the transistor is fully off: I_C = 0, with base current also zero because the emitter-base junction is not forward biased.

mcqs.q: Which region of a transistor gives amplification rather than switching?
options: The cutoff region, where collector current is zero
The saturation region, where collector current is maximum
The active region, where collector current is proportional to base current
Both cutoff and saturation together
mcqs.why: In the active region, between cutoff and saturation, collector current is proportional to base current, so the transistor works as an amplifier. Cutoff and saturation are the switch states.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a transistor used as a switch and as an amplifier?
options: As a switch it works in the active region; as an amplifier it works in cutoff
There is no difference; both use the same region
As a switch it needs four diodes; as an amplifier it needs two
As a switch it works only in cutoff (open, load OFF) and saturation (closed, load ON); as an amplifier it works in the active region
mcqs.why: A switch uses only cutoff, acting as an open switch with the load OFF, and saturation, acting as a closed switch with the load ON. An amplifier uses the active region, where collector current is proportional to base current.

chapters.title: Unit 18: Dawn of the Modern Physics

lessons.title: Relative Motion and Frames of Reference
lessons.notes_html:
Relative motion is the motion of a body as observed from a particular frame. The same motion looks different to different observers. A passenger in a moving train is at rest relative to the train but in motion relative to a person on the platform. Two cars at the same speed in the same direction appear at rest to each other. All motion is relative; there is no absolute rest.

Inertial and Non-Inertial Frames
