A frame of reference is the system from which motion is observed. An inertial frame is one in which Newton laws hold: it is at rest or moves with uniform velocity and has zero acceleration, so a free body stays at rest or in uniform motion.

A non-inertial frame is accelerated, so its velocity is variable. Newton laws do not hold in it unless fictitious forces are added. A train moving steadily is nearly inertial; a train speeding up or rounding a bend is non-inertial.

FeatureInertial frameNon-inertial frame
AccelerationZeroNon-zero
Newton lawsHold directlyNeed fictitious forces
ExampleTrain at steady speedRotating or speeding-up frame

mcqs.q: A passenger sitting in a moving train is at rest relative to what?
options: A person standing on the platform
The ground outside the train
A car moving on a nearby road
The train itself
mcqs.why: Relative motion is motion as observed from a particular frame. The passenger does not change position inside the train, so relative to the train the passenger is at rest, even though relative to the platform the passenger is moving.

mcqs.q: How does the same passenger in a moving train appear to a person standing on the platform?
options: In motion, moving with the train
At rest, because the passenger is sitting still
Moving backwards relative to the train
At absolute rest in space
mcqs.why: The notes give this exact example: a passenger in a moving train is at rest relative to the train but in motion relative to a person on the platform, because the observed motion depends on the observer frame.

mcqs.q: What is the correct statement about absolute rest?
options: The Earth is a state of absolute rest
All motion is relative; there is no absolute rest
A body sitting still on Earth is in absolute rest
Only objects in space can be in absolute rest
mcqs.why: The notes state directly that all motion is relative and there is no absolute rest. Whether a body is described as moving or at rest always depends on the frame from which it is observed.

mcqs.q: What is a frame of reference?
options: A fixed point that never moves in space
The path followed by a moving body
The system from which motion is observed
A device used to measure the speed of light
mcqs.why: The notes define a frame of reference as the system from which motion is observed. Different frames can give different descriptions of the same motion, which is the basis of relative motion.

mcqs.q: Which condition defines an inertial frame of reference?
options: It rotates at a constant rate
It speeds up steadily in a straight line
Newton laws fail in it unless extra forces are invented
It has zero acceleration and Newton laws hold in it directly
mcqs.why: An inertial frame is at rest or moves with uniform velocity, so its acceleration is zero. In such a frame Newton laws hold directly and a free body stays at rest or in uniform motion.

mcqs.q: In an inertial frame, what does a free body with no force on it do?
options: It stays at rest or keeps moving in uniform motion
It gradually slows down and stops by itself
It accelerates in the direction it last moved
It moves in a circle around the observer
mcqs.why: The notes state that in an inertial frame a free body stays at rest or in uniform motion, because Newton laws hold there. This behaviour is exactly what fails to hold in an accelerated frame.

mcqs.q: Why is a non-inertial frame different from an inertial frame?
options: It moves with uniform velocity in a straight line
It is accelerated, so Newton laws do not hold in it unless fictitious forces are added
It has zero acceleration at all times
It is always completely at rest
mcqs.why: A non-inertial frame is accelerated, so its velocity is variable. The notes state that Newton laws do not hold in it unless fictitious forces are added, unlike an inertial frame where they hold directly.

mcqs.q: A train moving steadily at constant speed is best described as which kind of frame?
options: A non-inertial frame
An absolute frame of rest
Nearly an inertial frame
A rotating frame
mcqs.why: The notes give a train moving steadily as nearly inertial, because it moves with uniform velocity and zero acceleration. A train speeding up or rounding a bend would instead be non-inertial.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an example of a non-inertial frame from the notes?
options: A train at steady speed on a straight track
A frame at rest on the platform
A frame moving with uniform velocity
A rotating or speeding-up frame
mcqs.why: The comparison table in the notes lists a rotating or speeding-up frame as the example of a non-inertial frame, because such a frame has non-zero acceleration, while the steady train is the inertial example.

mcqs.q: Two cars travel in the same direction, each at 70 km per hour. What is the speed of one car relative to the other?
options: 0 km per hour; they appear at rest to each other
70 km per hour
140 km per hour
35 km per hour
mcqs.why: Working: relative speed for motion in the same direction = 70 - 70 = 0 km per hour. The notes state that two cars at the same speed in the same direction appear at rest to each other.

lessons.title: Special Theory of Relativity
lessons.notes_html:
The special theory of relativity was proposed by Einstein in 1905. It deals with observers in inertial frames moving at constant velocity relative to each other, even at speeds near the speed of light.

The Two Postulates

First postulate: the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames of reference. No inertial frame is preferred.

Second postulate: the speed of light in free space is the same for all observers, whatever the motion of the source or the observer. If a light source moves towards the observer, the received speed is still the same.

c = 3 x 108 m s-1

  • c - speed of light in free space, the greatest speed any material body can approach

These postulates replace the old idea of absolute time and absolute length. Measurements of length, time and mass depend on the relative speed of the observer.

mcqs.q: Who proposed the special theory of relativity, and in which year?
options: Einstein, in 1905
Newton, in 1687
Planck, in 1900
Einstein, in 1915
mcqs.why: The notes state that the special theory of relativity was proposed by Einstein in 1905. It deals with observers in inertial frames, even at speeds near the speed of light.

mcqs.q: The special theory of relativity deals with observers in which kind of frames?
options: Accelerated frames only
Inertial frames moving at constant velocity relative to each other
Rotating frames only
Frames that are all at absolute rest
mcqs.why: The notes state that the theory deals with observers in inertial frames moving at constant velocity relative to each other. Accelerated, non-inertial frames are outside the scope of the special theory as presented here.

mcqs.q: What is the first postulate of the special theory of relativity?
options: The speed of light depends on the motion of the source
Time is absolute and the same for every observer
The laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames of reference
Length is absolute and never changes with motion
mcqs.why: The first postulate states that the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames of reference, and no inertial frame is preferred. The speed-of-light statement is the separate second postulate.

mcqs.q: What is the second postulate of the special theory of relativity?
options: The speed of light is greater when the source moves towards the observer
The speed of light is measured only in one preferred frame
The speed of light changes from one inertial frame to another
The speed of light in free space is the same for all observers, whatever the motion of the source or the observer
mcqs.why: The second postulate states that the speed of light in free space is the same for all observers, whatever the motion of the source or the observer. This replaces the old ideas of absolute time and absolute length.

mcqs.q: What is the value of the speed of light in free space given in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes give c = 3 x 10^8 m s^-1 for the speed of light in free space. They also state that c is the greatest speed any material body can approach.

mcqs.q: A light source moves towards an observer at 1 x 10^8 m s^-1. What speed of light does the observer receive?
options: 4 x 10^8 m s^-1, the sum of the two speeds
Still 3 x 10^8 m s^-1
2 x 10^8 m s^-1, the difference of the two speeds
1 x 10^8 m s^-1, the speed of the source
mcqs.why: Working: by the second postulate the received speed does not add the source speed, so it stays c = 3 x 10^8 m s^-1. The notes state explicitly that if a light source moves towards the observer, the received speed is still the same.

mcqs.q: Which old ideas do the two postulates of relativity replace?
options: The ideas of energy and momentum conservation
The idea that light travels in free space
The ideas of absolute time and absolute length
The idea that physics laws exist at all
mcqs.why: The notes state that the postulates replace the old idea of absolute time and absolute length. Measurements of length, time and mass instead depend on the relative speed of the observer.

mcqs.q: According to the notes, measurements of length, time and mass depend on what?
options: The colour of the object being measured
The temperature of the measuring instruments
The size of the laboratory used
The relative speed of the observer
mcqs.why: The notes state that measurements of length, time and mass depend on the relative speed of the observer. This dependence is developed in the next lesson as length contraction, time dilation and mass increase.

mcqs.q: Which statement about inertial frames follows from the first postulate?
options: No inertial frame is preferred over any other
One special inertial frame is the true rest frame
Only a frame at rest on Earth is a true inertial frame
A faster inertial frame has different laws of physics
mcqs.why: Because the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, the notes state that no inertial frame is preferred. An experiment cannot single out one inertial frame as the special rest frame.

mcqs.q: The speed of light c is described in the notes as what?
options: An average speed that fast rockets easily exceed
The greatest speed any material body can approach
The speed of sound in free space
A speed reached only by objects at rest
mcqs.why: The notes describe c, the speed of light in free space, as the greatest speed any material body can approach. The consequences of this limit, such as mass increase, are worked out in the following lesson.

lessons.title: Consequences of Special Theory of Relativity
lessons.notes_html:
The postulates lead to surprising results at high speeds: length contraction, time dilation, mass increase and mass-energy equivalence. A particle can move at the speed of light only if its rest mass is zero, like the photon; any other particle would need infinite energy to reach c.

L = L0 sqrt(1 - v2/c2)

  • L - length measured in motion, shorter than rest length; L0 - rest length; v - speed of object

T = T0 / sqrt(1 - v2/c2)

  • T - time interval measured by moving observer, longer than proper time; T0 - proper time in rest frame; a moving clock runs slower

m = m0 / sqrt(1 - v2/c2)

  • m - relativistic mass, increases with speed; m0 - rest mass

E = m c2

  • E - energy equivalent of mass m; even a small mass gives very large energy because c2 is huge

Worked Example: Length Contraction of a Rocket

How fast must a rocket go for its length to be contracted to 80 percent of its rest length?

Step 1: L / L0 = 0.80, so sqrt(1 - v2/c2) = 0.80.

Step 2: Squaring gives 1 - v2/c2 = 0.64, so v2/c2 = 0.36 and v = 0.6 c.

Step 3: v = 0.6 x 3 x 108 = 1.8 x 108 m s-1.

Answer: 1.8 x 108 m s-1.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives length contraction in the special theory of relativity?
options: L = L0 / sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2)
L = L0 sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2)
L = L0 sqrt(1 + v^2 / c^2)
mcqs.why: The notes give L = L0 sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2), where L is the length measured in motion and L0 is the rest length. Since the square root is less than 1, the moving length is shorter than the rest length.

mcqs.q: What does time dilation say about a moving clock?
options: A moving clock runs faster than a clock at rest
A moving clock keeps exactly the same time as a rest clock
A moving clock runs slower; its measured interval T is longer than the proper time T0
A moving clock stops completely at any speed
mcqs.why: The notes give T = T0 / sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2), so T is longer than the proper time T0 measured in the rest frame. They summarise this by saying a moving clock runs slower.

mcqs.q: How fast must a rocket go for its length to contract to 80 percent of its rest length?
mcqs.why: Full working: L / L0 = 0.80, so sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2) = 0.80. Squaring: 1 - v^2 / c^2 = 0.64, so v^2 / c^2 = 0.36 and v = 0.6 c. Then v = 0.6 x 3 x 10^8 = 1.8 x 10^8 m s^-1, the worked example answer in the notes.

mcqs.q: A rod has rest length 100 m and moves at 0.6 c. What is its contracted length?
mcqs.why: Full working: L = L0 sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2) = 100 x sqrt(1 - 0.36) = 100 x sqrt(0.64) = 100 x 0.8 = 80 m. The moving length is shorter than the 100 m rest length, as length contraction requires.

mcqs.q: A clock has proper time interval 10 s and moves at 0.6 c. What interval is measured for the moving clock?
options: 8 s
mcqs.why: Full working: T = T0 / sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2) = 10 / sqrt(1 - 0.36) = 10 / sqrt(0.64) = 10 / 0.8 = 12.5 s. The interval is longer than the proper time, which is the time dilation effect.

mcqs.q: A particle of rest mass 3 kg moves at 0.8 c. What is its relativistic mass?
options: 3 kg
4 kg
5 kg
1.8 kg
mcqs.why: Full working: m = m0 / sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2) = 3 / sqrt(1 - 0.64) = 3 / sqrt(0.36) = 3 / 0.6 = 5 kg. The relativistic mass is greater than the rest mass, because mass increases with speed.

mcqs.q: What energy is equivalent to a mass of 1 kg, using E = m c^2?
mcqs.why: Full working: E = m c^2 = 1 x (3 x 10^8)^2 = 1 x 9 x 10^16 = 9 x 10^16 J. The notes stress that even a small mass gives a very large energy because c^2 is huge.

mcqs.q: A proper time interval is 6 s for a clock moving at 0.8 c. What is the dilated interval?
options: 6 s
mcqs.why: Full working: T = T0 / sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2) = 6 / sqrt(1 - 0.64) = 6 / sqrt(0.36) = 6 / 0.6 = 10 s. Division by a factor smaller than 1 makes the measured interval longer than the proper time.

mcqs.q: Which particle can move at the speed of light, according to the notes?
options: Any particle, if it is given enough time to accelerate
Only a particle with zero rest mass, like the photon
An electron, because it is very light
A particle whose rest mass increases to a large value
mcqs.why: The notes state that a particle can move at the speed of light only if its rest mass is zero, like the photon. Any other particle would need infinite energy to reach c, so it can only approach c.

mcqs.q: What happens to the mass of a body as its speed increases towards c?
options: Its relativistic mass decreases towards zero
Its mass stays exactly equal to its rest mass at all speeds
Its relativistic mass increases, following m = m0 / sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2)
Its mass becomes negative at high speed
mcqs.why: The notes list mass increase as a consequence of relativity, with m = m0 / sqrt(1 - v^2 / c^2). As v grows the denominator shrinks, so m grows larger than the rest mass m0.

lessons.title: Blackbody Radiation
lessons.notes_html:
A blackbody is a perfect absorber and emitter of radiation. Blackbody radiation is the electromagnetic radiation it emits when heated. Its spectrum depends only on temperature, not on the material. No perfect blackbody exists in nature. The closest example is a hollow cavity with a very small hole: radiation entering is trapped by repeated reflections and almost fully absorbed, so the hole acts as a blackbody.

Laws of Blackbody Radiation

lambdamax T = 2.9 x 10-3 m K

  • Wien displacement law: lambdamax - wavelength of maximum emission; hotter bodies radiate most strongly at shorter wavelengths

E = σ T4

  • Stefan-Boltzmann law: E - total energy radiated per unit area per second; σ - Stefan constant; if T doubles, E increases sixteen times

Classical theory predicted energy rising without limit at short wavelengths, the ultraviolet catastrophe. Planck solved this with the quantum idea in the next lessons, giving Planck law for the full distribution.

mcqs.q: What is a blackbody?
options: A body that reflects all radiation falling on it
A body that emits only visible light
A perfect absorber and emitter of radiation
A body that absorbs radiation but never emits it
mcqs.why: The notes define a blackbody as a perfect absorber and emitter of radiation. Blackbody radiation is the electromagnetic radiation it emits when heated, and no perfect blackbody exists in nature.

mcqs.q: The spectrum of blackbody radiation depends on what?
options: Only on the material of the body
On the colour the body had before heating
On the shape of the container holding the body
Only on the temperature, not on the material
mcqs.why: The notes state that the spectrum of blackbody radiation depends only on temperature, not on the material. This is why laws such as the Wien and Stefan-Boltzmann laws are written purely in terms of temperature.

mcqs.q: What is the closest practical example of a blackbody given in the notes?
options: A hollow cavity with a very small hole
A polished silver mirror
A sheet of white paper in sunlight
A transparent glass window
mcqs.why: The notes state that the closest example is a hollow cavity with a very small hole: radiation entering is trapped by repeated reflections and almost fully absorbed, so the hole acts as a blackbody.

mcqs.q: What does the Wien displacement law state?
options: lambda_max T = 2.9 x 10^-6 m K
lambda_max T = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K
lambda_max / T = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K
lambda_max T^4 = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K
mcqs.why: The notes give the Wien displacement law as lambda_max T = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K, where lambda_max is the wavelength of maximum emission. Hotter bodies radiate most strongly at shorter wavelengths.

mcqs.q: A blackbody at 2900 K has its maximum emission at what wavelength?
mcqs.why: Full working: lambda_max = 2.9 x 10^-3 / T = 2.9 x 10^-3 / 2900 = 1 x 10^-6 m. This uses the Wien displacement law lambda_max T = 2.9 x 10^-3 m K from the notes.

mcqs.q: A blackbody at 5800 K has its maximum emission at what wavelength?
mcqs.why: Full working: lambda_max = 2.9 x 10^-3 / T = 2.9 x 10^-3 / 5800 = 5 x 10^-7 m. The hotter body peaks at a shorter wavelength than the 2900 K body, as the Wien law requires.

mcqs.q: What does the Stefan-Boltzmann law state?
options: E = sigma T^4, the total energy radiated per unit area per second
E = sigma T, the total energy radiated per unit area per second
E = sigma / T^4, the total energy radiated per unit area per second
E = sigma T^2, the total energy radiated per unit area per second
mcqs.why: The notes give the Stefan-Boltzmann law as E = sigma T^4, where E is the total energy radiated per unit area per second and sigma is the Stefan constant. The fourth power makes E very sensitive to temperature.

mcqs.q: If the temperature of a blackbody doubles, by what factor does the energy radiated per unit area per second increase?
options: Two times
Sixteen times
Four times
Eight times
mcqs.why: Full working: E = sigma T^4, so doubling T gives (2)^4 = 16 times the energy. The notes state this result directly: if T doubles, E increases sixteen times.

mcqs.q: If the temperature of a blackbody becomes three times as great, by what factor does E increase?
options: 9 times
27 times
81 times
3 times
mcqs.why: Full working: E = sigma T^4, so replacing T by 3T gives (3)^4 = 81 times the original energy. This follows the same fourth-power Stefan-Boltzmann law used in the notes for the doubling case.

mcqs.q: What was the ultraviolet catastrophe?
options: Classical theory predicted no radiation at all from hot bodies
Classical theory predicted energy falling to zero at long wavelengths only
An experiment in which ultraviolet light destroyed the cavity
Classical theory predicted energy rising without limit at short wavelengths
mcqs.why: The notes state that classical theory predicted energy rising without limit at short wavelengths, the ultraviolet catastrophe. Planck solved this with the quantum idea, giving the Planck law for the full distribution.

lessons.title: Particle Theory of Electromagnetic Radiations
lessons.notes_html:
Planck proposed that energy is not emitted continuously but in discrete packets called quanta. One quantum of radiation is a photon. This quantum hypothesis explained the blackbody distribution over all wavelengths.

E = h f

  • E - energy of one photon, unit J; h - Planck constant = 6.63 x 10-34 J s; f - frequency of radiation

E = h c / lambda

  • lambda - wavelength; c - speed of light; photon energy rises as wavelength falls

The dimension of Planck constant is [M L2 T-1], the same as angular momentum. Radiation therefore has a particle side as well as a wave side. The photon picture is the basis of the photoelectric effect, the Compton effect and pair production in this unit. Brighter light means more photons per second, while the colour decides the energy of each photon.

mcqs.q: What did Planck propose about the emission of energy?
options: Energy is emitted as a smooth continuous wave only
Energy is emitted only when the body is at rest
Energy packets grow smaller as frequency increases
Energy is not emitted continuously but in discrete packets called quanta
mcqs.why: The notes state that Planck proposed that energy is not emitted continuously but in discrete packets called quanta. This quantum hypothesis explained the blackbody distribution over all wavelengths.

mcqs.q: What is one quantum of radiation called?
options: A photon
A phonon
A positron
A quantum electron
mcqs.why: The notes state that one quantum of radiation is a photon. The photon picture is the basis of the photoelectric effect, the Compton effect and pair production in this unit.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the energy of one photon?
options: E = h / f
E = h f
E = f / h
E = h f^2
mcqs.why: The notes give E = h f, where E is the energy of one photon in joules, h is the Planck constant and f is the frequency of the radiation. Photon energy therefore increases in direct proportion to frequency.

mcqs.q: What is the value of the Planck constant given in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes give h, the Planck constant, as 6.63 x 10^-34 J s in the formula E = h f. Its dimension is [M L^2 T^-1], the same as angular momentum.

mcqs.q: What is the energy of a photon of frequency 1 x 10^15 Hz?
mcqs.why: Full working: E = h f = 6.63 x 10^-34 x 1 x 10^15 = 6.63 x 10^-19 J. The frequency multiplies the Planck constant directly, using h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s from the notes.

mcqs.q: What is the energy of a photon of frequency 5 x 10^14 Hz?
mcqs.why: Full working: E = h f = 6.63 x 10^-34 x 5 x 10^14 = 33.15 x 10^-20 = 3.315 x 10^-19 J. Halving the frequency compared with 1 x 10^15 Hz halves the photon energy, as E = h f requires.

mcqs.q: What is the energy of a photon of wavelength 500 nm, using E = h c / lambda?
mcqs.why: Full working: E = h c / lambda = (6.63 x 10^-34 x 3 x 10^8) / (500 x 10^-9) = 1.989 x 10^-25 / 5 x 10^-7 = 3.978 x 10^-19 J. Photon energy rises as wavelength falls, as the notes state.

mcqs.q: How is the photon energy E = h c / lambda related to wavelength?
options: Photon energy rises as wavelength rises
Photon energy does not depend on wavelength
Photon energy rises as wavelength falls
Photon energy falls as frequency rises
mcqs.why: The notes give E = h c / lambda and state that photon energy rises as wavelength falls. Wavelength is in the denominator, so a shorter wavelength means a larger photon energy.

mcqs.q: The dimension of the Planck constant is the same as that of what quantity?
options: Force, with dimension [M L T^-2]
Energy alone, with dimension [M L^2 T^-2]
Momentum, with dimension [M L T^-1]
Angular momentum, with dimension [M L^2 T^-1]
mcqs.why: The notes state that the dimension of the Planck constant is [M L^2 T^-1], the same as angular momentum. This follows from E = h f, since energy divided by frequency has these dimensions.

mcqs.q: What does brighter light of the same colour mean in the photon picture?
options: More photons per second, while the colour decides the energy of each photon
Each photon carries more energy than before
Each photon travels faster than the speed of light
Fewer photons per second, each with much more energy
mcqs.why: The notes state that brighter light means more photons per second, while the colour decides the energy of each photon. Radiation therefore has a particle side as well as a wave side.

lessons.title: Photoelectric Effect
lessons.notes_html:
The photoelectric effect, first observed by Hertz, is the emission of electrons from a metal surface when light of suitable frequency falls on it. The emitted electrons are photoelectrons. Einstein explained it with the photon picture: a photon transfers its energy to one electron.

Einstein Equation and Laws

h f = phi + K.E.max

  • h f - photon energy; phi - work function, the minimum energy to free an electron; K.E.max - maximum kinetic energy of photoelectron

K.E.max = h f - phi

  • Kinetic energy grows with frequency, not intensity; phi equals the threshold energy h f0

K.E.max = e Vs

  • Vs - stopping potential; e - electron charge; this gives K.E. from a voltage measurement

Laws: emission only if f exceeds the threshold frequency f0 = phi / h; photocurrent is proportional to intensity; K.E. depends on frequency only; emission is instantaneous. Alkali metals like potassium emit even for visible light, work function about 2 eV.

Worked Example: Photoelectrons from Potassium

Find the maximum K.E. of photoelectrons ejected from a potassium surface by ultraviolet radiation of wavelength 200 nm. The work function is 2.8 eV. Also find the stopping potential.

Step 1: Photon energy E = h c / lambda = (6.626 x 10-34 x 3 x 108) / (200 x 10-9) = 9.939 x 10-19 J.

Step 2: In eV, E = 9.939 x 10-19 / 1.602 x 10-19 = 6.2 eV.

Step 3: K.E.max = 6.2 - 2.8 = 3.4 eV.

Step 4: Stopping potential Vs = 3.4 V, since K.E.max = e Vs.

Answer: K.E.max = 3.4 eV and Vs = 3.4 V.

mcqs.q: What is the photoelectric effect?
options: The emission of electrons from a metal surface when light of suitable frequency falls on it
The emission of light from a metal when a current passes through it
The bending of light around the edge of a metal plate
The heating of a metal until it glows white
mcqs.why: The notes define the photoelectric effect, first observed by Hertz, as the emission of electrons from a metal surface when light of suitable frequency falls on it. The emitted electrons are called photoelectrons.

mcqs.q: What are the electrons emitted in the photoelectric effect called?
options: Thermions
Photoelectrons
Positrons
Free neutrons
mcqs.why: The notes state that the emitted electrons are photoelectrons. Einstein explained their emission with the photon picture: a photon transfers its energy to one electron.

mcqs.q: What is the Einstein photoelectric equation?
options: h f = phi - K.E.max
h f = phi x K.E.max
h f = phi + K.E.max
K.E.max = phi - h f
mcqs.why: The notes give h f = phi + K.E.max, where h f is the photon energy, phi is the work function and K.E.max is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectron. The photon energy is shared between freeing the electron and its kinetic energy.

mcqs.q: What is the work function phi of a metal?
options: The maximum kinetic energy of any photoelectron
The energy of the incoming photon
The stopping potential multiplied by the photon energy
The minimum energy needed to free an electron from the metal
mcqs.why: The notes define phi, the work function, as the minimum energy to free an electron, and state that phi equals the threshold energy h f0. Only the photon energy above phi appears as kinetic energy.

mcqs.q: Ultraviolet light of wavelength 200 nm falls on potassium of work function 2.8 eV. What is the photon energy?
options: 6.2 eV
3.4 eV
2.8 eV
9.0 eV
mcqs.why: Full working: E = h c / lambda = (6.626 x 10^-34 x 3 x 10^8) / (200 x 10^-9) = 9.939 x 10^-19 J. In eV: E = 9.939 x 10^-19 / 1.602 x 10^-19 = 6.2 eV, as in the worked example in the notes.

mcqs.q: For the same potassium example, photon energy 6.2 eV and work function 2.8 eV, what is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons?
options: 9.0 eV
3.4 eV
6.2 eV
2.8 eV
mcqs.why: Full working: K.E.max = h f - phi = 6.2 - 2.8 = 3.4 eV, using the Einstein equation h f = phi + K.E.max. This is the worked example answer given in the notes.

mcqs.q: For the same potassium example with K.E.max = 3.4 eV, what is the stopping potential?
mcqs.why: Full working: K.E.max = e Vs, so Vs = K.E.max / e = 3.4 eV / e = 3.4 V. The notes give this result directly: the stopping potential is 3.4 V since K.E.max = e Vs.

mcqs.q: A photon of energy 5 eV strikes a metal of work function 2 eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons?
options: 7 eV
5 eV
2 eV
3 eV
mcqs.why: Full working: K.E.max = h f - phi = 5 - 2 = 3 eV, from the Einstein equation h f = phi + K.E.max. The work function energy is used to free the electron and only the remainder becomes kinetic energy.

mcqs.q: Photoelectrons have a maximum kinetic energy of 2 eV. What stopping potential stops them?
options: 2 V
4 V
1 V
mcqs.why: Full working: K.E.max = e Vs, so Vs = K.E.max / e = 2 eV / e = 2 V. The notes give the relation K.E.max = e Vs, which lets kinetic energy be found from a voltage measurement.

mcqs.q: Which is a correct law of the photoelectric effect from the notes?
options: Emission occurs for any frequency if the light is bright enough and given enough time
Emission occurs only if the frequency exceeds the threshold frequency f0 = phi / h, and emission is instantaneous
Kinetic energy grows with intensity, not with frequency
There is a long time delay before electrons are emitted
mcqs.why: The notes list the laws: emission only if f exceeds the threshold frequency f0 = phi / h; photocurrent is proportional to intensity; K.E. depends on frequency only; and emission is instantaneous. Kinetic energy grows with frequency, not intensity.

lessons.title: Photocell and Solar Cell
lessons.notes_html:
A photocell is a device that converts light energy into electrical energy. When light of suitable frequency falls on its photosensitive surface, photoelectrons are emitted and the resulting current varies with the intensity of the light.

Uses of the Photocell

Photocells are used in automatic doors, burglar alarms, street-light controls and solar energy systems. In each case a change in light level changes the current, and that change switches another circuit on or off.

Solar Cell

A solar cell also converts light energy directly into electrical energy, using a semiconductor PN junction. Sunlight falling on the junction frees electron-hole pairs, and the junction field separates them to give a useful current and voltage. Solar cells put the photoelectric idea to work on a large scale for clean power, and photocells in alarms and controls use the same light-to-current principle on a small scale.

mcqs.q: What does a photocell do?
options: It converts electrical energy into light energy
It converts light energy into electrical energy
It converts heat energy into sound energy
It stores light energy as chemical energy permanently
mcqs.why: The notes define a photocell as a device that converts light energy into electrical energy. When light of suitable frequency falls on its photosensitive surface, photoelectrons are emitted and a current results.

mcqs.q: In a photocell, how does the resulting current behave?
options: The current stays fixed whatever the light level
The current varies only with the temperature of the room
The current varies with the intensity of the light
The current flows only when the light is switched off
mcqs.why: The notes state that when light of suitable frequency falls on the photosensitive surface, photoelectrons are emitted and the resulting current varies with the intensity of the light. That variation is what makes the photocell useful in control circuits.

mcqs.q: Which is a use of a photocell given in the notes?
options: Measuring the mass of an electron
Producing X-rays for hospitals
Splitting white light into a spectrum
Automatic doors
mcqs.why: The notes list photocells in automatic doors, burglar alarms, street-light controls and solar energy systems. In each case a change in light level changes the current, and that change switches another circuit on or off.

mcqs.q: How does a photocell control another circuit, such as a burglar alarm?
options: A change in light level changes the current, and that change switches the other circuit on or off
The photocell shines a brighter beam onto the other circuit
The photocell heats the other circuit until it melts a fuse
The photocell blocks all current permanently once light falls on it
mcqs.why: The notes explain that in alarms and controls a change in light level changes the current, and that change switches another circuit on or off. The photocell therefore works as a light-operated switch.

mcqs.q: Which list gives only uses of photocells named in the notes?
options: Television screens, radio transmitters and loudspeakers
Burglar alarms, street-light controls and solar energy systems
Electric motors, transformers and generators
Microscopes, telescopes and cameras lenses only
mcqs.why: The notes name automatic doors, burglar alarms, street-light controls and solar energy systems as uses of photocells. The other lists contain devices that are not given as photocell uses in this lesson.

mcqs.q: What does a solar cell convert, and by what means?
options: It converts heat energy into electrical energy using two metal junctions
It converts light energy into chemical energy in a battery electrolyte
It converts light energy directly into electrical energy using a semiconductor PN junction
It converts sound energy into electrical energy using a coil and magnet
mcqs.why: The notes state that a solar cell converts light energy directly into electrical energy using a semiconductor PN junction. Sunlight falling on the junction frees electron-hole pairs, which the junction field separates.

mcqs.q: In a solar cell, what does sunlight falling on the PN junction do?
options: It melts the junction so the two sides join into one conductor
It reflects off the junction and is stored as light in the cell
It frees protons that flow out as a beam of radiation
It frees electron-hole pairs, and the junction field separates them to give a useful current and voltage
mcqs.why: The notes state that sunlight falling on the junction frees electron-hole pairs, and the junction field separates them to give a useful current and voltage. This is how the solar cell delivers electrical power.

mcqs.q: How do solar cells and simple photocells compare in the notes?
options: Solar cells use the photoelectric idea on a large scale for clean power; photocells in alarms and controls use the same light-to-current principle on a small scale
Solar cells and photocells work on completely unrelated principles
Photocells produce large-scale power while solar cells only work alarms
Solar cells work in darkness while photocells need bright light
mcqs.why: The notes state that solar cells put the photoelectric idea to work on a large scale for clean power, and photocells in alarms and controls use the same light-to-current principle on a small scale.

mcqs.q: What must be true of the light falling on a photocell photosensitive surface for photoelectrons to be emitted?
options: The light must be of any frequency, however low
The light must be of suitable frequency
The light must fall on the surface for several hours first
The light must be reflected from a mirror before reaching the surface
mcqs.why: The notes state that photoelectrons are emitted when light of suitable frequency falls on the photosensitive surface. This connects the photocell back to the photoelectric effect and its threshold frequency.

mcqs.q: Which application relies on a photocell detecting a change in light level to control street lighting?
options: A solar panel heating water for houses
A burglar alarm sounding when a door opens mechanically
Street-light controls that switch lamps as the light level changes
An automatic door driven by an electric motor alone
mcqs.why: Street-light controls are listed in the notes as a photocell use. A change in light level changes the photocell current, and that change switches the lamp circuit on or off.

lessons.title: Photon Model of Light
lessons.notes_html:
In the photon model, light travels as particles called photons. Each photon carries energy and momentum, yet light also shows wave behaviour like diffraction. Diffraction does not verify the particle nature; the photoelectric effect, Compton effect and pair production do.

p = h f / c

  • p - momentum of a photon; h f - its energy; a photon has zero rest mass and always moves at c

p = h / lambda

  • Same momentum written with wavelength lambda; shorter wavelength means larger momentum

Einstein first explained that a photon can transfer its whole energy to a single electron. That single idea explains the threshold frequency, the frequency dependence of photoelectron energy, and why brighter light of the same frequency ejects more electrons but not faster ones. A photon at rest mass zero still carries energy and momentum, and it always travels at c in free space.

mcqs.q: In the photon model, how does light travel?
options: Only as a continuous wave with no particle behaviour
As particles that carry momentum but no energy
As particles called photons, each carrying energy and momentum
As slow massive particles that can be brought to rest
mcqs.why: The notes state that in the photon model light travels as particles called photons, and each photon carries energy and momentum. Yet light also shows wave behaviour like diffraction, so both sides are needed.

mcqs.q: Which phenomenon does NOT verify the particle nature of light, according to the notes?
options: The photoelectric effect
The Compton effect
Pair production
Diffraction
mcqs.why: The notes state clearly that diffraction does not verify the particle nature of light; it is a wave behaviour. The photoelectric effect, Compton effect and pair production do verify the particle nature.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the momentum of a photon in terms of its frequency?
options: p = h f / c
p = h f c
p = c / (h f)
p = h / (f c)
mcqs.why: The notes give p = h f / c, where p is the momentum of a photon and h f is its energy. Dividing the photon energy by c gives its momentum, since the photon always moves at c.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the momentum of a photon in terms of its wavelength?
options: p = h lambda
p = h / lambda
p = lambda / h
p = h lambda / c
mcqs.why: The notes give the same momentum written with wavelength as p = h / lambda. A shorter wavelength therefore means a larger momentum, because lambda is in the denominator.

mcqs.q: What is the momentum of a photon of wavelength 500 nm?
mcqs.why: Full working: p = h / lambda = 6.63 x 10^-34 / (500 x 10^-9) = 6.63 x 10^-34 / 5 x 10^-7 = 1.326 x 10^-27 kg m s^-1. This uses the photon momentum formula p = h / lambda from the notes.

mcqs.q: A photon has energy 6 x 10^-19 J. What is its momentum?
mcqs.why: Full working: p = h f / c = E / c = 6 x 10^-19 / (3 x 10^8) = 2 x 10^-27 kg m s^-1. The notes give p = h f / c, and h f is the photon energy E.

mcqs.q: What is true about the rest mass and speed of a photon?
options: A photon has zero rest mass and always moves at c
A photon has a small rest mass and can be slowed to rest
A photon has zero rest mass but moves slower than c in free space
A photon gains rest mass when its frequency increases
mcqs.why: The notes state that a photon at rest mass zero still carries energy and momentum, and it always travels at c in free space. Zero rest mass is what allows it to move at the speed of light.

mcqs.q: How does photon momentum change when the wavelength becomes shorter?
options: Shorter wavelength means smaller momentum
Shorter wavelength means larger momentum
Momentum stays the same for all wavelengths
Momentum becomes zero at short wavelengths
mcqs.why: The notes state that in p = h / lambda, a shorter wavelength means larger momentum. Since lambda is in the denominator, decreasing lambda increases p in inverse proportion.

mcqs.q: Einstein first explained that a photon can transfer what to a single electron?
options: Only half of its energy, keeping the rest
Its momentum but none of its energy
Its whole energy
Its rest mass, becoming an electron itself
mcqs.why: The notes state that Einstein first explained that a photon can transfer its whole energy to a single electron. That single idea explains the threshold frequency and the frequency dependence of photoelectron energy.

mcqs.q: Why does brighter light of the same frequency eject more electrons but not faster ones?
options: Brighter light makes each photon more energetic
Brighter light increases the speed of each photon beyond c
Brighter light lowers the work function of the metal
Brighter light means more photons, each still transferring the same energy set by the frequency
mcqs.why: The notes explain that the single-photon energy transfer idea explains why brighter light of the same frequency ejects more electrons but not faster ones: there are more photons, but each carries the same frequency-set energy.

lessons.title: Compton Effect
lessons.notes_html:
The Compton effect is the increase in wavelength of X-rays scattered by electrons in a target such as carbon. A photon collides with an electron at rest, loses energy and momentum to it, and is scattered with a longer wavelength. Only a particle picture can explain this, so the effect verifies the particle nature of light. Note: one short question in the book prints wave theory here; that is a misprint for particle nature.

Δlambda = (h / m0c)(1 - cos theta)

  • Δlambda - Compton shift, lambda prime minus lambda; theta - scattering angle; h / m0c = 2.43 x 10-12 m is the Compton wavelength

The shift is zero for no scattering and greatest, twice the Compton wavelength, for back scattering at 180 degrees.

Worked Example: Incident Wavelength from Compton Shift

A photon scatters from an electron at rest at 60 degrees. The Compton shift is triple the wavelength of the incident photon. Find the incident wavelength.

Step 1: Shift = 2.43 x 10-12 x (1 - cos 60 degrees). Cos 60 degrees = 0.5.

Step 2: Shift = 2.43 x 10-12 x 0.5 = 1.215 x 10-12 m.

Step 3: Given shift = 3 x lambda, so lambda = 1.215 x 10-12 / 3 = 4.05 x 10-13 m.

Answer: 4.05 x 10-13 m.

mcqs.q: What is the Compton effect?
options: The decrease in wavelength of X-rays passing through a crystal
The emission of electrons from a metal by visible light
The creation of an electron-positron pair by a gamma photon
The increase in wavelength of X-rays scattered by electrons in a target such as carbon
mcqs.why: The notes define the Compton effect as the increase in wavelength of X-rays scattered by electrons in a target such as carbon. Only a particle picture can explain it, so it verifies the particle nature of light.

mcqs.q: In the Compton effect, what happens to the photon during the collision?
options: It collides with an electron at rest, loses energy and momentum to it, and is scattered with a longer wavelength
It gains energy from the electron and leaves with a shorter wavelength
It is completely absorbed and no scattered photon appears
It passes through the electron unchanged in energy and wavelength
mcqs.why: The notes state that a photon collides with an electron at rest, loses energy and momentum to it, and is scattered with a longer wavelength. The wavelength increase is the Compton shift.

mcqs.q: What does the Compton effect verify about light?
options: The wave theory of light only
The particle nature of light
That photons have a large rest mass
That electrons have no momentum
mcqs.why: The notes state that only a particle picture can explain the Compton effect, so the effect verifies the particle nature of light. They also note that a book question printing wave theory here is a misprint for particle nature.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the Compton shift?
options: Delta lambda = (h / m0 c)(1 + cos theta)
Delta lambda = (m0 c / h)(1 - cos theta)
Delta lambda = (h / m0 c)(1 - cos theta)
Delta lambda = (h / m0 c) cos theta
mcqs.why: The notes give Delta lambda = (h / m0 c)(1 - cos theta), where Delta lambda is lambda prime minus lambda and theta is the scattering angle. The quantity h / m0 c = 2.43 x 10^-12 m is the Compton wavelength.

mcqs.q: What is the value of the Compton wavelength h / m0 c given in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes give h / m0 c = 2.43 x 10^-12 m as the Compton wavelength. The shift at any angle is this value multiplied by (1 - cos theta), so it is also the shift at 90 degrees.

mcqs.q: What is the Compton shift for back scattering at 180 degrees?
options: 4.86 x 10^-12 m, twice the Compton wavelength
2.43 x 10^-12 m, equal to the Compton wavelength
Zero, because the photon reverses direction
1.215 x 10^-12 m, half the Compton wavelength
mcqs.why: Full working: Delta lambda = 2.43 x 10^-12 x (1 - cos 180 degrees) = 2.43 x 10^-12 x (1 - (-1)) = 2.43 x 10^-12 x 2 = 4.86 x 10^-12 m. The notes state the shift is greatest, twice the Compton wavelength, for back scattering at 180 degrees.

mcqs.q: What is the Compton shift for scattering at 90 degrees?
options: Zero
mcqs.why: Full working: Delta lambda = 2.43 x 10^-12 x (1 - cos 90 degrees) = 2.43 x 10^-12 x (1 - 0) = 2.43 x 10^-12 m. At 90 degrees the shift equals the Compton wavelength itself.

mcqs.q: What is the Compton shift for scattering at 60 degrees?
mcqs.why: Full working: Delta lambda = 2.43 x 10^-12 x (1 - cos 60 degrees) = 2.43 x 10^-12 x (1 - 0.5) = 2.43 x 10^-12 x 0.5 = 1.215 x 10^-12 m. This is step 1 and 2 of the worked example in the notes.

mcqs.q: A photon scatters at 60 degrees and the Compton shift is triple the incident wavelength. What is the incident wavelength?
mcqs.why: Full working: shift at 60 degrees = 2.43 x 10^-12 x 0.5 = 1.215 x 10^-12 m. Given shift = 3 x lambda, lambda = 1.215 x 10^-12 / 3 = 4.05 x 10^-13 m, the worked example answer in the notes.

mcqs.q: At what scattering angle is the Compton shift zero?
options: At 0 degrees, when there is no scattering
At 90 degrees, sideways scattering
At 180 degrees, back scattering
At 60 degrees, the worked example angle
mcqs.why: Full working: Delta lambda = 2.43 x 10^-12 x (1 - cos 0 degrees) = 2.43 x 10^-12 x (1 - 1) = 0. The notes state the shift is zero for no scattering and greatest for back scattering at 180 degrees.

lessons.title: Pair Production
lessons.notes_html:
Pair production is the creation of matter from energy: a high-energy gamma photon passing near a nucleus disappears and produces an electron-positron pair. The positron is the antiparticle of the electron. Any extra photon energy appears as kinetic energy of the pair, and both particles have equal speeds in the symmetric case.

Emin = 2 x 0.511 MeV = 1.02 MeV

  • Minimum photon energy: each particle needs its rest energy 0.511 MeV, so the photon must supply at least 1.02 MeV

Annihilation

Annihilation is the reverse process. When an electron meets a positron, both disappear and their total energy is released as two gamma photons of 0.511 MeV each, travelling in opposite directions to conserve momentum.

FeaturePair productionAnnihilation
ChangeEnergy into matterMatter into energy
StartOne gamma photon near a nucleusElectron plus positron
EndElectron plus positronTwo gamma photons

Worked Example: Photon for a Pair with Kinetic Energy

An electron-positron pair, each with K.E. of 220 keV, is produced by a photon. Find the energy and wavelength of the photon.

Step 1: Photon energy = rest energies plus kinetic energies = 0.511 + 0.511 + 0.220 + 0.220 = 1.462 MeV, about 1.46 MeV.

Step 2: Convert: E = 1.462 x 1.602 x 10-13 J = 2.342 x 10-13 J.

Step 3: lambda = h c / E = 1.9878 x 10-25 / 2.342 x 10-13 = 8.49 x 10-13 m, about 8.5 x 10-13 m.

Answer: Energy 1.46 MeV, wavelength 8.5 x 10-13 m.

mcqs.q: What is pair production?
options: A high-energy gamma photon passing near a nucleus disappears and produces an electron-positron pair
An electron and positron disappear and produce two gamma photons
A photon splits into two photons of half the energy
An electron jumps between two energy levels in an atom
mcqs.why: The notes define pair production as the creation of matter from energy: a high-energy gamma photon passing near a nucleus disappears and produces an electron-positron pair. Annihilation is the reverse process.

mcqs.q: What is the positron?
options: A positively charged proton inside the nucleus
The antiparticle of the electron
An electron with extra kinetic energy
A photon with positive charge
mcqs.why: The notes state that the positron is the antiparticle of the electron. In pair production the gamma photon produces one electron and one positron, matter created from energy.

mcqs.q: What is the minimum energy a photon must have for pair production?
options: 2.04 MeV
1.02 MeV
mcqs.why: Full working: E_min = 2 x 0.511 MeV = 1.02 MeV, because each particle needs its rest energy 0.511 MeV. The notes give this minimum photon energy directly for creating the electron-positron pair.

mcqs.q: Where does any extra photon energy go in pair production, beyond the rest energies?
options: It is stored as extra rest mass of the nucleus only
It disappears, because energy need not be conserved
It is emitted as a second gamma photon of equal energy
It appears as kinetic energy of the pair
mcqs.why: The notes state that any extra photon energy appears as kinetic energy of the pair, and both particles have equal speeds in the symmetric case. The total photon energy is the rest energies plus the kinetic energies.

mcqs.q: What is annihilation?
options: An electron meets a positron, both disappear, and their total energy is released as two gamma photons of 0.511 MeV each
A gamma photon near a nucleus creates an electron-positron pair
An electron falls into the nucleus and is destroyed alone
Two photons collide and produce a single electron
mcqs.why: The notes define annihilation as the reverse of pair production: when an electron meets a positron, both disappear and their total energy is released as two gamma photons of 0.511 MeV each, travelling in opposite directions to conserve momentum.

mcqs.q: Why are the two gamma photons in annihilation emitted in opposite directions?
options: To conserve the number of photons
To conserve momentum
Because the photons repel each other electrically
Because the electron and positron were at different temperatures
mcqs.why: The notes state that the two gamma photons of 0.511 MeV each travel in opposite directions to conserve momentum. Their opposite momenta cancel, matching the near-zero total momentum of the pair.

mcqs.q: An electron-positron pair is produced, each particle having kinetic energy 220 keV. What is the energy of the photon that produced them?
options: About 1.02 MeV
About 0.44 MeV
About 1.46 MeV
About 2.92 MeV
mcqs.why: Full working: photon energy = rest energies plus kinetic energies = 0.511 + 0.511 + 0.220 + 0.220 = 1.462 MeV, about 1.46 MeV. This is step 1 of the worked example in the notes.

mcqs.q: For that same pair production, the photon energy is 1.462 MeV = 2.342 x 10^-13 J. What is the photon wavelength?
options: About 8.5 x 10^-12 m
About 4.25 x 10^-13 m
About 1.7 x 10^-12 m
About 8.5 x 10^-13 m
mcqs.why: Full working: lambda = h c / E = 1.9878 x 10^-25 / 2.342 x 10^-13 = 8.49 x 10^-13 m, about 8.5 x 10^-13 m. The photon energy in joules was 1.462 x 1.602 x 10^-13 = 2.342 x 10^-13 J, as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: A photon produces an electron-positron pair in which each particle has kinetic energy 100 keV. What is the photon energy?
options: 1.22 MeV
1.02 MeV
0.20 MeV
2.44 MeV
mcqs.why: Full working: photon energy = rest energies plus kinetic energies = 0.511 + 0.511 + 0.100 + 0.100 = 1.222 MeV, about 1.22 MeV. This applies the same energy account used in the worked example in the notes.

mcqs.q: Which comparison of pair production and annihilation is correct?
options: Both processes change energy into matter
Pair production changes energy into matter starting from one gamma photon near a nucleus; annihilation changes matter into energy starting from an electron plus a positron
Pair production starts from an electron plus a positron and annihilation starts from one gamma photon
Both processes end with two gamma photons
mcqs.why: The comparison table in the notes states: pair production is energy into matter, starting from one gamma photon near a nucleus and ending with an electron plus positron; annihilation is matter into energy, starting from electron plus positron and ending with two gamma photons.

lessons.title: Wave Nature of Particles
lessons.notes_html:
De Broglie proposed in 1924 that, just as light has both wave and particle properties, every moving material particle has a wave associated with it. This is the de Broglie hypothesis of wave-particle duality.

lambda = h / p

  • lambda - de Broglie wavelength; p - momentum of the particle; h - Planck constant

lambda = h / (m v)

  • m - mass of particle; v - its speed; the wavelength matters for light, fast particles like electrons and is negligible for ordinary objects

Davisson and Germer Experiment

Davisson and Germer scattered electrons accelerated through 54 V from a nickel crystal. The electrons showed diffraction, a wave property, with maximum intensity at a scattering angle of 50 degrees. The peak matched the de Broglie wavelength, proving the wave nature of particles.

Worked Example: De Broglie Wavelength of an Electron

Find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 3.3 kV.

Step 1: K.E. = e V = 1.602 x 10-19 x 3300 = 5.287 x 10-16 J.

Step 2: p = sqrt(2 m K.E.) = sqrt(2 x 9.11 x 10-31 x 5.287 x 10-16) = 3.104 x 10-23 kg m s-1.

Step 3: lambda = h / p = 6.626 x 10-34 / 3.104 x 10-23 = 2.135 x 10-11 m = 0.021 nm.

Answer: 0.021 nm. (The book printed answer of 0.38 nm is wrong; the correct value is 0.021 nm.)

mcqs.q: What did de Broglie propose in 1924?
options: Electrons move only as particles and never show wave behaviour
Every moving material particle has a wave associated with it, just as light has both wave and particle properties
Only photons have wavelengths; matter has none
The wavelength of a particle increases with its momentum
mcqs.why: The notes state that de Broglie proposed in 1924 that, just as light has both wave and particle properties, every moving material particle has a wave associated with it. This is the de Broglie hypothesis of wave-particle duality.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the de Broglie wavelength of a particle?
options: lambda = h p
lambda = p / h
lambda = h / p
lambda = h / (p c)
mcqs.why: The notes give lambda = h / p, where lambda is the de Broglie wavelength, p is the momentum of the particle and h is the Planck constant. Written with mass and speed it becomes lambda = h / (m v).

mcqs.q: For which particles does the de Broglie wavelength matter most, according to the notes?
options: Large slow objects such as cars and stones
Only for particles completely at rest
Equally for every object regardless of mass or speed
Light, fast particles like electrons; it is negligible for ordinary objects
mcqs.why: The notes state that with lambda = h / (m v), the wavelength matters for light, fast particles like electrons and is negligible for ordinary objects. Ordinary objects have such large momentum that their wavelength is far too small to observe.

mcqs.q: What did the Davisson and Germer experiment show?
options: Electrons scattered from a nickel crystal showed diffraction, a wave property, proving the wave nature of particles
Electrons passed through a crystal with no wave behaviour at all
Photons scattered from nickel produced an electron-positron pair
Electrons were shown to have zero wavelength at 54 V
mcqs.why: The notes state that Davisson and Germer scattered electrons from a nickel crystal and the electrons showed diffraction, a wave property. The peak matched the de Broglie wavelength, proving the wave nature of particles.

mcqs.q: In the Davisson and Germer experiment, through what potential were the electrons accelerated, and from what were they scattered?
options: Accelerated through 3.3 kV and scattered from a carbon target
Accelerated through 54 V and scattered from a nickel crystal
Accelerated through 54 V and scattered from a gold foil
Accelerated through 540 V and scattered from a nickel crystal
mcqs.why: The notes state that Davisson and Germer scattered electrons accelerated through 54 V from a nickel crystal. The electrons showed maximum intensity at a scattering angle of 50 degrees.

mcqs.q: At what scattering angle was the maximum intensity found in the Davisson and Germer experiment?
options: 90 degrees
180 degrees
50 degrees
60 degrees
mcqs.why: The notes state that the electrons showed diffraction with maximum intensity at a scattering angle of 50 degrees. The peak matched the de Broglie wavelength, proving the wave nature of particles.

mcqs.q: An electron is accelerated from rest through 3.3 kV. What kinetic energy does it gain?
mcqs.why: Full working: K.E. = e V = 1.602 x 10^-19 x 3300 = 5.287 x 10^-16 J. This is step 1 of the worked example in the notes for the de Broglie wavelength of an electron.

mcqs.q: For that electron, the momentum is p = sqrt(2 m K.E.). What value does this give?
mcqs.why: Full working: p = sqrt(2 m K.E.) = sqrt(2 x 9.11 x 10^-31 x 5.287 x 10^-16) = sqrt(9.635 x 10^-46) = 3.104 x 10^-23 kg m s^-1. This is step 2 of the worked example in the notes.

mcqs.q: What is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated from rest through 3.3 kV?
options: 2.1 nm
mcqs.why: Full working: lambda = h / p = 6.626 x 10^-34 / 3.104 x 10^-23 = 2.135 x 10^-11 m = 0.021 nm. The notes add that the book printed answer of 0.38 nm is wrong; the correct value is 0.021 nm.

mcqs.q: A particle has momentum 6.626 x 10^-23 kg m s^-1. What is its de Broglie wavelength?
mcqs.why: Full working: lambda = h / p = 6.626 x 10^-34 / 6.626 x 10^-23 = 1 x 10^-11 m. This applies the de Broglie formula lambda = h / p directly with the given momentum.

lessons.title: Electron Microscope
lessons.notes_html:
An electron microscope gives much higher magnification and resolving power than an optical microscope, so it can image extremely small specimens. Its working principle is the wave nature of electrons.

Working Principle

A beam of electrons accelerated through a high voltage has a very short de Broglie wavelength, much shorter than visible light. A shorter wavelength can resolve far smaller details, just as short-wavelength light gives small position uncertainty in measurement. Magnetic lenses focus the electron beam on the specimen, and the transmitted or scattered electrons form the magnified image.

Because electron wavelengths can be thousands of times smaller than light wavelengths, the electron microscope reveals viruses, crystal defects and fine cell structures that no light microscope can show. The specimen must be very thin and placed in vacuum, because air would scatter the electron beam.

mcqs.q: What advantage does an electron microscope have over an optical microscope?
options: It works without any lenses at all
It can image specimens in ordinary air at any thickness
Much higher magnification and resolving power, so it can image extremely small specimens
It gives lower magnification but brighter images
mcqs.why: The notes state that an electron microscope gives much higher magnification and resolving power than an optical microscope, so it can image extremely small specimens. Its working principle is the wave nature of electrons.

mcqs.q: What is the working principle of the electron microscope?
options: The photoelectric effect on a metal surface
The Compton scattering of X-rays by electrons
Pair production by gamma photons near a nucleus
The wave nature of electrons
mcqs.why: The notes state that the working principle of the electron microscope is the wave nature of electrons. A beam of electrons accelerated through a high voltage has a very short de Broglie wavelength, which gives the high resolving power.

mcqs.q: Why does the electron beam have such a short wavelength in an electron microscope?
options: The electrons are accelerated through a high voltage, giving them a very short de Broglie wavelength, much shorter than visible light
The electrons are slowed almost to rest before striking the specimen
The electrons travel through a coloured filter that shortens their wavelength
The specimen itself shortens the wavelength of any beam passing through it
mcqs.why: The notes state that a beam of electrons accelerated through a high voltage has a very short de Broglie wavelength, much shorter than visible light. A shorter wavelength can resolve far smaller details.

mcqs.q: Why does a shorter wavelength give better resolution in the microscope?
options: A shorter wavelength makes the image larger without adding detail
A shorter wavelength can resolve far smaller details
A shorter wavelength removes the need to focus the beam
A shorter wavelength lets the beam pass through thick specimens easily
mcqs.why: The notes state that a shorter wavelength can resolve far smaller details, just as short-wavelength light gives small position uncertainty in measurement. This is why electron wavelengths reveal structures light cannot show.

mcqs.q: What focuses the electron beam on the specimen in an electron microscope?
options: Glass lenses
Curved mirrors
Magnetic lenses
A pair of charged parallel plates only
mcqs.why: The notes state that magnetic lenses focus the electron beam on the specimen, and the transmitted or scattered electrons form the magnified image. Glass lenses cannot be used because electrons do not pass through them in this way.

mcqs.q: How is the magnified image formed in an electron microscope?
options: Reflected visible light from the specimen forms the image
Photons produced by annihilation inside the specimen form the image
The specimen emits photoelectrons that draw the image directly
The transmitted or scattered electrons from the specimen form the magnified image
mcqs.why: The notes state that magnetic lenses focus the beam on the specimen, and the transmitted or scattered electrons form the magnified image. The image therefore carries the fine detail resolved by the short electron wavelength.

mcqs.q: How do electron wavelengths compare with light wavelengths, according to the notes?
options: Electron wavelengths can be thousands of times smaller than light wavelengths
Electron wavelengths are about the same as light wavelengths
Electron wavelengths are thousands of times larger than light wavelengths
Electron wavelengths are slightly larger than visible light wavelengths
mcqs.why: The notes state that because electron wavelengths can be thousands of times smaller than light wavelengths, the electron microscope reveals viruses, crystal defects and fine cell structures that no light microscope can show.

mcqs.q: Which specimens does the notes say the electron microscope can reveal that no light microscope can show?
options: Planets, stars and distant galaxies
Viruses, crystal defects and fine cell structures
Whole animals and large organs
Sound waves travelling through air
mcqs.why: The notes list viruses, crystal defects and fine cell structures as things the electron microscope reveals that no light microscope can show. This follows from the thousands-of-times smaller electron wavelength.

mcqs.q: What condition must the specimen satisfy in an electron microscope, and why?
options: The specimen must be thick and kept in air so the beam slows down
The specimen must be heated until it emits its own electrons
The specimen must be very thin and placed in vacuum, because air would scatter the electron beam
The specimen must be coated with a thick layer of metal paint
mcqs.why: The notes state that the specimen must be very thin and placed in vacuum, because air would scatter the electron beam. Scattering by air molecules would destroy the fine image before it could form.

mcqs.q: The notes connect short wavelength with measurement by saying short-wavelength light gives what?
options: Large position uncertainty in measurement
Zero momentum for the particle being measured
Perfect knowledge of both position and momentum
Small position uncertainty in measurement
mcqs.why: The notes state that a shorter wavelength can resolve far smaller details, just as short-wavelength light gives small position uncertainty in measurement. This same idea underlies the uncertainty principle in the next lesson.

lessons.title: Uncertainty Principle
lessons.notes_html:
Heisenberg uncertainty principle states that position and momentum of a particle cannot both be determined with perfect accuracy at the same time. It is a fundamental limit of nature, not a limit of our instruments.

Uncertainty product = h / (4 pi)

  • Δx - uncertainty in position; Δp - uncertainty in momentum; in the simplified form used in this book the product is of the order of h

Energy-time product = h / (4 pi)

  • ΔE - uncertainty in energy; Δt - uncertainty in time; also of the order of h in simplified form

To locate an electron accurately we need short-wavelength light, but such photons give the electron a large uncertain kick and disturb its momentum. The two uncertainties always trade against each other.

Key Points

  • All motion is relative; an inertial frame has zero acceleration and Newton laws hold in it, a non-inertial frame is accelerated.
  • Relativity postulates: physics is the same in all inertial frames, and c is the same for all observers.
  • Moving lengths contract, moving clocks dilate, mass increases with speed, and E = m c2; only zero rest-mass particles travel at c.
  • Blackbody spectrum depends only on temperature; Wien law and Stefan law describe it, and Planck quanta E = h f explain it fully.
  • Photoelectric effect: h f = phi + K.E.max; emission needs f above threshold, K.E. depends on frequency, photocurrent on intensity.
  • A photon carries momentum p = h f / c = h / lambda; photocells and solar cells convert light into electricity.
  • Compton effect: scattered photons gain wavelength, proving the particle nature of light.
  • Pair production needs at least 1.02 MeV and creates an electron-positron pair; annihilation is its reverse.
  • Every particle has wavelength lambda = h / p, verified by Davisson and Germer diffraction and used in the electron microscope.
  • Uncertainty principle: position and momentum together cannot be known exactly; their uncertainties obey the Heisenberg relations.

mcqs.q: What does the Heisenberg uncertainty principle state?
options: Position and momentum can both be measured exactly with good enough instruments
Only position can ever be measured; momentum cannot be measured at all
Uncertainty applies only to large objects, never to electrons
Position and momentum of a particle cannot both be determined with perfect accuracy at the same time
mcqs.why: The notes state the Heisenberg uncertainty principle: position and momentum of a particle cannot both be determined with perfect accuracy at the same time. The two uncertainties always trade against each other.

mcqs.q: Is the uncertainty principle a limit of our instruments or a limit of nature?
options: It is a fundamental limit of nature, not a limit of our instruments
It is only a limit of present-day instruments
It applies only when the instruments are faulty
It disappears when short-wavelength light is used
mcqs.why: The notes state clearly that the uncertainty principle is a fundamental limit of nature, not a limit of our instruments. No improvement in apparatus can remove it, because the measurement itself disturbs the particle.

mcqs.q: What is the uncertainty product for position and momentum given in the notes?
options: Delta x Delta p = h
Delta x Delta p = h / (4 pi)
Delta x Delta p = 4 pi h
Delta x Delta p = h / 2
mcqs.why: The notes give the uncertainty product as h / (4 pi), where Delta x is the uncertainty in position and Delta p is the uncertainty in momentum. They add that in the simplified form used in the book the product is of the order of h.

mcqs.q: Using h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s, what is the value of the product h / (4 pi)?
options: About 5.28 x 10^-34 J s
About 1.66 x 10^-34 J s
About 5.28 x 10^-35 J s
About 8.33 x 10^-36 J s
mcqs.why: Full working: h / (4 pi) = 6.63 x 10^-34 / (4 x 3.14) = 6.63 x 10^-34 / 12.57 = 5.28 x 10^-35 J s. This is the uncertainty product Delta x Delta p given in the notes.

mcqs.q: If the position of an electron is known to within Delta x = 1 x 10^-10 m, what is the uncertainty in its momentum?
options: About 5.28 x 10^-35 kg m s^-1
About 5.28 x 10^-24 kg m s^-1
About 1.89 x 10^-25 kg m s^-1
About 5.28 x 10^-25 kg m s^-1
mcqs.why: Full working: Delta p = (h / (4 pi)) / Delta x = 5.28 x 10^-35 / 1 x 10^-10 = 5.28 x 10^-25 kg m s^-1. A very small position uncertainty forces a large momentum uncertainty, as the principle requires.

mcqs.q: What is the energy-time uncertainty product given in the notes?
options: Delta E Delta t = h / (4 pi)
Delta E Delta t = h c
Delta E Delta t = 4 pi / h
Delta E Delta t = h / 2
mcqs.why: The notes give the energy-time product as h / (4 pi), where Delta E is the uncertainty in energy and Delta t is the uncertainty in time. They add it is also of the order of h in the simplified form used in the book.

mcqs.q: Why does locating an electron accurately disturb its momentum?
options: The electron speeds up on its own whenever it is observed
Short-wavelength light is needed to locate it, but such photons give the electron a large uncertain kick and disturb its momentum
The light used is always too dim to affect the electron
The microscope lenses attract the electron magnetically
mcqs.why: The notes explain that to locate an electron accurately we need short-wavelength light, but such photons give the electron a large uncertain kick and disturb its momentum. The two uncertainties always trade against each other.

mcqs.q: If the uncertainty in position is made smaller, what happens to the uncertainty in momentum?
options: It also becomes smaller by the same factor
It stays exactly the same
It becomes larger, because the two uncertainties trade against each other
It becomes zero, giving perfect knowledge of momentum
mcqs.why: The notes state that the two uncertainties always trade against each other, since their product is fixed at h / (4 pi). Reducing Delta x must increase Delta p so the product stays the same.

mcqs.q: According to the key points of this lesson, which statement about relativity is correct?
options: Moving lengths expand and moving clocks run faster
Mass decreases with speed and E = m c
Only zero rest-mass particles are affected by relativity
Moving lengths contract, moving clocks dilate, mass increases with speed, and E = m c^2
mcqs.why: The key points in this lesson state that moving lengths contract, moving clocks dilate, mass increases with speed, and E = m c^2, and that only zero rest-mass particles travel at c. These summarise the consequences of special relativity.

mcqs.q: According to the key points of this lesson, which statement about the photoelectric effect is correct?
options: h f = phi + K.E.max; emission needs f above threshold, K.E. depends on frequency and photocurrent on intensity
h f = phi - K.E.max; K.E. depends on intensity and photocurrent on frequency
Emission needs intensity above a threshold value at any frequency
K.E. depends on both frequency and intensity equally
mcqs.why: The key points state the photoelectric effect as h f = phi + K.E.max, with emission needing f above threshold, K.E. depending on frequency and photocurrent on intensity. This matches the laws given in the photoelectric lesson.

lessons.title: Atomic Spectra
lessons.notes_html:
What Is an Atomic Spectrum?

An atomic spectrum is the set of wavelengths emitted or absorbed by the atoms of an element. To produce it, excite the atoms of a gas at low pressure by an electric discharge or by heating. When the excited electrons fall back to lower levels, the emitted light is analysed by a spectroscope.

Emission and Absorption Spectra

An emission spectrum has bright lines on a dark background. It is produced when excited atoms emit light of certain wavelengths.

An absorption spectrum has dark lines on a bright continuous background. It is produced when white light passes through a cool gas and the atoms absorb exactly those wavelengths that would excite their electrons. The dark lines are therefore called absorption lines.

Line, Band and Continuous Spectra

TypeAppearanceProduced by
Line spectrumSharp separate linesAtoms of a gas
Band spectrumGroups of close lines with sharp edgesMolecules
Continuous spectrumUnbroken range of all wavelengthsHot solids, liquids, gases at high pressure

Each element has its own characteristic lines, so spectra are used to identify elements. Light passed through a gas at low pressure gives an emission spectrum.

mcqs.q: What is an atomic spectrum?
options: The set of wavelengths emitted or absorbed by the atoms of an element
The set of colours seen in a rainbow after rain
The range of masses of the atoms of an element
The pattern of electrons arranged inside a solid
mcqs.why: The notes define an atomic spectrum as the set of wavelengths emitted or absorbed by the atoms of an element.

mcqs.q: How is an atomic spectrum produced in the method described in the notes?
options: Cooling a solid until it stops glowing completely
Exciting atoms of a gas at low pressure by an electric discharge or by heating
Passing an electric current through a thick metal bar
Dissolving the element in water and shining light on it
mcqs.why: Atoms of a gas at low pressure are excited by an electric discharge or by heating, and the emitted light is analysed by a spectroscope.

mcqs.q: What happens when excited electrons fall back to lower levels?
options: The atoms absorb white light continuously
The atoms gain mass and become heavier
The atoms emit light of certain wavelengths
The nucleus splits into smaller parts
mcqs.why: When excited electrons fall back to lower levels, the emitted light forms the spectrum that is analysed by a spectroscope.

mcqs.q: An emission spectrum has:
options: Dark lines on a bright continuous background
An unbroken range of all wavelengths
Groups of close lines with sharp edges only
Bright lines on a dark background
mcqs.why: An emission spectrum is produced when excited atoms emit light of certain wavelengths, giving bright lines on a dark background.

mcqs.q: An absorption spectrum is produced when:
options: White light passes through a cool gas and atoms absorb wavelengths that would excite their electrons
Excited atoms emit light in all directions
A hot solid glows with an unbroken spectrum
A gas at high pressure emits bright lines
mcqs.why: In absorption, white light passes through a cool gas and atoms absorb exactly those wavelengths that would excite their electrons, leaving dark lines.

mcqs.q: The dark lines in an absorption spectrum are called:
options: Emission lines
Absorption lines
Band edges
Continuous lines
mcqs.why: The dark lines formed when a cool gas absorbs its characteristic wavelengths are called absorption lines in the notes.

mcqs.q: A line spectrum, made of sharp separate lines, is produced by:
options: Molecules
Hot solids only
Atoms of a gas
Liquids only
mcqs.why: The table in the notes states that a line spectrum of sharp separate lines is produced by atoms of a gas.

mcqs.q: A band spectrum, made of groups of close lines with sharp edges, is produced by:
options: Atoms of a gas
Hot solids
Gases at high pressure only
Molecules
mcqs.why: Band spectra consist of groups of close lines with sharp edges and are produced by molecules, not by single atoms.

mcqs.q: A continuous spectrum, an unbroken range of all wavelengths, is produced by:
options: Hot solids, liquids and gases at high pressure
Atoms of a gas at low pressure
Molecules in a cool gas
A single excited atom
mcqs.why: The notes state that continuous spectra come from hot solids, liquids and gases at high pressure, giving an unbroken range of wavelengths.

mcqs.q: Why are spectra used to identify elements?
options: Every element gives exactly the same lines
Each element has its own characteristic lines
Spectra show the chemical price of an element
Spectra measure the temperature of a room
mcqs.why: Each element has its own characteristic lines, so its spectrum acts like a fingerprint and is used to identify the element.

lessons.title: Spectrum of Hydrogen Atom
lessons.notes_html:
Series in the Hydrogen Spectrum

The spectrum of hydrogen consists of several spectral series. Each series is formed by transitions ending on one particular orbit. Let p be the final orbit and n be the starting orbit, with n greater than p.

1 / λ = RH (1 / p2 - 1 / n2)

  • λ — wavelength of the line; RH — Rydberg constant, 1.0974 x 107 m-1
  • p — final orbit number; n — starting orbit number
SeriesFinal orbit pRegion
Lyman1Ultraviolet
Balmer2Visible
Paschen3Infrared
Brackett4Infrared
Pfund5Infrared

The Balmer Series

Balmer first identified four lines of this series. For Balmer, p = 2 and n = 3, 4, 5, ... The first four lines are red, blue-green, blue-violet and violet. The series limit, for n to infinity, is 3646 angstrom. Within each series the longest wavelength comes from the nearest higher level and the shortest from infinity.

Worked Example: Shortest Balmer Wavelength

Calculate the shortest wavelength of the Balmer series.

Step 1: Shortest wavelength means largest energy change, so n = infinity and p = 2.

Step 2: Use 1 / λ = RH (1 / 4 - 0) = RH / 4.

Step 3: λ = 4 / RH = 4 / (1.0974 x 107) = 3.645 x 10-7 m.

Answer: 3646 angstrom.

Worked Example: Longest Lyman Wavelength

Determine the longest wavelength in the Lyman series.

Step 1: Longest wavelength means smallest energy change, so n = 2 to p = 1.

Step 2: 1 / λ = RH (1 - 1 / 4) = 3 RH / 4.

Step 3: λ = 4 / (3 x 1.0974 x 107) = 1.215 x 10-7 m.

Answer: 1216 angstrom.

mcqs.q: In the hydrogen spectrum formula 1/lambda = R_H (1/p^2 - 1/n^2), p is:
options: The starting orbit number
The final orbit number
The Rydberg constant
The wavelength of the line
mcqs.why: In the notes p is the final orbit and n is the starting orbit, with n greater than p, and R_H is the Rydberg constant.

mcqs.q: What is the value of the Rydberg constant R_H given in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes give the Rydberg constant for hydrogen as R_H = 1.0974 x 10^7 m^-1, used in the series formula.

mcqs.q: The Lyman series is formed by transitions ending on orbit p = 1 and lies in the:
options: Visible region
Infrared region
X-ray region
Ultraviolet region
mcqs.why: The series table shows Lyman has final orbit 1 and lies in the ultraviolet, while Balmer is visible and the rest are infrared.

mcqs.q: The Balmer series is formed by transitions ending on which orbit, and in which region?
options: p = 2, visible region
p = 1, ultraviolet region
p = 3, infrared region
p = 4, infrared region
mcqs.why: For Balmer, p = 2 and n = 3, 4, 5, ..., and this series lies in the visible region of the spectrum.
