mcqs.q: Which series have final orbits p = 3, 4 and 5 respectively?
options: Lyman, Balmer and Paschen, all in the ultraviolet
Paschen, Brackett and Pfund, all in the infrared
Balmer, Paschen and Brackett, all in the visible
Pfund, Brackett and Paschen, all in the visible
mcqs.why: Paschen ends on 3, Brackett on 4 and Pfund on 5, and the notes place all three series in the infrared region.

mcqs.q: The first four Balmer lines, in order, are:
options: Violet, blue-violet, blue-green and red
Red, yellow, green and blue
Red, blue-green, blue-violet and violet
Ultraviolet, red, green and violet
mcqs.why: Balmer first identified four lines of this series: red, blue-green, blue-violet and violet, as listed in the notes.

mcqs.q: Within a series, the longest wavelength comes from:
options: The transition from infinity
The transition from the ground state of another atom
A transition between two equal levels
The transition from the nearest higher level
mcqs.why: The notes state that within each series the longest wavelength comes from the nearest higher level and the shortest from infinity.

mcqs.q: Calculate the shortest wavelength of the Balmer series.
options: 3646 angstrom
1216 angstrom
6561 angstrom
911 angstrom
mcqs.why: Shortest wavelength means n = infinity, p = 2: 1/lambda = R_H (1/4 - 0) = R_H/4, so lambda = 4 / (1.0974 x 10^7) = 3.645 x 10^-7 m = 3646 angstrom.

mcqs.q: Calculate the longest wavelength in the Lyman series.
options: 3646 angstrom
1216 angstrom
911 angstrom
18746 angstrom
mcqs.why: Longest wavelength means smallest change, n = 2 to p = 1: 1/lambda = R_H (1 - 1/4) = 3 R_H/4, so lambda = 4 / (3 x 1.0974 x 10^7) = 1.215 x 10^-7 m = 1216 angstrom.

mcqs.q: What is the series limit of the Balmer series?
options: 1216 angstrom, for n going to infinity
3646 angstrom, for n = 3 only
3646 angstrom, for n going to infinity
6561 angstrom, for n going to infinity
mcqs.why: The series limit is reached for n to infinity; for Balmer this gives lambda = 4 / R_H = 3646 angstrom, as worked in the notes.

lessons.title: Bohr's Atomic Model of the Hydrogen Atom
lessons.notes_html:
Bohr Postulates

Bohr's atomic model for hydrogen rests on three postulates. First, an electron in an allowed orbit does not radiate energy, so the atom is stable and the electron does not spiral into the nucleus. Second, only orbits with quantized angular momentum are allowed. Third, an electron radiates or absorbs energy only when it jumps between orbits.

m v r = n h / (2 π)

  • m — mass of electron; v — its speed; r — orbit radius
  • n — quantum number 1, 2, 3, ...; h — Planck constant

h f = Ehigher - Elower

  • f — frequency of emitted or absorbed photon; E — energy of the orbit

Radii of Orbits

Balancing the Coulomb attraction with the centripetal force and using the quantization condition gives quantized radii. This is called quantization of orbits: the electron can occupy only certain discrete orbits.

rn = n2 x 0.53 angstrom

  • rn — radius of orbit n; n — orbit number
  • The radius of the first orbit, 0.53 angstrom, is the Bohr radius.

So the second orbit has radius 4 x 0.53 = 2.12 angstrom, and the diameter of the hydrogen atom is 1.06 angstrom. When the electron rises from n = 1 to n = 2, the radius becomes four times larger.

Energies of Orbits

En = -13.6 / n2 eV

  • En — total energy in orbit n, unit eV; n — orbit number

The levels are -13.6 eV (n = 1), -3.4 eV (n = 2), -1.51 eV (n = 3), -0.85 eV (n = 4), -0.54 eV (n = 5) and 0 at infinity. The negative sign means the electron is bound to the nucleus and energy must be supplied to free it. On excitation the kinetic energy decreases and the potential energy increases. The Rydberg constant follows from the ground state energy:

RH = E1 / (h c)

  • E1 — 13.6 eV in joules; c — speed of light
  • Value: RH = 1.0974 x 107 m-1, dimensions [M0L-1T0].

Worked Example: Speed and Kinetic Energy

Calculate the speed of an electron of hydrogen in the second orbit and also find its kinetic energy.

Step 1: Speed in orbit n is vn = 2.19 x 106 / n m s-1.

Step 2: For n = 2, v = 2.19 x 106 / 2 = 1.09 x 106 m s-1.

Step 3: Kinetic energy is K.E. = 13.6 / n2 eV = 13.6 / 4 = 3.4 eV.

Answer: Speed 1.09 x 106 m s-1, kinetic energy 3.4 eV. (The book's printed speed 1.23 x 1012 m s-1 is wrong; it exceeds the speed of light. The correct value is 1.09 x 106 m s-1.)

Worked Example: Time Period of First Orbit

Determine the time period of the first Bohr orbit in hydrogen.

Step 1: r1 = 0.53 x 10-10 m and v1 = 2.19 x 106 m s-1.

Step 2: T = 2 π r1 / v1 = (2 x 3.14 x 0.53 x 10-10) / (2.19 x 106).

Step 3: T = 3.33 x 10-10 / 2.19 x 106 = 1.52 x 10-16 s.

Answer: About 1.53 x 10-16 s.

mcqs.q: According to Bohr's first postulate, an electron in an allowed orbit:
options: Radiates energy continuously and spirals into the nucleus
Radiates energy only at night
Does not radiate energy, so the atom is stable
Gains energy until it leaves the atom
mcqs.why: Bohr's first postulate says an electron in an allowed orbit does not radiate, so the atom is stable and the electron does not spiral into the nucleus.

mcqs.q: Bohr's quantization condition for angular momentum is:
options: m v r = h / (2 pi n^2)
m v = n h r / (2 pi)
m v r = 2 pi n / h
m v r = n h / (2 pi)
mcqs.why: Only orbits with quantized angular momentum are allowed, given by m v r = n h / (2 pi), where n = 1, 2, 3, ...

mcqs.q: An electron radiates or absorbs energy only when it:
options: Jumps between orbits
Stays in one allowed orbit
Moves in a circle at constant speed
Reaches the nucleus
mcqs.why: Bohr's third postulate says radiation or absorption, h f = E_higher - E_lower, occurs only when the electron jumps between orbits.

mcqs.q: The radius of orbit n in hydrogen is r_n = n^2 x 0.53 angstrom. What is the radius of the second orbit?
options: 1.06 angstrom
2.12 angstrom
4.77 angstrom
0.53 angstrom
mcqs.why: Using r_n = n^2 x 0.53 angstrom with n = 2: r_2 = 4 x 0.53 = 2.12 angstrom, exactly as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: The radius of the first Bohr orbit, 0.53 angstrom, is called:
options: The Rydberg radius
The atomic diameter
The Bohr radius
The series limit
mcqs.why: The notes call the radius of the first orbit, 0.53 angstrom, the Bohr radius, and the atom's diameter is twice it, 1.06 angstrom.

mcqs.q: Using E_n = -13.6 / n^2 eV, what is the energy of the third orbit?
mcqs.why: Using E_n = -13.6 / n^2 eV with n = 3: E_3 = -13.6 / 9 = -1.51 eV, matching the level list in the notes.

mcqs.q: What are the energies of orbits n = 4 and n = 5?
options: -0.85 eV and -0.54 eV
-0.54 eV and -0.85 eV
-1.51 eV and -0.85 eV
-3.4 eV and -1.51 eV
mcqs.why: E_4 = -13.6 / 16 = -0.85 eV and E_5 = -13.6 / 25 = -0.54 eV, as listed for the Bohr energy levels in the notes.

mcqs.q: The negative sign of the orbit energy E_n means:
options: The electron has negative mass
The electron is bound to the nucleus and energy must be supplied to free it
The electron moves backwards around the nucleus
The atom has lost all its energy
mcqs.why: A negative total energy means the electron is bound to the nucleus, and energy must be supplied to free it from the atom.

mcqs.q: Calculate the speed of an electron in the second Bohr orbit and its kinetic energy.
Calculate the time period of the first Bohr orbit, using r_1 = 0.53 x 10^-10 m and v_1 = 2.19 x 10^6 m s^-1.
options: About 1.52 x 10^-10 s
About 3.04 x 10^-16 s
About 1.52 x 10^-19 s
About 1.52 x 10^-16 s

lessons.title: Excitation and Ionization of an Atom
lessons.notes_html:
Excitation Energy and Potential

Excitation is raising an electron from the ground state to a higher energy state by supplying exactly the energy difference. This energy is the excitation energy. The excitation potential is the potential difference through which an electron must be accelerated to gain that energy.

For hydrogen, n = 1 to n = 2 needs 13.6 - 3.4 = 10.2 eV, so the first excitation potential is 10.2 V.

Ionization Energy and Potential

Ionization is removing the electron completely from the atom. The ionization energy for hydrogen from the ground state is:

E = 0 - (-13.6) = 13.6 eV

  • E — ionization energy, unit eV

The ionization potential is the potential difference that gives an electron this energy:

V = E / e = 13.6 V

  • V — ionization potential, unit volt; e — electronic charge

These potentials are measured by accelerating electrons through a known voltage and observing the energy at which excitation or ionization first occurs. An electron emits energy only when it jumps from a higher orbit to a lower orbit; while it stays in one allowed orbit it radiates nothing.

Worked Example: Wavelength of Emitted Radiation

An electron jumps from a level Ei = -2.2 eV to Ef = -7.5 eV. What is the wavelength of the emitted radiation?

Step 1: Photon energy E = Ei - Ef = -2.2 - (-7.5) = 5.3 eV.

Step 2: Use λ = h c / E with h c = 1240 eV nm.

Step 3: λ = 1240 / 5.3 = 234 nm.

Answer: 234 nm.

mcqs.q: Excitation of an atom means:
options: Removing the electron completely from the atom
Lowering an electron to the ground state
Splitting the nucleus into two parts
Raising an electron from the ground state to a higher energy state by supplying exactly the energy difference
mcqs.why: Excitation is raising an electron from the ground state to a higher state by supplying exactly the energy difference, called the excitation energy.

mcqs.q: The excitation potential is:
options: The potential difference through which an electron must be accelerated to gain the excitation energy
The voltage of the battery in a torch
The energy needed to remove an electron completely
The wavelength of the emitted photon in volts
mcqs.why: The excitation potential is the potential difference through which an electron must be accelerated to gain the excitation energy.

mcqs.q: For hydrogen, the energy needed to excite an electron from n = 1 to n = 2 is:
options: 3.4 eV
mcqs.why: Energy needed = E_2 - E_1 in magnitude = 13.6 - 3.4 = 10.2 eV, using E_1 = -13.6 eV and E_2 = -3.4 eV from the notes.

mcqs.q: The first excitation potential of hydrogen is:
options: 10.2 eV per metre
mcqs.why: The n = 1 to n = 2 excitation needs 10.2 eV, so an electron accelerated through 10.2 V gains exactly that energy; the first excitation potential is 10.2 V.

mcqs.q: Ionization of an atom means:
options: Raising the electron to the second orbit only
Moving the electron to a lower orbit
Adding a neutron to the nucleus
Removing the electron completely from the atom
mcqs.why: Ionization is removing the electron completely from the atom, taking it to zero energy at infinity.

mcqs.q: Calculate the ionization energy of hydrogen from the ground state.
options: 3.4 eV
mcqs.why: Ionization energy E = 0 - (-13.6) = 13.6 eV, because the ground state energy is -13.6 eV and the free electron has zero energy.

mcqs.q: The ionization potential of hydrogen from the ground state is:
mcqs.why: Ionization potential V = E / e = 13.6 eV / e = 13.6 V, the potential difference that gives an electron the ionization energy.

mcqs.q: How are excitation and ionization potentials measured, according to the notes?
options: By weighing the atom before and after heating
By counting the lines in a band spectrum
By accelerating electrons through a known voltage and observing the energy at which excitation or ionization first occurs
By measuring the size of the atom with a ruler
mcqs.why: These potentials are measured by accelerating electrons through a known voltage and observing where excitation or ionization first occurs.

mcqs.q: An electron emits energy only when it:
options: Stays in one allowed orbit
Jumps from a lower orbit to a higher orbit
Circles the nucleus at constant radius
Jumps from a higher orbit to a lower orbit
mcqs.why: While an electron stays in one allowed orbit it radiates nothing; it emits energy only on jumping from a higher orbit to a lower orbit.

mcqs.q: An electron jumps from E_i = -2.2 eV to E_f = -7.5 eV. Calculate the wavelength of the emitted radiation.
options: 234 nm
124 nm
468 nm
128 nm
mcqs.why: Photon energy E = E_i - E_f = -2.2 - (-7.5) = 5.3 eV. Then lambda = h c / E = 1240 eV nm / 5.3 eV = 234 nm.

lessons.title: Inner Shell Transitions and X-Rays
lessons.notes_html:
Inner Shell Transitions

In a heavy atom, if an inner-shell electron is knocked out, an electron from a higher shell falls into the vacancy. The photon emitted has energy equal to the difference between the two shells. Because inner-shell energies are large, these photons are characteristic x-rays, and their energies are characteristic of the element.

Production of X-Rays

In an x-ray tube, fast electrons strike a metal target. Some electrons are suddenly slowed down, giving continuous x-rays called bremsstrahlung. Others knock out inner-shell electrons, giving the characteristic lines superimposed on the continuous spectrum.

ΔE = h c / λ

  • ΔE — energy difference between the two levels; λ — wavelength of the x-ray

Worked Example: K X-Ray from Copper

The wavelength of K x-ray from copper is 1.377 x 10-10 m. What is the energy difference between the two levels?

Step 1: ΔE = h c / λ = (6.626 x 10-34 x 3 x 108) / (1.377 x 10-10).

Step 2: ΔE = 1.9878 x 10-25 / 1.377 x 10-10 = 1.4436 x 10-15 J.

Step 3: In eV, ΔE = 1.4436 x 10-15 / 1.602 x 10-19 = 9011 eV.

Answer: About 9.0 keV, close to the book value 9.025 keV; the small difference is from rounding of constants.

mcqs.q: Inner-shell transitions occur when:
options: An inner-shell electron is knocked out and an electron from a higher shell falls into the vacancy
An outer electron jumps to a higher shell
The nucleus emits an alpha particle
Two atoms collide and stick together
mcqs.why: In a heavy atom, if an inner-shell electron is knocked out, an electron from a higher shell falls into the vacancy, emitting a photon.

mcqs.q: The photons emitted in inner-shell transitions are:
options: Visible light lines of the Balmer series
Characteristic x-rays, whose energies are characteristic of the element
Infrared rays from molecular vibrations
Radio waves from the nucleus
mcqs.why: Because inner-shell energies are large, these photons are characteristic x-rays and their energies are characteristic of the element.

mcqs.q: In an x-ray tube, x-rays are produced when:
options: Slow neutrons strike a uranium rod
White light passes through a cool gas
Fast electrons strike a metal target
A gas is excited at low pressure
mcqs.why: The notes state that in an x-ray tube, fast electrons strike a metal target to produce x-rays.

mcqs.q: Bremsstrahlung x-rays are produced when:
options: Inner-shell electrons are knocked out of target atoms
Electrons fall from a higher shell into a vacancy
The target is heated until it melts
Electrons striking the target are suddenly slowed down
mcqs.why: Some electrons are suddenly slowed down on striking the target, giving continuous x-rays called bremsstrahlung.

mcqs.q: The characteristic x-ray lines in a tube spectrum come from:
options: Electrons knocking out inner-shell electrons of the target atoms
Electrons being suddenly slowed down
The cooling of the hot target
Light passing through the target
mcqs.why: Other electrons knock out inner-shell electrons, giving the characteristic lines superimposed on the continuous spectrum.

mcqs.q: In an x-ray spectrum, the characteristic lines are:
options: Completely separate from any continuous part
Superimposed on the continuous spectrum
Found only in the visible region
Produced only at low pressure
mcqs.why: The characteristic lines from inner-shell transitions appear superimposed on the continuous bremsstrahlung spectrum in the notes.

mcqs.q: The energy of an x-ray photon from a transition between two levels is related to its wavelength by:
options: Delta E = h c lambda
Delta E = lambda / (h c)
Delta E = h c / lambda
Delta E = h lambda / c
mcqs.why: The notes give Delta E = h c / lambda, where Delta E is the energy difference between the two levels and lambda is the x-ray wavelength.

mcqs.q: The wavelength of the K x-ray from copper is 1.377 x 10^-10 m. Calculate the energy difference between the two levels in joules.
Convert the copper K x-ray energy 1.4436 x 10^-15 J into electron-volts.
options: About 9011 eV, about 9.0 keV
About 901 eV, about 0.9 keV
About 14436 eV, about 14.4 keV
About 90 eV, about 0.09 keV
mcqs.why: Delta E in eV = 1.4436 x 10^-15 / 1.602 x 10^-19 = 9011 eV, which is about 9.0 keV, close to the book value of 9.025 keV.

mcqs.q: Why are inner-shell transition photons x-rays rather than visible light?
options: Because the target is made of copper
Because inner-shell energies are large, so the photon energies are large
Because the tube is evacuated
Because the electrons move slowly
mcqs.why: The notes explain that because inner-shell energies are large, the emitted photons have large energies and are characteristic x-rays.

lessons.title: Laser
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Laser Action?

LASER stands for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. A laser gives an intense, monochromatic and coherent beam. Laser action cannot occur with normal population; it needs population inversion.

Three Processes

Stimulated absorption raises atoms from the ground state to an excited state by absorbing photons. In spontaneous emission an excited atom falls on its own, emitting a photon in a random direction with random phase; this is the ordinary light of a bulb. In stimulated emission an incident photon causes an excited atom to fall, emitting a second photon identical in frequency, phase and direction.

In a normal population most atoms are in the ground state. In population inversion more atoms are in an excited state than in the ground state. This unnatural condition is created by pumping.

Metastable State

A metastable state is an excited state where an atom stays for about 10-3 s, instead of about 10-8 s for ordinary excited states. Its long lifetime lets atoms pile up there, so population inversion can be built and maintained. Stimulated emission occurs only when population inversion is in the metastable state. Repeated stimulated emission, amplified between two mirrors, produces the laser beam.

Helium-Neon Laser and Uses

The Helium-Neon laser is a gas laser. A mixture of helium and neon is excited by electric discharge; helium atoms transfer energy to neon atoms, creating population inversion between neon levels, and a continuous red beam of wavelength 632.8 nm is emitted.

Uses include reading CDs and DVDs, fibre-optic communication, laser printing, holography, eye surgery and medical treatment, cutting and welding, barcode scanners, weapons guidance and research into controlled fusion.

Key Points

  • Emission spectra have bright lines; absorption spectra have dark lines from a cool gas absorbing its own wavelengths.
  • Line spectra come from atoms, band spectra from molecules, continuous spectra from hot solids and liquids.
  • Hydrogen series: Lyman to n = 1 (ultraviolet), Balmer to n = 2 (visible), Paschen, Brackett and Pfund to n = 3, 4, 5 (infrared).
  • Bohr orbits obey m v r = n h / (2 π), with rn = n2 x 0.53 angstrom and En = -13.6 / n2 eV.
  • Negative energy means the electron is bound; 13.6 eV frees it from the ground state.
  • First excitation of hydrogen needs 10.2 eV (10.2 V); ionization needs 13.6 eV (13.6 V).
  • Characteristic x-rays come from inner-shell transitions; bremsstrahlung gives the continuous x-ray spectrum.
  • Laser action needs pumping, a metastable state and population inversion, so stimulated emission exceeds absorption.

mcqs.q: LASER stands for:
options: Light Absorption by Spontaneous Emission of Radiation
Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation
Light Amplification by Spontaneous Emission of Rays
Laser Amplification by Stimulated Energy Release
mcqs.why: The notes expand LASER as Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation, describing a laser beam's origin.

mcqs.q: A laser beam is described in the notes as:
options: Weak, multi-coloured and random
Intense, white and diverging in all directions
Intense, monochromatic and coherent
Monochromatic but with random phase only
mcqs.why: A laser gives an intense, monochromatic and coherent beam, unlike the ordinary light of a bulb described in the notes.

mcqs.q: Laser action cannot occur with a normal population; it needs:
options: Spontaneous emission only
A cool gas at low pressure
Complete ionization of all atoms
Population inversion
mcqs.why: Laser action needs population inversion, the unnatural condition where more atoms are in an excited state than in the ground state.

mcqs.q: Stimulated absorption is the process in which:
options: Atoms rise from the ground state to an excited state by absorbing photons
An excited atom falls on its own emitting a random photon
An incident photon makes an excited atom emit an identical photon
Atoms fall to the ground state without any photon
mcqs.why: Stimulated absorption raises atoms from the ground state to an excited state by absorbing photons, as defined in the notes.

mcqs.q: In spontaneous emission, an excited atom:
options: Falls only when a photon strikes it
Falls on its own, emitting a photon in a random direction with random phase
Emits a photon identical to an incoming photon
Stays excited for about 10^-3 s always
mcqs.why: In spontaneous emission an excited atom falls on its own, emitting a photon in a random direction with random phase; this is the ordinary light of a bulb.

mcqs.q: In stimulated emission, the second photon emitted is:
options: Different in frequency and random in direction
Identical in frequency but opposite in phase
Identical in frequency, phase and direction to the incident photon
Twice the frequency of the incident photon
mcqs.why: An incident photon causes an excited atom to fall, emitting a second photon identical in frequency, phase and direction.

mcqs.q: Population inversion is created by:
options: Cooling the gas
Spontaneous emission
Removing all mirrors
Pumping
mcqs.why: Population inversion, where more atoms are excited than in the ground state, is the unnatural condition created by pumping.

mcqs.q: A metastable state is an excited state where an atom stays for about:
options: 10^-3 s, instead of about 10^-8 s for ordinary excited states
10^-8 s, instead of about 10^-3 s for ordinary states
1 s, instead of about 10^-3 s for ordinary states
10^-5 s, the same as ordinary excited states
mcqs.why: A metastable state lasts about 10^-3 s instead of about 10^-8 s, so atoms pile up there and population inversion can be built and maintained.

mcqs.q: In the helium-neon laser, population inversion is created between neon levels because:
options: Neon atoms transfer energy to helium atoms
Helium atoms transfer energy to neon atoms after the mixture is excited by electric discharge
The mixture is cooled by liquid helium
Mirrors pump neon atoms directly with light
mcqs.why: A helium-neon mixture is excited by electric discharge; helium atoms transfer energy to neon atoms, creating population inversion between neon levels.

mcqs.q: The helium-neon laser emits a continuous beam of which colour and wavelength?
options: Green beam of wavelength 532 nm
Red beam of wavelength 364.6 nm
Red beam of wavelength 632.8 nm
Violet beam of wavelength 632.8 nm
mcqs.why: The helium-neon gas laser emits a continuous red beam of wavelength 632.8 nm, as stated in the notes.

lessons.title: Composition of Atomic Nuclei and Isotopes
lessons.notes_html:
Composition of the Nucleus

The nucleus is composed of protons and neutrons, together called nucleons. The proton was discovered by Rutherford and the neutron by Chadwick. The proton has the greatest mass among electron, positron, proton and photon.

The atomic number Z is the number of protons; it fixes the element and, in a neutral atom, equals the number of electrons. The mass number A is the total number of protons and neutrons. A nucleus is written as AZX, so the number of neutrons is A - Z. For example, 23592U has 235 - 92 = 143 neutrons.

The nucleus is tiny, about 10-14 m, compared with the atom, about 10-10 m, but it contains almost all the mass. The short-range strong nuclear force binds the nucleons and overcomes the repulsion between protons.

Atomic Mass Unit

The atomic mass unit (u) is one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. Carbon-12 is used as reference because it is stable, abundant and can be compared very accurately.

1 u = 1.6605 x 10-27 kg

  • u — atomic mass unit; energy equivalent 1 u = 931 MeV

Isotopes, Isobars, Isotones, Isomers

NameSameExample
IsotopesZ, different AHydrogen-1, -2, -3; carbon-12, carbon-14
IsobarsA, different ZSodium-22 and neon-22
IsotonesNeutron number A - ZCarbon-13 and nitrogen-14, both 7 neutrons
IsomersZ and A, different energy stateMetastable and ground states of technetium-99

Isotopes are nuclei of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. 2211Na and 2210Ne are isobars.

mcqs.q: The nucleus is composed of protons and neutrons, together called:
options: Isotopes
Nucleons
Photons
Leptons
mcqs.why: The notes state that the nucleus is composed of protons and neutrons, and together they are called nucleons.

mcqs.q: The proton was discovered by Rutherford and the neutron was discovered by:
options: Bohr
Balmer
Chadwick
Rydberg
mcqs.why: The notes credit Rutherford with the proton and Chadwick with the neutron, the two particles that make up the nucleus.

mcqs.q: Among electron, positron, proton and photon, which has the greatest mass?
options: Electron
Positron
Photon
Proton
mcqs.why: The notes state directly that the proton has the greatest mass among electron, positron, proton and photon.

mcqs.q: The atomic number Z is:
options: The number of protons, which fixes the element and equals the electron number in a neutral atom
The total number of protons and neutrons
The number of neutrons only
The mass of the nucleus in atomic mass units
mcqs.why: Z is the number of protons; it fixes the element and, in a neutral atom, equals the number of electrons, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: The mass number A is:
options: The number of protons only
The total number of protons and neutrons
The number of neutrons only
The number of electrons in a neutral atom
mcqs.why: A is the total number of protons and neutrons, so the number of neutrons in a nucleus is A - Z.

mcqs.q: Calculate the number of neutrons in 235 92 U.
options: 92 neutrons
235 neutrons
143 neutrons
327 neutrons
mcqs.why: Neutrons = A - Z = 235 - 92 = 143, using the notation A Z X given in the notes for uranium-235.

mcqs.q: The nucleus is about 10^-14 m in size, compared with the atom at about 10^-10 m, yet the nucleus:
options: Contains almost no mass of the atom
Contains half the mass of the atom
Is larger than the atom itself
Contains almost all the mass of the atom
mcqs.why: The notes stress that the tiny nucleus, about 10^-14 m against the atom's 10^-10 m, contains almost all the mass.

mcqs.q: The force that binds nucleons and overcomes the repulsion between protons is:
options: The short-range strong nuclear force
The gravitational force
The weak nuclear force only
The electrostatic attraction between protons
mcqs.why: The short-range strong nuclear force binds the nucleons and overcomes the repulsion between protons inside the nucleus.

mcqs.q: The atomic mass unit u is defined as:
options: The mass of a hydrogen-1 atom
One-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom
One-sixteenth of the mass of an oxygen atom
The mass of a single proton exactly
mcqs.why: 1 u is one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom; carbon-12 is the reference because it is stable, abundant and accurately comparable.

mcqs.q: 22 11 Na and 22 10 Ne, which have the same A but different Z, are:
options: Isotopes
Isotones
Isobars
Isomers
mcqs.why: Isobars have the same mass number A but different atomic number Z; the notes give sodium-22 and neon-22 as the example.

lessons.title: Mass Spectrograph
lessons.notes_html:
What Is a Mass Spectrograph?

A mass spectrograph is a device that separates the isotopes of an element by their masses and measures atomic masses accurately.

How It Works

Atoms of the element are ionized and accelerated into a magnetic field. The magnetic force bends their paths into circles whose radii depend on the mass-to-charge ratio. Lighter isotopes are bent more and heavier ones less, so the isotopes strike a photographic plate or detector at different positions. The positions give the masses and the intensities give the relative abundances.

This is why carbon-12 can serve as an accurate mass standard: its atoms can be compared very precisely in a mass spectrograph.

mcqs.q: A mass spectrograph is a device that:
options: Splits a heavy nucleus into two lighter nuclei
Counts radioactive decays per second
Separates the isotopes of an element by their masses and measures atomic masses accurately
Produces x-rays from a metal target
mcqs.why: The notes define a mass spectrograph as a device that separates isotopes by their masses and measures atomic masses accurately.

mcqs.q: In a mass spectrograph, the atoms of the element are first:
options: Fused together at high temperature
Cooled until they become a solid
Bombarded with slow neutrons
Ionized and accelerated into a magnetic field
mcqs.why: Atoms are ionized and accelerated into a magnetic field, whose force bends their paths into circles, according to the notes.

mcqs.q: In a mass spectrograph, the magnetic force bends ion paths into circles whose radii depend on:
options: The mass-to-charge ratio
The colour of the element
The temperature of the gas
The half-life of the isotope
mcqs.why: The radii of the circular paths depend on the mass-to-charge ratio, so different isotopes land at different positions.

mcqs.q: In a mass spectrograph, lighter isotopes are bent:
options: Less than heavier isotopes
More than heavier isotopes
Exactly the same as heavier isotopes
Not at all by the magnetic field
mcqs.why: Lighter isotopes are bent more and heavier ones less, so the isotopes strike the detector at different positions.

mcqs.q: In a mass spectrograph, the isotopes strike the photographic plate or detector at:
options: Exactly the same position always
Positions that give only their colours
Different positions, giving their masses
Random positions with no pattern
mcqs.why: The isotopes strike a photographic plate or detector at different positions, and the positions give the masses.

mcqs.q: In a mass spectrograph, the intensities of the isotope spots give:
options: The half-lives of the isotopes
The binding energies of the isotopes
The charges of the isotopes only
The relative abundances of the isotopes
mcqs.why: The notes state that the positions give the masses and the intensities give the relative abundances of the isotopes.

mcqs.q: Why can carbon-12 serve as an accurate mass standard, according to the notes on the mass spectrograph?
options: Its atoms can be compared very precisely in a mass spectrograph
It is the lightest of all elements
It has no isotopes at all
It is radioactive with a long half-life
mcqs.why: Carbon-12 can serve as an accurate mass standard because its atoms can be compared very precisely in a mass spectrograph.

mcqs.q: The working of a mass spectrograph is based on ions moving in:
options: An x-ray tube
A magnetic field
A nuclear reactor
A laser cavity between mirrors
mcqs.why: Ionized atoms are accelerated into a magnetic field, and the magnetic force bends their paths into mass-dependent circles.

mcqs.q: Two isotopes of the same element entering a mass spectrograph with the same charge will:
options: Follow identical circles because their charges are equal
Not be deflected at all
Follow circles of different radii because their masses differ
Fuse into a single heavier isotope
mcqs.why: With the same charge, the radius depends on mass, so isotopes of different mass follow circles of different radii and separate.

mcqs.q: A mass spectrograph measures atomic masses:
options: Only approximately, from the colour of light
By counting decays per second
From the wavelengths of spectral lines only
Accurately, by separating isotopes by mass
mcqs.why: The stated purpose of a mass spectrograph is to separate isotopes by their masses and measure atomic masses accurately.

lessons.title: Mass Defect and Binding Energy
lessons.notes_html:
Mass Defect

The mass of a nucleus is always less than the sum of the masses of its separate protons and neutrons. The missing mass is the mass defect. When nucleons bind together, part of their mass is converted into the energy that holds them together.

Δm = (Z mp + (A - Z) mn) - M

  • Δm — mass defect; mp, mn — proton and neutron masses; M — mass of nucleus

Binding Energy

Binding energy is the energy that holds the nucleons together, or the energy needed to break the nucleus into separate protons and neutrons.

B.E. = Δm c2

  • B.E. — binding energy; c — speed of light; 1 u of mass defect gives 931 MeV

The binding energy per nucleon, B.E. / A, measures stability. Larger value means a more stable nucleus. It rises to a maximum of about 8.8 MeV near 5626Fe, for mass numbers 50-60, stays near 8 MeV per nucleon over a broad range, then slowly falls. That is why 5626Fe has very high binding energy, medium nuclei are most stable, heavy nuclei release energy by fission and light nuclei by fusion.

Worked Example: Binding Energy of Nitrogen-14

Calculate mass defect, binding energy and binding energy per nucleon of 147N. Mass of the nucleus is 14.003074 u.

Step 1: Nitrogen-14 has 7 protons and 7 neutrons.

Step 2: Sum of nucleon masses = 7 x 1.007276 + 7 x 1.008665 = 14.111587 u.

Step 3: Δm = 14.111587 - 14.003074 = 0.108513 u.

Step 4: B.E. = 0.108513 x 931 = 101.03 MeV, about 101 MeV.

Step 5: B.E. per nucleon = 101 / 14 = 7.21 MeV, about 7.2 MeV.

Answer: Mass defect 0.108513 u, binding energy 101 MeV, 7.2 MeV per nucleon.

mcqs.q: The mass defect of a nucleus is:
options: The mass of the nucleus plus the nucleon masses
The mass gained when a nucleus splits
The mass of the electrons in the atom
The difference between the sum of the separate nucleon masses and the mass of the nucleus
mcqs.why: The mass of a nucleus is always less than the sum of its separate proton and neutron masses; the missing mass is the mass defect.

mcqs.q: The mass defect formula given in the notes is:
options: Delta m = (Z m_p + (A - Z) m_n) - M
Delta m = M - (Z m_p + (A - Z) m_n)
Delta m = (Z m_n + (A - Z) m_p) - M
Delta m = A - Z - M
mcqs.why: Delta m = (Z m_p + (A - Z) m_n) - M, where m_p and m_n are the proton and neutron masses and M is the mass of the nucleus.

mcqs.q: Binding energy is:
options: The kinetic energy of the electrons around the nucleus
The energy that holds the nucleons together, or the energy needed to break the nucleus into separate protons and neutrons
The energy released when an atom is ionized
The energy of a photon emitted by an atom
mcqs.why: Binding energy holds the nucleons together and equals the energy needed to break the nucleus into separate protons and neutrons.

mcqs.q: Binding energy is calculated from the mass defect by:
options: B.E. = Delta m / c^2, with 1 u giving 931 eV
B.E. = Delta m c, with 1 u giving 93.1 MeV
B.E. = Delta m c^2, with 1 u of mass defect giving 931 MeV
B.E. = Delta m x 0.693, with 1 u giving 931 MeV
mcqs.why: B.E. = Delta m c^2, and the notes state that 1 u of mass defect gives 931 MeV of binding energy.

mcqs.q: The binding energy per nucleon, B.E./A, measures:
options: Radioactivity, with a larger value meaning faster decay
The size of the nucleus in metres
The number of electrons in the atom
Stability, with a larger value meaning a more stable nucleus
mcqs.why: The binding energy per nucleon measures stability; a larger value means a more stable nucleus, according to the notes.

mcqs.q: The binding energy per nucleon rises to a maximum of about 8.8 MeV near:
options: 56 26 Fe, for mass numbers 50-60
14 7 N, for mass numbers 10-20
235 92 U, for mass numbers above 200
4 2 He, for mass numbers below 10
mcqs.why: B.E./A rises to a maximum of about 8.8 MeV near iron-56, for mass numbers 50-60, which is why iron-56 is very stable.

mcqs.q: Because B.E./A peaks at medium nuclei and then falls, heavy nuclei release energy by fission and light nuclei by:
options: Alpha decay only
Fusion
Ionization
Spontaneous emission
mcqs.why: Medium nuclei are most stable, so heavy nuclei release energy by fission and light nuclei by fusion, both moving toward the peak.

mcqs.q: For nitrogen-14, the sum of the masses of 7 protons and 7 neutrons is 7 x 1.007276 + 7 x 1.008665. Calculate this sum.
mcqs.why: Sum = 7 x 1.007276 + 7 x 1.008665 = 7.050932 + 7.060655 = 14.111587 u, step 2 of the nitrogen-14 worked example.

mcqs.q: The mass of the nitrogen-14 nucleus is 14.003074 u and the nucleon sum is 14.111587 u. Calculate its mass defect and binding energy.
options: 0.108513 u and about 10.1 MeV
1.08513 u and about 101 MeV
0.0108513 u and about 1010 MeV
0.108513 u and about 101 MeV

mcqs.q: Calculate the binding energy per nucleon of nitrogen-14, whose total binding energy is about 101 MeV.
options: About 7.2 MeV per nucleon
About 14.4 MeV per nucleon
About 101 MeV per nucleon
About 3.6 MeV per nucleon
mcqs.why: B.E. per nucleon = B.E. / A = 101 / 14 = 7.21 MeV, about 7.2 MeV per nucleon, as in the worked example.

lessons.title: Radioactivity
lessons.notes_html:
What Is Radioactivity?

Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiations from unstable nuclei. Radioactive elements have atomic number greater than 82; examples are uranium, radium and polonium. Decay is unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical combination, because it is a nuclear process. The rate of decay depends on the number of undecayed nuclei present.

Parent and Daughter Nuclei

The decaying nucleus is the parent nucleus and the new nucleus formed is the daughter nucleus.

DecayChange in ZChange in A
Alpha decayFalls by 2Falls by 4
Beta decayRises by 1No change
Gamma decayNo changeNo change, only energy lost

In beta decay a neutron changes into a proton, so the mass number stays the same. Alpha, beta and gamma rays are not emitted simultaneously because each decay is a separate event: the nucleus decays by one mode at a time, and gamma emission only removes excess energy from an already formed excited nucleus.

Properties of the Radiations

RayIonizing powerPenetrating power
AlphaHighestLeast
BetaMiddleMiddle
GammaLeastHighest

Units of Activity

The SI unit is the becquerel: 1 Bq = 1 disintegration per second. The older unit is the curie, the activity of 1 gram of radium.

1 Ci = 3.7 x 1010 Bq

  • Ci — curie, unit of radioactivity; Bq — becquerel

mcqs.q: Radioactivity is:
options: The spontaneous emission of radiations from unstable nuclei
The emission of light from excited atoms
The splitting of a nucleus by a slow neutron in a reactor
The joining of two light nuclei at high temperature
mcqs.why: Radioactivity is defined in the notes as the spontaneous emission of radiations from unstable nuclei.

mcqs.q: Radioactive elements have atomic number:
options: Less than 10, such as hydrogen and helium
Greater than 82, such as uranium, radium and polonium
Exactly 26, such as iron
Between 1 and 20 only
mcqs.why: The notes state that radioactive elements have atomic number greater than 82; examples are uranium, radium and polonium.

mcqs.q: Radioactive decay is unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical combination because:
options: It is a chemical process
It depends on the electrons in the atom
It is a nuclear process
It happens only in a vacuum
mcqs.why: Decay is a nuclear process, so it is unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical combination, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: In radioactive decay, the decaying nucleus is called the parent nucleus and the new nucleus formed is the:
options: Tracer nucleus
Isomer nucleus
Target nucleus
Daughter nucleus
mcqs.why: The decaying nucleus is the parent nucleus and the new nucleus formed from it is the daughter nucleus.

mcqs.q: In alpha decay, the atomic number Z and mass number A change by:
options: Z falls by 2 and A falls by 4
Z rises by 1 and A does not change
Z and A both stay the same
Z falls by 1 and A falls by 1
mcqs.why: The decay table shows alpha decay lowers Z by 2 and A by 4, because an alpha particle carries 2 protons and 4 nucleons.

mcqs.q: In beta decay, a neutron changes into a proton, so:
options: Z falls by 2 and A falls by 4
Z rises by 1 and A does not change
Z and A both fall by 1
Only energy is lost, with no change in Z
mcqs.why: In beta decay a neutron changes into a proton, so the mass number stays the same while Z rises by 1.

mcqs.q: In gamma decay:
options: Z falls by 2 and A falls by 4
Z rises by 1 with A unchanged
Neither Z nor A changes; only energy is lost
A falls by 4 with Z unchanged
mcqs.why: Gamma decay changes neither Z nor A; the nucleus only loses excess energy as a gamma ray, according to the decay table.

mcqs.q: Alpha, beta and gamma rays are not emitted simultaneously because:
options: The nucleus is too small to emit more than one ray
Gamma rays block alpha and beta rays
All three rays are actually the same ray
Each decay is a separate event and the nucleus decays by one mode at a time
mcqs.why: Each decay is a separate event; the nucleus decays by one mode at a time and gamma emission only removes excess energy from an excited nucleus.

mcqs.q: Comparing ionizing and penetrating power, alpha has the highest ionizing power but the least penetrating power, while gamma has:
options: The least ionizing power and the highest penetrating power
The highest ionizing power and the highest penetrating power
Middle ionizing power and middle penetrating power
No ionizing power and no penetrating power
mcqs.why: The properties table gives alpha highest ionizing and least penetrating, beta middle in both, and gamma least ionizing but highest penetrating.

mcqs.q: The SI unit of activity is the becquerel, where 1 Bq equals:
options: 100 disintegrations per second, and 1 Ci = 3.7 x 10^8 Bq
1 disintegration per second, and 1 Ci = 3.7 x 10^10 Bq
1 disintegration per minute, and 1 Ci = 3.7 x 10^10 Bq
1 disintegration per second, and 1 Ci = 3.7 x 10^6 Bq
mcqs.why: 1 Bq = 1 disintegration per second. The curie is the activity of 1 gram of radium, and 1 Ci = 3.7 x 10^10 Bq.

lessons.title: Radioactive Decay Equation
lessons.notes_html:
Laws of Radioactive Decay

The laws are: the rate of decay is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present; the decay constant is characteristic of the substance and independent of external conditions; and the number of nuclei falls exponentially with time.

The decay constant λ is the probability per unit time that a given nucleus will decay. Its unit is s-1.

A = λ N

  • A — activity, rate of decay; N — number of undecayed nuclei

Decay Equation

dN / dt = -λ N

  • dN / dt — rate of change of N; minus sign shows N decreases

Integrating from N0 at t = 0 to N at time t gives the radioactive decay equation:

N = N0 e-λ t

  • N0 — number of nuclei at t = 0; t — time; e — base of natural logarithm

Half-Life

The half-life T1/2 is the time for half the nuclei to decay. Setting N = N0 / 2 gives:

T1/2 = 0.693 / λ

  • T1/2 — half-life; after n half-lives the fraction left is (1 / 2)n

Worked Example: Decay Constant of Krypton

The half-life of krypton (Z = 36) is 3.16 minutes. Find its decay constant.

Step 1: Convert half-life to seconds: T = 3.16 x 60 = 189.6 s.

Step 2: λ = 0.693 / T = 0.693 / 189.6.

Step 3: λ = 3.655 x 10-3 s-1.

Answer: About 3.66 x 10-3 s-1.

After five half-lives, a sample keeps (1 / 2)5 = 1 / 32 = 0.031 of its nuclei, as for carbon-14 with half-life 5700 years.

mcqs.q: The first law of radioactive decay states that the rate of decay is:
options: Proportional to the temperature of the sample
Proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present
Constant and independent of the sample size
Proportional to the square of the time elapsed
mcqs.why: The laws state the rate of decay is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present, giving A = lambda N.

mcqs.q: The decay constant lambda is:
options: The time for half the nuclei to decay, with unit s
The number of nuclei in the sample, with unit Bq
The probability per unit time that a given nucleus will decay, with unit s^-1
The energy released per decay, with unit MeV
mcqs.why: Lambda is the probability per unit time that a given nucleus will decay; it is characteristic of the substance and its unit is s^-1.

mcqs.q: Activity A is related to the number of undecayed nuclei N by:
options: A = N / lambda
A = lambda / N
A = lambda N^2
A = lambda N
mcqs.why: The notes give A = lambda N, where A is the activity or rate of decay and N is the number of undecayed nuclei.

mcqs.q: The radioactive decay equation obtained by integrating dN/dt = -lambda N is:
options: N = N_0 e^(-lambda t)
N = N_0 e^(lambda t)
N = N_0 - lambda t
N = N_0 / (lambda t)
mcqs.why: Integrating from N_0 at t = 0 to N at time t gives N = N_0 e^(-lambda t); the minus sign shows N decreases with time.

mcqs.q: The half-life T_1/2 is:
options: The time for all the nuclei to decay, given by 1 / lambda
The time for half the nuclei to decay, given by T_1/2 = 0.693 / lambda
The time for one nucleus to decay, given by lambda / 0.693
The average energy of decay, given by 0.693 lambda
mcqs.why: Setting N = N_0 / 2 in the decay equation gives T_1/2 = 0.693 / lambda, the time for half the nuclei to decay.

mcqs.q: After n half-lives, the fraction of nuclei left is:
options: 1 - (1/2)^n of the original mass in grams
mcqs.why: The notes state that after n half-lives the fraction left is (1/2)^n, halving again with each successive half-life.

mcqs.q: The half-life of krypton (Z = 36) is 3.16 minutes. First convert this half-life to seconds.
mcqs.why: T = 3.16 x 60 = 189.6 s, step 1 of the worked example, converting the half-life from minutes to seconds.

mcqs.q: Calculate the decay constant of krypton, whose half-life is 189.6 s.
options: About 3.66 x 10^-3 s
About 3.66 s^-1
mcqs.why: Lambda = 0.693 / T = 0.693 / 189.6 = 3.655 x 10^-3 s^-1, about 3.66 x 10^-3 s^-1, as in the worked example.

mcqs.q: What fraction of a sample remains after five half-lives?
mcqs.why: Fraction left = (1/2)^5 = 1/32 = 0.03125, about 0.031, the value given in the notes for five half-lives.

mcqs.q: Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5700 years. What fraction remains after 11400 years?
mcqs.why: 11400 years is n = 11400 / 5700 = 2 half-lives, so the fraction left = (1/2)^2 = 1/4 of the original nuclei.

lessons.title: Radiation Detectors
lessons.notes_html:
Geiger-Muller Counter

The Geiger-Muller counter (GM counter) detects and counts ionizing particles. It is a gas-filled tube with a central wire anode at high positive voltage. An entering particle ionizes the gas, and the ions are accelerated so strongly that they cause an avalanche of further ionization, giving an electrical pulse that is counted. Each pulse corresponds to one particle.

Solid State Detector

A solid state detector uses a semiconductor crystal such as silicon instead of gas. An ionizing particle creates electron-hole pairs in the crystal, and the applied voltage sweeps them to the electrodes, producing a pulse whose size is proportional to the particle energy. So it both counts the radiation and measures its energy.

mcqs.q: A Geiger-Muller (GM) counter is used to:
options: Measure the energy of each particle precisely
Separate isotopes by their masses
Detect and count ionizing particles
Slow down fast neutrons in a reactor
mcqs.why: The GM counter detects and counts ionizing particles; each electrical pulse it produces corresponds to one particle.

mcqs.q: A GM counter consists of:
options: A semiconductor crystal of silicon only
A photographic plate in a magnetic field
A metal target struck by fast electrons
A gas-filled tube with a central wire anode at high positive voltage
mcqs.why: The notes describe the GM counter as a gas-filled tube with a central wire anode at high positive voltage.

mcqs.q: In a GM counter, an entering particle ionizes the gas, and the ions then:
options: Are accelerated so strongly that they cause an avalanche of further ionization, giving a counted pulse
Are collected slowly with no further ionization
Fuse with the gas atoms to form new elements
Emit a flash of visible light that is photographed
mcqs.why: The ions are accelerated so strongly that they cause an avalanche of further ionization, giving an electrical pulse that is counted.

mcqs.q: In a GM counter, each electrical pulse corresponds to:
options: One hundred particles
One particle
One complete radioactive decay chain
One half-life of the source
mcqs.why: The notes state directly that in a GM counter each pulse corresponds to one particle entering the tube.

mcqs.q: A solid state detector uses, instead of gas:
options: A gas-filled tube with a wire anode
A photographic plate
A semiconductor crystal such as silicon
A thick concrete shield
mcqs.why: A solid state detector uses a semiconductor crystal such as silicon instead of the gas used in a GM counter.

mcqs.q: In a solid state detector, an ionizing particle creates:
options: An avalanche in a gas-filled tube
Bright lines on a dark background
New isotopes of the element
Electron-hole pairs in the crystal
mcqs.why: An ionizing particle creates electron-hole pairs in the semiconductor crystal, which are then swept to the electrodes.

mcqs.q: In a solid state detector, the applied voltage sweeps the electron-hole pairs to the electrodes, producing a pulse whose size is:
options: Proportional to the particle energy
Always the same whatever the particle energy
Proportional to the half-life of the particle
Inversely proportional to the particle energy
mcqs.why: The pulse size is proportional to the particle energy, so the solid state detector both counts radiation and measures its energy.

mcqs.q: Unlike a GM counter, a solid state detector can:
options: Only count radiation, never measure energy
Both count the radiation and measure its energy
Detect radiation without any applied voltage
Separate isotopes by mass-to-charge ratio
mcqs.why: Because its pulse size is proportional to particle energy, the solid state detector both counts the radiation and measures its energy.

mcqs.q: The GM counter works because an entering particle first:
options: Creates electron-hole pairs in silicon
Knocks out an inner-shell electron from copper
Ionizes the gas in the tube
Splits a heavy nucleus in the tube
mcqs.why: Detection in a GM counter starts when an entering particle ionizes the gas, after which the avalanche produces the counted pulse.

mcqs.q: Which detector uses an avalanche of ionization in a gas to produce its pulse?
options: The solid state detector
The mass spectrograph
The ionization chamber in an x-ray tube
The Geiger-Muller counter
mcqs.why: In the GM counter the accelerated ions cause an avalanche of further ionization in the gas, giving the electrical pulse that is counted.

lessons.title: Nuclear Reaction
lessons.notes_html:
What Is a Nuclear Reaction?

A nuclear reaction is a process in which a change occurs in a nucleus when it is struck by a nuclear particle. Its kinds include elastic scattering, where the particle bounces off unchanged; inelastic scattering, where the nucleus is left excited; transmutation; fission; fusion; and radioactive decay.

Transmutation

Transmutation is the conversion of the nucleus of one element into the nucleus of another element. It happens naturally in radioactive decay and artificially by bombarding a nucleus. In Rutherford's first artificial transmutation, nitrogen-14 bombarded with alpha particles changes into oxygen-17 and a proton.

Q = Δm x 931 MeV

  • Q — energy of reaction in MeV; Δm — mass of reactants minus mass of products, in u
  • Positive Q means energy is released; negative Q means energy is absorbed.

Worked Example: Reaction Energy

Determine the energy of 147N + 42He → 178O + 11H. Masses: nitrogen-14 = 14.003074 u, helium-4 = 4.002603 u, oxygen-17 = 16.999131 u, hydrogen-1 = 1.007825 u.

Step 1: Reactants = 14.003074 + 4.002603 = 18.005677 u.

Step 2: Products = 16.999131 + 1.007825 = 18.006956 u.

Step 3: Δm = 18.005677 - 18.006956 = -0.001279 u.

Step 4: Q = -0.001279 x 931 = -1.191 MeV.

Answer: -1.191 MeV; energy is absorbed, not released.

mcqs.q: A nuclear reaction is:
options: A chemical change in the electron shells of an atom
The emission of light by an excited atom
The movement of electrons in a metal wire
A process in which a change occurs in a nucleus when it is struck by a nuclear particle
mcqs.why: The notes define a nuclear reaction as a process in which a change occurs in a nucleus when it is struck by a nuclear particle.

mcqs.q: In elastic scattering, a nuclear reaction kind listed in the notes:
options: The particle bounces off unchanged
The nucleus is left excited
The nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei
One element changes into another element
mcqs.why: In elastic scattering the particle bounces off unchanged, while in inelastic scattering the nucleus is left excited.

mcqs.q: In inelastic scattering:
options: The particle bounces off unchanged
The nucleus is left excited
Two light nuclei join together
The nucleus decays spontaneously
mcqs.why: The notes distinguish inelastic scattering, where the nucleus is left excited, from elastic scattering, where the particle bounces off unchanged.

mcqs.q: Transmutation is:
options: The bouncing of a particle off a nucleus unchanged
The emission of gamma rays with no change in Z or A
The conversion of the nucleus of one element into the nucleus of another element
The slowing of fast neutrons by a moderator
mcqs.why: Transmutation converts the nucleus of one element into the nucleus of another, naturally in decay and artificially by bombardment.

mcqs.q: In Rutherford's first artificial transmutation, nitrogen-14 bombarded with alpha particles changes into:
options: Oxygen-17 and a neutron
Carbon-14 and a proton
Oxygen-16 and an alpha particle
Oxygen-17 and a proton
mcqs.why: Nitrogen-14 bombarded with alpha particles changes into oxygen-17 and a proton, in Rutherford's first artificial transmutation.

mcqs.q: The energy of a nuclear reaction is calculated by:
options: Q = Delta m x 931 MeV, where Delta m is reactants mass minus products mass in u
Q = Delta m x 0.693 MeV, where Delta m is in kg
Q = Delta m / 931 MeV, where Delta m is products minus reactants
Q = Delta m c, where Delta m is in grams
mcqs.why: The notes give Q = Delta m x 931 MeV, with Delta m the mass of reactants minus mass of products, in atomic mass units.

mcqs.q: A positive Q value for a nuclear reaction means:
options: Energy is absorbed
Energy is released
No energy change occurs
The reaction cannot take place at all
mcqs.why: Positive Q means energy is released; negative Q means energy is absorbed, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: For 14 7 N + 4 2 He -> 17 8 O + 1 1 H, the reactant masses sum to 14.003074 + 4.002603 u and the products to 16.999131 + 1.007825 u. Calculate both sums.
options: Reactants 18.006956 u, products 18.005677 u
Reactants 18.005677 u, products 18.056956 u
Reactants 18.005677 u, products 18.006956 u
Reactants 17.005677 u, products 18.006956 u
mcqs.why: Reactants = 14.003074 + 4.002603 = 18.005677 u. Products = 16.999131 + 1.007825 = 18.006956 u, steps 1 and 2 of the worked example.

mcqs.q: Using reactants 18.005677 u and products 18.006956 u, calculate Q for the nitrogen transmutation reaction.
options: +1.191 MeV, so energy is released
-0.191 MeV, so energy is absorbed
-11.91 MeV, so energy is absorbed
-1.191 MeV, so energy is absorbed
mcqs.why: Delta m = 18.005677 - 18.006956 = -0.001279 u. Q = -0.001279 x 931 = -1.191 MeV; the negative sign means energy is absorbed, not released.

mcqs.q: Transmutation happens naturally in radioactive decay and artificially by:
options: Bombarding a nucleus
Heating a gas at low pressure
Passing white light through a cool gas
Accelerating electrons through a known voltage
mcqs.why: The notes state transmutation happens naturally in radioactive decay and artificially by bombarding a nucleus with particles.

lessons.title: Nuclear Fission
lessons.notes_html:
Nuclear Fission

Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 into two lighter nuclei when struck by a slow neutron. About 200 MeV is released per fission in general, and on average 2.5 fresh neutrons are emitted. If these neutrons cause further fissions, a self-sustaining chain reaction results.

The Nuclear Reactor

A nuclear reactor controls the chain reaction. Its parts are: fuel, uranium-235 in fuel rods; a moderator such as heavy water or graphite, which slows fast neutrons to thermal speeds because slow neutrons are far more likely to cause fission; control rods of boron or cadmium, which absorb neutrons and regulate the rate; a coolant to carry away heat; and a thick concrete shield.

A fast reactor needs no moderator: it uses highly enriched uranium or plutonium fuel where fast neutrons still cause enough fissions, and it can breed new fuel from uranium-238.

Worked Example: Fission Energy

Calculate the energy released in: neutron + 23592U → 14156Ba + 9236Kr + 3 neutrons. Masses: neutron = 1.008665 u, uranium-235 = 235.043924 u, barium-141 = 140.913740 u, krypton-92 = 91.926270 u.

Step 1: Reactants = 1.008665 + 235.043924 = 236.052589 u.

Step 2: Products = 140.913740 + 91.926270 + 3 x 1.008665 = 235.866005 u.

Step 3: Δm = 236.052589 - 235.866005 = 0.186584 u.

Step 4: Q = 0.186584 x 931 = 173.7 MeV.

Answer: About 174 MeV for this fission channel.

mcqs.q: Nuclear fission is:
options: The splitting of a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 into two lighter nuclei when struck by a slow neutron
The joining of two light nuclei into a heavier nucleus
The spontaneous emission of an alpha particle
The conversion of a neutron into a proton
mcqs.why: Fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 into two lighter nuclei when struck by a slow neutron.

mcqs.q: In general, the energy released per fission is about:
options: 20 MeV, with on average 25 fresh neutrons emitted
200 MeV, with on average 2.5 fresh neutrons emitted
200 MeV, with on average 25 fresh neutrons emitted
2000 MeV, with on average 2.5 fresh neutrons emitted
mcqs.why: The notes state about 200 MeV is released per fission in general, and on average 2.5 fresh neutrons are emitted.

mcqs.q: A self-sustaining chain reaction results when:
options: The control rods absorb all the neutrons
The coolant carries away all the heat
The neutrons emitted in fission cause further fissions
The fuel rods are removed from the reactor
mcqs.why: If the neutrons from one fission cause further fissions, a self-sustaining chain reaction results, as described in the notes.

mcqs.q: In a nuclear reactor, the fuel is:
options: Boron or cadmium in control rods
Heavy water or graphite
Deuterium and tritium gas
Uranium-235 in fuel rods
mcqs.why: The reactor parts list gives the fuel as uranium-235 in fuel rods, controlled by moderator, control rods, coolant and shielding.

mcqs.q: The moderator in a reactor, such as heavy water or graphite, serves to:
options: Slow fast neutrons to thermal speeds, because slow neutrons are far more likely to cause fission
Absorb neutrons and regulate the reaction rate
Carry away the heat produced by fission
Shield workers from radiation outside the reactor
mcqs.why: A moderator slows fast neutrons to thermal speeds because slow neutrons are far more likely to cause fission of uranium-235.

mcqs.q: Control rods of boron or cadmium in a reactor:
options: Slow neutrons down to thermal speeds
Absorb neutrons and regulate the rate of the reaction
Act as the fuel for the chain reaction
Carry heat away from the core
mcqs.why: Control rods of boron or cadmium absorb neutrons and regulate the rate, while the moderator slows neutrons and the coolant removes heat.

mcqs.q: A fast reactor differs from an ordinary reactor because it:
options: Needs two moderators instead of one
Uses only slow neutrons at ordinary temperatures
Needs no moderator and uses highly enriched uranium or plutonium fuel
Cannot breed new fuel from uranium-238
mcqs.why: A fast reactor needs no moderator; it uses highly enriched uranium or plutonium where fast neutrons still cause enough fissions, and it can breed fuel from uranium-238.

mcqs.q: For neutron + 235 92 U -> 141 56 Ba + 92 36 Kr + 3 neutrons, reactants total 236.052589 u and products total 235.866005 u. Calculate the mass defect.
mcqs.why: Delta m = reactants - products = 236.052589 - 235.866005 = 0.186584 u, step 3 of the fission worked example.

mcqs.q: Calculate the energy released in the fission channel with mass defect 0.186584 u.
options: About 174 MeV
About 17.4 MeV
About 2000 MeV
About 101 MeV
mcqs.why: Q = Delta m x 931 = 0.186584 x 931 = 173.7 MeV, about 174 MeV for this fission channel, as worked in the notes.

mcqs.q: The purpose of the coolant and the thick concrete shield in a reactor is, respectively, to:
options: Slow down neutrons, and absorb neutrons
Carry away heat, and shield against radiation
Carry away heat, and act as fuel
Regulate the rate, and slow down neutrons
mcqs.why: The parts list gives a coolant to carry away heat and a thick concrete shield, alongside fuel, moderator and control rods.

lessons.title: Nuclear Fusion
lessons.notes_html:
Nuclear Fusion

Nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy because the product has larger binding energy per nucleon. A typical fusion reaction releases about 28 MeV in the book comparison, for example forming helium in the Sun.

Fusion releases more energy per nucleon than fission: fusing hydrogen into helium raises binding energy per nucleon from about 1 MeV to about 7 MeV, a gain of about 6 MeV per nucleon, while fission of uranium-235 gains only about 0.9 MeV per nucleon.

FissionFusion
ProcessHeavy nucleus splitsLight nuclei join
NeedsSlow neutronTemperature of millions of degrees
Energy per eventAbout 200 MeVAbout 17-28 MeV

Why Fusion Is Difficult

The positively charged nuclei repel each other strongly. They can fuse only if given very high kinetic energies, which means temperatures of millions of degrees, and confining such hot material without cooling on walls is extremely difficult. Fission, by contrast, needs only a slow neutron at ordinary temperatures.

Fusion in the Sun

The Sun generates energy by fusion in its core through the proton-proton chain: two protons fuse to deuterium, deuterium fuses with a proton to helium-3, and two helium-3 nuclei fuse to helium-4 plus two protons. Overall four protons become one helium nucleus, releasing about 28 MeV, which reaches the surface and is radiated as sunlight.

Worked Example: Deuterium-Tritium Fusion

Calculate the energy of 21H + 31H → 42He + neutron. Masses: hydrogen-2 = 2.014102 u, hydrogen-3 = 3.016049 u, helium-4 = 4.002603 u, neutron = 1.008665 u.

Step 1: Reactants = 2.014102 + 3.016049 = 5.030151 u.

Step 2: Products = 4.002603 + 1.008665 = 5.011268 u.

Step 3: Δm = 5.030151 - 5.011268 = 0.018883 u.

Step 4: Q = 0.018883 x 931 = 17.58 MeV.

Answer: About 17.6 MeV released.

mcqs.q: Nuclear fusion is:
options: The splitting of a heavy nucleus by a slow neutron
The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy because the product has larger binding energy per nucleon
The emission of radiations from unstable nuclei
The knocking out of an inner-shell electron
mcqs.why: Fusion joins two light nuclei into a heavier nucleus and releases energy because the product has larger binding energy per nucleon.

mcqs.q: Fusion releases more energy per nucleon than fission because fusing hydrogen into helium raises B.E. per nucleon from about 1 MeV to about 7 MeV, a gain of:
options: About 0.9 MeV per nucleon, while fission gains about 6 MeV per nucleon
About 60 MeV per nucleon, while fission gains about 9 MeV per nucleon
About 6 MeV per nucleon, while fission of uranium-235 gains only about 0.9 MeV per nucleon
About 6 MeV per nucleon, the same gain as fission
mcqs.why: Gain = 7 - 1 = about 6 MeV per nucleon for fusion, while fission of uranium-235 gains only about 0.9 MeV per nucleon.

mcqs.q: Fusion is difficult mainly because:
options: Light nuclei are too rare to be used as fuel
Fusion needs a slow neutron that is hard to produce
The product nucleus is always radioactive
The positively charged nuclei repel each other strongly and need temperatures of millions of degrees to fuse
mcqs.why: Positively charged nuclei repel strongly; they fuse only at temperatures of millions of degrees, and confining such hot material is extremely difficult.

mcqs.q: In contrast to fusion, fission needs only:
options: A slow neutron at ordinary temperatures
A temperature of millions of degrees
Confinement away from container walls
Very high kinetic energies for the nuclei
mcqs.why: The notes contrast fusion's millions of degrees with fission, which needs only a slow neutron at ordinary temperatures.

mcqs.q: The Sun generates energy by fusion in its core through the:
options: Uranium fission chain reaction
Proton-proton chain
Carbon-14 decay chain
Bremsstrahlung process
mcqs.why: The Sun's core energy comes from the proton-proton chain: protons form deuterium, then helium-3, then helium-4 plus two protons.

mcqs.q: Overall in the proton-proton chain, four protons become:
options: One helium nucleus, releasing about 200 MeV
Two helium nuclei, releasing about 28 MeV
One helium nucleus, releasing about 28 MeV
One helium nucleus, absorbing about 28 MeV
mcqs.why: Overall four protons become one helium nucleus, releasing about 28 MeV, which reaches the surface and is radiated as sunlight.

mcqs.q: In the proton-proton chain, the step after two protons fuse to deuterium is:
options: Deuterium splits into two protons again
Two deuterium nuclei form uranium
Helium-3 fuses with a neutron to form helium-4 directly
Deuterium fuses with a proton to form helium-3
mcqs.why: The chain runs: two protons to deuterium, deuterium with a proton to helium-3, and two helium-3 nuclei to helium-4 plus two protons.

mcqs.q: For 2 1 H + 3 1 H -> 4 2 He + neutron, reactants total 2.014102 + 3.016049 u and products total 4.002603 + 1.008665 u. Calculate the mass defect.
mcqs.why: Reactants = 5.030151 u; products = 5.011268 u. Delta m = 5.030151 - 5.011268 = 0.018883 u, steps 1 to 3 of the worked example.

mcqs.q: Calculate the energy released in the deuterium-tritium fusion with mass defect 0.018883 u.
options: About 1.76 MeV
About 17.6 MeV
About 176 MeV
About 28 MeV exactly for this reaction
mcqs.why: Q = Delta m x 931 = 0.018883 x 931 = 17.58 MeV, about 17.6 MeV released, as worked in the notes for D-T fusion.

mcqs.q: According to the comparison table, a typical fusion event releases about 17-28 MeV while a fission event releases about:
options: 28 MeV per event, more per nucleon than fusion
17.6 MeV per event, exactly like D-T fusion
200 MeV per event, but less per nucleon than fusion
6 MeV per event, less than any fusion event
mcqs.why: The table gives fission about 200 MeV and fusion about 17-28 MeV per event, yet fusion gives more energy per nucleon than fission.

lessons.title: Radiation Exposure and Dose
lessons.notes_html:
Radiation Exposure

Radiation exposure is the amount of ionizing radiation absorbed by a body, measured by the charge it produces in air or by the energy deposited per unit mass.

Measurement and Units

QuantityUnitMeasured by
ExposureRoentgenIonization chamber
Absorbed doseRad or grayDosimeter
Dose equivalentRem or sievertFilm badge, TLD dosimeter

A dosimeter, such as a film badge or thermoluminescent dosimeter, is worn by workers and records their accumulated dose. A GM counter counts individual particles, and an ionization chamber measures the ionization current produced by the radiation. Keeping exposure records protects workers who handle radioactive sources.

mcqs.q: Radiation exposure is:
options: The number of particles counted per second by a detector
The half-life of a radioactive source near the body
The amount of ionizing radiation absorbed by a body, measured by the charge it produces in air or the energy deposited per unit mass
The temperature rise of a body in sunlight
mcqs.why: Exposure is the amount of ionizing radiation absorbed by a body, measured by charge produced in air or energy deposited per unit mass.

mcqs.q: Exposure is measured in roentgen using an:
options: Film badge
GM counter
Mass spectrograph
Ionization chamber
mcqs.why: The units table shows exposure in roentgen is measured by an ionization chamber, which measures the ionization current produced.

mcqs.q: Absorbed dose is measured in rad or gray using a:
options: Dosimeter
Ionization chamber
Spectroscope
GM counter only
mcqs.why: The table gives absorbed dose in rad or gray, measured by a dosimeter such as a film badge or thermoluminescent dosimeter.

mcqs.q: Dose equivalent is measured in rem or sievert using a:
options: Mass spectrograph
Film badge or TLD dosimeter
X-ray tube
Solid state detector only
mcqs.why: The table gives dose equivalent in rem or sievert, measured by a film badge or TLD (thermoluminescent) dosimeter.

mcqs.q: A dosimeter, such as a film badge or thermoluminescent dosimeter, is worn by workers to:
options: Count individual particles one by one
Measure the ionization current in air
Record their accumulated dose
Separate the isotopes they handle
mcqs.why: A dosimeter is worn by workers and records their accumulated dose, and keeping exposure records protects workers handling sources.

mcqs.q: A GM counter differs from an ionization chamber in that a GM counter:
options: Measures accumulated dose on a film, while a chamber counts particles
Measures dose equivalent in sievert, while a chamber measures exposure
Separates isotopes, while a chamber records dose
Counts individual particles, while an ionization chamber measures the ionization current produced by the radiation
mcqs.why: The notes state a GM counter counts individual particles, and an ionization chamber measures the ionization current produced by radiation.

mcqs.q: Which quantity is matched with the wrong unit in the options?
options: Absorbed dose measured in roentgen
Exposure measured in roentgen
Absorbed dose measured in gray
Dose equivalent measured in sievert
mcqs.why: Exposure is measured in roentgen; absorbed dose is measured in rad or gray, so absorbed dose in roentgen is the wrong match.

mcqs.q: TLD in the notes stands for the thermoluminescent dosimeter, which is a type of:
options: Counter that counts individual particles
Dosimeter worn to record accumulated dose
Chamber that measures ionization current
Spectrograph that separates isotopes
mcqs.why: A film badge or thermoluminescent dosimeter (TLD) is a dosimeter worn by workers to record their accumulated dose.

mcqs.q: Keeping exposure records is important because it:
options: Increases the activity of radioactive sources
Makes radioactive decay happen faster
Protects workers who handle radioactive sources
Removes the need for shielding in a reactor
mcqs.why: The notes state that keeping exposure records protects workers who handle radioactive sources.

mcqs.q: The energy deposited per unit mass in a body corresponds to which quantity in the table?
options: Exposure, in roentgen
Dose equivalent, in rem only
Activity, in becquerel
Absorbed dose, in rad or gray
mcqs.why: Exposure is defined by charge in air or energy deposited per unit mass, and absorbed dose, in rad or gray, is the deposited-energy quantity in the table.

lessons.title: Biological Effect of Radiations
lessons.notes_html:
Biological Effect of Radiations

Ionizing radiations damage living cells by ionizing atoms and molecules in the tissue. The harm depends on the dose, the type of radiation and the tissue exposed. Alpha rays are the most ionizing, so they are very harmful inside the body, while gamma rays penetrate deeply and can damage organs from outside.

Radiation can damage DNA. Rapidly dividing cells, such as cancer cells, are affected most strongly, which is the basis of radiotherapy. Large doses harm healthy tissue as well, so in all medical and industrial uses the dose to healthy tissue and to workers must be kept as low as possible, with shielding and careful control of exposure.

mcqs.q: Ionizing radiations damage living cells by:
options: Heating the tissue like an oven
Making the tissue magnetic
Removing neutrons from the tissue
Ionizing atoms and molecules in the tissue
mcqs.why: The notes state that ionizing radiations damage living cells by ionizing atoms and molecules in the tissue.

mcqs.q: The harm from radiation depends on:
options: The dose, the type of radiation and the tissue exposed
The colour of the radiation source only
The time of day the exposure occurs
The chemical name of the source only
mcqs.why: The harm depends on the dose, the type of radiation and the tissue exposed, according to the notes.

mcqs.q: Alpha rays are very harmful inside the body because they are:
options: The most penetrating of the radiations
The most ionizing of the radiations
Completely non-ionizing
Able to pass through thick concrete
mcqs.why: Alpha rays are the most ionizing, so they are very harmful inside the body, even though they penetrate least from outside.

mcqs.q: Gamma rays can damage organs from outside the body because they:
options: Are the most ionizing at the skin surface
Stop at the surface of the skin
Penetrate deeply
Travel only a few millimetres in air
mcqs.why: Gamma rays penetrate deeply and can damage organs from outside, unlike alpha rays which are most harmful inside the body.

mcqs.q: Radiation can damage which important molecule in cells, according to the notes?
options: Haemoglobin only
Insulin
Chlorophyll
DNA
mcqs.why: The notes state that radiation can damage DNA, which is why its effects on living cells can be serious.

mcqs.q: Rapidly dividing cells are affected most strongly by radiation, which is the basis of:
options: Radiotherapy for cancer
Diagnosis with tracers
The mass spectrograph
The GM counter
mcqs.why: Rapidly dividing cells such as cancer cells are affected most strongly, which is the basis of radiotherapy.

mcqs.q: Why must the dose in medical and industrial uses be kept as low as possible?
options: Because radiation becomes non-ionizing at large doses
Because large doses harm healthy tissue as well
Because large doses make sources decay faster
Because healthy tissue is never affected by radiation
mcqs.why: Large doses harm healthy tissue as well, so the dose to healthy tissue and workers must be kept as low as possible.

mcqs.q: Protection of healthy tissue and workers from radiation is achieved by:
options: Increasing the dose for shorter times
Removing all dosimeters from workers
Shielding and careful control of exposure
Using alpha sources inside the body freely
mcqs.why: The notes call for shielding and careful control of exposure so doses to healthy tissue and workers stay as low as possible.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly compares alpha and gamma harm?
options: Gamma is very harmful inside; alpha penetrates deeply from outside
Both are harmless inside and outside the body
Alpha penetrates deeply; gamma is most ionizing inside
Alpha is very harmful inside the body; gamma penetrates deeply and damages organs from outside
mcqs.why: Alpha rays are the most ionizing and very harmful inside the body, while gamma rays penetrate deeply and damage organs from outside.

mcqs.q: Cancer cells are targeted by radiotherapy because, compared with most healthy cells, they are:
options: Rapidly dividing and so affected most strongly by radiation
Completely resistant to ionization
The only cells that contain DNA
Unable to absorb any radiation dose
mcqs.why: Rapidly dividing cells, such as cancer cells, are affected most strongly by radiation, which is the basis of radiotherapy.

lessons.title: Biological and Medical Uses of Radiations
lessons.notes_html:
Diagnosis with Tracers

In diagnosis, a small amount of a radioactive isotope called a tracer is introduced into the body, and its gamma rays are detected from outside to image the organ and its working. Examples from the book are iodine-131 for the thyroid and technetium-99m for general scanning.

Treatment of Cancer

In treatment, called radiotherapy, cancerous tissue is exposed to carefully aimed gamma rays, for example from cobalt-60, or to implanted radioactive sources. The radiation damages the DNA of the rapidly dividing cancer cells and destroys them, while the dose to healthy tissue is kept as low as possible. In this way radioactive radiations are used both to diagnose and to treat fatal diseases like cancer.

mcqs.q: In diagnosis with tracers, a tracer is:
options: A small amount of a radioactive isotope introduced into the body
A large dose of cobalt-60 aimed at a tumour
A detector worn by a radiation worker
A non-radioactive dye seen by x-rays only
mcqs.why: In diagnosis, a small amount of a radioactive isotope called a tracer is introduced into the body to image an organ and its working.

mcqs.q: In tracer diagnosis, the organ is imaged by:
options: Counting alpha particles inside the organ
Detecting the tracer's gamma rays from outside the body
Measuring the patient's temperature change
Photographing the organ with visible light
mcqs.why: The tracer's gamma rays are detected from outside to image the organ and its working, as described in the notes.

mcqs.q: Iodine-131 is used as a tracer for which organ, according to the book examples?
options: The heart
The liver only
The thyroid
The bones only
mcqs.why: The book examples are iodine-131 for the thyroid and technetium-99m for general scanning, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: Technetium-99m is used in diagnosis for:
options: Thyroid imaging only
Treating cancer tumours
Measuring worker dose
General scanning
mcqs.why: The notes give technetium-99m as the tracer used for general scanning, while iodine-131 is used for the thyroid.

mcqs.q: Treatment of cancer with radiation is called:
options: Radiotherapy
Tracer diagnosis
Transmutation
Population inversion
mcqs.why: In treatment, called radiotherapy, cancerous tissue is exposed to carefully aimed gamma rays to destroy the cancer cells.

mcqs.q: In radiotherapy, gamma rays may come from:
options: Iodine-131 tracers in the thyroid only
Cobalt-60, or from implanted radioactive sources
A GM counter placed on the skin
A helium-neon laser beam
mcqs.why: Radiotherapy uses carefully aimed gamma rays, for example from cobalt-60, or implanted radioactive sources, according to the notes.

mcqs.q: Radiotherapy destroys cancer cells by:
options: Heating the whole body until tumours melt
Changing cancer cells into healthy isotopes
Damaging the DNA of the rapidly dividing cancer cells
Blocking the blood supply with a tracer
mcqs.why: The radiation damages the DNA of the rapidly dividing cancer cells and destroys them, as explained in the notes.

mcqs.q: During radiotherapy, the dose to healthy tissue must be:
options: Made equal to the tumour dose
Increased to protect healthy cells
Ignored because healthy tissue is unaffected
Kept as low as possible
mcqs.why: The dose to healthy tissue is kept as low as possible while the aimed gamma rays destroy the cancerous tissue.

mcqs.q: Radioactive radiations are used in medicine both to:
options: Diagnose diseases with tracers and treat fatal diseases like cancer
Diagnose diseases only, never to treat them
Treat cancer only, never to diagnose disease
Measure radiation dose for workers
mcqs.why: The notes conclude that radiations are used both to diagnose and to treat fatal diseases like cancer.
